title: Sounds and Letters
sub: The alphabet, classical pronunciation, vowel length and the stress rule

blocks.p: The Romans wrote with 23 letters: A B C D E F G H I K L M N O P Q R S T V X Y Z. *K* survives in only a handful of words (*Kalendae*, ‘the first day of the month’), and *Y* and *Z* were added for Greek loanwords (*lyra*, *zōna*). There was no *J* and no *W*, and *U* and *V* were one and the same letter. Modern school editions — and this app — write *u* for the vowel and *v* for the consonant (*servus*, *vīvus*), and use *i* for both the vowel and the consonant (*iam* ‘already’, *Iūlius*).

The good news: Latin spelling is almost perfectly phonetic. Each letter stands for one sound, and every letter is pronounced — the only weak one is *h*, which educated Romans pronounced and uneducated ones often dropped.

Every Latin vowel is either **short** or **long**; a long vowel is held roughly twice as long. The Romans seldom marked the difference in writing, so modern books put a **macron** (ā ē ī ō ū) over long vowels. Short vowels get no mark. Long and short vowels also differ a little in quality, much like English *bit* / *beet* or *full* / *fool*.

table.title: The vowels
table.note: Short a as in Italian ‘casa’, long ā as in ‘father’. Short e as in ‘pet’, long ē like the vowel of ‘they’ without the glide. Short i as in ‘bit’, long ī as in ‘machine’. Short o as in British ‘pot’, long ō as in ‘go’ but pure. Short u as in ‘put’, long ū as in ‘rule’. Y (only in Greek words) is the French u or German ü.

blocks.p: Length is not decoration: it keeps words and forms apart. *mālum* ‘apple’ vs. *malum* ‘evil’; *lēvis* ‘smooth’ vs. *levis* ‘light’; *ōs* ‘mouth’ vs. *os* ‘bone’; *rosa* ‘the rose’ (subject) vs. *rosā* ‘with the rose’. Learn every word **with** its macrons — they will also tell you where the stress falls.

table.title: Diphthongs (each is one syllable)
table.note: ae rhymes with English ‘eye’, au with ‘how’, oe with ‘boy’. The last three are rare. A diphthong always counts as long.

table.title: Consonants that differ from English
table.note: Double consonants are held longer, as in Italian: annus [ˈanːʊs]. The aspirates ph, th, ch occur in Greek loanwords and sound like the p, t, k of English ‘pot, top, kit’.

blocks.tip: Classical Latin had no soft c and no soft g: *Caesar* was [ˈkai̯sar] — which is why the Germanic peoples who borrowed the title early still say **Kaiser**. And *v* was English *w*: Caesar’s *vēnī, vīdī, vīcī* sounded like ‘way-nee, wee-dee, wee-kee’.

blocks.pitfall: Do not skip double consonants: *annus* ‘year’ and *anus* ‘old woman’ differ only by the length of the *n*. Italian still works this way: *anno* ‘year’ vs. *ano* ‘anus’, *nonno* ‘grandfather’ vs. *nono* ‘ninth’.

table.title: Classical vs. Church pronunciation
table.note: Church Latin, still used in the Catholic liturgy and in choral singing, follows Italian habits: c and g soften before e, i, ae, oe; v is [v]; ae and oe are plain e; ti before a vowel is [tsi]. This app teaches the classical pronunciation.

blocks.p: To find the stress you need to know whether the **penult** — the next-to-last syllable — is heavy or light. A syllable is **heavy** if its vowel is long or a diphthong (*a-mī-cus*), or if its vowel is followed by two consonants (*pu-el-la*, *fe-nes-tra*; *x* counts as two, since it is [ks]). Otherwise it is **light** (*do-mi-nus*). A plosive followed by *r* or *l* (*tr*, *cr*, *pl*…) usually does not count as two consonants.

Latin stress follows one rule, often called the **penult law**. Words of two syllables are stressed on the first: *RO-sa*, *PA-ter*. In longer words, look at the penult: if it is **heavy**, it takes the stress (*a-MĪ-cus*, *pu-EL-la*); if it is **light**, the stress moves one syllable further back, to the antepenult (*DO-mi-nus*). Stress never falls on the last syllable, and never further back than the third from the end.

table.title: The penult law at work
table.note: Long vowel or two consonants in the penult → stress on the penult. Short vowel + single consonant in the penult → stress on the antepenult. Note that the long ē of fēmina is irrelevant: only the penult decides.

blocks.pitfall: *habēre* ‘to have’ and *legere* ‘to read’ look alike, but the macron changes everything: ha-BĒ-re vs. LE-ge-re. Without macrons you cannot pronounce Latin correctly — which is why dictionaries and this app always print them.

items.en: I came, I saw, I conquered. (Caesar)
The die is cast. (Caesar at the Rubicon)
Seize the day. (Horace)
items.lit: Pluck the day.

items.en: I think, therefore I am. (Descartes)
eternal Rome — say it RŌ-ma ai-TER-na

afterlife.title: How Latin sounds became Romance sounds

blocks.p: Italian, Spanish, French, Portuguese and Romanian are spoken Latin after two thousand years of wear. Three changes explain a great deal of what you hear today: *c* and *g* softened before front vowels, *v* moved from [w] to [v] or [b], and vowel **length** turned into vowel **quality**. The stress, by contrast, mostly stayed exactly where the penult law put it.

compare.title: c and g before e and i
compare.note: Latin [k] before e, i became [tʃ] in Italian and Romanian (cento, cer), [θ] in Castilian Spanish ([s] in Latin America), and [s] in French and Portuguese. G before e, i became [dʒ] in Italian and Romanian, [ʒ] in French and Portuguese, and disappeared in Spanish hielo. A bare ‘hundred’ is cien in Spanish and cem in Portuguese (ciento, cento appear in 101 and up); Romanian replaced centum with sută, a Slavic loan. Before a, o, u, c stayed [k] — except in French, where ca- became cha- [ʃa].

compare.title: v: from [w] to [v] and [b]
compare.note: Latin [w] became [v] almost everywhere; in Spanish, v and b now sound the same ([b], or [β] between vowels). English wine and wall (from vallum ‘rampart’) were borrowed by Germanic speakers while Latin v was still [w].

blocks.p: Spoken Latin also lost the difference between long and short vowels. Instead, short *e* and *o* became open vowels [ɛ ɔ], and under stress these often broke into diphthongs — *ie* and *uo* in Italian, *ie* and *ue* in Spanish. Portuguese kept simple vowels; Romanian diphthongised *e* but not *o*.

compare.title: The stressed syllable stays put
compare.note: Syllables after the stress tended to wear away, but the stressed one survived: French, which dropped almost everything after it, is stressed on its last syllable precisely because that was the Latin stressed one. Romanian says prieten (a Slavic word) for ‘friend’. One systematic shift: Spanish and Portuguese moved infinitives like vēndere to -ér (vender), while Italian vèndere and Romanian vínde keep the Latin stress — Italian still contrasts avére with vèndere exactly as Latin contrasted habēre with vēndere.

parts.title: How Latin sounds became Romance sounds

title: What Cases Are
sub: Six cases, free word order and prepositions

blocks.p: In English, *the dog bites the man* and *the man bites the dog* use the same words; only the **order** tells you who bites whom. Latin does it differently: the **ending** of each noun shows its job in the sentence. These ending-sets are called **cases**. Because the endings carry the meaning, the order of the words is free.

items.en: The dog bites the man.
The dog bites the man. (stress on ‘the man’)
The man bites the dog.

blocks.p: *canis* and *vir* are subject forms; *canem* and *virum* are object forms. Change the ending and you change the meaning — change the order and you only change the emphasis.

table.title: What each case does
rows: possession, belonging, part of a whole
indirect object: the person who receives or benefits
direct object; motion towards; after many prepositions
means, manner, separation, place and time; after many prepositions
by, with, from, in, on, at
table.note: A seventh case, the locative (‘at …’), survives only with names of towns and small islands and a few words: Rōmae ‘at Rome’, domī ‘at home’, rūrī ‘in the country’.

items.en: The girl sings. (nominative = subject)
The girl’s rose is beautiful. (genitive = possession)
Marcus gives the girl a rose. (dative = indirect object)
Marcus sees the girl. (accusative = direct object)
Marcus walks with the girl. (ablative after cum)
You too, Brutus? (vocative = direct address; Shakespeare’s Caesar)

blocks.p: Notice that *puellae* appears twice with two different jobs — genitive in the second sentence, dative in the third. Latin endings are often ambiguous out of context; the rest of the sentence settles it. Every noun belongs to one of five **declensions** (families of endings); you will meet them one by one, starting in the next chapter.

The neutral order of Latin prose is **Subject – Object – Verb**: *Mārcus puellam videt*. But any order is grammatical, and good writers use the first and last positions for emphasis. Poets go further and separate words that belong together, trusting the endings to reunite them.

items.en: I sing of arms and the man. (first words of Virgil’s Aeneid)
items.lit: Arms and-man I-sing.

items.en: The sailor sees the girl.
items.lit: Girl (object) sees sailor (subject).

blocks.pitfall: Never translate by position. In *Puellam videt nauta* the first word is the object: the *-am* ending says so. Find the verb, then find the nominative that goes with it, then the accusative — whatever order they come in.

blocks.p: Prepositions in Latin are followed by a fixed case — usually the **accusative** or the **ablative**. As a rough guide, motion *towards* goes with the accusative; position, separation and accompaniment go with the ablative. Two very common prepositions take either case, with a change of meaning: *in* + accusative ‘into, onto’, *in* + ablative ‘in, on’; *sub* + accusative ‘(going) under’, *sub* + ablative ‘(being) under’.

table.title: Common prepositions
rows: ad (to), ante (before), apud (at the house of), circum (around), contrā (against), inter (between), per (through), post (after), prope (near), trāns (across)
ā / ab (from, by), cum (with), dē (down from, about), ē / ex (out of), prō (for, in front of), sine (without)

items.en: He walks into the villa. (in + accusative = motion)
He lives in the villa. (in + ablative = position)

blocks.tip: Accusatives in the singular almost always end in **-m** (*puellam, virum, canem*). Ablatives in the singular end in a vowel, usually long (*puellā, virō*). If you see a noun after *cum*, *sine*, *dē*, *ē/ex* or *ā/ab*, expect the ablative.

afterlife.title: Cases in Romance: lost — except where they weren’t

blocks.p: In spoken Latin, final *-m* faded away and the difference between long and short vowels disappeared. *Rosa*, *rosam* and *rosā* ended up sounding the same, and the case system collapsed. Its work was taken over by two tools that Latin already had: **prepositions** (*dē* for the genitive, *ad* for the dative) and a **fixed word order** (subject – verb – object) for telling subject from object.

compare.title: Endings replaced by prepositions — except in Romanian
rows: Doy el libro a la chica.
Je donne le livre à la fille.
gloss: I give the book to the girl.
compare.note: Italian della = di + la, alla = a + la; Portuguese da = de + a, à = a + a. Romanian alone needs no preposition: fetei is a genitive-dative form of fata ‘the girl’.

blocks.p: **Romanian** is the one major Romance language that kept a case distinction in its nouns: a nominative-accusative and a genitive-dative, marked mainly on the definite article, which Romanian attaches to the end of the noun. The genitive-dative plural *-lor* continues Latin *illōrum* ‘of those’. Romanian also kept a **vocative**: *Doamne!* ‘O Lord!’ comes straight from Latin *domine*.

table.title: Romanian: two cases on the article
table.note: Casa e mare ‘The house is big’ — ușa casei ‘the door of the house’ — Dau apă lupului ‘I give water to the wolf’.

blocks.p: Everywhere else, cases survive in the **pronouns** — just as in English, where *I / me / my*, *he / him / his* and *who / whom / whose* are the last remains of the old Germanic cases. Romance languages distinguish a subject form, an object form and often a separate ‘to …’ form.

compare.title: ‘I’, ‘me’, ‘to me’
compare.note: Italian, Spanish, French and Portuguese use one clitic for ‘me’ and ‘to me’; Romanian keeps them apart (mă / îmi), like Latin mē / mihi. The stressed forms used after prepositions — Spanish para mí, Portuguese para mim, Romanian mie — continue the Latin dative mihi.

compare.title: ‘he’, ‘him’, ‘to him’: three cases of ille
compare.note: The Latin demonstrative ille ‘that’ became the third-person pronoun (see Chapter 12). Italian gli, Spanish le and Portuguese lhe continue the dative illī; French lui (and Italian lui, Romanian lui) go back to a Late Latin dative illui, remodelled on cui ‘to whom’.

parts.title: Cases in Romance: lost — except where they weren’t

title: The First Declension
sub: Nouns in -a, and the verb ‘to be’

blocks.p: The **first declension** is the family of nouns whose nominative ends in *-a* and genitive in *-ae*. Dictionaries list a noun by these two forms plus its gender: *rosa, rosae* f. ‘rose’. The genitive is what identifies the declension, so always learn it.

Nearly all first-declension nouns are **feminine**: *puella* ‘girl’, *fēmina* ‘woman’, *terra* ‘earth’, *aqua* ‘water’, *via* ‘road’, *vīta* ‘life’, *patria* ‘homeland’, *īnsula* ‘island’, *silva* ‘forest’, *fortūna* ‘luck’. A few nouns for men’s occupations are **masculine**: *nauta* ‘sailor’, *agricola* ‘farmer’, *poēta* ‘poet’, *pīrāta* ‘pirate’.

table.title: rosa, rosae f. ‘rose’
table.note: Endings: -a, -ae, -ae, -am, -ā, -a | -ae, -ārum, -īs, -ās, -īs, -ae. The vocative is always the same as the nominative in this declension.

blocks.p: Two small irregularities: *dea* ‘goddess’ and *fīlia* ‘daughter’ have dative and ablative plurals in *-ābus* (*deābus*, *fīliābus*), to keep them apart from *deīs* ‘gods’ and *fīliīs* ‘sons’.

blocks.pitfall: The endings overlap. *rosae* can be genitive singular, dative singular, nominative plural or vocative plural; *rosīs* can be dative or ablative plural; and *rosa* and *rosā* differ only in the length of the final vowel. The verb usually decides: *Rosae pulchrae sunt* (plural verb → nominative plural) ‘The roses are beautiful’.

table.title: sum, esse ‘to be’ — present tense
table.note: sum ‘I am’, es ‘you are’, est ‘he / she / it is; there is’, sumus ‘we are’, estis ‘you (pl.) are’, sunt ‘they are; there are’.

blocks.p: Latin does not need subject pronouns: the ending of the verb already says who is meant, so *est* alone means ‘he is’, ‘she is’, ‘it is’ or ‘there is’. In prose, *est* and *sunt* usually come last. A noun or adjective that describes the subject after ‘to be’ is in the **nominative**, not the accusative: *Iūlia puella est* ‘Julia is a girl’.

items.en: Rome is in Italy.
The girls are in the street.
The sailor gives the girl a rose.
Farmers love the land.

items.t: Ubi est Iūlia? In silvā est.
items.en: Where is Julia? She is in the forest.
Fortune is blind. (Cicero)

blocks.tip: Masculine *nauta*, *agricola* and *poēta* look feminine but take masculine adjectives: *nauta bonus* ‘a good sailor’ (Chapter 6). Gender belongs to the word’s meaning, not to its ending.

blocks.p: Romance nouns usually continue the Latin **accusative**, the case that was used most and after most prepositions — minus the final *-m*, which was already silent in spoken Latin. In the first declension that means *rosam* → *rosa*. Because the *-a* survived nearly everywhere, the first declension is the most recognisable in Romance, and its nouns stayed **feminine**.

compare.title: First-declension nouns in Romance
compare.note: French reduced final -a to a silent -e; Romanian turned it into -ă. Romanian roză is a later learned word — the everyday Romanian word for ‘rose’ is trandafir. Portuguese lua lost the n between vowels, as Portuguese regularly does.

blocks.p: **Plurals** split Romance in two. Italian and Romanian plurals in *-e* match the Latin **nominative** plural *-ae*; Spanish, Portuguese and French plurals in *-s* continue the **accusative** plural *-ās*. This east–west split runs through the whole Romance world and returns with the second declension (Chapter 4).

compare.title: Plurals: -ae or -ās?
compare.note: French plural -s is silent today, but you can still hear it in liaison: les étoiles [lez‿etwal].

blocks.p: A humble first-declension word took over the whole family of ‘house’ words: Latin *casa* meant a hut or cottage (the proper word was *domus*), but it became *casa* in Italian, Spanish and Portuguese and *casă* in Romanian. French went its own way with *maison* (from *mānsiōnem*), yet *casa* survives there too: in *chez* ‘at the home of’.

compare.title: ‘is’ and ‘are’
compare.note: The full present tense of ‘to be’ is compared in Chapter 5.

blocks.p: English borrowed many first-declension words, some still with their Latin plurals: *alga – algae*, *larva – larvae*, *vertebra – vertebrae*, *nebula – nebulae*, *formula – formulae* (or *formulas*). The *-ae* is the Latin nominative plural.

title: The Second Declension
sub: Masculines in -us and -er, neuters in -um

blocks.p: The **second declension** has genitive singular *-ī*. Most of its nouns are masculine and end in *-us* (*dominus, dominī* m. ‘master’); others end in *-er* (*puer, puerī* m. ‘boy’); and the neuters end in *-um* (*templum, templī* n. ‘temple’).

table.title: dominus, dominī m. ‘master, lord’
table.note: Endings: -us, -ī, -ō, -um, -ō, -e | -ī, -ōrum, -īs, -ōs, -īs, -ī.

blocks.p: This is the only place in Latin where the **vocative** differs from the nominative: *-us* becomes *-e* (*Mārce!*, *Brūte!*, *domine!*), and nouns and names in *-ius* contract to *-ī* (*fīlī!* ‘son!’, *Vergilī!*). The vocative of *meus* ‘my’ is *mī*: *mī fīlī* ‘my son’.

Nouns in *-er* have no ending in the nominative and vocative singular. Some keep the *e* throughout, others drop it after the nominative — the genitive tells you which. *vir, virī* ‘man’ declines like *puer*.

table.title: puer, puerī ‘boy’ and ager, agrī ‘field’
table.note: Like puer: gener ‘son-in-law’, socer ‘father-in-law’, vir (virī). Like ager: liber, librī ‘book’, magister, magistrī ‘teacher’.

blocks.tip: English derivatives show which stem a noun uses: *puerile* (puer-), but *agriculture* (agr-), *library* (libr-), *magistrate* (magistr-).

blocks.p: Two rules hold for **every neuter noun in Latin**, in every declension: (1) the nominative, accusative and vocative are always identical; (2) in the plural those three cases always end in *-a*. Common neuters: *bellum* ‘war’, *dōnum* ‘gift’, *verbum* ‘word’, *vīnum* ‘wine’, *oppidum* ‘town’, *caelum* ‘sky’, *ōvum* ‘egg’.

blocks.pitfall: A neuter plural in *-a* looks like a first-declension feminine singular: *templa* ‘temples’, *verba* ‘words’, *bella* ‘wars’. Check the dictionary entry — and remember that not every *-us* noun is second declension: *corpus, corporis* n. is third, *manus, manūs* f. is fourth. Latin *vīrus* is a neuter with no attested plural, which is why English says *viruses*, never *viri*.

items.en: The master calls the slave.
The boys are working in the field.
The teacher tells the boys a story.
Spoken words fly away, written ones remain.
items.lit: Words fly, written things stay.

items.en: In wine (there is) truth.
To err is human.

afterlife.title: Masculine -us, and the death of the neuter

blocks.p: Second-declension masculines passed into Romance smoothly: the accusative *lupum* lost its *-m*, and the remaining *-u* became *-o* in Italian, Spanish and Portuguese, disappeared in French and Romanian.

compare.title: Second-declension nouns in Romance
compare.note: Spoken Latin preferred the slangy caballus ‘nag’ to the literary equus; equus survives only in learned words such as equestrian.

blocks.p: The **neuter** gender did not survive in Italian, Spanish, French or Portuguese. Neuter nouns in *-um* simply became masculine, since *-um* and *-us* had fallen together: *templum* → *il tempio*, *el templo*, *le temple*, *o templo*; *vīnum* → *il vino*, *el vino*, *le vin*, *o vinho*.
But the neuter **plural** in *-a* left traces. Because it looked feminine, some neuter plurals were reanalysed as feminine **singulars**: a ‘mass of leaves’ became ‘a leaf’.

compare.title: Neuter plurals that became feminine singulars
compare.note: All the Romance forms are feminine singulars, though their Latin sources were neuter plurals.

blocks.p: **Italian** kept something even closer to the Latin neuter: a group of nouns that are masculine in the singular but take a plural in *-a*, which behaves as feminine: *l’uovo – le uova* (Latin *ōvum – ōva*), *il braccio – le braccia* (*bracchium – bracchia*), *il labbro – le labbra* (*labrum – labra*). The pattern was so alive that it spread to nouns that were never neuter: *il dito – le dita*, although Latin *digitus* was masculine.

**Romanian** went furthest: it kept a full third gender, traditionally called neuter (or *ambigen*). These nouns are **masculine in the singular and feminine in the plural**, exactly like the Italian relics, but there are thousands of them. Their plurals in *-uri* go back to Latin neuter plurals in *-ora* such as *tempora* → *timpuri*.

table.title: The Romanian neuter: masculine in the singular, feminine in the plural
table.note: The adjective shows the switch: un ou bun ‘a good egg’ (masculine form) but două ouă bune ‘two good eggs’ (feminine form). Compare un (m.) / două (f.).

blocks.p: The plurals split east and west, as in the first declension. Italian and Romanian *-i* match the Latin **nominative** plural *-ī*; Spanish, Portuguese and French *-s* continue the **accusative** plural *-ōs*.

English keeps Latin second-declension plurals in learned words: *alumnus – alumni*, *fungus – fungi*, *stimulus – stimuli*; and neuters: *datum – data*, *medium – media*, *curriculum – curricula*, *bacterium – bacteria*. *Data* and *media* are, strictly speaking, Latin neuter plurals.

parts.title: Masculine -us, and the death of the neuter

title: The Present Tense
sub: The four conjugations, sum and possum

blocks.p: A Latin verb is listed with four **principal parts**: *amō, amāre, amāvī, amātum* — ‘I love, to love, I loved, loved’. The second part, the **infinitive**, tells you which of the four **conjugations** the verb belongs to. For the present tense you need only the first two parts.

table.title: The four conjugations
table.note: amāre ‘to love’, monēre ‘to warn, advise’, regere ‘to rule’, capere ‘to take’, audīre ‘to hear’.

blocks.p: All Latin active verbs share one set of personal endings: **-ō** (or **-m**) ‘I’, **-s** ‘you’, **-t** ‘he/she/it’, **-mus** ‘we’, **-tis** ‘you (pl.)’, **-nt** ‘they’. Add them to the stem and you have the present tense. Because the ending shows the person, subject pronouns are normally left out: *amat* = ‘he loves’, ‘she loves’ or ‘it loves’.

table.title: Present active of the four conjugations
table.note: Long vowels shorten before final -t and -nt and before another vowel: amat, monet, audit, moneō, audiunt. In the 1st conjugation the stem vowel vanishes in amō (from amā-ō).

blocks.p: The Latin present covers all three English presents: *amō* is ‘I love’, ‘I am loving’ and ‘I do love’. To make a verb negative, put *nōn* in front of it: *nōn amō* ‘I don’t love’.

blocks.tip: To tell the 2nd conjugation from the 3rd, look at the infinitive’s macron: *monēre* (mo-NĒ-re, 2nd) vs. *regere* (RE-ge-re, 3rd). The 3rd conjugation is the odd one out: its stem vowel changes (*regis, regit, regunt*). The *-iō* verbs (*capiō, faciō ‘do’, fugiō ‘flee’*) keep their *i* only before a vowel: *capiō, capiunt* but *capis, capit*.

table.title: sum ‘I am’ and possum ‘I can’
table.note: possum is pot- ‘able’ + sum: pot- before a vowel (pot-es), pos- before s (pos-sum).

blocks.p: *possum* is followed by an infinitive, just like English *can*: *Natāre possum* ‘I can swim’; *Nōn possum dormīre* ‘I can’t sleep’.

items.en: I think, therefore I am. (Descartes)
While I breathe, I hope.
The teacher warns the boys.
The pupils listen to the teacher.
How are you?
items.lit: What are you doing?

items.en: They can because they think they can. (Virgil)
items.lit: They are able, because they seem to be able.

blocks.pitfall: In the 3rd conjugation the 1st person singular and the 3rd plural do not follow the *-i-* of the other forms: *regō, regis, regit, regimus, regitis, regunt* — note the *-unt*. Students often write *regint* — there is no such form.

blocks.p: The Latin present survived in every Romance language, and the old personal endings *-ō, -s, -t, -mus, -tis, -nt* can still be traced in them. Spanish and Portuguese have kept them most faithfully; French still writes them but no longer pronounces most of them; Italian and Romanian dropped final *-s* and use *-i* for ‘you’.

compare.title: cantāre ‘to sing’ — present
compare.note: French chante, chantes, chantent are all pronounced [ʃɑ̃t]: the endings survive only in spelling.

compare.title: amāre ‘to love’ — present
compare.note: Romanian lost amāre and says iubi, a Slavic loan. But its endings are Latin: -esc, -ești, -ește come from the Latin suffix -ēscō / -īscō, the same one found in Italian finisco ‘I finish’ and French (nous) finissons.

blocks.p: The verb ‘to be’ is irregular everywhere — but irregular in recognisably Latin ways. Note **Spanish** *eres* ‘you are’: it is not the Latin present *es* but the Latin **future** *eris* ‘you will be’, pressed into service because *es* ‘you are’ and *es* ‘he is’ had become identical.

compare.title: sum ‘to be’ — present
compare.note: Italian sono and Romanian sunt serve both as ‘I am’ and ‘they are’. Romanian also has short forms: e for este, s for sunt. Spanish and Portuguese have a second verb, estar, from Latin stāre ‘to stand’.

blocks.p: *possum, posse* was too irregular to last. Spoken Latin rebuilt it as a regular second-conjugation verb on the stem of *potes, potest* (reconstructed as *potēre*): hence Italian *potere*, Spanish and Portuguese *poder*, French *pouvoir*, Romanian *a putea*.

title: Adjectives of the First and Second Declension
sub: bonus, bona, bonum: agreement and position

blocks.p: Latin adjectives change their endings to match the noun they describe. The most common type borrows its endings from the two declensions you already know: **second declension** for the masculine and neuter, **first declension** for the feminine. Dictionaries give the three nominatives: *bonus, bona, bonum* ‘good’, *magnus, -a, -um* ‘big’, *parvus, -a, -um* ‘small’, *multus, -a, -um* ‘much, many’.

Adjectives in *-er* behave like *puer* and *ager*: some keep the *e* (*līber, lībera, līberum* ‘free’; *miser, misera, miserum* ‘wretched’), others drop it outside the masculine nominative (*pulcher, pulchra, pulchrum* ‘beautiful’; *sacer, sacra, sacrum* ‘holy’; *niger, nigra, nigrum* ‘black’). The feminine form tells you which.

table.title: Adjectives in -er
table.note: English keeps the same split: liberal (līber-) but pulchritude (pulchr-).

blocks.p: An adjective **agrees** with its noun in **gender, number and case**. That does not mean the endings rhyme: the adjective follows its own pattern, whatever declension the noun belongs to. *nauta* is a masculine first-declension noun, so ‘a good sailor’ is *nauta bonus*; *corpus* is a third-declension neuter, so ‘a healthy body’ is *corpus sānum*.

blocks.pitfall: Don’t match endings by eye. *agricola bonus*, *agricolae bonī*, *agricolam bonum* are all correct, and *agricola bona* is wrong: the farmer is masculine. Ask ‘which noun does it go with, and what are that noun’s gender, number and case?’ — then pick the form from the table.

blocks.p: Most adjectives **follow** their noun: *vir bonus* ‘a good man’, *rēs pūblica* ‘the state’. Adjectives of quantity and size usually **precede**: *multī puerī* ‘many boys’, *magnum oppidum* ‘a large town’. Any adjective may come first for emphasis, and in poetry an adjective can stand far from its noun — agreement shows where it belongs.

Adjectives are often used **as nouns**: *bonī* ‘good men, the good’, *Rōmānī* ‘the Romans’, *multa* ‘many things’, *bona* ‘goods, property’. The gender supplies the missing noun: masculine for people, neuter for things.

items.en: The farmer is good.
The little girl loves the beautiful rose.

items.t: Multī puerī in magnō oppidō habitant.
items.en: Many boys live in the big town.
The wretched slaves work in the fields.
A healthy mind in a healthy body. (Juvenal)

blocks.tip: Juvenal’s line is a perfect agreement drill: *mēns* (3rd decl., feminine, nominative) takes *sāna*; *corpore* (3rd decl., neuter, ablative) takes *sānō*. Neither adjective ending rhymes with its noun, and both are right.

afterlife.title: bonus → buono, bueno, bon, bom, bun

blocks.p: Romance adjectives continue the Latin *bonus, bona* type directly. The masculine comes from *bonum* (*-um* > *-o*, as in nouns), the feminine from *bonam* (> *-a*). The neuter merged with the masculine, except in Romanian (see Chapter 4).

compare.title: First/second-declension adjectives in Romance
compare.note: Latin pl- became Italian pi- (pieno), Spanish ll- (lleno) and Portuguese ch- (cheio). French aveugle replaced caecus with a phrase, ab oculīs ‘without eyes’; Romanian orb comes from Latin orbus ‘bereft’.

blocks.p: **Agreement** survived intact: Romance adjectives still agree in gender and number, just as Latin ones did — only the case agreement has gone, along with the cases.

compare.title: Agreement in gender and number
compare.note: Latin niger, nigra, nigrum → Italian nero, Spanish and Portuguese negro, French noir, Romanian negru: every language still marks masculine vs. feminine and singular vs. plural on the adjective. (Portuguese also uses preto for the colour.)

blocks.p: Latin adjectives also live on in English phrases where the agreement is still visible: *bonā fidē* ‘in good faith’ (ablative feminine, agreeing with *fidē*), *magnum opus* ‘great work’ (neuter), *terra incognita* ‘unknown land’ (feminine).

parts.title: bonus → buono, bueno, bon, bom, bun

title: The Third Declension
sub: Consonant stems, i-stems and neuters

blocks.p: The **third declension** contains more nouns than any other, of all three genders. Its genitive singular ends in *-is*. The nominative is unpredictable — *rēx* ‘king’, *nox* ‘night’, *homō* ‘human being’, *corpus* ‘body’, *nōmen* ‘name’ — so you must learn every noun with its genitive: *rēx, rēgis*; *nox, noctis*; *homō, hominis*; *corpus, corporis*; *nōmen, nōminis*. Take away the *-is* and you have the **stem** to which all the other endings are added.

table.title: rēx, rēgis m. ‘king’ and homō, hominis m. ‘human being’
table.note: The vocative is the same as the nominative throughout the third declension. Masculine and feminine nouns share the same endings: -, -is, -ī, -em, -e | -ēs, -um, -ibus, -ēs, -ibus.

table.title: Neuters: corpus, corporis ‘body’ and nōmen, nōminis ‘name’
table.note: The neuter rule again: accusative = nominative, and the plural of both ends in -a.

blocks.tip: Gender guides for the third declension: abstract nouns in *-tās*, *-tūdō* and *-tiō* are feminine (*lībertās, magnitūdō, nātiō*); most nouns in *-or* are masculine (*amor, timor*); nouns in *-men*, in *-us* with genitive *-oris* / *-eris*, and in *-e*, *-al*, *-ar* are neuter (*nōmen, corpus, genus, mare, animal*). Words for men and women follow their sex (*pater* m., *māter* f.).

blocks.p: Some third-declension nouns once had stems ending in *-i-*, and it still shows in a few endings — above all the genitive plural **-ium** instead of *-um*. Three groups:

**(1)** Masculine and feminine nouns with the **same number of syllables** in the nominative and genitive (‘parisyllabic’): *cīvis, cīvis* ‘citizen’, *hostis* ‘enemy’, *nāvis* ‘ship’ → *cīvium, hostium, nāvium*. **(2)** Nouns in *-s* or *-x* whose **stem ends in two consonants**: *urbs, urbis* ‘city’, *nox, noctis*, *mōns, montis* ‘mountain’, *pars, partis* ‘part’ → *urbium, noctium, montium, partium*. **(3)** **Neuters** in *-e*, *-al*, *-ar*: *mare* ‘sea’, *animal*, *exemplar* — these also have ablative singular *-ī* and plural *-ia*.

table.title: i-stems: cīvis m. ‘citizen’, urbs f. ‘city’, mare n. ‘sea’
table.note: The accusative plural in -īs is an older alternative found in many texts. animal, animālis declines like mare: animālī, animālia, animālium.

blocks.pitfall: The nominative can look nothing like the rest of the word: *iter, itineris* ‘journey’; *caput, capitis* ‘head’; *opus, operis* ‘work’; *lac, lactis* ‘milk’; *Iuppiter, Iovis* ‘Jupiter’. And watch for look-alikes: *ōs, ōris* ‘mouth’ but *os, ossis* ‘bone’. If you meet an unfamiliar form, work back from the genitive stem.

items.en: The king rules the city.
I am a Roman citizen. (Cicero)
Oh, the times! Oh, the customs! (Cicero)
Man is a wolf to man. (after Plautus)
The law is harsh, but it is the law.
The name is an omen.

blocks.p: Romance nouns descend from the **accusative** (the main ‘oblique’ case), not the nominative. In the first two declensions the difference hardly matters, but in the third it is decisive: the nominative is often shorter or different, and it is the longer stem of *noctem*, *pontem*, *flōrem* that lives on. That is why learning the genitive pays off twice — it gives you both the Latin stem and the Romance word.

compare.title: Third-declension nouns: from the accusative
compare.note: Spoken Latin treated lac as lacte. Spanish can is literary — the everyday word is perro; Romanian ‘bridge’ is pod, a Slavic word, while punte survives with a narrower meaning.

blocks.p: A handful of words continue the **nominative** instead. Latin *homō, hominem* gave two different results: Italian *uomo* and Romanian *om* come from the nominative *homō*, while Spanish *hombre*, Portuguese *homem* and French *homme* come from the accusative *hominem*. Italian still shows both in one noun: singular *uomo* (< *homō*), plural *uomini* (< *hominēs*).

**Old French** kept a two-case system (subject case vs. oblique case) until the 13th–14th centuries. When it collapsed, a few nouns survived in **both** forms, which drifted apart into separate words:

compare.title: French doublets: nominative vs. accusative
compare.note: On dit… ‘one says, people say’ is literally ‘man says’ — compare German man sagt.

blocks.p: With the loss of the neuter, third-declension neuters became masculine in Italian, Spanish, Portuguese and French (*tempus* → *il tempo*, *el tiempo*, *o tempo*, *le temps*). And some nouns changed gender for no grammatical reason at all. French turned most Latin masculines with accusative *-ōrem* into feminines (*la couleur, la douleur, la fleur* from *colōrem, dolōrem, flōrem*).

compare.title: Gender on the move
compare.note: Romanian shows the definite article attached at the end (marea = ‘the sea’) and keeps a neuter class, so lapte can stay neuter. Spanish sailors and poets also say la mar.

blocks.p: English borrowed third-declension words from the **stem**, not the nominative: *nocturnal* (noct-), *regal* (rēg-), *corporal* (corpor-), *nominal* (nōmin-), *itinerary* (itiner-), *capital* (capit-). Knowing the genitive explains them all.

title: Third-Declension Adjectives
sub: fortis, ācer, fēlīx, ingēns

blocks.p: The second great family of adjectives takes its endings from the **third declension**, i-stem type: ablative singular **-ī**, genitive plural **-ium**, neuter plural **-ia**. These adjectives are grouped by how many different forms they have in the nominative singular:

**Two endings** (the most common): *fortis* (m./f.), *forte* (n.) ‘strong, brave’ — also *omnis* ‘every, all’, *brevis* ‘short’, *trīstis* ‘sad’, *facilis* ‘easy’, *dulcis* ‘sweet’, *gravis* ‘heavy’. **Three endings**: *ācer* (m.), *ācris* (f.), *ācre* (n.) ‘sharp, keen’. **One ending**: *fēlīx* ‘lucky, happy’, *ingēns* ‘huge’, *audāx* ‘bold’, *prūdēns* ‘wise’ — for these the dictionary gives the genitive: *fēlīx, fēlīcis*; *ingēns, ingentis*.

table.title: fortis, forte ‘strong, brave’
table.note: Masculine and feminine are identical: vir fortis ‘a brave man’, fēmina fortis ‘a brave woman’.

table.title: ācer, ācris, ācre ‘sharp, keen’
table.note: Only the nominative singular has three forms; everything else is like fortis. celer, celeris, celere ‘swift’ keeps its e throughout.

table.title: fēlīx ‘lucky’ (gen. fēlīcis) and ingēns ‘huge’ (gen. ingentis)
table.note: Present participles decline like ingēns: amāns, amantis ‘loving’ (but with ablative -e when used as a verb: amante).

blocks.tip: The ablative singular is the quickest way to tell a third-declension adjective from a noun: adjectives have **-ī** (*fortī, ācrī, fēlīcī*), most nouns have **-e** (*rēge, homine*). *cum rēge fortī* ‘with the brave king’.

blocks.p: Agreement works exactly as before — gender, number and case, not rhyme. A third-declension adjective can describe a noun of any declension, and a first/second-declension adjective can describe a third-declension noun: *puella fortis*, *dominus fortis*, *bellum ingēns*; *rēx bonus*, *urbs magna*.

blocks.pitfall: *fortis* can be nominative **or** genitive singular; *fortēs* nominative **or** accusative plural; *forte* is neuter (and also an adverb, ‘by chance’). Don’t assume an *-is* adjective goes with an *-is* noun: in *fēmina fortis* both are nominative, in *rēgis fortis* both are genitive, and in *puellae fortis* (‘of the brave girl’) only the case matches.

items.en: Fortune favours the brave. (proverb, in Terence)
Love conquers all. (Virgil)
Art is long, life is short.

items.t: Nihil est ab omnī parte beātum.
items.en: Nothing is blessed in every respect. (Horace)

items.t: Fēlīx quī potuit rērum cognōscere causās.
items.en: Happy the man who has been able to learn the causes of things. (Virgil)
The brave soldier fights with a sharp sword.

blocks.tip: The months *September*, *Octōber*, *November*, *December* are three-ending adjectives like *ācer*, agreeing with an understood *mēnsis* ‘month’ (m.): *mēnsis September*, *Kalendae Septembrēs* ‘the first of September’. They mean ‘seventh, eighth, ninth, tenth’ because the old Roman year began in March.

blocks.p: A Latin third-declension adjective like *fortis* had **one form** for masculine and feminine. Most Romance languages kept that: Italian, Spanish and Portuguese adjectives in *-e* (or a consonant) do not change for gender — *un uomo forte, una donna forte*; *un hombre fuerte, una mujer fuerte*.

compare.title: Third-declension adjectives in Romance
compare.note: Romanian foarte ‘very’ is fortis turned into an adverb; ‘big’ in Romanian is mare. Spoken Latin said virdis for viridis. French heureux does not come from fēlīx: it is built on heur ‘luck’, from Latin augurium ‘omen’ (as in bonheur, malheur). Romanian fericit ‘happy’ is derived from ferice, which continues fēlīx.

blocks.p: **French** went its own way. In Old French, *grant* and *fort* had one form for both genders, just like Latin *grandis*, *fortis*. Later French built new feminines on the model of *bon / bonne*: *grande*, *forte*, *verte*. But fossils of the old system remain in fixed compounds — *grand-mère*, *grand-rue*, *grand-chose*, *à grand-peine* — where a feminine noun still takes the bare *grand*. Grammarians once wrote *grand’mère* with an apostrophe, wrongly believing an *e* had been dropped.

compare.title: One form for two genders
compare.note: Only French marks the feminine (forte, douce). Romanian puternic ‘strong’ comes from a putea ‘to be able’, but dulce keeps one form for both genders, just like the Latin. Spanish agua is feminine but takes un before stressed a-.

blocks.p: English borrowed these adjectives mostly in learned forms: *fortitude*, *felicity*, *dulcet*, *viridian*, *acrid*, *omnibus* (literally ‘for all’, the dative-ablative plural of *omnis*).

title: Imperfect and Future
sub: Two more tenses built on the present stem

blocks.p: The **imperfect** describes the past as ongoing, repeated or habitual: *amābam* ‘I was loving, I used to love, I kept loving’. It is formed from the present stem plus the tense sign **-bā-** and the personal endings (*-m, -s, -t, -mus, -tis, -nt*). The 1st and 2nd conjugations add *-bā-* directly to the stem vowel (*amā-ba-m, monē-ba-m*); the 3rd and 4th insert a long *ē* (*reg-ēba-m, capi-ēba-m, audi-ēba-m*).

table.title: Imperfect active
table.note: The ā of -bā- shortens before -m, -t and -nt: amābam, amābat, amābant.

blocks.p: The **future** is formed in two different ways. The **1st and 2nd conjugations** use **-b-** with the vowels *ō, i, u*: *amābō, amābis, amābit, amābimus, amābitis, amābunt*. The **3rd and 4th conjugations** use **-a-** in the first person singular and **-ē-** everywhere else: *regam, regēs, reget, regēmus, regētis, regent*.

blocks.tip: A classroom mnemonic: 1st and 2nd conjugations ‘go **bo-bi-bu**’ in the future (*amābō, amābis, amābunt*); 3rd and 4th have ‘**one a, then all e’s**’ (*regam, regēs, reget…*).

blocks.pitfall: In the 3rd conjugation a single vowel separates present from future: *regit* ‘he rules’, *reget* ‘he will rule’; *regimus* ‘we rule’, *regēmus* ‘we shall rule’. And don’t mistake a 3rd-conjugation future for a 2nd-conjugation present: *regēs* ‘you will rule’ looks like *monēs* ‘you warn’. Know each verb’s conjugation.

items.en: I am not what I used to be. (Horace)
The boys were playing in the garden.

items.t: Ōlim in Italiā rēx potēns habitābat.
items.en: Once upon a time a powerful king lived in Italy.
Tomorrow I will come to Rome.
Our friends will wait for us.
I shall not wholly die. (Horace, on his poetry)
items.lit: Not all (of me) will die.

afterlife.title: The imperfect lives on; the future was rebuilt

blocks.p: The **imperfect** is one of the great survivors: every Romance language still has it, used much as in Latin for background, description and habit. The *-b-* is still audible in Italian *-vo* and Spanish *-aba*; elsewhere it has worn away.

compare.title: The Latin imperfect in Romance
compare.note: Spanish and Portuguese lost the b in the 2nd/3rd-conjugation type (-ēbam > -ía). French generalised that type to all verbs, so chantais has the ending of avais. Old Italian said io cantava; the -o of cantavo was added later by analogy with the present. French était comes from stābat ‘he was standing’, not from erat. Romanian iubeam is a Slavic verb with Latin imperfect endings.

blocks.p: The **Latin future** did not survive. In spoken Latin it had become a liability: once *b* and *v* merged, *amābit* ‘he will love’ sounded like *amāvit* ‘he loved’; and in the 3rd conjugation, future *reget* and present *regit* fell together when the vowel system changed. Speakers replaced it with a phrase: the **infinitive** + *habeō* ‘I have (to)’ — *cantāre habeō* ‘I have to sing’ → ‘I will sing’. The two words fused into one, and the endings of the Romance future are simply the present tense of ‘to have’.

compare.title: cantāre habeō → the Romance future
compare.note: Romanian took a different auxiliary: voi cânta is literally ‘I want to sing’, with voi from Latin volō ‘I want’ — just like English will, which once meant ‘want’. Everyday Romanian also says o să cânt, or am să cânt (literally ‘I have to sing’).

table.title: French: the future endings are the verb avoir
table.note: Italian shows the same thing: ho, hai, ha … hanno → canterò, canterai, canterà … canteranno.

blocks.p: The proof that the Romance future was once two words survives in **European Portuguese**, where an object pronoun can still be wedged between the infinitive and the ending (‘mesoclisis’). Old Spanish did the same (*darte he* ‘I will give you’).

items.en: I will give you the book tomorrow.
items.lit: give-you-I.have the book tomorrow

items.en: I will love you forever.

blocks.p: The same trick produced a brand-new tense that Latin never had, the **conditional**: infinitive + the imperfect of *habēre* → Spanish *cantaría*, Portuguese *cantaria*, French *chanterais* (*chanter* + *-ais* as in *avais*). Italian used the perfect *ebbi* ‘I had’ instead: *canterei*. And one form of the old Latin future still lives on, disguised: Spanish *eres* ‘you are’ is the Latin future *eris* ‘you will be’.

parts.title: The imperfect lives on; the future was rebuilt

title: The Perfect System
sub: Perfect, pluperfect and future perfect active

blocks.p: The Latin **perfect** does the work of two English tenses: the simple past (*amāvī* ‘I loved’) and the present perfect (‘I have loved’). It is built on a separate stem — the **perfect stem** — which you find in the **third principal part**: *amō, amāre, amāvī, amātum*: the third part, *amāvī*, gives the stem *amāv-*. The perfect has its own set of endings, used for no other tense.

table.title: Perfect active
table.note: The 3rd plural also has a poetic form in -ēre (amāvēre). Contracted forms are common: amāstī for amāvistī, amārunt for amāvērunt, audiit for audīvit. possum has perfect potuī.

blocks.p: The 1st and 4th conjugations are mostly regular (*-āvī*, *-īvī*), and many 2nd-conjugation verbs take *-uī*. The 3rd conjugation is a museum of older formations. There are five main types:

table.title: Types of perfect stem
table.note: love, hear, warn, have, say, write, send, give, run, sing, come, see, read, make / do, drive / do, defend. In dīxī and rēxī, x is simply c or g + s. Reduplication repeats the first consonant with a vowel (de-dī, cu-currī, ce-cinī); lengthening makes the stem vowel long, sometimes changing it (faciō → fēcī, agō → ēgī).

blocks.tip: There is no reliable way to predict a 3rd-conjugation perfect — learn all four principal parts together, aloud, as a single word: *regō-regere-rēxī-rēctum*. Caesar’s *vēnī, vīdī, vīcī* is three lengthened perfects in a row (*veniō, videō, vincō*).

blocks.pitfall: The macron can be the only difference between present and perfect: *venit* ‘he comes’ vs. *vēnit* ‘he came’; *legit* ‘he reads’ vs. *lēgit* ‘he read’; *fugit* ‘he flees’ vs. *fūgit* ‘he fled’. In the 3rd plural, keep apart *amāvērunt* (perfect), *amāverant* (pluperfect) and *amāverint* (future perfect).

blocks.p: The two remaining tenses of the perfect system are built on the same perfect stem, with endings that look like the imperfect and future of *sum*. The **pluperfect** (‘I had loved’) = perfect stem + *eram, erās, erat…*; the **future perfect** (‘I will have loved’) = perfect stem + *erō, eris, erit…*, except for the 3rd plural *-erint*.

table.title: Pluperfect and future perfect of amāre
table.note: Every verb works the same way: rēxeram, vēneram, fueram ‘I had been’; rēxerō, vēnerō, fuerō ‘I will have been’.

blocks.p: Latin uses the **future perfect** much more strictly than English. When one future event will be finished before another, Latin says so: *Sī Rōmam vēneris, Forum vidēbis* ‘If you come (literally ‘will have come’) to Rome, you will see the Forum’. English uses a present tense here.

items.en: I came, I saw, I conquered. (Caesar)
I have built a monument more lasting than bronze. (Horace)
We were Trojans; Troy is no more. (Virgil)
items.lit: We have been Trojans, Ilium has been.

items.en: They are dead. (Cicero, announcing the execution of the Catilinarian conspirators)
items.lit: They have lived.

items.en: The boys had already run home.
If you come to Rome, you will see the Forum.
items.lit: If you will have come to Rome…

blocks.p: The Latin perfect became the Romance **simple past**: Italian *passato remoto*, Spanish *pretérito perfecto simple* (or *indefinido*), French *passé simple*, Portuguese *pretérito perfeito*, Romanian *perfect simplu*. Even the old irregular perfects survived — they are the ‘irregular preterites’ that learners of Spanish and Italian still have to memorise.

compare.title: The Latin perfect in Romance
compare.note: Spoken Latin already contracted cantāvit to something like cantaut, hence -ò, -ó, -ou. Romanian perfect cântă is stressed on the last syllable, unlike the present cântă (stressed on the first). Spanish hice and Portuguese fiz keep the vowel change of fēcī; Italian feci, French fis and Romanian făcui all continue the same Latin form.

blocks.p: Meanwhile spoken Latin built a new **compound perfect** from *habēre* + past participle: *librum scrīptum habeō* ‘I have the book (in a) written (state)’ → ‘I have written the book’. This is the source of Italian *ho scritto*, Spanish *he escrito*, French *j’ai écrit*, Romanian *am scris*. In spoken French and Romanian, and in much of northern Italy, the compound form has pushed the simple past out of everyday speech. Spanish and Portuguese still use the simple past all the time — and Portuguese *tenho escrito* means ‘I have been writing’, not ‘I have written’.

compare.title: ‘Yesterday I sang’: simple or compound?
compare.note: Italian cantai is still normal in Tuscany and the south, and in writing; the French passé simple (je chantai) is now almost purely literary; Romanian perfect simplu survives in speech mainly in Oltenia.

blocks.p: The **pluperfect** had an unusual afterlife. **Portuguese** still has the Latin pluperfect indicative, with its original meaning: *cantara* ‘I had sung’ (from *cantāveram*), *fora* ‘I had been’, *dissera* ‘I had said’ — today mostly literary, while speech prefers *tinha cantado*. In **Spanish** the same forms in *-ra* shifted to become the imperfect **subjunctive**: *si yo cantara* ‘if I sang’; Spanish journalists and writers still sometimes use them in their old pluperfect sense (*el libro que escribiera en 1950*).

compare.title: The Latin pluperfect in Portuguese and Spanish
gloss: I had sung → pt. ‘I had sung’, es. ‘(if) I sang’
I had been → pt. ‘I had been’, es. ‘(if) I were’
I had said → pt. ‘I had said’, es. ‘(if) I said’
I had done → pt. ‘I had done’, es. ‘(if) I did’

blocks.p: Romanian’s pluperfect (*cântasem* ‘I had sung’) is built instead on the Latin **pluperfect subjunctive** (*cantāvissem*), the same form that gave the imperfect subjunctive of the western languages: Italian *cantassi*, Spanish *cantase*, French *chantasse*, Portuguese *cantasse*. And the **future perfect** lives on in the Portuguese **future subjunctive**: *quando eu fizer* ‘when I do’ goes back mainly to Latin *fēcerō*.

title: Personal Pronouns and Possessives
sub: ego, tū, is, ea, id — and the reflexive sē, suus

table.title: Personal pronouns: 1st and 2nd person
table.note: The genitives are rare and never mean ‘my’ or ‘your’: nostrum is partitive (ūnus nostrum ‘one of us’), nostrī objective (memor nostrī ‘mindful of us’).

blocks.p: Because the verb ending already shows the person, the nominatives *ego, tū, nōs, vōs* are used only for **emphasis or contrast**: *Ego labōrō, tū dormīs* ‘**I** am working, **you** are sleeping’. With the ablative, *cum* ‘with’ is attached to the end: *mēcum* ‘with me’, *tēcum*, *nōbīscum*, *vōbīscum*.

‘My, your, our’ are ordinary adjectives that agree with the thing possessed: *meus, mea, meum* ‘my’ and *tuus, -a, -um* ‘your’ decline like *bonus*; *noster, nostra, nostrum* ‘our’ and *vester, vestra, vestrum* ‘your (pl.)’ like *pulcher*. The masculine vocative of *meus* is *mī*: *mī fīlī* ‘my son’. Latin often leaves the possessive out when it is obvious: *Patrem amō* ‘I love my father’.
Latin has no true third-person personal pronoun. Its place is taken by the weak demonstrative *is, ea, id* ‘he, she, it; that’, which can also be used as an adjective: *ea puella* ‘that girl’.

table.title: is, ea, id
table.note: eius ‘his, her, its’ and eōrum / eārum ‘their’ are the genitives used for possession by someone other than the subject.

blocks.p: When ‘him(self), her(self), them(selves)’ refers back to the **subject** of the sentence, Latin uses the reflexive pronoun *sē*. It has no nominative (it can never be the subject) and the same forms for singular and plural. The matching possessive is *suus, sua, suum* ‘his own, her own, their own’.

items.en: Marcus praises his (own) friend.
Marcus praises his friend (someone else’s).
Marcus praises himself.
Marcus praises him (another man).

blocks.pitfall: English *his* is ambiguous; Latin is not. If ‘his’ means the subject’s own, use *suus* (which agrees with the thing owned); if it means someone else’s, use the genitive *eius*, which never changes. Writing *Mārcus amīcum eius laudat* when you mean Marcus’s own friend is one of the commonest mistakes in Latin composition.

items.en: The Lord be with you.
Do not touch me. (John 20:17)

items.t: Sī valēs, bene est; ego valeō.
items.en: If you are well, that is good; I am well. (standard opening of a Roman letter)

items.t: Homō sum: hūmānī nīl ā mē aliēnum putō.
items.en: I am human: I consider nothing human foreign to me. (Terence)
I like it.
items.lit: It pleases to me.

blocks.p: Personal pronouns are where the Latin case system survives best in Romance (see Chapter 2). The subject pronouns descend directly from *ego, tū, nōs, vōs*, and the unstressed object forms *mē, tē, sē* became the little **clitic** pronouns that sit next to the verb in every Romance language.

compare.title: Subject pronouns
compare.note: Spanish nosotros, vosotros are nōs, vōs + otros ‘others’ — ‘we others’, like French nous autres. Portuguese vós is archaic; speakers say vocês.

compare.title: Object clitics
compare.note: Mi vedi? ¿Me ves? Tu me vois ? Vês-me? Mă vezi? — ‘Do you see me?’ The reflexive sē also gave the impersonal ‘one’ construction: Italian si dice, Spanish se dice, Portuguese diz-se, Romanian se spune ‘it is said’.

compare.title: ‘with me’, ‘with you’
compare.note: Spanish and Portuguese kept Latin mēcum, tēcum, sēcum — and then, no longer feeling the -cum as ‘with’, put another con / com in front: conmigo is literally ‘with with-me’.

compare.title: Possessives
compare.note: Spanish uses the short forms mi, tu, su before a noun (mi casa) and mío, tuyo, suyo after it (una amiga mía). All five languages continue the spoken Latin form voster rather than classical vester.

blocks.p: The careful Latin distinction between *suus* and *eius* did not survive in the west: Spanish *su libro* can mean ‘his, her, its, their or your (formal) book’. Romanian comes closest to Latin, using genitive pronouns for other people’s property — *cartea lui* ‘his book’, *cartea ei* ‘her book’, *cartea lor* ‘their book’ — much as Latin used *eius* and *eōrum*. Those genitives, like Italian *loro* and French *leur* ‘their’, come not from *is, ea, id*, which vanished, but from *ille* — the subject of the next chapter.

title: Demonstratives
sub: hic, iste, ille, ipse, īdem

blocks.p: Latin has a richer set of ‘pointing’ words than English *this* and *that*. Each can be used as an adjective (*hic liber* ‘this book’) or on its own as a pronoun (*hic* ‘this man, he’):

*hic* ‘this (here, near me)’ · *iste* ‘that (near you)’ — often contemptuous, ‘that … of yours’ · *ille* ‘that (over there)’; also ‘the famous’ · *ipse* ‘-self, the very’ · *īdem* ‘the same’. You already know the weakest of them, *is, ea, id* (Chapter 11).

table.title: hic, haec, hoc ‘this’
table.note: Note haec in three places: feminine nominative singular, neuter nominative and accusative plural.

table.title: ille, illa, illud ‘that’
table.note: iste, ista, istud declines exactly like ille: istīus, istī, istum, istam, istud…

blocks.p: Apart from the genitive in *-īus* and dative in *-ī*, *ille* and *iste* use ordinary *bonus* endings. This **pronominal declension** is shared by nine common adjectives, remembered by the acronym **UNUS NAUTA**: *ūnus* ‘one’, *ūllus* ‘any’, *nūllus* ‘no’, *sōlus* ‘alone’, *neuter* ‘neither’, *alius* ‘other’, *uter* ‘which of two’, *tōtus* ‘whole’, *alter* ‘the other (of two)’. So: *tōtīus urbis* ‘of the whole city’, *nūllī virō* ‘to no man’.

table.title: ipse, ipsa, ipsum ‘-self’ and īdem, eadem, idem ‘the same’
table.note: īdem is simply is, ea, id + -dem; m before d becomes n (eum-dem → eundem). Masculine īdem has a long ī, neuter idem a short i.

blocks.pitfall: *ipse* is not the reflexive. *Caesar sē laudat* ‘Caesar praises himself’ (object = subject: reflexive *sē*). *Caesar ipse vēnit* ‘Caesar came himself / Caesar in person came’ (emphasis: *ipse*). English uses *himself* for both.

blocks.tip: *ille* placed after a noun often means ‘that famous’: *Mēdēa illa* ‘the famous Medea’, *Alexander ille* ‘the great Alexander’. And *hic … ille* together mean ‘the latter … the former’ — *hic* is the one nearer in the text.

items.t: Hic liber meus est, ille tuus.
items.en: This book is mine, that one is yours.

items.t: Ō tempora, ō mōrēs! Senātus haec intellegit, cōnsul videt; hic tamen vīvit.
items.en: Oh, the times! Oh, the customs! The senate knows these things, the consul sees them — and yet this man lives. (Cicero, against Catiline)
This is my body. (Vulgate)

items.t: Idem velle atque idem nōlle, ea dēmum firma amīcitia est.
items.en: To want the same things and to reject the same things — that, in the end, is true friendship. (Sallust)
Who will guard the guards themselves? (Juvenal)
That boy of yours does nothing.

afterlife.title: ille: how the article was born

blocks.p: Classical Latin had **no articles**: *lupus* means ‘a wolf’ or ‘the wolf’. In spoken Latin, *ille* ‘that’ was used so often to point back to something already mentioned that it weakened into a simple ‘the’. Every Romance language built its **definite article** from it — the masculine from *illum* / *ille*, the feminine from *illam* / *illa*. Portuguese lost the *l* (*lo* → *o*, *la* → *a*), and Romanian attaches the article to the **end** of the noun: *lupul* ‘the wolf’ (from *lupum illum*), *capra* ‘the goat’.

compare.title: Definite articles from ille
compare.note: The Latin column shows the late spoken use of ille as ‘the’, not classical Latin. Spanish los, las continue the accusatives illōs, illās; Italian i (and gli) the nominative illī. The indefinite article (it. un / una, es. un / una, fr. un / une, pt. um / uma, ro. un / o) comes from ūnus ‘one’ everywhere.

items.en: The wolf sees the goat.

items.t: Văd un lup și o capră.
items.en: I see a wolf and a goat.

blocks.p: *ille* also became the **third-person pronoun** — ‘he, she, they’ — replacing *is, ea, id*. Its genitive plural *illōrum* ‘of those’ became the word for **‘their’** in three languages.

compare.title: Pronouns from ille
compare.note: Italian egli and ella are literary; everyday lui, lei come from late datives (illui, illaei). Spanish uses su and Portuguese seu / deles for ‘their’.

blocks.p: **iste** lost its sneer and became the ordinary word for ‘this’, often reinforced with *ecce* / *eccum* ‘look!’. Spanish and Portuguese *este* continue plain *iste*; Italian *questo* comes from *eccum istum*, Romanian *acest* from *ecce iste*. ‘That’ was built the same way on *ille*: Italian *quello*, Spanish *aquel*, Portuguese *aquele*, Romanian *acel*. French *ce, cet, cette* also go back to *ecce* + *iste* / *ille*.

compare.title: ‘this’ and ‘that’
compare.note: Spanish ese and Portuguese esse ‘that (near you)’ come from ipse. Romanian acest(a) and acel(a) add a final -a when used as pronouns or after the noun: omul acesta ‘this man’.

blocks.p: **ipse** was reinforced with the emphatic suffix *-met* and the superlative ending into a spoken form *metipsimus*, the source of Spanish *mismo*, Portuguese *mesmo*, French *même* and Italian *medesimo* ‘same, -self’; Italian *stesso* is *istum ipsum*.

**hic** died out almost completely, surviving only in fossils: Spanish *ahora* and Portuguese *agora* ‘now’ come from *hāc hōrā* ‘at this hour’; Spanish *pero* and Italian *però* ‘but, however’ from *per hoc* ‘because of this’; French *avec* ‘with’ from *apud hoc*. Best of all, *hoc* ‘this (is so)’ was the medieval word for **yes**: in the south of France people said *oc*, in the north *oïl* (from *hoc ille*, today’s *oui*) — hence the names *langue d’oc* (Occitan) and *langue d’oïl* for the two halves of the French-speaking world.
In English, Latin demonstratives survive in learned phrases: *ad hoc* ‘for this (purpose)’, *post hoc*, *ipso facto* ‘by that very fact’, *idem* ‘the same (author)’, *i.e.* = *id est* ‘that is’.

parts.title: ille: how the article was born

title: The Fourth and Fifth Declensions
sub: manus, cornū, diēs, rēs

blocks.p: The **fourth declension** is recognised by its genitive singular in **-ūs**. Most of its nouns are masculine and end in *-us* in the nominative — *frūctus* ‘fruit’, *exercitus* ‘army’, *senātus* ‘senate’, *cursus* ‘course’, *metus* ‘fear’, *spīritus* ‘breath, spirit’ — but a few are feminine (*manus* ‘hand’, *domus* ‘house’, *Īdūs* ‘the Ides’), and a few neuters end in *-ū* (*cornū* ‘horn’, *genū* ‘knee’).

table.title: manus, manūs f. ‘hand’ and cornū, cornūs n. ‘horn’
table.note: Vocative = nominative. Endings: -us, -ūs, -uī, -um, -ū | -ūs, -uum, -ibus, -ūs, -ibus. Neuters: -ū throughout the singular; -ua, -uum, -ibus in the plural.

blocks.pitfall: Three declensions have nominatives in *-us*, and only the genitive tells them apart: *dominus, dominī* (2nd), *manus, manūs* (4th), *corpus, corporis* (3rd, neuter). Within the 4th declension, the macron is everything: *manus* (nom. sg.) vs. *manūs* (gen. sg., nom. pl., acc. pl.).

blocks.p: *domus* ‘house, home’ mixes 2nd- and 4th-declension forms (abl. *domō*, acc. pl. *domōs* or *domūs*), and has a **locative**. Its three ‘place’ forms are used **without a preposition**, like the names of towns: *domī* ‘at home’, *domum* ‘(to) home’, *domō* ‘from home’.

table.title: domus, domūs f. ‘house, home’
table.note: The forms in -ō, -ōs and -ōrum are borrowed from the second declension.

blocks.p: The **fifth declension** is small: genitive singular **-eī** (or **-ēī** after a vowel). Its nouns are feminine except *diēs* ‘day’ (usually masculine) and *merīdiēs* ‘midday’. Only *diēs* and *rēs* have a complete plural; the others — *spēs* ‘hope’, *fidēs* ‘faith, trust’, *faciēs* ‘face’ — are used mostly in the singular.

table.title: diēs, diēī m. ‘day’ and rēs, reī f. ‘thing’
table.note: The e stays long between two vowels (diēī) but is short after a consonant (reī, fideī, speī).

blocks.tip: *rēs* is the most flexible noun in Latin: ‘thing, matter, affair, fact, event, property, situation’. Translate it by context, and learn the set phrases: *rēs pūblica* ‘the state’ (literally ‘the public thing’), *rēs gestae* ‘deeds, achievements’, *rēs novae* ‘revolution’, *quam ob rem* ‘for which reason, therefore’.

items.en: Seize the day. (Horace)
I have lost a day. (the emperor Titus, on a day when he had helped no one)
One hand washes the other. (Petronius)
items.lit: A hand washes a hand.

items.en: Master the subject, and the words will follow. (Cato the Elder)

items.t: Rēs pūblica in magnō perīculō est.
items.en: The state is in great danger.
Today I am staying at home.

blocks.p: The fourth and fifth declensions were small and irregular, and spoken Latin absorbed them into the bigger ones: most fourth-declension nouns joined the second (*frūctus* → *frutto*, *fruto*, *fruit*), fifth-declension nouns mostly joined the first (*faciēs* → spoken *facia*). But the old genders sometimes stayed put — which is why Italian and Spanish have a feminine noun in *-o*.

compare.title: Fourth-declension nouns in Romance
compare.note: Italian la mano and Spanish la mano are feminine despite their -o: they kept the gender of Latin manus. Italian plural le mani. French corne (f.) comes from the neuter plural cornua, like Italian le corna and Romanian coarne ‘horns’.

blocks.p: *domus* lost out to humble *casa* as the word for ‘house’ (Chapter 3), but it survives in Italian *duomo* ‘cathedral’ — the *domus Deī*, ‘house of God’ — which English borrowed (via French) as *dome*.

compare.title: Fifth-declension nouns in Romance
compare.note: Italian dì is literary — the everyday giorno, like French jour, comes from diurnum ‘daily’. French keeps -di only in the days of the week (lundi, mardi …) and midi ‘noon’ (medius diēs). Spanish día and Portuguese dia are masculine although they end in -a, because Latin diēs was masculine; Romanian zi (ziua ‘the day’) is feminine. Everyday ‘face’ is cara in Spanish and Portuguese (from Greek), visage in French.

blocks.p: And *rēs* ‘thing’? It was replaced by *causa* ‘cause, legal case’, which became the ordinary word for ‘thing’: Italian and Spanish *cosa*, French *chose*, Portuguese *coisa*. (Romanian uses *lucru*, from Latin *lucrum* ‘profit’.) But *rēs* survives in a famous paradox: French *rien* ‘nothing’ comes from the accusative *rem* ‘a thing’. Used constantly in negative sentences — *ne … rien* ‘not a thing’ — it absorbed the negative meaning, just as *personne* ‘a person’ came to mean ‘nobody’. Spanish and Portuguese *nada* ‘nothing’ has a similar story: it is Latin *(rem) nātam* ‘a thing born’.

compare.title: ‘thing’ and ‘nothing’
compare.note: None of the words for ‘nothing’ continue Latin nihil, which survives only in learned words like annihilate and nihilism.

blocks.p: English uses many fourth-declension nouns unchanged: *status*, *census*, *consensus*, *apparatus*, *prospectus*. Their Latin plural would be *-ūs* (*statūs*), never *-ī* — so ‘stati’ is a false Latinism; English says *statuses*. From the fifth declension come *per diem* ‘per day’, *republic* (*rēs pūblica*) and *rebus*, a puzzle told ‘by things’ (*rēbus*) instead of words.

title: Relative and Interrogative Pronouns
sub: quī, quae, quod and quis, quid

blocks.h: The relative pronoun: quī, quae, quod

blocks.p: The **relative pronoun** introduces a clause that describes a noun: ‘the girl *who* sings’, ‘the book *which* I read’. Latin has one relative, *quī, quae, quod*, for ‘who, whom, whose, which, that’.

table.title: quī, quae, quod ‘who, which’
table.note: cuius and cui are pronounced as two syllables and one: [ˈkʊj.jʊs], [kʊi̯].

blocks.p: The golden rule: the relative takes its **gender and number** from the noun it refers to (its **antecedent**), but its **case** from its own job inside the relative clause. In *Puella quam vidēs soror mea est*, *quam* is feminine singular because *puella* is, but accusative because it is the object of *vidēs*.

items.t: Puella quam vidēs soror mea est.
items.en: The girl whom you see is my sister.

items.t: Puer cui librum dedī amīcus meus est.
items.en: The boy to whom I gave the book is my friend.

items.t: Vir cuius fīlium vīdistī rēx est.
items.en: The man whose son you saw is the king.

items.t: Pater noster, quī es in caelīs…
items.en: Our Father, who art in heaven… (the Lord’s Prayer)
He who is silent is taken to consent. (legal maxim)
He whom the gods love dies young. (Plautus)

blocks.tip: When a relative clause has no antecedent, supply ‘he who’, ‘those who’, ‘what’: *Quī tacet…* ‘(He) who is silent…’. And when a sentence *begins* with a relative, it often just links back to the previous sentence: *Quae cum ita sint* ‘Since these things are so’, *Quā dē causā* ‘For this reason’.

blocks.p: To ask ‘who?’ or ‘what?’, Latin uses *quis* (m./f.) and *quid* (n.). In the singular they differ from the relative only in the nominative and the neuter accusative; in the plural they are identical to it.

table.title: quis, quid ‘who? what?’ (singular)
table.note: Plural: quī, quae, quae; quōrum, quārum, quōrum; quibus… — exactly like the relative.

blocks.p: ‘Which …?’ used with a noun is the **interrogative adjective**, identical in form to the relative: *Quī vir?* ‘Which man?’, *Quae fēmina?* ‘Which woman?’, *Quod templum?* ‘Which temple?’. Other question words: *ubi* ‘where’, *quō* ‘where to’, *unde* ‘where from’, *quandō* ‘when’, *cūr* ‘why’, *quōmodo* ‘how’, *quot* ‘how many’, *quantus* ‘how big’, *quālis* ‘of what kind’, *uter* ‘which of two’. A plain yes/no question adds *-ne* to its first word: *Vidēsne?* ‘Do you see?’.

items.en: How are you?
items.lit: What are you doing?

items.en: Lord, where are you going? (John 13:36)
Who will guard the guards themselves? (Juvenal)
Which was to be proved. (Q.E.D.)

blocks.pitfall: *quī* and *quis* are not interchangeable. *quī* (with *quae, quod*) is the relative ‘who, which’ and the adjective ‘which …?’; *quis* (with *quid*) is the pronoun ‘who?’. Also watch *quae*: it can be feminine singular nominative, feminine plural nominative, or neuter plural nominative/accusative. And *quod* is often not a pronoun at all but the conjunction ‘because’.

afterlife.title: che, que, qui — and Romanian care

blocks.p: Like the nouns, the relative pronoun lost most of its cases. In the west, one invariable word does nearly everything: Italian *che*, Spanish and Portuguese *que*, French *qui* (subject) / *que* (object) — all from the Latin forms *quī, quem, quid* and *quod*, which had fallen together. Romanian chose a different Latin word: *care*, from *quālis* ‘of what kind’.

compare.title: The relative pronoun
compare.note: French still keeps a subject/object distinction (qui / que), a faint echo of quī / quem. Romanian marks a personal object with pe and repeats it with the clitic o: pe care o văd.

blocks.p: A few oblique forms survived too. Italian *cui*, straight from the Latin dative, is used after prepositions: *la persona a cui scrivo* ‘the person to whom I write’, *il libro di cui parlo* ‘the book I’m talking about’. Spanish *cuyo* and Portuguese *cujo* ‘whose’ come from the genitive *cuius* and, like Latin possessives, agree with the thing possessed: *la mujer cuyo hijo…*, *la mujer cuya hija…*. And Spanish *quien*, Portuguese *quem* ‘who(m)’ continue the accusative *quem*.

*quālis* ‘of what kind’, which became Romanian *care*, also gave the western languages their formal relative with the article: Italian *il quale*, Spanish *el cual*, French *lequel*, Portuguese *o qual* — ‘the which’.

compare.title: Question words
compare.note: Latin quōmodo ‘in what way’ gave come, cómo, comme, como and Romanian cum; French comment adds -ment. French ‘how much’ is combien, a new formation (Old French com bien). ‘Where’: French où continues ubi; Portuguese onde and Romanian unde continue unde ‘from where’; Spanish dónde is dē unde and Italian dove is dē ubi.

blocks.p: English borrowed Latin relative and interrogative forms as nouns: a *quorum* (genitive plural, ‘of whom’ — from commissions naming members ‘of whom’ a certain number had to be present), a *quota* (from *quota pars* ‘how great a part’), *quality* and *quantity* (from *quālitās*, *quantitās*), and *quid pro quo* ‘something for something’.

parts.title: The relative pronoun: quī, quae, quod
che, que, qui — and Romanian care

title: Numbers and Time
sub: Cardinals, ordinals, and how Latin says ‘when’ and ‘how long’

table.title: Latin numbers
table.note: Ordinals are ordinary adjectives like bonus: prīma lūx ‘first light’, secundus annus ‘the second year’. Compound numbers: vīgintī ūnus or ūnus et vīgintī ‘21’.

blocks.p: Only *ūnus*, *duo*, *trēs*, the hundreds from 200 to 900, and the plural *mīlia* decline. All the other cardinals — *quattuor* to *centum* — are **indeclinable**: *decem puerī*, *decem puellārum*, *cum decem puerīs*.

table.title: ūnus ‘one’
table.note: ūnus belongs to the UNUS NAUTA group (Chapter 12): genitive -īus, dative -ī.

blocks.p: *mīlle* ‘a thousand’ is an indeclinable adjective: *mīlle mīlitēs* ‘a thousand soldiers’. But its plural *mīlia* is a neuter **noun**, followed by a genitive: *duo mīlia mīlitum* ‘two thousand(s) of soldiers’.

blocks.tip: 18 and 19 are counted **down** from 20: *duodēvīgintī* ‘two-from-twenty’, *ūndēvīgintī* ‘one-from-twenty’ — the same subtractive idea as the Roman numerals IV, IX, XL, XC. With Roman numerals, a smaller numeral before a larger one subtracts: this year, 2026, is MMXXVI.

blocks.pitfall: Don’t confuse *ūndecim* ‘eleven’ with *ūndēvīgintī* ‘nineteen’, or *duodecim* ‘twelve’ with *duodēvīgintī* ‘eighteen’ — the little *dē* ‘from’ changes everything. And *sex* ‘six’, *sextus* ‘sixth’ have nothing to do with English *sex* (from *sexus*).

blocks.p: Latin answers ‘**when?**’ and ‘**within what time?**’ with the plain **ablative**, without a preposition: *tertiā hōrā* ‘at the third hour’, *hieme* ‘in winter’, *eō annō* ‘in that year’, *paucīs diēbus* ‘within a few days’. It answers ‘**how long?**’ with the **accusative**: *trēs annōs* ‘for three years’, *tōtam noctem* ‘all night long’. The accusative also measures **distance**: *mīlle passūs* ‘a mile’ (literally ‘a thousand paces’).
Age is expressed with *nātus* ‘born’ and an accusative of duration: *decem annōs nātus* ‘ten years old’, literally ‘born ten years’.

items.en: They left at first light. (ablative: time when)
In winter the ships stay in the harbour.
I will be back within a few days.
I lived in Rome for three years. (accusative: duration)

items.t: Rōmulus septem et trīgintā annōs rēgnāvit.
items.en: Romulus reigned for thirty-seven years. (after Livy)
The boy is ten years old.
We walked a mile.

blocks.p: The numbers from one to ten are among the most stable words in any language, and the Romance ones are unmistakably Latin. Two need comment: Romanian replaced *centum* with *sută*, a Slavic loan, and Spanish and Portuguese have short forms for a bare ‘hundred’ (*cien*, *cem*).

compare.title: One to ten, a hundred, a thousand
compare.note: Romanian is the odd one out in sound: Latin qu- became p- (quattuor → patru, like aqua → apă), and -ct- became -pt- (octō → opt, like noctem → noapte). Portuguese keeps the gender of ‘two’ (dois m., duas f.), as Romanian does (doi m., două f.) — like Latin duo, duae. Romanian mie comes from the plural mīlia.

blocks.p: From eleven upwards the languages diverge. Latin built the teens as ‘one-ten’ (*ūn-decim*), and Italian, Spanish, French and Portuguese kept that pattern for the lower teens before switching to ‘ten-and-seven’: Italian after 16 (*sedici* → *diciassette*), French after 16 (*seize* → *dix-sept*), Spanish and Portuguese after 15 (*quince* → *dieciséis*). **Romanian** rebuilt the whole series on the Slavic model ‘one-upon-ten’: *unsprezece* = *un* + *spre* (from Latin *super*) + *zece* — the words are Latin, the pattern is Slavic. The Romanian tens follow the same model: *douăzeci* is literally ‘two tens’.

compare.title: Eleven and beyond
compare.note: Brazilian Portuguese writes dezesseis, dezessete. Standard French counts by twenties from 70 to 99 (soixante-dix ‘sixty-ten’, quatre-vingts ‘four twenties’), but Belgian and Swiss French keep Latin-style septante and nonante (and in parts of Switzerland huitante).

compare.title: Saying your age
compare.note: Latin is ‘born ten years’; every Romance language says ‘I have ten years’ instead.

blocks.p: The **days of the week** were named, in late antiquity, after the seven planets: *diēs Lūnae* ‘day of the Moon’, *diēs Mārtis* ‘of Mars’, and so on. The Church replaced the Saturn and Sun days with *sabbatum* ‘Sabbath’ and *(diēs) dominica* ‘the Lord’s day’. **Portuguese** went further: following the Church’s practice of numbering the days, it calls Monday to Friday ‘second to sixth *feira*’ (from Latin *fēria*, ‘feast day’) — a custom associated with St Martin of Braga in the 6th century.

compare.title: Days of the week
compare.note: Italian -dì and French -di are diēs. English kept the pagan scheme but swapped in Germanic gods: Tiw for Mars (Tuesday), Woden for Mercury (Wednesday), Thor for Jupiter (Thursday), Frigg for Venus (Friday); Saturday keeps Saturn.

blocks.p: The months, too, are Latin in all six languages. *September* to *December* still mean ‘seventh’ to ‘tenth’ month, from the time when the Roman year began in March; *Iūlius* and *Augustus* were renamed in honour of Julius Caesar and the emperor Augustus.

title: The Passive Voice
sub: Present, imperfect and future passive; the agent with ā / ab

blocks.p: In the **active** voice the subject does something: *Puella rosam amat* ‘The girl loves the rose’. In the **passive** the subject undergoes it: *Rosa ā puellā amātur* ‘The rose is loved by the girl’. English builds its passive from two words, ‘is’ + participle. Latin, in the three tenses of the present system, needs only one: it simply swaps the active personal endings for passive ones.

table.title: Active and passive personal endings
table.note: Where the active ends in -ō, the passive adds -r (amō → amor); where it ends in -m, the passive replaces it with -r (amābam → amābar). The 2nd singular has a shorter form in -re, common in poetry and in the imperfect and future (amābāre, amābere).

blocks.tip: The passive signature is the letter **r**: *-or, -ris, -tur, -mur, -ntur*. Only the 2nd plural *-minī* breaks the pattern — it is probably a fossilised participle, related to Greek *-μενοι* and to Latin *alumnus*, originally ‘one being nourished’.

table.title: Present passive
table.note: I am loved, I am warned, I am ruled, I am heard, I am taken. The 3rd conjugation has a short e in regeris; -iō verbs like capiō keep their i before o and u (capior, capiuntur).

blocks.p: The **present passive infinitive** ends in *-rī* — except in the 3rd conjugation, which has a plain *-ī*: *amārī* ‘to be loved’, *monērī* ‘to be warned’, *audīrī* ‘to be heard’, but *regī* ‘to be ruled’, *capī* ‘to be taken’, *mittī* ‘to be sent’.

The **imperfect** passive keeps the tense sign *-bā-* and adds the passive endings: *amābar* ‘I was being loved, I used to be loved’. The **future** keeps its two patterns (Chapter 9): *-bor, -beris, -bitur…* in the 1st and 2nd conjugations, *-ar, -ēris, -ētur…* in the 3rd and 4th.

table.title: Imperfect passive
table.note: capere goes like audīre: capiēbar, capiēbāris …

table.title: Future passive
table.note: I shall be loved, warned, ruled, heard. capere: capiar, capiēris, capiētur …

blocks.pitfall: In the 3rd conjugation a single vowel length separates two tenses: *regeris* ‘you are ruled’ (present) but *regēris* ‘you will be ruled’ (future). Watch the 2nd singular in *-re*, too: *amābere* ‘you will be loved’ is not an infinitive.

blocks.p: The person (or animal, or god) by whom an action is done — the **agent** — goes into the ablative with **ā** (before consonants) or **ab** (before vowels and *h*): *ā puellā*, *ab amīcō*. A thing or instrument takes the **plain ablative**, without a preposition — the ablative of means: *gladiō vulnerātur* ‘he is wounded with a sword’.

items.en: Gaul is being conquered by Caesar.
The city is defended by high walls.
The letters were being carried by a slave.
You will be praised by everyone.
The world wants to be deceived. (proverb)

items.t: Tempora mūtantur, nōs et mūtāmur in illīs.
items.en: Times change, and we change with them. (proverb)
items.lit: Times are changed, and we are changed in them.

items.en: This is the way to the stars. (Virgil)
items.lit: Thus it is gone to the stars.

blocks.p: The Latin passive often has a **reflexive** or **intransitive** meaning that English expresses with an active verb: *movētur* ‘it moves’, *vertitur* ‘it turns’, *lavor* ‘I wash (myself)’, *mūtantur* ‘they change’. Intransitive verbs can even form an **impersonal passive** in the 3rd singular, meaning ‘people do X’ or ‘there is X-ing’: *pugnātur* ‘there is fighting’, *ītur* ‘people go’, *bene vīvitur* ‘people live well’.

blocks.tip: To turn an active sentence into a passive one: the object (accusative) becomes the subject (nominative), the verb takes passive endings, and the old subject becomes *ā / ab* + ablative. *Caesar Galliam vincit* → *Gallia ā Caesare vincitur*.

blocks.p: Not one Romance language kept the one-word passive: there is no Italian, Spanish or French descendant of *amātur*. The cause lies in the perfect. *Amātus est* (Chapter 17) originally meant ‘he was loved, he has been loved’, but speakers came to hear it as ‘he **is** loved’ — *est* is, after all, a present tense.
