Once *amātus est* meant ‘is loved’, the old *amātur* was redundant, and a new passive made of ‘to be’ + participle took over every tense.

compare.title: ‘The letter is written by the girl’
rows: La lettera è scritta dalla ragazza.
La carta es escrita por la chica.
La lettre est écrite par la fille.
A carta é escrita pela menina.
gloss: The letter is written by the girl.
compare.note: The preposition for the agent varies: Italian da (usually derived from dē + ab), French par (from per), Spanish and Portuguese por (pela = por + a), Romanian de (from dē). In everyday Spanish and Portuguese the active (La chica escribe la carta) is far more common than this passive.

blocks.p: Italian added a second auxiliary, **venire** ‘to come’, for the action as opposed to the state: *La porta viene chiusa alle otto* ‘The door is (gets) closed at eight’, while *La porta è chiusa* usually means ‘The door is closed’ (not open). Spanish and Portuguese mark the state with their second verb ‘to be’, *estar*: *La puerta está cerrada*, *A porta está fechada*. And Italian **andare** + participle expresses obligation: *Questo libro va letto* ‘This book must be read’.

Above all, Romance languages avoid the passive altogether when nobody in particular is the agent. Instead they use the **reflexive** pronoun from Latin *sē* — literally ‘the house sells itself’. Because the verb agrees with the thing sold (Italian *si vendono case*, Spanish *se venden casas*, Portuguese *vendem-se casas* ‘houses for sale’), this really is a passive in reflexive dress.

compare.title: The reflexive passive
gloss: it is sold, it is for sale
wine is drunk, people drink wine
compare.note: Classical Latin usually supplied the passive of vendō ‘sell’ from a different verb, vēneō ‘be on sale’ (literally ‘go to sale’), 3 sg. vēnit. Italian shop signs keep an old word order, Vendesi ‘for sale’, Affittasi ‘to let’ — just like Portuguese Vende-se. French prefers on (from homō ‘man’) for ‘people in general’.

blocks.p: The Latin **impersonal passive** has a close modern counterpart in the Italian impersonal *si*: Latin *Sīc ītur ad astra* ‘thus one goes to the stars’, Italian *Di qui si va al mare* ‘this way to the sea’; Latin *bene vīvitur* ‘people live well’, Italian *si vive bene*, Spanish *se vive bien*.

English kept nothing of the Latin passive forms either — but it borrowed the vocabulary of undergoing: *passive*, *passion* and *patient* all come from *patior, passus* ‘suffer, undergo’ (Chapter 18).

title: The Perfect Passive
sub: The perfect passive participle, and tenses built with esse

blocks.p: The fourth principal part of most verbs is the **supine** in *-um*: *amō, amāre, amāvī, amātum*. Replace *-um* with *-us, -a, -um* and you have the **perfect passive participle** (PPP): *amātus* ‘loved, having been loved’. It is an ordinary adjective of the *bonus* type (Chapter 6) and agrees with its noun in gender, number and case.

table.title: Perfect passive participles
table.note: Like the perfect stem, the supine of a 3rd-conjugation verb cannot be predicted: learn it as part of the principal parts.

blocks.tip: The participle stem is the source of most English words from Latin verbs: *āct-* → act, action; *fact-* → fact, factory; *scrīpt-* → script, description; *miss-* → mission, missile; *vīs-* → vision, visible; *dict-* → dictum, dictionary; *capt-* → captive, capture.

blocks.h: Perfect, pluperfect and future perfect passive

blocks.p: The three passive tenses of the perfect system are not single words but phrases: the participle + a form of *esse*. The **perfect** uses the present of *sum* — *amātus sum* ‘I was loved, I have been loved’; the **pluperfect** uses the imperfect — *amātus eram* ‘I had been loved’; the **future perfect** uses the future — *amātus erō* ‘I shall have been loved’. The participle agrees with the subject: *Rōma condita est*, *Rōmānī victī sunt*, *bellum cōnfectum est*.

table.title: Perfect-system passive of amāre
table.note: Feminine amāta sum, amātae sumus; neuter amātum est, amāta sunt. The perfect passive infinitive is amātus esse ‘to have been loved’. Forms with fuī and fueram (amātus fuit) also occur, and became much more common in later Latin.

blocks.pitfall: *Amātus est* is a **past** tense: ‘he was loved’ or ‘he has been loved’ — never ‘he is loved’, which is *amātur*. Speakers of Italian, French or Spanish fall into this trap easily, because their *è amato*, *est aimé*, *es amado* mean exactly ‘is loved’. The Afterlife below explains why.

blocks.p: The PPP is used constantly as an adjective, and Latin uses it to pack a whole clause into one word. *Urbs capta* is ‘the captured city’; *Hostēs victī fūgērunt* is ‘The enemy, defeated, fled’ or ‘After they had been defeated, the enemy fled’. Its time is **before** that of the main verb.

A noun + participle often stands where English uses an abstract noun: *ab urbe conditā* ‘from the city founded’ = ‘from the founding of the city’ (Livy’s title for his history of Rome, which counted the years from 753 BC); *post rēgēs exāctōs* ‘after the expulsion of the kings’; *Sicilia āmissa* ‘the loss of Sicily’.

items.en: The die is cast. (Caesar at the Rubicon, as reported by Suetonius)
items.lit: The die has been thrown.

items.t: Gallia est omnis dīvīsa in partēs trēs.
items.en: Gaul as a whole is divided into three parts. (Caesar)
Rome was founded by Romulus.
Carthage was destroyed by the Romans.
The captured city was set on fire.
The letter had already been written.
items.lit: The letters had already been written.

items.en: It is finished. (John 19:30)

blocks.tip: Caesar’s *dīvīsa est* describes a **state** (‘is divided’) rather than a past event (‘was divided’). This double meaning is exactly the crack through which the Romance passive grew.

blocks.p: Because the PPP is an adjective, it can describe the object of *habeō* ‘I have’: *Litterās scrīptās habeō* ‘I have the letter in a written state’, ‘I have the letter (already) written’. Classical writers used this to stress a completed result: *cognitum habeō* ‘I have (it) found out’, i.e. ‘I know for certain’. These were still two separate ideas — possession plus a state — but they were the seed of a new tense.

afterlife.title: From ‘I have it written’ to ‘I have written’

blocks.p: In spoken Latin both patterns of this chapter were reinterpreted. **esse + participle** stopped being a past tense and became the new present passive (*amātus est* → *è amato* ‘is loved’, Chapter 16). **habēre + participle** stopped meaning ‘to possess something in a finished state’ and became a new past tense: *habeō litterās scrīptās* → ‘I have written the letter’. The participle stopped agreeing, *habēre* became a mere auxiliary, and the construction spread even to verbs with no object at all (Italian *ho dormito* ‘I have slept’).

compare.title: ‘I have written the letter’
compare.note: Italian ho, Spanish he, French ai and Romanian am all come from habeō. Portuguese prefers the simple past here: its compound tenho escrito, built with ter (from tenēre ‘to hold’), means ‘I have been writing (lately)’ (Chapter 10).

blocks.p: Traces of the old agreement survive. In French and Italian the participle still agrees with a direct object that comes **before** it — just as *scrīptās* agreed with *litterās*. And Spanish *tener* + participle keeps the original Latin meaning, agreement included: *Tengo escritas tres cartas* ‘I have three letters written’, i.e. finished and ready.

compare.title: Agreement: ‘I have written them’ (the letters)
compare.note: Italian scritte and French écrites are feminine plural, agreeing with le / les, like Latin scrīptās with eās. Spanish and Romanian never make the participle agree in this tense.

blocks.p: The choice of auxiliary is a legacy too. In **Italian** and **French**, verbs of motion and change of state (‘come, go, arrive, be born, die, become’) and all reflexive verbs form their compound past with **‘to be’**, and the participle agrees with the subject: *è venuta*, *elle est venue* ‘she has come’. These look exactly like Latin deponent perfects such as *nātus est* ‘he was born’ and *mortuus est* ‘he died’ (Chapter 18). Old Spanish and Old Portuguese did the same (Old Spanish *es venido* ‘he has come’) but later generalised *haber* and *ter*; Romanian uses *avea* for every verb.

compare.title: ‘to have’ or ‘to be’?
gloss: he was born, has been born
compare.note: Portuguese answers with its simple past (Chapter 10). Romanian a se naște ‘to be born’ is reflexive: s-a născut is literally ‘himself has born’, still with the auxiliary a from avea.

blocks.p: A rule of thumb for Italian and French: if the subject **undergoes** a change rather than doing something to something, the auxiliary is *essere* / *être* — very often the same verbs that were deponent or passive in Latin. English once had the same split: older English said *he is come* and still says *Christ is risen*.

parts.title: Perfect, pluperfect and future perfect passive
From ‘I have it written’ to ‘I have written’

title: Deponent and Semi-Deponent Verbs
sub: Passive forms with active meanings

blocks.h: Passive in form, active in meaning

blocks.p: Some Latin verbs have **passive forms but active meanings**. *Hortor* means ‘I encourage’, not ‘I am encouraged’; *sequitur* means ‘he follows’. Roman grammarians called them *verba dēpōnentia*, ‘verbs that lay aside’ (*dēpōnō*) their active forms. There are a few hundred of them, many very common, so they must be recognised at sight.

A deponent has only **three principal parts**: the present, the infinitive (passive in form), and the perfect (participle + *sum*): *hortor, hortārī, hortātus sum* ‘encourage’. The conjugation is exactly the passive you already know (Chapters 16–17) — only the translation changes.

table.title: Common deponent verbs
table.note: orior has some 3rd-conjugation forms (oritur ‘it rises’). Future participles: moritūrus ‘about to die’, oritūrus ‘about to rise’.

table.title: sequor ‘follow’
table.note: I follow, I was following, I shall follow, I followed / have followed. Infinitive sequī ‘to follow’; pluperfect secūtus eram ‘I had followed’.

blocks.pitfall: Translate deponents **actively**, whatever their endings: *Hostēs secūtī sumus* is ‘We followed the enemy’, not ‘we were followed’; *loquī* is ‘to speak’, not ‘to be spoken’. The only way to know is to learn which verbs are deponent — the dictionary entry (*-or, -ī, -us sum*) tells you.

blocks.p: Deponents borrow a few active forms: the **present participle** (*sequēns* ‘following’), the **future participle** (*secūtūrus* ‘about to follow’) and the future infinitive (*secūtūrus esse*). Their **perfect participle** is active in meaning: *secūtus* ‘having followed’, *locūtus* ‘having spoken’, *profectus* ‘having set out’. This is a real asset, because ordinary Latin verbs have no perfect active participle at all: ‘having seen’ cannot be said with *vīsus*, which means ‘having been seen’.

Five deponents take their object in the **ablative**, not the accusative: *ūtor* ‘use’, *fruor* ‘enjoy’, *fungor* ‘perform’, *potior* ‘take possession of’, *vescor* ‘feed on’. *Gladiō ūtitur* ‘He uses a sword’; *vītā fruimur* ‘we enjoy life’; *urbe potītī sunt* ‘they took possession of the city’.

blocks.tip: Remember the five ablative deponents as **PFFUV**: *potior, fruor, fungor, ūtor, vescor*.

blocks.p: One verb behaves like a deponent without being one: *videor* is simply the passive of *videō* ‘I am seen’, but its usual meaning is ‘I seem’: *vidētur* ‘he seems, it seems (good)’.
A handful of **semi-deponent** verbs are active in the present system but deponent in the perfect system:

table.title: Semi-deponent verbs
table.note: audet ‘he dares’, ausus est ‘he dared’; solet ‘he usually does’, solitus est ‘he used to’. The reverse also exists: revertor ‘return’ is deponent in the present system but has an active perfect, revertī ‘I returned’.

items.en: While we talk, envious time will have fled. (Horace)
From the moment we are born, we are dying. (Manilius)
items.lit: Being born, we die.

items.en: Hannibal crossed the Alps.
Caesar set out from Rome.
The soldiers use swords.
Fortune favours the bold. (after Virgil)
He who keeps silent is taken to consent. (legal maxim)
items.lit: Who is silent seems to consent.

blocks.tip: English is full of deponent participles: *sequor, secūtus* → sequence, consecutive, persecute; *loquor, locūtus* → eloquent, elocution; *patior, passus* → patient, passion, passive; *nāscor, nātus* → native, nation, nature; *ūtor, ūsus* → use, utility; *gradior, gressus* → progress, aggressive; *orior, ortus* → origin, orient; *experior, expertus* → experience, expert.

blocks.p: Deponents were an oddity that spoken Latin did not keep. Late Latin writers and inscriptions increasingly give them active endings, and no Romance language has a single deponent verb — the category itself disappeared. The verbs that survived simply became ordinary active verbs.

compare.title: Deponents turned active
gloss: to wonder at → it. ‘aim, gaze at’, es. / pt. ‘look at’, fr. ‘see one’s reflection’, ro. ‘wonder’
compare.note: Romanian a naște means ‘to give birth’; ‘to be born’ is reflexive, a se naște — and ‘to wonder’ is a se mira (mă mir ‘I wonder’). The reflexive pronoun has taken over the job of the deponent’s passive form. Spanish and Portuguese padecer go back to an extended form *patēscere. Romanian has no heir of sequī and says urma. French miroir ‘mirror’ belongs to the family of mīrārī.

blocks.p: There were two routes to a new active verb. Usually the deponent simply took active endings, as above. Sometimes the **perfect participle** became the base of a brand-new verb: *ūsus* (from *ūtor*) gave spoken Latin *ūsāre* ‘to use’, and *oblītus* (from *oblīvīscor* ‘forget’) gave *oblītāre* ‘to forget’.

compare.title: New verbs from deponent participles
compare.note: Words in brackets come from other roots. French user now mostly means ‘to wear out’; the everyday ‘to use’ is utiliser or se servir de.

blocks.p: Even ‘to speak’ shows the deponents’ fate. Classical *loquī* vanished, but Spanish *hablar* and Portuguese *falar* come from another deponent, *fābulārī* ‘to chat’, which went active like all the rest. Italian *parlare* and French *parler* come from Church Latin *parabolāre* ‘to tell parables’; Romanian *vorbi* is Slavic. Only the learned family of *loquor* lives on: Italian *eloquente*, Spanish *elocuente*, English *eloquent*, *loquacious*.

There is a neat link with Chapter 17. The verbs that were deponent in Latin because the subject undergoes the action — *nāscor* ‘be born’, *morior* ‘die’, *proficīscor* ‘set out’ — are exactly the kind of verbs that take ‘to be’ in Italian and French compound tenses. Latin *nātus est* and *mortuus est* line up with *è nato, è morto* and *il est né, il est mort* — the same shape, nearly two thousand years apart.

parts.title: Passive in form, active in meaning

title: Irregular Verbs
sub: eō ‘go’, ferō ‘carry’, volō ‘want’, fīō ‘become’, edō ‘eat’

blocks.p: Besides *sum* and *possum* (Chapter 5), Latin has a handful of irregular verbs. They are few, but they are among the most frequent words in the language, and they have dozens of compounds. Their irregularities are mostly in the **present system**; the perfect system is regular once you know the principal parts.

table.title: eō ‘go’
table.note: Infinitive īre; imperative ī, īte; present participle iēns, euntis; present subjunctive eam. The perfect also appears as īvī. The stem is ī-, which becomes e- before a, o, u: eō, eunt, eam, euntis.

blocks.p: *eō* has many compounds, all conjugated the same way: *abeō* ‘go away’, *adeō* ‘approach’, *exeō* ‘go out’, *ineō* ‘go in, begin’, *pereō* ‘perish’ (‘go through, be lost’), *redeō* ‘go back’, *trānseō* ‘go across’, *praetereō* ‘go past’, *subeō* ‘go under, undergo’.

blocks.tip: English has kept *eō* in stage directions — *exit* ‘he goes out’, *exeunt* ‘they go out’ — and in *transit*, *transient*, *initial* (*initium* ‘a going in’), *circuit*, *ambition* (*ambitiō* ‘going around’ canvassing for votes), *obituary* (*obitus* ‘a going down, death’), *sedition* (‘a going apart’) and *preterite* (*praeteritus* ‘gone by’).

table.title: ferō — present
table.note: Infinitives ferre, ferrī; imperative fer, ferte. Wherever a connecting vowel would come before r, s or t, ferō simply leaves it out. Everything else is regular 3rd conjugation: imperfect ferēbam, future feram, ferēs, feret …

blocks.p: The perfect *tulī* and the supine *lātum* come from two different roots (*tulī* is related to *tollō* ‘lift’ and *tolerō* ‘endure’). Compounds of *ferō* therefore have three very different-looking stems, and the prefix usually assimilates (Chapter 30):

table.title: Compounds of ferō
table.note: The ablative case is the casus ablātīvus, the ‘taking-away case’ — named from ablātum. A legislator is a lēgis lātor, ‘proposer of a law’.

blocks.h: volō, nōlō, mālō ‘want, not want, prefer’

table.title: volō, nōlō, mālō — present
table.note: Infinitives velle, nōlle, mālle; perfects voluī, nōluī, māluī. Imperfect volēbam; future volam, volēs …; present subjunctive velim, nōlim, mālim. Only nōlō has an imperative: nōlī, nōlīte (Chapter 21). Older texts write volt, voltis.

blocks.p: *nōlō* is *nē* + *volō* ‘not want’; *mālō* is *magis* + *volō* ‘want more’, i.e. ‘prefer’, and is followed by *quam* ‘than’: *Mālō pācem quam bellum* ‘I prefer peace to war’.

blocks.h: fīō, fierī, factus sum ‘become, be made, happen’

blocks.p: *faciō* ‘make, do’ has no regular passive in the present system. Instead Latin uses a separate verb, *fīō*, which is active in form but means ‘be made’, ‘become’ or ‘happen’. In the perfect system it borrows the passive of *faciō*: *factus sum* ‘I became, was made’.

table.title: fīō ‘become, be made’
table.note: Infinitive fierī; present subjunctive fīam, fīās, fīat. The i is long except in fit and before er (fierī, fierem). Quid fit? ‘What is happening?’ Cōnsul factus est ‘He was made consul’.

blocks.p: *edō* is a regular 3rd-conjugation verb with a set of short alternative forms that look just like *sum* — except that their *e* is long.

table.title: edō ‘eat’ — present
table.note: Infinitive edere or ēsse; perfect ēdī; present subjunctive edam (older edim). Imperative ēs, ēste.

blocks.pitfall: Lookalikes: *ēst* ‘he eats’ vs. *est* ‘he is’; *ēsse* ‘to eat’ vs. *esse* ‘to be’; *vīs* ‘you want’ vs. *vīs* ‘force’ (acc. *vim*); *it* ‘he goes’ vs. English *it*. And *fit* is not ‘fit’ but ‘it becomes, it happens’.

items.en: Thus passes the glory of the world. (from the old papal coronation rite)

items.t: Ībant obscūrī sōlā sub nocte per umbram.
items.en: They went on, dim figures in the lonely night, through the shadows. (Virgil)
The Fates lead the willing and drag the unwilling. (Seneca)

items.t: Graecia capta ferum victōrem cēpit et artēs intulit agrestī Latiō.
items.en: Captive Greece took her savage conqueror captive and brought the arts into rustic Latium. (Horace)
Force makes a way. (Virgil)
items.lit: A way is made by force.

items.t: Ēsse oportet ut vīvās, nōn vīvere ut edās.
items.en: You should eat to live, not live to eat. (Rhetorica ad Herennium)
Death before dishonour. (motto)
items.lit: I prefer to die rather than to be disgraced.

afterlife.title: Go, want, eat — rebuilt from spare parts

blocks.p: Irregular verbs are the most used, and therefore the most worn. Latin *īre* was a particularly fragile verb: forms like *it* ‘he goes’ and *īs* ‘you go’ were a single vowel and a consonant. In every Romance language ‘to go’ is a **patchwork** of several Latin verbs. In Italian, Spanish, French and Portuguese most of the present comes from *vādere* ‘to stride, to go’; *īre* survives in the infinitive, future and imperfect of some languages; and Spanish and Portuguese took their past tense from *esse*.

compare.title: ‘to go’ — present
compare.note: Italian vado, vai, va, vanno, Spanish voy, vas, va, van, French vais, vas, va, vont and Portuguese vou, vais, vai, vão all go back to vādere. Portuguese ides (the old vós form) is Latin ītis.

compare.title: ‘to go’ — other tenses
gloss: I was going, used to go
compare.note: Spanish iba and Portuguese ia continue the imperfect ībam; the futures iré, irai, irei are īre + habeō (Chapter 9). Spanish and Portuguese fui means both ‘I went’ and ‘I was’: it is Latin fuī ‘I was’, which took over the past of ‘go’.

blocks.p: Where do Italian *andare*, French *aller* (with *allons, allez, allais*) and Spanish and Portuguese *andar* ‘to walk’ come from? Nobody knows for certain. The most popular candidate for *aller* is *ambulāre* ‘to walk’, but the sound changes are irregular; for *andare* / *andar*, proposals include *ambulāre*, *ambitāre* and several others. None is generally accepted. What is certain is that *ambulāre* survives regularly in Romanian *umbla* ‘to walk about’, and that Romanian ‘go’, *merge*, is Latin *mergere* ‘to dip, to plunge’ — a meaning that shifted to ‘to go’ only in the east.

*volō* became an ordinary 2nd-conjugation verb in spoken Latin (*volēre*), whence Italian *volere*, French *vouloir* and Romanian *vrea* (*vreau* ‘I want’). From *volō* also came Romanian’s future auxiliary: *voi cânta* ‘I will sing’ is literally ‘I want to sing’ (Chapter 9). Spanish and Portuguese replaced *velle* with *quaerere* ‘to seek, to ask for’, which gave *querer* ‘to want, to love’ — *te quiero* ‘I love you’ is literally ‘I seek you’.

*ferre* did not survive as a simple verb — Romance ‘carry’ is Italian *portare*, French *porter* (from *portāre*), Spanish *llevar*, Portuguese *levar* (from *levāre* ‘lift’), Romanian *purta* or *duce*. But two compounds came through by inheritance, rebuilt as regular verbs: *sufferre* ‘to bear up under’ → Italian *soffrire*, Spanish *sufrir*, French *souffrir*, Portuguese *sofrer*, Romanian *suferi*; and *offerre* → Italian *offrire*, French *offrir* (Spanish *ofrecer*, Portuguese *oferecer* add the suffix *-ecer*).

*fīō* left a surprising heir: Romanian ‘to be’ is *a fi*, from *fierī*, and its subjunctive *să fiu, să fie* comes from *fīam, fīat*. *edere* ‘to eat’ disappeared everywhere, replaced by more vivid verbs: *comedere* ‘to eat up’ and *mandūcāre* ‘to chew, to munch’.

compare.title: ‘to eat’
compare.note: Spanish and Portuguese comer continue comedere; French manger and Romanian mânca continue mandūcāre. Italian mangiare is most likely a borrowing from Old French (the native Tuscan form was manicare). The old verb lives on in English edible, from Late Latin edibilis.

parts.title: volō, nōlō, mālō ‘want, not want, prefer’
Go, want, eat — rebuilt from spare parts

title: Comparison of Adjectives and Adverbs
sub: -ior and -issimus, the irregulars, quam and the ablative of comparison

blocks.p: Adjectives have three degrees: **positive** *altus* ‘high’, **comparative** *altior* ‘higher’, **superlative** *altissimus* ‘highest, very high’. Latin builds both new degrees with endings, as English does with *-er* and *-est* — but Latin uses them for adjectives of any length: *prūdentior* is ‘more prudent’, *prūdentissimus* ‘most prudent’.

To form them, take the stem — the genitive singular minus its ending (*alt-ī*, *fort-is*, *fēlīc-is*) — and add **-ior** (neuter **-ius**) for the comparative, **-issimus, -a, -um** for the superlative.

table.title: Declension of the comparative: altior, altius
table.note: The comparative is a 3rd-declension adjective, but not an i-stem: ablative -e, genitive plural -um, neuter plural -a (altiōra, never altiōria). The superlative declines like bonus.

blocks.p: Two groups have special superlatives. Adjectives in **-er** add *-rimus* to the nominative: *līber* → *līberrimus*, *pulcher* → *pulcherrimus*, *ācer* → *ācerrimus*, *celer* → *celerrimus*. Six adjectives in **-ilis** take *-limus*: *facilis* → *facillimus*, *difficilis* → *difficillimus*, *similis* → *simillimus*, *dissimilis* → *dissimillimus*, *gracilis* → *gracillimus*, *humilis* → *humillimus*. Other *-ilis* adjectives are regular: *ūtilis* → *ūtilissimus*.

table.title: Irregular comparison
table.note: plūs is a neuter noun in the singular — plūs vīnī ‘more (of) wine’ — but an adjective in the plural: plūrēs, plūra ‘more, several’. The last five have no proper positive; they are built on prepositions and adverbs.

blocks.tip: Adjectives ending in a vowel + *-us* (*idōneus* ‘suitable’, *dubius* ‘doubtful’, *necessārius* ‘necessary’) do not add endings; they use the adverbs **magis** ‘more’ and **maximē** ‘most’: *magis idōneus*, *maximē idōneus*. Remember *magis* — it has a great future in Spanish, Portuguese and Romanian.

blocks.p: ‘Than’ is **quam**, with the same case on both sides: *Lūx clārior est quam nox* ‘Light is brighter than night’. When the first term is nominative or accusative, Latin can drop *quam* and put the second term in the **ablative of comparison**: *Lūx clārior est nocte*. The amount of difference is also in the ablative: *multō maior* ‘much bigger’ (‘bigger by much’), *paulō post* ‘a little later’, and *quō … eō* ‘the … the’.

The degrees have some idiomatic uses. A comparative alone can mean ‘rather’ or ‘too’: *senior* ‘rather old’, *audācior* ‘too bold’. A superlative alone often means ‘very’: *vir fortissimus* ‘a very brave man’. **quam** + superlative means ‘as … as possible’: *quam celerrimē* ‘as quickly as possible’, *quam plūrimī* ‘as many as possible’.

Adverbs are made from 1st/2nd-declension adjectives with **-ē** (*lātus* → *lātē* ‘widely’), and from 3rd-declension adjectives with **-iter** or, after *-nt-*, **-er** (*fortis* → *fortiter*, *prūdēns* → *prūdenter*). The comparative adverb is the neuter of the comparative adjective, *-ius*; the superlative ends in *-issimē*.

blocks.pitfall: *melius*, *fortius*, *altius* can be either the neuter comparative adjective (*bellum fortius*) or the comparative adverb (*fortius pugnant* ‘they fight more bravely’). And *minus* is not ‘minus’ but ‘less’; *magis* is ‘more’ (in degree), *plūs* ‘more’ (in quantity).

items.en: Faster, higher, stronger. (Olympic motto, 1894)

items.en: A living dog is better than a dead lion. (Ecclesiastes 9:4)
Of all these, the bravest are the Belgae. (Caesar)
Nothing is more lovable than virtue. (Cicero)

items.en: Rome is much bigger than Ostia.

Come as quickly as possible!

afterlife.title: plūs or magis? The Romance comparative

blocks.p: The comparative in *-ior* did not survive in spoken Latin. Romance languages instead put an adverb meaning ‘more’ before the ordinary adjective — the old Latin method of *magis idōneus*, extended to every adjective. But which adverb? Here Romance splits famously in two: Italian and French chose **plūs**, while Spanish, Portuguese and Romanian (and Catalan *més*) kept **magis**.

compare.title: ‘longer’, ‘clearer’, ‘more’
compare.note: Spanish largo means ‘long’ — a false friend for English large.

blocks.p: The split is usually explained geographically. *Magis* is the older word, and it survives at the **edges** of the Roman world — Iberia in the west, Dacia in the east — while the newer *plūs* spread through the **centre**, Gaul and Italy, too late to reach the periphery. Linguists use this pattern (an old form at both edges, a newer one in the middle) as a general rule of thumb for Romance.

*Magis* left other traces in the *plūs* languages, in disguise. Italian *ma* and French *mais* ‘but’ come from *magis* ‘rather’; so do Spanish *mas* and Portuguese *mas* ‘but’. Italian *mai* ‘ever’ is *magis* too, and French *jamais* and Spanish *jamás* ‘never’ are *iam magis* ‘already more’.

compare.title: magis in disguise
compare.note: Spanish mas ‘but’ is literary; everyday Spanish says pero. Italian non … mai ‘never’ uses magis alone. Romanian dar and niciodată have other origins.

blocks.p: A few old comparatives were too common to die: those of ‘good’, ‘bad’, ‘big’ and ‘small’, and the adverbs ‘better’ and ‘worse’. They survive everywhere except Romanian, which says simply *mai bun* ‘more good’.

compare.title: The surviving comparatives
compare.note: French pire and moindre continue the Latin nominatives peior and minor, meilleur the accusative meliōrem. French majeur is a learned word; the inherited form of maior is maire ‘mayor’ — the source of English mayor.

blocks.p: The superlative *-issimus* lives on as an intensifier meaning ‘very’: Italian *bellissimo*, Spanish *buenísimo*, Portuguese *lindíssimo*. Italian has used it without a break; Spanish and Portuguese *-ísimo / -íssimo* became common only in the Renaissance, under the influence of Latin and Italian. French keeps it in a few words (*rarissime*, *richissime*), and Romanian not at all. The ‘most’ superlative is simply the comparative with the definite article: *il più lungo*, *el más largo*, *le plus long*, *o mais longo*, *cel mai lung*.

compare.title: ‘very long’, ‘the longest’
compare.note: French très comes from trāns ‘across, beyond’; Romanian foarte ‘very’ from forte ‘strongly’; Romanian cel is ecce ille, the demonstrative of Chapter 12.

blocks.p: The learned superlatives returned as ordinary words: Italian *ottimo, pessimo, massimo, minimo*, Spanish *óptimo, pésimo, máximo, mínimo*, Portuguese *ótimo* (in Brazil, simply ‘great!’). English borrowed *superior, inferior, major, minor, prior, senior, junior* and *ulterior*, and from Italian music *fortissimo*, *pianissimo* — and *generalissimo*.

parts.title: plūs or magis? The Romance comparative

title: Commands and Address
sub: The imperative, prohibitions with nōlī, and the vocative

blocks.p: The **present imperative** gives a direct command. The singular is simply the **present stem** — the infinitive without *-re*; the plural adds **-te** (3rd conjugation *-ite*).

table.title: Present imperative active
table.note: love! warn! rule! hear! take!

table.title: Short and irregular imperatives
table.note: be! go! carry! say! lead! do!  Four verbs drop the -e of the singular: dīc, dūc, fac, fer. Compounds of faciō with a weakened vowel keep it: perfice ‘complete!’.

blocks.p: Deponent verbs, having no active forms, use the **passive** imperative: singular in **-re**, plural in **-minī**. The singular looks exactly like an active infinitive, which is a classic trap.

table.title: Imperative of deponents
table.note: Sequere mē! ‘Follow me!’

blocks.p: Latin also has a **future imperative** in *-tō* (plural *-tōte*), used for general rules, laws and instructions that apply from now on: *Salūs populī suprēma lēx estō* ‘The safety of the people shall be the highest law’ (Cicero). A few verbs use it as their only imperative: *mementō* ‘remember!’ (from *meminī*), *scītō* ‘know!’.

blocks.tip: Roman greetings are imperatives: *Salvē!* / *Salvēte!* ‘Be well!’ = ‘Hello!’; *Valē!* / *Valēte!* ‘Be strong!’ = ‘Goodbye!’; *Avē!* ‘Hail!’

blocks.p: Classical prose does not normally negate an imperative with *nē* (that is poetic or colloquial). The usual prohibition is **nōlī** (plural **nōlīte**) — the imperative of *nōlō* ‘be unwilling’ — + the **infinitive**: *Nōlī timēre* ‘Don’t be afraid’, literally ‘be unwilling to fear’. A second, more abrupt way is **nē** + the **perfect subjunctive** (Chapter 24): *Nē timueris* ‘Don’t be afraid’.

table.title: Prohibitions
table.note: Both mean ‘Don’t be afraid’.

blocks.p: The **vocative** is the case for calling or addressing someone. In almost every noun it is the same as the nominative. The one distinctive form is in the 2nd declension: nouns in **-us** have a vocative in **-e**, and nouns in **-ius** contract to **-ī**. *meus* has the vocative *mī*. The interjection *ō* often comes before it: *ō fortūna!*

table.title: Vocatives
table.note: Deus ‘God’ has the vocative Deus. In the plural, the vocative always equals the nominative.

items.en: Seize the day. (Horace)
items.lit: Pluck the day.

items.en: Dare to be wise. (Horace)
Make haste slowly. (a favourite saying of Augustus)
Do not touch me. (John 20:17)

items.t: Audī, fīlī mī, disciplīnam patris tuī.
items.en: Hear, my son, your father’s instruction. (Proverbs 1:8)
You too, Brutus? (Shakespeare’s Latin; Suetonius reports Caesar’s last words in Greek)
Remember that you must die.
items.lit: Remember to die.

blocks.pitfall: Three traps: (1) *sequere*, *hortāre* are imperatives (‘follow!’, ‘encourage!’), not infinitives; (2) *dīc, dūc, fac, fer* have no *-e*; (3) the vocative of *-ius* nouns is *-ī*, so *Vergilī!*, not *Vergilie!*

blocks.p: The imperative singular survived remarkably well: *venī* ‘come!’ and *cantā* ‘sing!’ are still recognisable everywhere. Even the short Latin imperatives *dīc* and *fac* left heirs in Italian *di’, fa’* and Spanish *di, haz*. In the plural, Spanish *-d* (*venid, cantad*) and Portuguese *vinde, cantai* continue Latin *-te*; French, Italian and Romanian plurals coincide with the present indicative.

compare.title: Imperatives
compare.note: Portuguese vinde and cantai are the old vós forms, now used mainly in prayers and literature; ordinary plural commands use the subjunctive (venham, cantem). Spanish venid, cantad are used in Spain; Latin America says vengan, canten.

blocks.p: Latin *nōlī* + infinitive did not survive. But Romance prohibitions still divide into two Latin-like types. **Italian** and **Romanian** use the plain **infinitive** for the negative singular: *Non parlare!*, *Nu vorbi!* ‘Don’t speak!’. **Spanish** and **Portuguese** use the **subjunctive**, just as Latin did with *nē* + subjunctive: *¡No hables!*, *Não fales!*. **French** simply negates the imperative.

compare.title: Prohibitions
compare.note: Italian and Romanian use the infinitive only in the singular; their plural prohibitions use the ordinary plural form. Romanian se teme ‘to be afraid’ is reflexive, hence nu te teme.

blocks.p: The **vocative** case died out in the west, but **Romanian** kept it — a striking survival. Masculine nouns take **-e**, exactly as in Latin, or **-ule** (with the article); feminines take **-o**, an ending borrowed from Slavic. *Doamne!* ‘O Lord!’ is Latin *domine* (Chapter 2).

compare.title: Calling someone
compare.note: Only Romanian still marks the vocative with an ending. Italian Signore, Spanish Señor and French Seigneur come from senior ‘elder’ (Chapter 20).

title: Infinitives and Indirect Statement
sub: Six infinitives and the accusative-and-infinitive

blocks.p: So far you have met the present infinitive, active (*amāre*) and passive (*amārī*). A full Latin verb has **six** infinitives: present, perfect and future, each active and passive. Their ‘tense’ is relative: the present means ‘at the same time’, the perfect ‘earlier’, the future ‘later’.

table.title: The infinitives of amāre and regere
table.note: to love, to have loved, to be going to love / to be loved, to have been loved, to be going to be loved. The perfect active is the perfect stem + -isse; the perfect passive and future active are participle + esse, and the participle agrees with its subject. The future passive (supine + īrī) is rare. esse has fuisse ‘to have been’ and futūrus esse or fore ‘to be going to be’.

blocks.p: An infinitive can act as a neuter noun, the subject of *est*: *Errāre hūmānum est* ‘To err is human’. It also completes verbs like *possum, volō, dēbeō, cupiō, audeō*: *Venīre nōn possum* ‘I cannot come’.

blocks.h: Indirect statement: the accusative and infinitive

blocks.p: After verbs of **saying, thinking, knowing and perceiving** — *dīcō, nūntiō, negō, putō, crēdō, sciō, spērō, audiō, videō, sentiō* — Latin has no word for ‘that’. Instead, the subject of the reported statement goes into the **accusative** and its verb into the **infinitive**. This is the **accusative and infinitive** (AcI): *Dīcit puerum venīre* ‘He says (that) the boy is coming’, literally ‘He says the boy to be coming’.

table.title: The tense of the infinitive is relative
table.note: He says that he is coming / that he came / that he will come. — He said that he was coming / that he had come / that he would come. The Latin infinitive stays the same; only the English changes.

blocks.p: Two details matter. First, the reflexive: if the reported subject is the same person as the speaker, Latin uses **sē**; if it is someone else, *eum, eam, eōs*: *Dīcit sē venīre* ‘He says that he (himself) is coming’, *Dīcit eum venīre* ‘He says that he (another man) is coming’. Second, participles in the infinitive agree with the accusative subject: *Dīxit urbem captam esse* ‘He said the city had been captured’; *esse* is often left out: *Spērō tē ventūrum* ‘I hope you will come’.

With passive verbs of saying and seeming the construction becomes **nominative and infinitive**: *Homērus caecus fuisse dīcitur* ‘Homer is said to have been blind’; *Vidētur esse fēlīx* ‘He seems to be happy’. English does the same: ‘is said to have been’.

items.en: He says that he is going to Rome.
I believe that the gods exist.
I know that I know nothing. (after Socrates)

items.t: Thalēs aquam dīxit esse initium rērum.
items.en: Thales said that water was the origin of all things. (Cicero)
The messenger said that the enemy had come.
I hope that you will come soon.
Homer is said to have been blind.

blocks.tip: To spot an AcI, look for a verb of saying or thinking, then an **accusative** and an **infinitive** that belong together. Insert ‘that’, make the accusative the subject, and give the infinitive a tense relative to the main verb.

blocks.pitfall: English ‘I hope to come’ has no subject; Latin needs one, and needs the future: *Spērō mē ventūrum esse*. And do not translate ‘that’ with *quod* or *ut*: classical Latin says *Dīcō eum venīre*, never *Dīcō quod venit* — although, as the Afterlife shows, that is exactly what later Latin did say.

blocks.p: In Late Latin, especially in Christian texts and the Bible translation of Jerome (the Vulgate), indirect statements were increasingly expressed with a conjunction — *quod*, *quia* or *quoniam* — and an ordinary finite verb, as in Greek. *Ūnum sciō, quia caecus cum essem, modo videō* ‘One thing I know: that whereas I was blind, now I see’ (John 9:25). The AcI survived in writing, but in speech it gave way to a ‘that’ clause.

Every Romance language now uses such a clause. The conjunction — Italian *che*, Spanish, French and Portuguese *que*, Romanian *că* — descends from one or more of the Latin relatives and conjunctions *quid, quod, quia*; exactly which is still debated.

compare.title: Indirect statements
rows: Je crois que les dieux existent.
gloss: I say that he is coming.
I believe that the gods exist.
He said that he would come.
compare.note: Italian credere che takes the subjunctive (esistano). For ‘would come’ Italian uses the perfect conditional (sarebbe venuto), Spanish, French and Portuguese the conditional; Romanian simply keeps the future of the original words, va veni ‘he will come’.

blocks.p: The AcI did not vanish completely. After verbs of **perception** — ‘see, hear’ — and in French and Italian after ‘make, let’, Romance still uses an object + infinitive, the direct heir of the Latin pattern: Latin *Eum videō venīre*.

compare.title: Accusative + infinitive after ‘see’
compare.note: Romanian prefers a gerund (venind) here. English has its own version in I believe him to be honest, they consider her to be the best — very close to Crēdō eum honestum esse.

blocks.p: **Portuguese** has an infinitive found almost nowhere else: the **personal** or **inflected infinitive**, which takes person endings. It lets Portuguese keep an infinitive where other languages need a full clause: *É melhor sairmos agora* ‘It’s better for us to leave now’; *para fazermos* ‘so that we do / for us to do’. Galician shares it. Its origin is disputed: some derive it from the Latin imperfect subjunctive (*facerem, facerēs…*), others see it as a Portuguese innovation.

table.title: Portuguese personal infinitive: fazer ‘to do’
table.note: Trouxe o livro para lermos juntos ‘I brought the book for us to read together’. Antes de saíres, fecha a janela ‘Before you leave, close the window’.

blocks.p: **Romanian** went the opposite way. Like its Balkan neighbours (compare Modern Greek *θέλω να τραγουδήσω*), it replaced most infinitives with *să* + subjunctive: *Vreau să cânt* ‘I want to sing’, literally ‘I want that I sing’. Its old long infinitive survives only as a noun: *cântare* ‘song, singing’.

parts.title: Indirect statement: the accusative and infinitive

title: Participles and the Ablative Absolute
sub: Present, perfect and future participles; the most Roman construction of all

blocks.p: A participle is a verbal adjective: it has tense and voice like a verb, but agrees with a noun like an adjective. Ordinary Latin verbs have three. You know the **perfect passive** (*amātus*, Chapter 17). The **present active** ends in *-ns, -ntis* (*amāns* ‘loving’); the **future active** in *-ūrus, -a, -um*, built on the supine stem (*amātūrus* ‘about to love, going to love’).

table.title: The participles
table.note: loving, ruling, hearing, taking / (having been) loved, ruled, heard, taken / about to love, rule, hear, take. Vowels before -ns are long; before -nt- they are short: amāns, amantis. Irregular: iēns, euntis ‘going’; sum has no present participle in classical Latin, and its future participle is futūrus.

blocks.p: The present participle declines like a 3rd-declension adjective of one ending (*fēlīx*, Chapter 8). Its ablative singular is **-e** when it is used as a verb (*puerō cantante* ‘while the boy sings’) and **-ī** when it is used as a plain adjective (*ā puerō sapientī*).

The participle’s tense is **relative to the main verb**: present = at the same time, perfect = before, future = after (or intended). Latin uses participles far more than English, and they often have to be translated with a clause — ‘while’, ‘when’, ‘after’, ‘because’, ‘although’, ‘who’: *Puerōs rīdentēs audīvī* ‘I heard the boys laughing’; *Hostēs victī fūgērunt* ‘After they were defeated, the enemy fled’; *Moritūrī tē salūtant* ‘Those who are about to die salute you’.
The future participle with *sum* forms the **active periphrastic**, ‘be about to, intend to’: *Bellum gestūrus sum* ‘I am about to wage war’; *Rōmam itūrus erat* ‘He was going to go to Rome’.

blocks.pitfall: Latin has **no present passive participle** (‘being loved’) and **no perfect active participle** (‘having loved’) — except for deponents, whose perfect participle is active (*secūtus* ‘having followed’, Chapter 18). ‘Having seen the city, he left’ must be turned round: ‘with the city seen, he left’ — which brings us to the ablative absolute.

blocks.p: A noun (or pronoun) and a participle in the **ablative**, standing apart from the rest of the sentence, form an **ablative absolute** (*absolūtus* ‘loosened, free’). It sets the scene — time, cause, condition or circumstance — for the main clause: *Urbe captā, hostēs discessērunt* ‘The city having been captured, the enemy left’, i.e. ‘After the city was captured…’ or simply ‘With the city taken…’.

Because *esse* has no present participle, two nouns, or a noun and an adjective, can form an ablative absolute on their own: *Cicerōne cōnsule* ‘Cicero being consul’ = ‘in Cicero’s consulship’ (63 BC); *mē puerō* ‘when I was a boy’; *Caesare vīvō* ‘while Caesar was alive’.

blocks.tip: To spot an ablative absolute: a noun + participle in the ablative, usually at the start and set off by commas, whose noun is **not** the subject or object of the main verb. Translate it first as ‘with X …-ed / …-ing’, then choose the best conjunction: when, after, since, although, if.

items.en: Hail, emperor, those who are about to die salute you. (Suetonius)
I fear the Greeks even when they bring gifts. (Virgil)
items.lit: I fear the Greeks even bearing gifts.

items.t: Hīs rēbus cognitīs, Caesar ad castra rediit.
items.en: When he learned this, Caesar returned to the camp.
items.lit: These things having been learned…

items.en: In Cicero’s consulship the conspiracy was exposed.
We set out at sunrise.
items.lit: With the sun rising…

items.en: The boys ran home laughing.
God willing.

blocks.p: English has borrowed several ablative absolutes ready-made: *mūtātīs mūtandīs* ‘with the things that need changing changed’ (the second word is a gerundive, Chapter 28), *Deō volente*, *mē iūdice* ‘in my judgement’, literally ‘with me as judge’.

The present participle lost most of its verbal power in Romance, but it lived on as an **adjective** and, above all, as a **noun** for a person or thing that does something. Many are learned words taken from written Latin, but the pattern is the same everywhere.

compare.title: Present participles that became nouns
compare.note: Italian also calls the east levante ‘rising’ and the west ponente ‘setting’ — two more participles (Spanish levante, poniente). Romanian amant, student and orient are modern loans.

blocks.p: The **ablative of the gerund** (*cantandō* ‘by singing’, Chapter 28) became the Romance **gerund**: Italian, Spanish and Portuguese *cantando*, Romanian *cântând*. In French, *-andō* and the participle *-antem* fell together as *-ant*, so *chantant* is both. This gerund now does much of the work of the Latin present participle.

compare.title: ‘He came in singing’
compare.note: In European Portuguese, a + infinitive often replaces the gerund in everyday speech (estou a cantar ‘I am singing’), while Brazil keeps the gerund (estou cantando).

blocks.p: The **absolute construction** survives too — no longer in the ablative, since the cases had gone, but with the same shape: a participle + a noun, set before the main clause. It is especially common with past participles in Italian, Spanish and Portuguese, and is felt as rather formal in French.

compare.title: ‘When the war was over, he went home’
rows: Finita la guerra, tornò a casa.
Terminada la guerra, volvió a casa.
La guerre finie, il rentra chez lui.
Terminada a guerra, voltou para casa.
După terminarea războiului, s-a întors acasă.
gloss: The war (being) over, he went home.
compare.note: Romanian rarely uses a participle this way and prefers a noun phrase: după terminarea războiului ‘after the end of the war’.

blocks.p: Some absolutes froze into prepositions. Late and Medieval Latin *dūrante bellō* ‘with the war lasting’ gave Italian, Spanish and Portuguese *durante* ‘during’ — and, through French *durant*, English *during*. *Nōn obstante* ‘(this) not standing in the way’ became *nonostante*, *no obstante*, *nonobstant*, *não obstante* and English *notwithstanding*, which is a word-for-word translation.

compare.title: Participles frozen into prepositions
gloss: ‘not standing in the way’ → despite, nevertheless
compare.note: The usual French word for ‘during’, pendant, is another participle: ‘hanging, pending’.

title: The Subjunctive: Forms
sub: Present, imperfect, perfect and pluperfect subjunctive

blocks.p: Every verb form so far has been **indicative** — the mood of facts and questions about facts. Latin has a second mood, the **subjunctive**, for what is willed, wished, possible, imagined, or simply dependent on another verb: ‘Long live the king!’, ‘if I were rich’, ‘so that he may come’. English has only scraps of it (*God save the Queen*, *if I were you*); Latin uses it constantly.
The subjunctive has **four tenses**: present, imperfect, perfect and pluperfect — there is no future. This chapter gives the forms; the next three show what they are used for.

The present subjunctive changes the characteristic vowel. The 1st conjugation swaps its *ā* for **e**; all the others add **a** to the present stem. The endings are the usual ones, with *-m* in the 1st singular.

table.title: Present subjunctive active
table.note: capere: capiam, capiās … possum: possim, possīs … The passive simply uses passive endings: amer, amēris, amētur, amēmur, amēminī, amentur; regar, regāris, regātur …

blocks.tip: The vowels of the present subjunctive in conjugation order — *e, ea, a, ia* — are captured by the English mnemonic ‘w**e** f**ea**r **a** l**ia**r’ (or ‘l**e**t’s b**ea**t **a** l**ia**r’).

blocks.pitfall: Do not take every *e* for a subjunctive or every *a* for an indicative: *monet* is indicative, *amet* subjunctive. And in the 3rd and 4th conjugations the 1st singular *regam*, *audiam* is both future indicative and present subjunctive; the other persons differ (*regēs* future, *regās* subjunctive).

blocks.p: The imperfect subjunctive is the easiest form in Latin: take the **present active infinitive** and add the endings *-m, -s, -t, -mus, -tis, -nt* (with long *ē* in most persons). It works even for the irregular verbs: *esse* → *essem*, *posse* → *possem*, *velle* → *vellem*, *īre* → *īrem*, *ferre* → *ferrem*.

table.title: Imperfect subjunctive active
table.note: Passive: amārer, amārēris, amārētur, amārēmur, amārēminī, amārentur. esse also has an alternative imperfect subjunctive forem, forēs, foret …

blocks.p: The **perfect** subjunctive adds *-erim, -erīs, -erit…* to the perfect stem; it looks like the future perfect except in the 1st singular (*amāverim* vs. *amāverō*). The **pluperfect** subjunctive is the second easy one: the **perfect active infinitive** + endings, *amāvisse* → *amāvissem*. The passives use the participle with the subjunctive of *sum*: *amātus sim*, *amātus essem*.

table.title: Perfect and pluperfect subjunctive of amāre
table.note: Every verb works the same way: rēxerim, rēxissem; fuerim, fuissem; vēnerim, vēnissem. Contracted pluperfects are common: amāssem for amāvissem, audīssem for audīvissem.

table.title: Irregular verbs in the subjunctive (1st singular)
table.note: sim, velim, nōlim, mālim keep an old subjunctive in -i-; all the imperfects are infinitive + -m.

items.en: Long live the king!
items.lit: May the king live!

items.en: So let us rejoice while we are young. (medieval student song)
May he (or she) rest in peace.
Let justice be done, though the heavens fall. (legal maxim)
May the earth lie light on you. (Roman epitaph formula)
If only I had not done it!
What am I to do?

blocks.p: The Romance languages still have a subjunctive — and a lively one, especially in Italian, Spanish and Portuguese. But only one Latin tense came through with its meaning unchanged: the **present subjunctive**. Its 1st-conjugation vowel *e* is still clearly visible.

compare.title: The present subjunctive
compare.note: Romanian -e in să cânte, against indicative cântă, is the Latin -et of cantet. Spanish sea and Portuguese seja come from the subjunctive of sedēre ‘to sit’ (sedeat), which merged with esse; Romanian să fie is fīat (Chapter 19).

blocks.p: The Latin **imperfect** subjunctive (*cantārem*) vanished from all five languages. Its place was taken — already in spoken Latin — by the **pluperfect** subjunctive, which had come to be used in unreal conditions where Classical Latin had the imperfect (Chapter 27). In its contracted form *cantāssem* it became the ordinary **imperfect subjunctive** of Italian, Spanish, French and Portuguese. Romanian kept the same forms with their old pluperfect meaning, but moved them into the indicative: *cântasem* ‘I had sung’ (Chapter 10).

compare.title: The Latin pluperfect subjunctive in Romance
compare.note: Spanish has a second imperfect subjunctive in -ra (cantara, fuera, hiciera), from the Latin pluperfect indicative (Chapter 10). The French imperfect subjunctive is now purely literary; in speech, que je chante serves for both.

blocks.p: **Portuguese** preserves something no other major Romance language has kept: a **future subjunctive**, used after *se* ‘if’, *quando* ‘when’ and in relative clauses about the future: *se eu cantar* ‘if I sing’, *quando eu fizer* ‘when I do’. It continues the Latin **future perfect** (*cantāverō*), which had largely merged with the perfect subjunctive (*cantāverim*). Old Spanish had it too, and it survives in legal language and proverbs.

compare.title: The Portuguese future subjunctive
gloss: if I am / if I go
compare.note: Spanish hiciere, fuere, viere are now archaic or legal. A proverb keeps them alive: Adonde fueres, haz lo que vieres ‘Wherever you go, do as you see done’ — the Spanish ‘When in Rome’.

blocks.p: **Romanian** reduced the subjunctive to a single tense, the present, always introduced by **să** — itself Latin *sī* ‘if’. Only the 3rd person has a distinct form (*să cânte*, *să fie*); the other persons are identical to the indicative. A perfect subjunctive *să fi cântat* ‘that I (may) have sung’ is formed with the invariable *fi*.

title: Subjunctive Uses: Wishes, Purpose, Result
sub: Independent subjunctives; ut and nē clauses

blocks.p: In a main clause the subjunctive expresses an attitude to the action rather than a fact. Four uses are common; the negative is **nē** for wishes and commands, **nōn** for the others.

**1. Exhortation and command (jussive).** The 1st plural means ‘let us’, the 3rd person ‘let him, let them’: *Gaudeāmus!* ‘Let us rejoice!’; *Eāmus!* ‘Let’s go!’; *Vīvat rēx!* ‘Long live the king!’; *Fīat lūx* ‘Let there be light’. With *nē*: *Nē nōs indūcās in tentātiōnem* ‘Lead us not into temptation’ (the Lord’s Prayer).

**2. Wishes (optative)**, often with *utinam* ‘if only’. The tense shows whether the wish can still come true: present for a possible wish (*Utinam veniat!* ‘I do hope he comes!’), imperfect for an unreal wish about the present (*Utinam adesset!* ‘If only he were here!’), pluperfect for an unreal wish about the past (*Utinam nē vēnissem!* ‘If only I had not come!’).
**3. Deliberation**, in questions about what to do: *Quid faciam?* ‘What am I to do?’; *Quō eam?* ‘Where should I go?’
**4. Possibility (potential)**, ‘would, could, might’: *Aliquis dīcat* ‘Someone might say’; *Velim* ‘I should like’; *Crēderēs* ‘You would have thought’.

items.en: So let us rejoice!
May they rest in peace.
Let them hate, as long as they fear. (Accius; Caligula’s favourite line, says Suetonius)

items.t: Utinam populus Rōmānus ūnam cervīcem habēret!
items.en: If only the Roman people had a single neck! (Caligula, in Suetonius)
What am I to do?

blocks.p: A **purpose** (final) clause says why something is done. It is introduced by **ut** ‘so that, in order that’ or, if negative, **nē** ‘so that … not, lest’, and its verb is in the subjunctive: **present** after a main verb in a present or future tense, **imperfect** after a past tense (the sequence of tenses, Chapter 26). English usually translates with a simple ‘to’: *Venit ut mē videat* ‘He comes to see me’; *Vēnit ut mē vidēret* ‘He came to see me’.

Two variants are worth knowing. A **relative** pronoun with the subjunctive can express purpose: *Lēgātōs mīsit quī pācem peterent* ‘He sent envoys to ask for peace’ (‘who were to ask’). And **quō** replaces *ut* before a comparative: *quō facilius* ‘so that … more easily’.

items.t: Rōmānī lēgātōs mīsērunt ut pācem peterent.
items.en: The Romans sent envoys to ask for peace.

items.t: Portās claudunt nē hostēs urbem intrent.
items.en: They are closing the gates so that the enemy cannot enter the city.

items.t: Spectātum veniunt, veniunt spectentur ut ipsae.
items.en: They come to watch — and they come to be watched themselves. (Ovid, on Roman women at the theatre)
You should eat in order to live.

blocks.pitfall: In prose, an English infinitive of purpose (‘he came **to see**’) is **never** a Latin infinitive: it is *ut* + subjunctive, a relative clause, or a gerund construction (Chapter 28). And *ut* has other meanings: with the **indicative** it means ‘as’ or ‘when’ (*ut dīxī* ‘as I said’, *ut vīdit* ‘when he saw’).

blocks.h: Result clauses: ut and ut nōn

blocks.p: A **result** (consecutive) clause says what happened as a consequence. It too uses **ut** + subjunctive, but it is usually announced by a signal word in the main clause — *tam* ‘so’ (with adjectives and adverbs), *ita* or *sīc* ‘so, in such a way’, *tantus* ‘so great’, *tālis* ‘such’, *tot* ‘so many’, *adeō* ‘to such a degree’ — and its negative is **ut nōn**, never *nē*.

table.title: Purpose or result?
rows: Signal word in the main clause
tam, ita, sīc, tantus, tālis, tot, adeō
table.note: After nē (and sī, nisi, num), aliquis ‘someone’ loses its ali-: nē quis ‘so that no one’.

items.t: Tam fortis erat ut nēmō eum vincere posset.
items.en: He was so strong that no one could beat him.

items.t: Ita vīxit ut omnēs eum amārent.
items.en: He lived in such a way that everyone loved him.

items.t: Tantus erat timor ut nēmō dormīret.
items.en: The fear was so great that nobody slept.

items.t: Eādem nocte accidit ut esset lūna plēna.
items.en: That same night it happened that there was a full moon. (Caesar)

blocks.tip: To tell purpose from result, look **back** from the *ut*: a signal word (*tam, ita, tantus…*) means result. Then look at the negative: *nē* is purpose, *ut nōn* is result. Verbs like *accidit ut* ‘it happens that’ and *efficiō ut* ‘I bring it about that’ also take result clauses.

blocks.p: The same *ut / nē* clause reports **commands and requests** after verbs such as *imperō* ‘order’, *rogō* ‘ask’, *hortor* ‘urge’, *persuādeō* ‘persuade’, *moneō* ‘warn’: *Hortātur mīlitēs ut fortiter pugnent* ‘He urges the soldiers to fight bravely’; *Tē rogō nē abeās* ‘I ask you not to go away’. (But *iubeō* ‘order’ takes the accusative and infinitive.) After verbs of **fearing** the logic is reversed: *Timeō nē veniat* ‘I am afraid he will come’, *Timeō ut veniat* ‘I am afraid he will not come’ — the clause is the wish turned inside out.

afterlife.title: che, que, ca să: subjunctive clauses in Romance

blocks.p: Romance languages kept the principle: a clause of purpose takes the **subjunctive**. Only the conjunction changed — *ut* died out, and new compound conjunctions were built around the general-purpose *che / que*: Italian *perché*, *affinché*; Spanish and Portuguese *para que*; French *pour que*, *afin que*; Romanian *ca să*.

compare.title: Purpose clauses
rows: Te lo dico perché tu lo sappia.
Te lo digo para que lo sepas.
Je te le dis pour que tu le saches.
gloss: I’m telling you so that you know.
So that he does not fall.

blocks.p: When the subject of the purpose clause is the same as that of the main clause, the western languages prefer a preposition + **infinitive** — something classical prose avoided: Italian *per*, Spanish and Portuguese *para*, French *pour*. Romanian, which has largely given up the infinitive (Chapter 22), keeps the subjunctive clause.

**Result** clauses went the other way. Latin put them in the subjunctive even when the result was a plain fact; the Romance languages use the **indicative**, because the result really happened. Latin *tam* survives in Spanish *tan* and Portuguese *tão*.

compare.title: ‘He was so strong that no one could beat him’
rows: Tam fortis erat ut nēmō eum vincere posset.
Era così forte che nessuno poteva batterlo.
Era tan fuerte que nadie podía vencerlo.
Il était si fort que personne ne pouvait le battre.
Era tão forte que ninguém o podia vencer.
Era atât de puternic încât nimeni nu-l putea învinge.
gloss: He was so strong that no one could beat him.

blocks.p: The independent subjunctive of wishes and commands survives in two forms. The ordinary one is **que / che / să + subjunctive**: Spanish *¡Que entre!*, French *Qu’il entre !*, Italian *Che entri!*, Romanian *Să intre!* ‘Let him come in!’. And a few fixed formulas keep the bare Latin subjunctive, without any conjunction: *Vīvat rēx!* is still Italian *Viva il re!*, Spanish *¡Viva el rey!*, French *Vive le roi !*, Portuguese *Viva o rei!*, Romanian *Trăiască regele!*

compare.title: Wishes and exhortations
compare.note: The Italian 1st plural ending -iamo (andiamo, cantiamo) originally belonged to the subjunctive (Latin -eāmus, -iāmus) and spread to the indicative; Italian ‘let’s go!’ and ‘we go’ are therefore the same word. French Ainsi soit-il ‘so be it’ and Spanish Así sea are further bare subjunctives.

parts.title: Result clauses: ut and ut nōn
che, que, ca să: subjunctive clauses in Romance

title: cum-Clauses, Indirect Questions and the Sequence of Tenses
sub: When, since, although; asking indirectly; keeping tenses in step

blocks.p: As a preposition, *cum* means ‘with’ and takes the ablative. As a **conjunction** it introduces a clause, and its meaning depends partly on the mood of its verb.
With the **indicative**, *cum* simply fixes a time: ‘when, at the time when, whenever’. *Cum Rōmam vēnerō, tē vīsam* ‘When I come to Rome, I shall visit you’.

With the **subjunctive**, *cum* has three meanings. **Circumstantial** ‘when, as’ — the standard way of setting the scene in narrative, with the imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive: *Cum Caesar in Galliā esset…* ‘When Caesar was in Gaul…’. **Causal** ‘since’: *Cum sīs fessus, dormī* ‘Since you are tired, sleep’. **Concessive** ‘although’, often with *tamen* ‘nevertheless’ in the main clause: *Cum dīves sit, tamen nōn est beātus* ‘Although he is rich, he is not happy’.

items.t: Cum esset Caesar in citeriōre Galliā, crēbrī ad eum rūmōrēs afferēbantur.
items.en: While Caesar was in Nearer Gaul, frequent rumours were brought to him. (Caesar, adapted)
When he had seen the enemy, he gave the signal.
Since you are tired, go to sleep.

items.t: Cum dīves sit, tamen nōn est beātus.
items.en: Although he is rich, he is not happy.
Their silence is a shout. (Cicero)
items.lit: When they are silent, they shout.

blocks.pitfall: Do not translate every *cum* + subjunctive as ‘when’. Ask which makes sense: ‘when’, ‘since’ or ‘although’ — a *tamen* in the main clause settles it for ‘although’. And check whether *cum* is not simply the preposition: *cum amīcīs* ‘with friends’.

blocks.p: A question reported after a verb of asking, knowing, telling, wondering or doubting is an **indirect question**. It keeps its question word — *quis, quid, cūr, ubi, unde, quō, quandō, quōmodo, quam* — but its verb goes into the **subjunctive**: direct *Quid facis?* ‘What are you doing?’ → *Rogō quid faciās* ‘I ask what you are doing’. ‘Whether’ is *-ne* or *num*; ‘whether … or’ is *utrum … an*.

Since the subjunctive has no future, a future in an indirect question uses the **future participle + sim / essem** (the active periphrastic, Chapter 23): *Nesciō quid factūrus sit* ‘I don’t know what he will do’.

items.en: I don’t know what to do.
items.lit: I don’t know what I should do.

items.en: He asked why I was coming.
Tell me where you have been.

items.t: Ōdī et amō. Quārē id faciam, fortasse requīris. Nesciō, sed fierī sentiō et excrucior.
items.en: I hate and I love. Why do I do that, perhaps you ask. I don’t know, but I feel it happening, and I am in torment. (Catullus 85)

blocks.p: In subordinate clauses with the subjunctive — purpose, result, indirect questions, *cum*-clauses — the tense of the subjunctive is chosen by the **main verb**. If the main verb is **primary** (present, future, future perfect, or a perfect meaning ‘have done’), the subjunctive is **present** for the same time or later, **perfect** for earlier time. If the main verb is **historic** (imperfect, perfect meaning ‘did’, pluperfect), the subjunctive is **imperfect** or **pluperfect**.

table.title: Sequence of tenses in indirect questions
table.note: I ask what you are doing / what you did / what you will do. — I asked what you were doing / what you had done / what you would do.

blocks.tip: English does much the same without noticing: ‘I ask what you **are** doing’ but ‘I asked what you **were** doing’. Latin is simply more systematic: present ↔ imperfect, perfect ↔ pluperfect.

blocks.p: Italian, Spanish and Portuguese kept a living **sequence of tenses** — Italian schools still call it by its Latin name, *consecutio temporum*, or *concordanza dei tempi*; Spanish grammars speak of *concordancia de tiempos*. After a past main verb, a present subjunctive shifts to the imperfect subjunctive — the Romance imperfect subjunctive that comes from the Latin pluperfect (Chapter 24). French has almost lost the rule in speech, because its imperfect subjunctive is now literary; Romanian never had it, because it has only one subjunctive tense.

compare.title: ‘I want you to come’ — ‘I wanted you to come’
compare.note: Spanish also says viniese, the form in -se. Literary French would write que tu vinsses, which today sounds pompous or comic. In Romanian, să vii stays the same whatever the main verb.

blocks.p: **Indirect questions** went over to the indicative almost everywhere. Only Italian still allows the subjunctive in a careful style — a direct descendant of the Latin rule.

compare.title: ‘I don’t know where he is’
rows: Je ne sais pas où il est.
gloss: I don’t know where he is.
compare.note: Everyday Italian also says Non so dov’è, with the indicative.

blocks.p: The conjunction *cum* itself did not survive; ‘when’ in every Romance language comes from *quandō*. The preposition *cum* ‘with’ did survive — except in French, which replaced it with *avec*, from Latin *apud hoc* ‘with this’. And Romanian *cum* is a false friend: it means ‘how’, and comes from *quōmodo* ‘in what way’, like Italian *come*, Spanish *como* and French *comme*.

Concessive clauses — Latin *cum* + subjunctive, *quamvīs* + subjunctive, *quamquam* + indicative — show the same split as before: Italian *benché* and *sebbene*, French *bien que* and *quoique*, and Portuguese *embora* all take the **subjunctive**; Spanish *aunque* takes the subjunctive or the indicative depending on meaning; Romanian *deși* takes the **indicative**.

compare.title: ‘although he is rich’
compare.note: Spanish aunque sea rico means ‘even if he is (or may be) rich’.

title: Conditional Sentences
sub: Real, possible and unreal conditions with sī and nisi

blocks.p: A conditional sentence has two halves: the ‘if’ clause (the **protasis**), introduced by **sī** ‘if’ or **nisi** ‘if not, unless’, and the main clause (the **apodosis**). Latin sorts conditions by how real the speaker thinks they are, and shows this with the mood and tense of **both** verbs.

table.title: The types of condition
table.note: If you say this, you are wrong. — If you said this, you were wrong. — If you say this (lit. ‘will have said’), you will be wrong. — If you should say this, you would be wrong. — If you were saying this (now), you would be wrong. — If you had said this, you would have been wrong.

blocks.p: **Simple** conditions state no opinion about reality: indicative in both halves, in any tense. **Future** conditions come in two strengths. The vivid one uses the indicative — and, with Latin precision, the **future perfect** in the *sī*-clause, since the condition must be fulfilled before the result (Chapter 10). The less vivid one, ‘if you should …, you would …’, uses the **present subjunctive** in both halves.

**Unreal** (contrary-to-fact) conditions describe what is not, or was not, the case. They use the subjunctive one step back in time: the **imperfect** subjunctive for the present (*Sī Rōmae essem…* ‘If I were in Rome [but I am not]…’), the **pluperfect** subjunctive for the past (*Sī Rōmae fuissem…* ‘If I had been in Rome…’). The two can be mixed: *Sī hoc fēcissēs, nunc fēlīx essēs* ‘If you had done this, you would be happy now’.

blocks.pitfall: English ‘if I **were**’ and ‘if I **had** been’ look like past tenses; Latin uses the subjunctive — imperfect for the present, pluperfect for the past. Do not translate *sī essem* as ‘if I was’ in the past: it means ‘if I were (now)’. And remember the future perfect where English uses a present: *Sī vēneris* ‘if you come’.

blocks.tip: Read the **mood** first. Indicative: the speaker is neutral (‘if …, then …’). Present subjunctive: a mere possibility (‘if … should …, would …’). Imperfect subjunctive: unreal now (‘if … were …’). Pluperfect subjunctive: unreal in the past (‘if … had …’).

Other conditional words: *nisi* ‘unless, if … not’; *sīn* ‘but if’; *sī nōn* ‘if not’ (when one word is negated); and *dum*, *modo*, *dummodo* + subjunctive ‘provided that’: *Ōderint dum metuant* ‘Let them hate, provided they fear’.

items.t: Sī valēs, bene est; ego valeō.
items.en: If you are well, good; I am well. (standard opening of a Roman letter)
If you want peace, prepare for war. (after Vegetius)

items.t: Nisi ūtile est quod facimus, stulta est glōria.
items.en: Unless what we do is useful, our glory is foolish. (Phaedrus)
If it should happen, I would not be surprised.
If I were in Rome, I would visit you.
If you had kept quiet, you would have remained a philosopher. (medieval proverb, after Boethius)

items.t: Ō mihi praeteritōs referat sī Iuppiter annōs!
items.en: Oh, if only Jupiter would give me back the years that are gone! (Virgil)

blocks.p: Latin had no special form for ‘would’: it used the subjunctive. The Romance languages created a brand-new mood, the **conditional**, by the same trick that produced their future (Chapter 9): the **infinitive** + a past tense of *habēre*. Spanish, Portuguese and French used the imperfect, *habēbam* (*cantāre habēbam* → *cantaría, cantaria, chanterais*); standard Italian used the perfect, *habuī* (*cantāre habuī* → *canterei*). Romanian built its conditional differently, with an auxiliary before the infinitive.

compare.title: The conditional ‘I would sing’
compare.note: The Latin column shows what Latin used instead: the imperfect subjunctive. Spanish -ía, French -ais are the imperfect endings of haber / avoir (había, avais). Italian -ebbe, -ebbero match ebbe, ebbero ‘he had, they had’. Early Italian poetry also used forms from habēbam (saria ‘would be’), borrowed from Sicilian and Provençal.

blocks.p: The Romanian auxiliary *aș, ai, ar, am, ați, ar* is a puzzle. It is clearly not the Latin *habēbam*; most scholars connect it with forms of *avea* ‘have’ or *vrea* ‘want’, but its exact origin is still disputed.

**Unreal conditions** show the same family resemblance with local differences. Italian, Spanish and Portuguese put the *if*-clause in the imperfect subjunctive and the main clause in the conditional. French uses the plain **imperfect indicative** after *si* — never the conditional. Romanian uses the conditional in both halves. And Spanish has a choice in the *si*-clause between *tuviese* (from the Latin pluperfect subjunctive *tenuissem*) and the more common *tuviera* — from the Latin pluperfect **indicative** *tenueram* ‘I had held’ (Chapter 10).

compare.title: Unreal conditions
rows: Si j’avais le temps, je viendrais.
Dacă aș avea timp, aș veni.
Se avessi avuto tempo, sarei venuto.
Si hubiera tenido tiempo, habría venido.
Si j’avais eu le temps, je serais venu.
Se tivesse tido tempo, teria vindo.
Dacă aș fi avut timp, aș fi venit.
gloss: If I had time, I would come.
If I had had time, I would have come.
compare.note: Spanish often uses the -ra form in the main clause too: Si hubiera tenido tiempo, hubiera venido. This echoes its origin as a Latin pluperfect indicative — and Latin itself sometimes used the indicative in the main clause of an unreal condition, especially with verbs like poteram ‘I could have’ and dēbēbam ‘I ought to have’.

blocks.p: The little word *sī* went two ways. In the west it stayed ‘if’: Italian and Portuguese *se*, Spanish and French *si*. In Romanian it became *să*, the marker of the subjunctive (Chapter 24) — so Romanian needed a new ‘if’, *dacă*, built from *de* + *că* ‘that’.

title: Gerund, Gerundive and the Passive Periphrastic
sub: The art of loving, and Carthage that must be destroyed

blocks.p: The **gerund** is a noun made from a verb, like English ‘-ing’ in ‘the art of **loving**’. It is neuter singular and is formed from the present stem + **-nd-** + 2nd-declension endings. It has no nominative: as a subject, Latin uses the infinitive (*Errāre hūmānum est*). The other cases are the gerund’s.

table.title: The gerund
table.note: monēre: monendī; capere: capiendī; īre: eundī. The genitive with causā or grātiā also expresses purpose: discendī causā ‘for the sake of learning’.

items.en: We learn by teaching. (after Seneca)

items.t: Gutta cavat lapidem nōn vī, sed saepe cadendō.
items.en: A drop hollows the stone not by force but by falling often. (proverb, after Ovid)
We have come to learn.
items.lit: We have come for learning.

items.en: One learns by making mistakes. (proverb)

blocks.tip: English has kept gerund genitives in Latin phrases: *modus operandī* ‘way of working’, *modus vīvendī* ‘way of living (together)’, *onus probandī* ‘burden of proving’, *ars amandī* ‘art of loving’.

blocks.p: The **gerundive** looks like the gerund but is an **adjective**, *-ndus, -nda, -ndum*, declined like *bonus*, and **passive** in meaning: ‘to be …-ed, needing to be …-ed’. *Liber legendus* is ‘a book to be read’, ‘a book that must be read’. Deponents have one too, and it is passive as well: *hortandus* ‘to be encouraged’.

The gerundive has two main jobs. First, when a gerund would have a direct object, Latin prefers to turn the phrase round and make the noun agree with a gerundive: not *ad capiendum urbem* ‘for capturing the city’, but **ad urbem capiendam**, ‘for the city to-be-captured’. The meaning is the same; the style is better. *Lēgātōs ad pācem petendam mīsērunt* ‘They sent envoys to ask for peace’.

Second, the gerundive + **esse** expresses **obligation** or **necessity**: *Carthāgō dēlenda est* ‘Carthage is to-be-destroyed’, i.e. ‘must be destroyed’. This is the **passive periphrastic**. The person who has to do the action goes into the **dative** (the dative of agent), not *ā / ab* + ablative: *Haec epistula mihi scrībenda est* ‘This letter must be written by me’ = ‘I must write this letter’. With intransitive verbs the construction is impersonal: *Mihi eundum est* ‘I must go’.

items.en: Moreover, I think that Carthage must be destroyed. (Cato the Elder, as tradition reports his refrain)
Now we must drink. (Horace, celebrating Cleopatra’s defeat)
items.lit: Now it is to be drunk.

items.t: Caesarī omnia ūnō tempore erant agenda.
items.en: Caesar had to do everything at once. (Caesar)
items.lit: All things were to be done by Caesar at one time.

items.en: There is no arguing about taste. (medieval proverb)
I have to go home.
Which was to be proved. (Q.E.D., after Euclid)

blocks.pitfall: Keep the gerund (a noun, active: *amandī* ‘of loving’) apart from the gerundive (an adjective, passive: *amandus* ‘to be loved’). And remember the **dative** of agent with the gerundive: *mihi* in *mihi legendum est* is ‘by me’, not ‘to me’. Finally, *dēlenda est* never means ‘is being destroyed’ — that would be *dēlētur*.

afterlife.title: Gerunds, and things to be done

blocks.p: The **ablative of the gerund**, *cantandō* ‘by singing’, became the Romance **gerund** — one of the most stable forms in the family. It also took over most of the work of the Latin present participle (Chapter 23). In French it merged with the participle in *-ant* and is used with *en*: *en chantant*.

With ‘to be’ or ‘to stand’ the gerund forms the Romance **progressive**: Italian *sto cantando*, Spanish *estoy cantando*, Brazilian Portuguese *estou cantando* — literally ‘I stand singing’, from *stāre*. European Portuguese prefers *estou a cantar*; French says *je suis en train de chanter*; Romanian simply uses the present.

compare.title: ‘I am singing’
rows: Je suis en train de chanter.

blocks.p: The **passive periphrastic** did not survive as such. Romance expresses obligation with ‘must’ (from *dēbēre*: *dovere, deber, devoir, dever*), with ‘have to’ (*tener que*, *ter de*), or — closest of all to *dēlenda est* — Italian **andare** + participle: *Cartagine va distrutta*.

compare.title: ‘Carthage must be destroyed’
compare.note: Italian also says deve essere distrutta. Romanian trebui ‘must’ is a Slavic loan.

blocks.p: The gerundive’s best-known afterlife is in **English**, which borrowed a whole series of ‘things to be done’ straight from Latin, mostly from the language of the Church, the law and mathematics.

compare.title: Gerundives in English
gloss: things to be read (lives of saints read aloud)
(a question) to be referred to the people
(the faith) to be spread — from the Vatican’s Congregātiō dē propāgandā fidē, 1622
she who must be loved — a 17th-century coinage
she who must be admired — coined by Shakespeare in The Tempest

blocks.p: In the Romance languages gerundives survive as learned words — Italian *laureando* ‘a student about to graduate’ and *dottorando* ‘doctoral candidate’, Spanish *doctorando*, mathematical *dividendo* and *sumando* — and in a few inherited words of surprising meaning:

compare.title: Gerundives in Romance
gloss: ‘things to be done’ → it. ‘chore, business’; es. ‘estate, ranch; the Treasury’; pt. ‘farm; the Treasury; cloth’
compare.note: Spain’s Ministry of Finance is still the Ministerio de Hacienda — literally the ministry of ‘things to be done’.

parts.title: Gerunds, and things to be done

title: How the Cases Are Used
sub: Genitive, dative and ablative; place and time: Rōmae, domī, rūrī

blocks.p: Chapter 2 introduced the six cases with their core meanings. In real texts each case does a range of jobs, and recognising them is the key to fluent reading. This chapter collects the most important uses of the three ‘difficult’ cases — genitive, dative and ablative — and the rules for place and time.

table.title: Uses of the genitive
rows: eager for glory · full of wine
I remember you · I forget you
table.note: The partitive genitive is used even where English says ‘some’ or nothing at all: quid novī? ‘what’s new?’ (lit. ‘what of new?’).

table.title: Uses of the dative
rows: I give the boy a book.
Caesar was in command of the army.
We learn not for school but for life.
like his father · dear to all
table.note: Nōn scholae sed vītae discimus turns Seneca on his head: he complained of the opposite, nōn vītae sed scholae discimus (Letters 106).

blocks.pitfall: Many common verbs take the **dative** where English has a direct object: *crēdō* ‘believe’, *faveō* ‘favour’, *noceō* ‘harm’, *pāreō* ‘obey’, *parcō* ‘spare’, *persuādeō* ‘persuade’, *placeō* ‘please’, *serviō* ‘serve’, *resistō* ‘resist’, *imperō* ‘command’, *ignōscō* ‘forgive’. So *Tibi crēdō*, never *tē crēdō*. In the passive they become impersonal: *mihi persuāsum est* ‘I have been persuaded’ (lit. ‘it has been persuaded to me’).

blocks.p: The Latin ablative is three old cases in one: a true ablative of **separation** (‘from’), an **instrumental** (‘with, by’), and a **locative** (‘in, at’). Most of its uses fall into one of these three groups.

table.title: Uses of the ablative
rows: to free from fear · to do without wine
out of love · out of fear
to excel in courage · lame in one foot
at the third hour · within a few days
table.note: See Chapters 15 (time), 16 (agent), 18 (ūtor, fruor …), 20 (comparison) and 23 (ablative absolute).

blocks.p: Normally place is expressed with prepositions: *in* + accusative ‘into’, *in* + ablative ‘in’, *ab / ex* + ablative ‘from’. But with the names of **cities, towns and small islands**, and with the three nouns *domus* ‘home’, *rūs* ‘countryside’ and *humus* ‘ground’, Latin uses **no preposition**: the accusative for ‘to’, the ablative for ‘from’, and an old **locative** case for ‘at, in’.

table.title: Where? Where to? Where from?
table.note: In the singular of the 1st and 2nd declensions the locative looks like the genitive (Rōmae, Corinthī); elsewhere it looks like the ablative or dative. Also domī mīlitiaeque ‘at home and in the field’, i.e. in peace and war.

blocks.tip: Prepositions creep back with country names and to stress the vicinity: *in Italiā* ‘in Italy’ (Italy is not a town), *ad Rōmam* ‘to the neighbourhood of Rome, near Rome’. And note *domum* ‘homewards’: *Domum redeō* ‘I am going back home’, without any preposition.

items.en: My name is Julia.
items.lit: To me the name is Julia.
