items.t: Helvētiī quoque reliquōs Gallōs virtūte praecēdunt.
items.en: The Helvetii, too, surpass the other Gauls in courage. (Caesar)

items.t: Rōmae vīvit, sed rūrī nātus est.
items.en: He lives in Rome, but he was born in the country.
I am going back home.
What’s new?
items.lit: What of new?

items.t: Sī fueris Rōmae, Rōmānō vīvitō mōre.
items.en: When you are in Rome, live in the Roman way. (medieval verse, after St Ambrose)

afterlife.title: Prepositions take over — and Romanian holds out

blocks.p: When the case endings wore away (Chapter 2), their jobs passed to **prepositions**. *Dē* ‘down from, about’ took over the genitive; *ad* ‘to’ took over the dative; and the many ablative uses were shared out among *cum*, *dē*, *per*, *prō* and others. The change began inside Latin itself: classical *ūnus ex multīs* ‘one of many’ and Caesar’s *paucī dē nostrīs* ‘a few of our men’ already sit beside the partitive genitive, and the Vulgate writes *dē pāne illō edat* ‘let him eat of that bread’ (1 Corinthians 11:28) — the ancestor of the French partitive *du pain*.

compare.title: Cases replaced by prepositions
rows: Ho dato un libro al ragazzo.
Le di un libro al chico.
J’ai donné un livre au garçon.
gloss: I gave the boy a book.
compare.note: Romanian băiatului is a genitive-dative form: it means both ‘of the boy’ and ‘to the boy’, with no preposition. Spanish and Romanian also repeat the indirect object as a pronoun: le di … al chico, i-am dat băiatului. Even Romanian uses a preposition (de) for ‘a glass of’.

blocks.p: **Romanian** is the great exception. It kept a **genitive-dative** distinct from the nominative-accusative, marked mostly on the definite article that it attaches to the end of the noun: *băiatul* ‘the boy’, *băiatului* ‘of / to the boy’; *fata* ‘the girl’, *fetei* ‘of / to the girl’. Like Latin, it uses the same form for ‘of’ and ‘to’ in the feminine singular — compare Latin *puellae*, which is both genitive and dative.

The ablative left fossils that nobody notices any more. The most productive is the Romance **adverb in -mente**: Latin *clārā mente* ‘with a clear mind’ became Italian *chiaramente*, Spanish and Portuguese *claramente*, French *clairement* ‘clearly’. The adjective is feminine because *mēns* was feminine — and in Spanish and Portuguese the suffix is still so independent that it can be shared: *clara y lentamente* ‘clearly and slowly’. Romanian simply uses the adjective as an adverb: *clar*, *încet*.

compare.title: Ablative fossils
compare.note: French aujourd’hui is ‘on the day of today’: au jour d’hui, with hui from hodiē. Spanish luego ‘then, later’ and Portuguese logo ‘soon’ are another ablative, locō ‘on the spot’. Romanian azi is formed differently.

blocks.p: The **locative** survives in place names. Many French cities are named after the Gaulish tribe that lived there, in the Latin ablative-locative plural ‘among the …’: *Paris* (the Parisii), *Reims* (the Remi), *Poitiers* (the Pictavi), *Tours* (the Turones). *Aix* in Provence is *Aquīs* ‘at the waters’ — the hot springs of *Aquae Sextiae*.

parts.title: Prepositions take over — and Romanian holds out

title: Word Formation
sub: Prefixes, assimilation, vowel weakening, suffixes and compounds

blocks.p: Latin vocabulary is built like a construction kit: a root, plus **prefixes** in front and **suffixes** behind. Once you know some twenty prefixes and a dozen suffixes, a single root unlocks a whole family — *mittō* ‘send’ gives *admittō, committō, dīmittō, ēmittō, immittō, omittō, permittō, prōmittō, remittō, submittō, trānsmittō*, and English has nearly all of them. Most compounds are verbs, made from a preposition and a simple verb.

table.title: The main prefixes
rows: ad- (ac-, af-, ag-, al-, ap-, ar-, as-, at-)
table.note: Keep apart in- ‘in, into’ and the negative in- ‘un-, not’, which is a different prefix that attaches to adjectives and nouns: incertus ‘uncertain’, impius ‘undutiful’, ignōtus ‘unknown’.

blocks.p: When a prefix ending in a consonant meets a root beginning with a different consonant, the prefix usually **assimilates** — it becomes like (*ad* + *similis*) the following sound, making a double consonant. The word *assimilation* is itself an example. Before *p, b, m*, a final *n* becomes *m*: *con* + *pōnō* → *compōnō*.

blocks.tip: Double consonants in English words of Latin origin — *accept, affect, aggressive, allude, announce, appear, arrive, assist, attend, collect, correct, effect, illegal, immense, irregular, occur, offer, oppose, succeed, suffer, suggest, support* — are almost always the fingerprint of an assimilated prefix.

blocks.p: In compounds, the short vowel of the root often **weakens**. This goes back to a prehistoric stage when Latin words were stressed on the first syllable, so the root vowel of a compound was unstressed and was reduced. The rules: short *a* and *e* become *i* in an open syllable (*faciō* → *efficiō*, *teneō* → *contineō*) but *a* becomes *e* in a closed one (*factum* → *effectum*); the diphthong *ae* becomes *ī* (*caedō* → *incīdō*); *au* becomes *ū* (*claudō* → *inclūdō*).

table.title: Vowel weakening
table.note: incipiō ‘take on’ is the ordinary word for ‘begin’; dēcīdō ‘cut off’ gave English decide — to cut the question short.

blocks.pitfall: Weakening can make two compounds collide: *occīdō* ‘kill’ (from *caedō* ‘cut’) and *occidō* ‘fall, die, set’ (from *cadō* ‘fall’) differ only in the length of one vowel. The setting sun, *sōl occidēns*, gave us the *Occident*; *occīdō* gave nothing so poetic.

table.title: The most productive suffixes
table.note: -āris replaces -ālis when the stem already contains an l (populāris, mīlitāris, cōnsulāris), to avoid two l’s close together. mūsculus is a ‘little mouse’ — the Romans thought a flexing muscle looked like one; libellus is a ‘little book’, then a written complaint.

blocks.p: Latin made fewer noun compounds than Greek or German, but there are many, usually linked with *-i-*: *agricola* ‘field-tiller’ (*ager* + *colō*), *artifex* ‘craftsman’ (*ars* + *faciō*), *pontifex* ‘priest’, traditionally explained as ‘bridge-maker’, *signifer* ‘standard-bearer’ (*signum* + *ferō*), *carnivorus* ‘flesh-eating’, *magnanimus* ‘great-souled’, *aequinoctium* ‘equal night’, *omnipotēns* ‘all-powerful’, *frātricīda* ‘brother-killer’ (*frāter* + *caedō*, with weakening). Some compounds were made from whole phrases: *manūmittō* ‘set free (a slave)’ is ‘send from the hand’.

items.en: He has left, gone off, escaped, broken out. (Cicero, on Catiline’s flight from Rome)
Never despair. (Horace)
items.lit: Nothing is to be despaired of.

items.en: Well begun is half done. (proverb)
items.lit: The beginning is half of the whole.

items.en: Divide and rule. (political maxim)
Experience teaches. (proverb)

blocks.tip: Take a word apart before you look it up. *Prīncipium* is *prīmus* + *capiō* (‘first-taking’) with weakening; *imperō* is *in* + *parō* ‘prepare against’; *cōnsuētūdō* ‘custom’ is *con* + *suēscō* ‘get used to’ + *-tūdō*. *Experientia* hides two prefixes, *ex* and *per*.

blocks.p: Latin prefixes and suffixes reached the modern languages by two routes. Words **inherited** by the spoken language were worn down by centuries of sound change; words **borrowed** later from written Latin — the ‘learned’ words — kept their Latin shape almost intact. Because educated speakers of all these languages kept borrowing from the same Latin source, the learned vocabulary is a shared European stock, and the suffixes match almost perfectly.

compare.title: Latin -tiō in seven languages
compare.note: Each language’s ending is fixed: -zione, -ción, -tion, -ção, -ție or -țiune, -tion. Romanian has two learned endings, -ție and -țiune, which entered the language by different routes. In the last row the Romance words are inherited, so they look different — except Romanian rațiune, which is learned.

compare.title: More Latin suffixes
compare.note: Romanian împărat is inherited, with sound changes typical of Romanian; it means ‘emperor’. Romanian cetate means ‘fortress, citadel’ — the everyday Romanian ‘city’ is oraș, from Hungarian. Portuguese nobre shows the Portuguese tendency to change l to r after a consonant.

blocks.p: Sometimes the same Latin word entered a language **twice**, once by each route, producing **doublets** with different meanings: French *frêle* ‘frail’ and *fragile*, both from *fragilis*; *loyal* and *légal* from *lēgālis*; *hôtel* and *hôpital* from *hospitāle*; Spanish *llamar* ‘to call’ and *clamar* ‘to cry out’ from *clāmāre*; *colgar* ‘to hang’ and *colocar* ‘to place’ from *collocāre*; Italian *vezzo* ‘habit, charm’ and *vizio* ‘vice’ from *vitium*. English, borrowing from French, often took both.

compare.title: Inherited and learned: doublets through French
compare.note: In each pair the first word was inherited (and worn down) in French, the second borrowed later from written Latin. French sevrer now means ‘to wean’.

title: From Latin to Romance
sub: Vulgar Latin, the Appendix Probi, and the first words of the daughter languages

blocks.p: The Latin of this book is the polished written language of Cicero, Caesar and Virgil. Alongside it, Romans of every class spoke a looser everyday Latin — Roman writers called it *sermō cottīdiānus*, ‘everyday speech’. Modern scholars call it **Vulgar Latin**, from *vulgus* ‘the common people’. It was not a different language, and not only the speech of the poor: it was Latin as it was actually spoken, changing generation by generation while the written standard stayed almost frozen. The Romance languages grew out of this spoken Latin, not out of the Latin of books.

Since speech leaves no recordings, we reconstruct Vulgar Latin from indirect evidence: graffiti scratched on the walls of **Pompeii** before AD 79; letters on wooden tablets from **Vindolanda** on Hadrian’s Wall; the freedmen’s chatter at Trimalchio’s dinner in **Petronius**; the travel diary of the pilgrim **Egeria** (late 4th century); misspellings on gravestones; Christian texts written for ordinary people; the complaints of grammarians — and the evidence of the Romance languages themselves.

The most famous of those complaints is the **Appendix Probī**, a list of about 227 corrections in the form ‘say A, **not** B’, preserved in a 7th- or 8th-century manuscript from the monastery of Bobbio and named after the grammarian Probus, whose work it follows. Its own date is disputed — estimates range from the 3rd to the 6th century. Its anonymous author wanted to stamp out ‘mistakes’; instead he gave us a snapshot of real speech, because the forms he condemned are very often the ones the Romance languages continue.

compare.title: ‘Say A, not B’ — and what Romance says
gloss: ear — from the diminutive auricula ‘little ear’
compare.note: The Appendix is written without macrons, so they are left out here. Brackets mark a word from another root. Every ‘wrong’ form wins: Romance continues oclus, oricla, veclus, virdis, calda, mesa and vinia — and Italian even spells acqua exactly as the grammarian forbade.

blocks.p: The list shows several changes at work. Unstressed vowels next to the stress dropped out (**syncope**): *oc(u)lus*, *vet(u)lus*, *cal(i)da*, *vir(i)dis*. The new cluster *-tl-* became *-cl-* (*vetlus* → *veclus*). An *e* or *i* before another vowel became a consonantal glide, *vinea* → *vinia* [ˈvinja], which later produced Italian *gn*, Spanish *ñ* and Portuguese *nh*. And speakers loved **diminutives**: the ear was *auricula* ‘little ear’, not *auris*.

Final **-m** had been weak for centuries: in classical verse it is elided before a vowel, and Pompeian graffiti often leave it out. Its loss made *rosam* sound like *rosa*, one of the blows that toppled the case system (Chapter 2). It survives only in a few monosyllables, as a nasal or *-n*: French *rien* from *rem*, Spanish *quien* from *quem*. **h** went silent even earlier; Catullus mocks a certain Arrius for sticking false h’s on his words to sound refined — *chommoda* for *commoda*, *hīnsidiās* for *īnsidiās*.

items.t: Quisquis ama valia, peria qui nosci amare.
items.en: Good luck to every lover, and death to anyone who can’t love! (graffito at Pompeii, spelled as the writer spoke; classical Latin would write Quisquis amat valeat, pereat quī nescit amāre)

items.t: Quod hodiē nōn est, crās erit: sīc vīta trūditur.
items.en: What isn’t here today will be here tomorrow — that’s how life rolls on. (a freedman talking, in Petronius)
Wine is life. (Trimalchio at his dinner party, in Petronius)

blocks.p: The Pompeian graffito shows, in one line, two changes that shaped much of Romance: final *-t* has gone (*ama, peria, nosci*), and an *e* before a vowel has become a glide (*valia* for *valeat*, *peria* for *pereat*). Petronius, for his part, puts colloquialisms into his freedmen’s mouths that the Romance languages would later make standard: *bellus* ‘nice, pretty’ for *pulcher*, and diminutives everywhere.

The greatest change was the **collapse of the vowel system**. Classical Latin had ten vowels, five short and five long, and length alone could tell words apart (*malum* ‘evil’, *mālum* ‘apple’). In speech, length was lost and replaced by differences of quality: long vowels were pronounced close, short vowels open. In most of the Romance world short *i* fell together with long *ē* as a close [e], short *u* with long *ō* as a close [o], while short *e* and short *o* became open [ɛ] and [ɔ]. Under stress these open vowels often broke into **diphthongs**: *e* → *ie*, *o* → Italian *uo*, Spanish *ue*, French *eu*. Italian and French diphthongised only in open syllables, Spanish in closed ones too; Portuguese kept the open vowels without diphthongs.

compare.title: The vowel collapse
gloss: fly — short u → o (ro. keeps u)
land — es. ie even in a closed syllable
new — short o → uo, ue, eu
compare.note: All the Latin vowels in this table are short. Romanian went its own way with the back vowels — short u stayed u, as in muscă — and has its own diphthongs, ea and oa: seară ‘evening’ (from sēra), roată ‘wheel’, moare ‘dies’.

blocks.p: Consonants divided the Romance world along a line that runs across northern Italy from La Spezia to Rimini. To the **west** and north (Spanish, Portuguese, French, northern Italian dialects), *p, t, k* between vowels became *b, d, g* — and in French often disappeared. To the **east** and south (Tuscan Italian, Romanian) they stayed put.

compare.title: East and west of La Spezia–Rimini
compare.note: Italian and Romanian keep k, t, p; Spanish and Portuguese have g, d, b; French has lost the consonant or made it v. Spanish hormiga also shows the Spanish change of initial f to h.

blocks.p: Spoken Latin steadily replaced endings with separate words — a shift from **synthetic** to **analytic** grammar. Most of the changes have appeared in the Afterlife panels of this book. The demonstrative *ille* became the definite article (Italian *il*, Spanish *el*, French *le*, Portuguese *o*, Romanian *-ul* at the end of the noun), and *ūnus* the indefinite article; Sardinian made its article from *ipse* instead (*su, sa*). Word order, once free and usually verb-final, settled into **subject – verb – object**, because without case endings word order was the only way to tell who did what to whom.

table.title: From synthetic to analytic
rows: amātus est → è amato, es amado, est aimé
habeō amātum → ho amato, he amado, j’ai aimé
plūs / magis + adjective → più bello, más bello
dīcō quod venit → dico che viene
dē puerō, ad puerum → del ragazzo, al ragazzo

blocks.p: Spoken Latin also had its own vocabulary — usually more vivid, more colloquial or more regular than the literary word. Again and again the Romance languages continue the humble word, not the classical one.

compare.title: Classical word and spoken word
gloss: head — testa was a ‘pot, shell’; es. / pt. from capitia, ro. cap from caput
mouth — bucca was a ‘cheek’; ro. gură is gula ‘throat’
compare.note: Italian also kept capo ‘head, chief’ beside testa. Romanian, isolated from the rest, often kept a different word: cal, gură, frumos.

blocks.p: For centuries, people who spoke early Romance still **wrote** Latin, however badly; the spoken language was simply ‘the way one talks Latin’. The moment when people realised they were speaking something else came gradually — earliest in Gaul, where French had moved furthest from writing. In 813 the Council of Tours told priests to preach *in rūsticam Rōmānam linguam*, ‘in the rustic Roman language’, so that their congregations could understand. Thirty years later we meet the first substantial text in a Romance language.

On 14 February 842, in Strasbourg, two grandsons of Charlemagne — Louis the German and Charles the Bald — swore an alliance against their brother Lothair. So that each army could understand, Louis swore in the Romance language of Charles’s men, and Charles in the Germanic language of Louis’s. Their cousin, the historian Nithard, copied both oaths into his Latin chronicle. These **Strasbourg Oaths** are the birth certificate of French.

items.t: Pro Deo amur et pro christian poblo et nostro commun salvament, d’ist di in avant, in quant Deus savir et podir me dunat, si salvarai eo cist meon fradre Karlo…
items.en: For the love of God and for the Christian people and our common salvation, from this day on, as far as God gives me knowledge and power, I will help this brother of mine, Charles… (Strasbourg Oaths, 842)

table.title: Latin, the Oaths, and French today
table.note: There are no articles yet. Deo stands without a preposition for ‘of God’ — a remnant of the case system. salvarai is already salvāre + habeō, the new future of Chapter 9. Final vowels have mostly gone (amur, christian) except a supporting -e / -o after consonant groups (fradre, nostro).

blocks.p: Italian has a riddle. Around the year 800, a scribe in Verona jotted a few lines in the margin of a prayer book: the **Indovinello Veronese** (‘Veronese riddle’), discovered in 1924. Scholars still argue whether it is very bad Latin or very early Italian — which is exactly the point.

items.t: Se pareba boves, alba pratalia araba, et albo versorio teneba, et negro semen seminaba.
items.en: He drove oxen before him, ploughed white fields, held a white plough, and sowed black seed. (Indovinello Veronese, c. 800)

blocks.p: The answer is the writer’s own hand: the oxen are the fingers, the white field the parchment, the white plough the quill, the black seed the ink. Note *pareba, araba, teneba, seminaba* — Latin *parābat, arābat, tenēbat, sēminābat* without their final *-t*, just as in Italian *(egli) arava*. The first securely Italian document is a legal formula from Capua, the **Placiti Cassinesi** of 960: *Sao ko kelle terre, per kelle fini que ki contene, trenta anni le possette parte sancti Benedicti* ‘I know that those lands, within the boundaries described here, have been held for thirty years by the monastery of Saint Benedict’.

table.title: The first texts
rows: Glosas Emilianenses — notes in early Ibero-Romance in the margin of a Latin manuscript at San Millán de la Cogolla
Letter of Neacșu of Câmpulung, warning the city of Brașov of Ottoman troop movements

blocks.p: Here, then, is the family portrait. **Italian** stayed closest to Latin in sound, keeping final vowels and double consonants: *noctem* → *notte*, *plēnum* → *pieno*. **Spanish** made diphthongs of *e* and *o* (*tierra, nuevo*), turned initial *f* into *h* (*hijo, hacer*) and *cl-, pl-, fl-* into *ll-* (*llamar, lleno, llama*). **Portuguese** developed nasal vowels (*mão, pão*), dropped *l* and *n* between vowels (*dor, lua*) and turned *cl-, pl-, fl-* into *ch-* (*chamar, cheio, chama*). **French** changed most: the stress moved to the end of the word, final vowels faded, *ca-* became *cha-* (*cantāre* → *chanter*), and Frankish left its mark. **Romanian**, cut off from the west after Rome abandoned Dacia about AD 271, kept cases, the neuter and the vocative, attached its article to the end of the noun (*lupul* ‘the wolf’), turned *l* between vowels into *r* (*sōlem* → *soare*), *ct* into *pt* (*noctem* → *noapte*), and absorbed many Slavic words.

compare.title: Family traits
gloss: white — the west borrowed Germanic *blank ‘shining’; Romanian kept albus
to know — the west used sapere ‘to taste, to be wise’; Romanian kept scīre

compare.title: One prayer, six languages
compare.note: Romanian tată ‘father’ comes from the Latin nursery word tata ‘daddy’; care ‘who, which’ from quālis; sfinți ‘to hallow’ is Slavic. Spanish estás and Portuguese estais use estar, from stāre ‘to stand’.

blocks.p: These five are only the best known. The same family includes Catalan, Occitan, Galician, Sardinian, Corsican, Romansh, Ladin, Friulian, Aromanian and hundreds of local dialects — and, through the learned words of Chapter 30, half the vocabulary of English. Latin did not die: it turned into its daughters, and every time one of them speaks, it is still, in a sense, Latin being spoken.

title: The Alphabet and Pronunciation
sub: Twenty-four letters, three ways to read them, and how they reached English

blocks.p: The Greeks borrowed their alphabet from the Phoenicians, probably in the 8th century BC, and made one decisive change: they turned Phoenician signs for consonants that Greek did not need into **vowels**. *Aleph*, a throat consonant, became *alpha*; *he* became *epsilon*; *yod* became *iota*; *ayin* became *omicron*. The result was the first alphabet to write vowels and consonants alike — and, through a western Greek variant taken over by the Etruscans and the Romans, the ancestor of the letters you are reading now.

Early Greek cities used local variants. Athens officially adopted the Ionic alphabet in 403/2 BC, and that is the alphabet of all our texts. It had only capitals. The small letters grew out of Byzantine handwriting of the 9th century AD; accents and breathings were invented by Alexandrian scholars around 200 BC but written regularly only in Byzantine manuscripts (Chapter 2). Modern editions use capitals only for proper names and for the first word of a paragraph or a quotation — not for every sentence.

table.title: The Greek alphabet
table.note: Sigma is written ς at the end of a word and σ everywhere else: σεισμός ‘earthquake’ (English seismic). Plain π τ κ had no puff of breath, as in French or Italian.

blocks.p: **Vowel length** matters in Greek as in Latin. *η* and *ω* are always long, *ε* and *ο* always short; *α*, *ι* and *υ* can be either, and ordinary texts do not show which — dictionaries and grammars mark the long ones *ᾱ ῑ ῡ*. You will need this for the accent rules in Chapter 2. The letter names themselves are Semitic words (*aleph* ‘ox’, *beth* ‘house’); *epsilon* ‘plain e’, *omicron* ‘small o’, *omega* ‘big o’ and *upsilon* ‘plain u’ are Byzantine names — classical Athenians simply said *εἶ*, *οὖ*, *ὦ* and *ὖ*.

blocks.tip: Capital *Η* once stood for the sound h — the Romans took it over with that value, hence our letter H. East Ionic speakers had lost their h-sound and recycled the letter for long open e. When Athens adopted the Ionic alphabet it was left with an h-sound and no letter to write it: that gap is filled by the rough breathing (Chapter 2).

blocks.pitfall: Several small letters look like Latin letters with a different value: *ν* is n (not v), *ρ* is r (not p), *η* is a long e (not n), *γ* is g (not y), *χ* is ch (not x), *ω* is a long o (not w). So *νῦν* ‘now’ is *nyn*, and *ἡμῖν* ‘to us’ is *hēmin*. Among the capitals, *Η* is eta, *Ρ* is rho, *Χ* is chi and *Β* is beta.

table.title: Diphthongs (each is one long syllable)
table.note: ει and ου began as true diphthongs (e + i, o + u) but had become simple long vowels by the classical period; the name stuck. Breathing and accent stand on the second letter of a diphthong: αὐτός, οἶκος, εἰμί.

blocks.p: In the long diphthongs *ᾱι*, *ηι*, *ωι* the iota stopped being pronounced in the Hellenistic period. Medieval scribes wrote it small **under** the vowel — the **iota subscript**: *ᾳ ῃ ῳ*. Nobody pronounces it today, but it is grammatically vital: *τῷ* is a dative, *τό* is not. After a capital it is written on the line (the iota adscript).

*θ φ χ* were **aspirated stops** in classical Attic: t, p, k followed by a puff of breath, like the English *t*, *p*, *k* of *top*, *pot*, *cat* — and they contrasted with plain *τ π κ*, which had no puff. They were not yet the fricatives of later Greek (th as in *thin*, f, German ch). That is why the Romans spelled them with an *h*: *theātrum*, *philosophia*, *chorus*.

blocks.tip: Greek spelling itself shows that *φ θ χ* were *π τ κ* + h. When a word ending in *π τ κ* meets a word beginning with h (rough breathing), the stop turns into its aspirated partner: *κατά* + *ἡμέραν* → *καθ’ ἡμέραν* ‘every day’ (Modern Greek *καθημερινός* ‘daily’), and *ἐπί* + *ἡμέρα* gives *ἐφήμερος* ‘lasting a day’, English *ephemeral*.

blocks.p: *ζ ξ ψ* are **double consonants**. *ξ* is *κ γ χ* + *σ*, and *ψ* is *π β φ* + *σ*; they appear whenever a stem ending in a k- or p-sound meets an ending in *σ*: *φύλακ-ς* → *φύλαξ* ‘guard’ (genitive *φύλακος*), *Κύκλωπ-ς* → *Κύκλωψ* ‘Cyclops’ (genitive *Κύκλωπος*). *ζ* was pronounced [zd] in classical Attic, later [z]: *Ἀθήναζε* ‘to Athens’ is *Ἀθήνας* + *-δε* ‘to’.

*γ* before another velar (*γ κ ξ χ*) is pronounced [ŋ], like the n of *ink* or *finger*: *ἄγγελος* [áŋgelos] ‘messenger’, *ἄγκυρα* ‘anchor’, *σφίγξ* ‘sphinx’. The Romans heard a nasal and wrote *n*: *angelus*, *ancora*, *sphinx*.

No one has heard Plato speak, but spelling mistakes in inscriptions, transcriptions into Latin, the descriptions of ancient grammarians, puns, verse and even animal noises allow a confident reconstruction of 5th–4th-century Attic. In practice you will meet three pronunciations: **reconstructed Attic**, which aims at the classical sound; **Erasmian**, the school tradition named after Erasmus, who argued in 1528 that Greek letters should be given their ancient values, and which in practice reads them through the habits of each country; and **Modern Greek** pronunciation, used in Greece for every stage of the language.

table.title: Where the three pronunciations differ
table.note: Erasmian varies from country to country: English speakers often read υ as ‘oo’, German speakers as ü. Modern Greek has also lost all vowel length, and its accent is a stress rather than a pitch (Chapter 2). Letters not listed sound much the same in all three systems.

blocks.p: A favourite piece of evidence: the comic poet Cratinus, in the 5th century BC, wrote a sheep’s bleat as *βῆ βῆ*. Sheep say *bē bē*, not *vi vi* — so in his day *β* was still [b] and *η* an open e, not the Modern [v] and [i].

Which system should you use? Choose one and stay consistent. This book describes the classical values, because they explain Greek spelling, verse and the way Greek words were written in Latin; each chapter’s afterlife shows what became of them in Modern Greek.

items.en: Know yourself. (gnōthi seauton — inscribed at Delphi)
Nothing in excess. (mēden agan — inscribed at Delphi)
Best of all is water. (ariston men hydōr — Pindar, Olympian 1)
Everything flows. (panta rhei — a later summary of Heraclitus’ teaching)
Fine things are hard. (chalepa ta kala — a proverb quoted by Plato)
I have found it! (heurēka — Archimedes, as the story goes)
In the beginning was the Word. (en archēi ēn ho logos — John 1:1)

blocks.p: Modern Greek writes the same 24 letters, but most of them have changed their sound. *β γ δ* became the fricatives [v ɣ ð]; *θ φ χ* became [θ f x]; vowel length vanished; and six different spellings collapsed into the single sound [i]: *η*, *ι*, *υ*, *ει*, *οι* and the rare *υι*. This merger is called **itacism**, after the Modern name of eta, *ήτα* [ˈita]. Most of these changes took place in the Koine and early Byzantine periods; *υ* and *οι* were the last to reach [i], around the 10th century.

table.title: Modern Greek values
table.note: Because β δ γ had become fricatives, Modern Greek needed new spellings for [b d g]: μπ, ντ, γκ, as in μπάλα ‘ball’, ντομάτα ‘tomato’, γκρίζος ‘grey’.

blocks.p: Itacism turns Modern spelling into a memory test: *λύρα* ‘lyre’ and *λίρα* ‘pound (currency)’ are both [ˈlira]; *κοινή* ‘common’ and *κινεί* ‘moves’ are both [ciˈni]. But the spelling is historical — it preserves the ancient forms — so Ancient Greek makes Modern spelling easy, and Modern Greek gives you thousands of ancient words for free.

table.title: One word, two pronunciations
table.note: In the Attic column ´ marks a high pitch and ˆ a rising-falling pitch (Chapter 2). Modern δώρο has lost its final -ν.

afterlife.title: From Greek letters to Roman ones

blocks.p: The Romans borrowed thousands of Greek words and names and wrote them with fixed equivalents. English took most of these words from Latin and inherited the Roman spelling — which is why *philosophy* has *ph* and *y*, and *psalm* a silent *p*.

compare.title: Greek → Latin → English
gloss: κ → c, soft before e and i in English

blocks.p: Diphthongs became Latin ones: *αι → ae*, *οι → oe*, *ου → ū*, and *ει* usually *ī* (*Νεῖλος → Nīlus* ‘Nile’). Endings were Latinized: *-ος → -us*, *-ον → -um* (*μουσεῖον* ‘shrine of the Muses’ → *mūsēum*). English later reduced *ae* and *oe* to *e* — completely in American spelling (*pedagogue*, *economy*, *encyclopedia*), only partly in British (*encyclopaedia*, *oesophagus*).

A few English words skip Latin and transliterate Greek directly, with *k*: *kinetic* (*κινητικός*), *kudos* (*κῦδος* ‘glory’), *kaleidoscope*. And the word *alphabet* itself is simply *alpha* + *beta*, through Latin *alphabētum*.

parts.title: From Greek letters to Roman ones

title: Accents, Breathings and Punctuation
sub: The little marks above the letters, the accent rules, and a question mark that looks like a semicolon

blocks.p: Every word that begins with a vowel or a diphthong carries a **breathing**. The **smooth breathing** ( ᾿ ) means nothing at all; the **rough breathing** ( ῾ ) means the word begins with an h-sound. The breathing stands over a small letter, over the **second** letter of a diphthong, and in front of a capital. Initial *ρ* and initial *υ* always take the rough breathing.

table.title: Smooth and rough
table.note: The Greek names are ψιλή ‘bare’ (smooth) and δασεῖα ‘thick, hairy’ (rough).

blocks.tip: The rough breathing is a descendant of the letter *Η* (Chapter 1). Scholars split the old h-sign in half: the left half became the rough breathing, the right half the smooth one, and both were later rounded into the hooks you see today.

blocks.p: The accent marks were introduced around 200 BC by the Alexandrian scholar Aristophanes of Byzantium, to help readers pronounce the classics correctly. They did not mark stress but **pitch**: the accented syllable was sung higher, and Dionysius of Halicarnassus says the voice moved within an interval of about a fifth. In the course of the Roman imperial period this pitch accent turned into a stress accent, and that is how everyone reads it today — Erasmians and Greeks alike: stress the syllable that carries the mark.

table.title: The three accents
rows: any of the last three syllables
the high pitch held down before the next word
last syllable only, in place of an acute
rise and fall on one long vowel
last two syllables, long vowels and diphthongs only

blocks.p: Greek grammars count syllables from the end: the last is the **ultima**, the one before it the **penult**, the one before that the **antepenult** — no accent can go further back. What matters for the accent is the length of the **vowel** in each syllable (consonants play no part, unlike in Latin): *η ω* and diphthongs are long, *ε ο* short, *α ι υ* either. One exception you will meet constantly: final *-αι* and *-οι* count as **short** (*ἄνθρωποι*, *θάλατται*).

**(1)** The acute can stand on any of the last three syllables, but on the antepenult only if the ultima is short: *ἄνθρωπος*, but *ἀνθρώπου*. **(2)** The circumflex stands only on a long vowel or diphthong, only on the last two syllables, and on the penult only if the ultima is short. **(3)** Conversely, an accented long penult before a short ultima **must** be circumflex: *δῶρον* ‘gift’ (never *δώρον*), but *δώρου* when the ultima is long.

table.title: Five possible positions
table.note: Linguists still use these terms; English oxytone is Greek ὀξύτονος ‘sharp-toned’.

blocks.p: **Nouns and adjectives** have a **persistent** accent: it stays on the syllable where the nominative has it, and moves only when rules 1–3 force it to. You cannot predict the nominative accent — learn it with the word — but the rest follows. Oxytones of the first two declensions add one twist: they take a circumflex in the genitive and dative, *ποταμός, ποταμοῦ, ποταμῷ*.

table.title: Persistent accent at work
table.note: A long ultima (-ου, -ων) pulls the acute of ἄνθρωπος forward to the penult and turns the circumflex of δῶρον into an acute. In ἄνθρωποι and δῶρα the ultima is short (-οι counts as short, neuter -α is short), so the accent returns home.

blocks.p: **Verbs** have a **recessive** accent: it goes as far back from the end as the rules allow, so you can predict it. *παιδεύω* ‘I educate’ (long ultima: penult), *παιδεύομεν* ‘we educate’ (short ultima: antepenult), *ἐπαίδευον* ‘I was educating’.

blocks.pitfall: An acute on the **last** syllable becomes **grave** when another word follows without punctuation: *ποταμός* but *ὁ ποταμὸς ῥεῖ* ‘the river flows’. Before a comma, a full stop or an enclitic it stays acute. The interrogative *τίς / τί* ‘who? what?’ is the exception: it never turns grave (*τί λέγεις;* ‘what are you saying?’).

blocks.p: Some short words have no accent of their own. **Proclitics** lean forward on the next word: the articles *ὁ ἡ οἱ αἱ*, the prepositions *ἐν, εἰς, ἐκ*, *οὐ* ‘not’, *εἰ* ‘if’, *ὡς* ‘as’. **Enclitics** lean back on the word before: most forms of *εἰμί* ‘I am’ (*ἐστί, εἰσί*), *τις / τι* ‘someone, something’, *μου, μοι, με*, *σου, σοι, σε*, *τε* ‘and’, *γε* ‘at least’. An enclitic may give the preceding word a second accent: *ἄνθρωπός τις* ‘some man’, *δῶρόν ἐστιν* ‘it is a gift’. For now, simply recognise them.

blocks.tip: Accents and breathings keep words apart: *εἰμί* ‘I am’ but *εἶμι* ‘I shall go’; *τίς* ‘who?’ but *τις* ‘someone’; *νόμος* ‘law’ but *νομός* ‘pasture, district’; *οὐ* ‘not’ but *οὗ* ‘where’.

table.title: Punctuation
rows: question mark: τίς εἶ; ‘who are you?’
raised dot: a semicolon or colon
apostrophe: an elided vowel, ἀλλ’ ἐγώ for ἀλλὰ ἐγώ
diaeresis: two vowels said separately, Ἀτρεΐδης ‘son of Atreus’
table.note: Modern editions add capitals for direct speech and quotation marks; ancient books had almost no punctuation and no spaces between words.

blocks.p: **Elision**: a short final vowel is dropped before a word beginning with a vowel, and an apostrophe marks the gap: *ἀλλ’ ἐγώ*, *δι’ ἀνθρώπων*. Before a rough breathing the consonant left behind turns aspirate: *ἀπό* + *ἡμῶν* → *ἀφ’ ἡμῶν* ‘from us’. **Crasis** fuses two words into one, marked with a **coronis** that looks like a smooth breathing: *καὶ ἐγώ* → *κἀγώ*, *τὸ ὄνομα* → *τοὔνομα*, *τὰ ἄλλα* → *τἆλλα*.

items.t: λέγει αὐτῷ ὁ Πιλᾶτος· τί ἐστιν ἀλήθεια;
items.en: Pilate says to him: What is truth? (John 18:38)
Sing, goddess, of the wrath of Achilles, son of Peleus. (Iliad 1.1 — note the grave on θεὰ and the diaeresis)
Man is the measure of all things. (Protagoras)
One thing I know: that I know nothing. (later saying based on Plato’s Socrates)
Who are you?

items.t: ὦ ξεῖν’, ἀγγέλλειν Λακεδαιμονίοις ὅτι τῇδε κείμεθα, τοῖς κείνων ῥήμασι πειθόμενοι.
items.en: Stranger, tell the Spartans that here we lie, obedient to their words. (Simonides, on the dead of Thermopylae)
items.lit: O stranger, announce to the Lacedaemonians that here we lie, obeying the words of those men

blocks.p: By Byzantine times the pitch accent had long become a stress accent, and *η, ι, υ, ει, οι* were all [i] — but Greeks went on writing three accents and two breathings that no longer matched their speech. In **1982** Greece officially adopted the **monotonic** system: one accent mark, the *τόνος*, on the stressed syllable of every word of two or more syllables; no breathings; no iota subscript; the diaeresis kept (*καΐκι* ‘caique’). One-syllable words are unaccented except where the mark keeps two words apart: *ή* ‘or’ vs *η* ‘the’, *πού* ‘where?’ vs *που* ‘that, which’, *πώς* ‘how?’ vs *πως* ‘that’. The Church and some writers and publishers still use polytonic.

The **position** of the accent has survived remarkably well: Modern stress usually falls on the syllable that carried the ancient accent, and many nouns still shift it exactly as the ancient rules require. Modern Greek also still distinguishes *νόμος* ‘law’ from *νομός* ‘prefecture’.

compare.title: Ancient accent rules inside Modern Greek

blocks.p: The h-sound written by the rough breathing faded from speech in the Koine period, so Modern Greek has no h at all: *ιστορία* is [istoˈria]. But Latin had borrowed Greek words while the h was still alive and spelled it out, so English keeps it: an English *h-* or *rh-* in a Greek word betrays a rough breathing. Words with a smooth breathing have no h: *ἀγωνία* → *agony*, *ἰδέα* → *idea*, *ὀρθός* → *ortho-*.

compare.title: Rough breathing as English h
compare.note: The everyday Modern word for water is νερό, from νεαρὸν (ὕδωρ) ‘fresh (water)’; ὕδωρ survives in learned compounds such as υδραυλικός ‘plumber’.

blocks.p: Even the names of punctuation marks are Greek: *comma* is *κόμμα* ‘a piece cut off’, *colon* is *κῶλον* ‘limb, clause’, *period* is *περίοδος* ‘a going round’, and *apostrophe* and *diaeresis* are *ἀπόστροφος* and *διαίρεσις* ‘division’.

title: The Article and the Second Declension
sub: ὁ ἡ τό, five cases, and nouns in -ος and -ον

blocks.p: Unlike Latin, Greek has a **definite article** ‘the’: *ὁ* (masculine), *ἡ* (feminine), *τό* (neuter). There is no indefinite article: *ἄνθρωπος* is ‘a human being’ or just ‘a man’, *ὁ ἄνθρωπος* ‘the human being’. Greek uses its article more than English does — with abstract nouns (*ἡ ἀρετή* ‘virtue’), with whole classes (*ὁ ἄνθρωπος* ‘man, mankind’) and often with names (*ὁ Σωκράτης*).

Greek nouns have **five cases**, listed in Greek grammars in this order: **nominative** (subject, and the complement of ‘to be’), **genitive** (‘of’, and with prepositions ‘from’), **dative** (‘to, for’; ‘with, by means of’; ‘in, at’), **accusative** (direct object; with prepositions ‘to, into’) and **vocative** (address). There is no ablative: the jobs of the Latin ablative are shared out between the genitive (‘from’) and the dative (‘with, by, in’).

table.title: The article ὁ ἡ τό ‘the’
table.note: ὁ ἡ οἱ αἱ have a rough breathing and no accent (they are proclitics); every other form begins with τ-. In a sentence the acutes turn grave: τὸν λόγον. There is no vocative article; the interjection ὦ is used instead: ὦ φίλε ‘my friend’.

blocks.tip: Learn the article first and perfectly — it is the key to everything else. Noun endings are often ambiguous; the article almost never is. Notice how its endings mirror the noun endings: *τοῦ λόγου, τῷ λόγῳ, τὸν λόγον, τοὺς λόγους*.

blocks.p: The second declension has **masculines in -ος** and **neuters in -ον**, both with genitive *-ου*. A dictionary lists a noun with its genitive ending and article: *λόγος, -ου, ὁ* ‘word, speech, reason’; *δῶρον, -ου, τό* ‘gift’. This is the same inherited declension as Latin *dominus* and *dōnum* — and *δῶρον* and *dōnum* even come from the same root, ‘give’.

table.title: λόγος, -ου, ὁ ‘word, speech, reason’
table.note: Endings: -ος, -ου, -ῳ, -ον, -ε | -οι, -ων, -οις, -ους, -οι.

table.title: ἄνθρωπος, -ου, ὁ ‘human being, man’
table.note: Persistent accent (Chapter 2): whenever the ending is long (-ου, -ῳ, -ων, -οις, -ους) the accent moves from the antepenult to the penult. -οι counts as short, so ἄνθρωποι keeps it on the antepenult.

table.title: δῶρον, -ου, τό ‘gift’
table.note: Neuters differ from masculines only in the nominative, accusative and vocative: -ον in the singular, -α in the plural. The circumflex of δῶρον becomes acute before a long ending: δώρου.

blocks.p: The **neuter rule**, true of every Greek (and Latin) neuter: nominative, accusative and vocative are always identical, and in the plural they end in short *-α* — compare Latin *dōnum, dōna*.

blocks.pitfall: A **neuter plural subject takes a singular verb** in Attic: *τὰ ζῷα τρέχει* ‘the animals run’ (literally ‘runs’). Greeks felt a neuter plural as a collective ‘lot’. Homer and the New Testament often ignore the rule, but in Plato and Xenophon a singular verb with *τά* is normal.

blocks.p: A small but important group of second-declension nouns are **feminine**: *ἡ ὁδός* ‘road’, *ἡ νῆσος* ‘island’, *ἡ νόσος* ‘disease’, *ἡ βίβλος* ‘book’, *ἡ παρθένος* ‘maiden’, *ἡ ἤπειρος* ‘mainland’, *ἡ ψῆφος* ‘pebble, vote’, as well as most trees and many towns and islands (*ἡ Κόρινθος*, *ἡ Ῥόδος*). They decline exactly like *λόγος* but take the feminine article and feminine adjectives. Latin has the same quirk: *fāgus* ‘beech’, *pīnus* ‘pine’ and *humus* ‘soil’ are feminine.

table.title: ὁδός, -οῦ, ἡ ‘road, way’
table.note: An oxytone of the second declension takes a circumflex in the genitive and dative: ὁδοῦ, ὁδῷ, ὁδῶν, ὁδοῖς. So do ποταμός ‘river’, θεός ‘god’, ἀδελφός ‘brother’.

blocks.pitfall: Compounds of *ὁδός* are feminine too, though their English descendants give no hint: *ἡ μέθοδος* ‘pursuit, method’, *ἡ περίοδος* ‘circuit, period’, *ἡ ἔξοδος* ‘way out, exodus’, *ἡ εἴσοδος* ‘entrance’, *ἡ σύνοδος* ‘meeting, synod’.

blocks.p: Many relations are expressed with prepositions, each governing a fixed case: *ἐν* + dative ‘in’, *εἰς* + accusative ‘into, to’, *ἐκ* (*ἐξ* before a vowel) + genitive ‘out of’, *ἀπό* + genitive ‘away from’, *πρός* + accusative ‘towards’, *σύν* + dative ‘together with’. Notice the logic: motion **towards** → accusative, motion **from** → genitive, **rest** at a place → dative. The dative alone often expresses the instrument: *λίθοις βάλλει* ‘he pelts (him) with stones’. A genitive placed between article and noun shows possession: *ὁ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἵππος* ‘the man’s horse’.

items.t: Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος, καὶ ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεόν, καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος.
items.en: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. (John 1:1)
Man is by nature a political animal. (Aristotle, Politics — ‘is’ is left out)

items.t: ὁ θεὸς τοῖς ἀνθρώποις δῶρα πέμπει.
items.en: The god sends gifts to men.

items.t: ὁ δοῦλος τοὺς ἵππους εἰς τὸν ἀγρὸν ἄγει.
items.en: The slave leads the horses into the field.

items.t: οἱ ἄνθρωποι ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ εἰσιν.
items.en: The people are in the road.

items.t: τὰ δῶρα ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ ἐστίν.
items.en: The gifts are in the house.
items.lit: the gifts in the house is

items.en: Greetings, my friend.

blocks.tip: In John 1:1 the article tells you which noun is the subject. In *θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος* the subject is *ὁ λόγος*, the one with the article; *θεός* without it is the predicate — ‘the Word was God’, not ‘God was the Word’.

blocks.p: Greek also has a **dual** number for pairs: *τὼ ἀνθρώπω* ‘the two men’. It is common in Homer and still alive in classical Attic, but rare enough to be left for later.

afterlife.title: The article and the -ος nouns today

blocks.p: The Modern Greek article is the ancient one, minus breathings, accents and the dative. Two changes stand out: the feminine nominative plural is now *οι*, like the masculine (*αἱ* would sound [e]), and the feminine accusative plural is *τις*.

The **dative** was gradually abandoned in speech between late antiquity and the Middle Ages. Its jobs went to *σε* (from *εἰς*) + accusative and, for the indirect object, to the genitive: *δίνω το βιβλίο στον φίλο μου* or *του δίνω το βιβλίο* ‘I give him the book’. Fossilised datives survive in set phrases: *τοις εκατό* ‘per cent’ (literally ‘in the hundreds’), *εν τω μεταξύ* ‘meanwhile’, *εν ολίγοις* ‘in short’, *δόξα τω Θεώ* ‘glory to God’, and *εντάξει* ‘OK’, from *ἐν τάξει* ‘in order’.

compare.title: λόγος then and now
compare.note: Apart from the lost dative and the final -ν of the accusative, the masculine -ος declension has hardly changed in 2,500 years. Neuters lost their -ν too: δῶρον → δώρο, βιβλίον → βιβλίο.

blocks.p: Feminines in *-ος* survive mainly in learned words: *η μέθοδος*, *η περίοδος*, *η οδός* in street names (*οδός Ερμού* ‘Hermes Street’), and the signs every visitor reads, *ΕΙΣΟΔΟΣ* ‘entrance’ and *ΕΞΟΔΟΣ* ‘exit’. The everyday word for ‘road’ is *ο δρόμος*.

compare.title: Second-declension words in Modern Greek and English
compare.note: Modern άλογο ‘horse’ is ancient ἄλογον ‘without reason’, a dumb beast; νησί continues the diminutive νησίον ‘islet’. Peloponnese is Πελοπόννησος ‘island of Pelops’; Theodore is ‘gift of god’.

parts.title: The article and the -ος nouns today

title: The First Declension
sub: Feminines in -α and -η, masculines in -ης and -ας, and Attic θάλαττα

blocks.p: The **first declension** is the Greek counterpart of Latin *rosa*: mostly **feminine** nouns ending in *-α* or *-η*, with genitive *-ας* or *-ης*, plus a group of **masculines** in *-ης* and *-ας*. The singular comes in several flavours; the **plural is the same for all**: *-αι, -ῶν, -αις, -ας, -αι*.

Which flavour a noun belongs to depends on one sound change. Early Attic-Ionic turned every inherited long *ᾱ* into *η* — but Attic kept (or restored) *ᾱ* **after ε, ι or ρ**. So *χώρα* ‘land’ (after ρ) keeps its *α* throughout the singular, while *γνώμη* ‘judgement’ and *τιμή* ‘honour’ have *η*.

table.title: Long-vowel feminines: χώρα ‘land’, γνώμη ‘judgement’, τιμή ‘honour’
table.note: Like χώρα: ἡμέρα ‘day’, οἰκία ‘house’, ἀγορά ‘market-place’, θεά ‘goddess’. Like γνώμη: ψυχή ‘soul’, ἀρχή ‘beginning, rule’, φωνή ‘voice’, ἐπιστολή ‘letter’. χῶραι and γνῶμαι have a circumflex because final -αι counts as short.

blocks.p: A second group has a **short** *-α* in the nominative. After *ε, ι, ρ* the *α* again stays in the genitive and dative singular (*μοῖρα, μοίρας* ‘fate’); after any other sound those two cases switch to *η* (*θάλαττα, θαλάττης* ‘sea’; *μοῦσα, μούσης* ‘muse’).

table.title: Short-α feminines: θάλαττα ‘sea’, μοῦσα ‘muse’, μοῖρα ‘fate’
table.note: Like θάλαττα and μοῦσα: γλῶττα ‘tongue’, δόξα ‘opinion, glory’, τράπεζα ‘table’. Like μοῖρα: γέφυρα ‘bridge’, ἀλήθεια ‘truth’.

blocks.tip: Long or short *α*? Let the accent tell you (Chapter 2). *θάλαττα*, accented on the antepenult, and *μοῦσα*, with a circumflex on a long penult, can only have a **short** final *α*. *χώρα*, with an acute on a long penult, must have a **long** one.

blocks.pitfall: Two traps in every first-declension noun. (1) The genitive plural is **always** *-ῶν* with a circumflex, whatever the accent of the nominative: *θάλαττα* → *θαλαττῶν*, *γνώμη* → *γνωμῶν* (it is contracted from older *-άων*, which Homer still uses). (2) *χώρας* is both genitive singular and accusative plural — only the article or the context decides: *τῆς χώρας* ‘of the land’, *τὰς χώρας* ‘the lands’ (object).

blocks.p: Masculine first-declension nouns add *-ς* in the nominative and borrow the genitive *-ου* from the second declension. Many name people by their occupation: *πολίτης* ‘citizen’, *στρατιώτης* ‘soldier’, *ναύτης* ‘sailor’, *ποιητής* ‘poet’, *κριτής* ‘judge’, *νεανίας* ‘young man’, *ταμίας* ‘treasurer’. Nouns in *-της* have a vocative in short *-α*: *ὦ πολῖτα* ‘citizen!’.

table.title: πολίτης ‘citizen’ and νεανίας ‘young man’
table.note: The plural is identical to the feminine plural. The ι of πολίτης is long, hence the circumflex in πολῖτα and πολῖται; the ι of νεανίας is short, so νεανίαι keeps an acute.

blocks.p: Latin has the same small class of masculines in *-a* (*nauta, agricola*), and it absorbed Greek masculines in *-ης* into it: *ποιητής* → *poēta*, *ἀθλητής* → *athlēta*, *προφήτης* → *prophēta*, *πειρατής* → *pīrāta*.

Where Attic has **ττ**, Ionic and most other dialects have **σσ**: Attic *θάλαττα, γλῶττα, πράττω* ‘I do’, *τέτταρες* ‘four’ against *θάλασσα, γλῶσσα, πράσσω, τέσσαρες*. Even in Athens the choice was a matter of style: comedy, the orators, Plato and Xenophon write *ττ*, but tragedy and Thucydides prefer the grander-sounding *σσ*. Ionic also has *η* where Attic keeps *α* after *ε ι ρ*: Herodotus writes *χώρη* and *ἡμέρη*.

items.en: The sea! The sea! (the cry of Xenophon’s Ten Thousand on sighting the Black Sea — Anabasis 4.7)
Tell me, Muse, of the man of many turns (Odyssey 1.1 — vocative Μοῦσα)
Let us begin our song from the Muses of Helicon. (Hesiod, Theogony 1 — epic genitive plural -άων)

items.t: ἡ γλῶσσ’ ὀμώμοχ’, ἡ δὲ φρὴν ἀνώμοτος.
items.en: My tongue has sworn, but my mind is unsworn. (Euripides, Hippolytus 612 — tragedy’s σσ)

items.t: οἱ νεανίαι ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ εἰσιν.
items.en: The young men are in the market-place.

items.t: ὁ ποιητὴς τοῖς πολίταις τὴν ἀλήθειαν λέγει.
items.en: The poet tells the citizens the truth.

items.t: καὶ γνώσεσθε τὴν ἀλήθειαν, καὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια ἐλευθερώσει ὑμᾶς.
items.en: And you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free. (John 8:32)

blocks.p: The first declension is alive and well in Modern Greek: *η χώρα* ‘country’, *η γνώμη* ‘opinion’, *η θάλασσα* ‘sea’, *η μούσα* ‘muse’, *η τιμή* ‘honour; price’ (ancient *τιμή* also meant both), *ο πολίτης* ‘citizen’. Three things changed: the dative disappeared; the feminine plural now ends in **-ες**, an ending taken over from the third declension (Chapter 7); and the switch from *α* to *η* in the genitive is gone — Modern says *της θάλασσας*, not *θαλάσσης*.

compare.title: ‘Sea’ then and now
compare.note: The genitive plural still carries its ancient stress on the ending.

compare.title: ‘Citizen’ then and now
compare.note: Modern masculines in -ης have dropped the borrowed genitive -ου: the singular is simply πολίτης, πολίτη, πολίτη.

blocks.p: In the *ττ / σσ* contest, the Koine chose **σσ**, and Modern Greek continues the Koine: *θάλασσα*, *γλώσσα*, *τέσσερις*. Only a handful of Attic forms came back as learned words, mostly through the formal *katharevousa* of the 19th and 20th centuries: *ήττα* ‘defeat’, *ελάττωμα* ‘defect’, formal *πράττω* ‘act’.

compare.title: First-declension words in Modern Greek and English
compare.note: Masculines in -ης reached English through Latin -a, which English then dropped: poet, athlete, prophet, pirate, despot, hypocrite.

title: The Present Tense and εἰμί
sub: Present active indicative and infinitive of ω-verbs; the verb ‘to be’

blocks.p: A Greek verb form tells you person, number, tense, voice (active, middle, passive) and mood (indicative, subjunctive, optative, imperative), and there are infinitives and participles besides. We start with the commonest form of the commonest type: the **present active indicative** of the so-called **ω-verbs**, whose first person singular ends in *-ω*. That first person is the dictionary form: Greek, like Latin, lists *λύω* ‘I loosen, free’, not ‘to loosen’.

Each form is built from **stem + thematic vowel + ending**. The thematic vowel is *ο* before *μ* and *ν*, *ε* elsewhere, though in the singular it has merged with the endings: *λύ-ο-μεν* ‘we loosen’, *λύ-ε-τε* ‘you (pl.) loosen’, but *λύεις, λύει*.

table.title: λύω ‘I loosen, free’ — present active indicative
table.note: Infinitive: λύειν ‘to loosen’. The bracketed -ν (‘movable nu’) is added before a vowel and at the end of a sentence: λύουσιν αὐτούς. The accent is recessive (Chapter 2): λύω, λύομεν, λύουσι.

blocks.p: The present means ‘I loosen’, ‘I am loosening’ or ‘I do loosen’ — Greek, like Latin, makes no distinction. Subject pronouns are not needed: *γράφει* is ‘he writes’, ‘she writes’ or ‘it writes’; *ἐγώ* ‘I’ and *σύ* ‘you’ appear only for emphasis or contrast.

compare.title: Greek and Latin present tense side by side
compare.note: λέγω ‘say’ (originally ‘pick out, count’) and legō ‘gather, read’ come from the same root, and both conjugations go back to the same Indo-European pattern. Doric Greek still had -οντι in the 3rd plural (λέγοντι), close to Latin -unt; Attic -ουσι developed from that older -οντι. Another cognate trio: φέρω, ferō, bear.

blocks.p: Useful ω-verbs: *ἄγω* ‘lead’, *ἀκούω* ‘hear’, *βλέπω* ‘look, see’, *γράφω* ‘write’, *διδάσκω* ‘teach’, *ἐθέλω* (or *θέλω*) ‘be willing, want’, *ἔχω* ‘have, hold’, *θύω* ‘sacrifice’, *κλέπτω* ‘steal’, *λέγω* ‘say’, *λείπω* ‘leave’, *μανθάνω* ‘learn’, *πέμπω* ‘send’, *πιστεύω* ‘trust, believe’, *φέρω* ‘carry, bring’, *φεύγω* ‘flee’, *φυλάττω* ‘guard’.

blocks.tip: Hang the verbs on English words: *γράφω* → *graphic, biography*; *ἀκούω* → *acoustic*; *διδάσκω* → *didactic*; *κλέπτω* → *kleptomania*; *λύω* → *analysis, paralysis*; *λείπω* → *ellipse, eclipse*; *φέρω* → *metaphor, amphora*; *πέμπω* → *pomp* (*πομπή* ‘a sending, procession’).

blocks.p: ‘Not’ with an indicative is *οὐ*, which becomes *οὐκ* before a smooth breathing and *οὐχ* before a rough one: *οὐ γράφω* ‘I am not writing’, *οὐκ ἔχω* ‘I do not have’, *οὐχ ἁρπάζει* ‘he does not snatch’. Questions are marked by the Greek question mark *;* and often by a question word: *τί* ‘what? why?’, *ποῦ* ‘where?’, or *ἆρα*, which simply announces a yes/no question: *ἆρα γράφεις;* ‘are you writing?’.

The present infinitive ends in *-ειν*: *λύειν* ‘to loosen’, *γράφειν* ‘to write’. It completes verbs of wanting and being able, *ἐθέλω μανθάνειν* ‘I want to learn’, and impersonal expressions such as *δεῖ* ‘it is necessary’ and *ἔξεστι* ‘it is allowed’: *δεῖ φεύγειν* ‘we must flee’. With the neuter article it becomes a noun that can be declined: *τὸ μανθάνειν* ‘learning, the act of learning’, *τοῦ μανθάνειν* ‘of learning’.

table.title: εἰμί ‘I am’ — present indicative
table.note: Infinitive: εἶναι ‘to be’. Every form except εἶ is enclitic, so in sentences it often loses its accent or throws an extra one onto the word before: ἄνθρωπός ἐστιν. Paradigms print the forms accented.

blocks.p: The 3rd singular is written **ἔστι(ν)** with the accent on the first syllable when it means ‘there is, exists’ or ‘it is possible’, at the start of a sentence, and after *οὐκ*: *ἔστι θεός* ‘there is a god’, *οὐκ ἔστι* ‘it is not so; it is impossible’. As a link verb, *εἰμί* takes a **nominative** complement — and it is often simply left out: *σοφὸς ὁ ἀνήρ* ‘the man is wise’.

compare.title: ‘To be’ in Greek, Latin and English
compare.note: One Indo-European verb lies behind all three columns: English is (German ist) matches ἐστί and est, and am matches εἰμί, which comes from an older ἐσμί (Aeolic Greek still said ἔμμι). The English plural are comes from a different root.

blocks.pitfall: Watch the last letter: *λύει* ‘he loosens’, *λύεις* ‘you loosen’, *λύειν* ‘to loosen’. In *εἰμί*, *ἐστί* ‘he is’ and *ἐστέ* ‘you (pl.) are’ differ by a single vowel.

items.en: I am writing a letter.
The teacher teaches the young men.
Are you telling the truth?
I am not willing to run away.

items.t: δεῖ τοὺς πολίτας τοὺς νόμους φυλάττειν.
items.en: The citizens must guard the laws.
items.lit: it is necessary the citizens to guard the laws

items.en: We are human beings, not gods.

items.t: ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ φῶς τοῦ κόσμου.
items.en: I am the light of the world. (John 8:12)

blocks.p: The present tense is one of the most stable things in the Greek language. Four of the six endings of *γράφω* are spelled exactly as they were in Plato’s day; the first plural *-ομεν* became *-ουμε* (formal *-ομε*), and the third plural *-ουσι* became *-ουν* or *-ουνε*.

The **infinitive**, on the other hand, **died**. Already in the Koine, *ἵνα* ‘so that’ + subjunctive began to replace it after verbs of wanting — Salome says *θέλω ἵνα ἐξαυτῆς δῷς μοι… τὴν κεφαλὴν Ἰωάννου* ‘I want you to give me at once the head of John’ (Mark 6:25). In Modern Greek *ἵνα* has shrunk to *να*, and every infinitive is a *να*-clause: *θέλω να γράψω* ‘I want to write’, literally ‘I want that I write’. Modern dictionaries therefore list verbs by the first person — as ancient ones always did.

compare.title: Life without an infinitive
compare.note: Romanian, Bulgarian and Albanian replaced the infinitive in exactly the same way: it is one of the shared features of the Balkan languages. Romanian să plays the part of Greek να.

blocks.p: Traces of the infinitive remain. The form used in the Modern perfect, *έχω γράψει* ‘I have written’, descends from an old aorist infinitive, and grammars still call it the *απαρέμφατο* ‘infinitive’. Philosophy keeps a few as nouns: *το είναι* ‘being’, as in the phrase *το είναι και το φαίνεσθαι* ‘being and seeming’.

‘To be’ changed its look: Modern *είμαι* has **middle** endings, like *έρχομαι* ‘I come’ (Chapter 9). Its 3rd person *είναι* looks like the ancient infinitive *εἶναι*, but it is usually traced to medieval *ἔνι* ‘is’ (from *ἔνεστι* ‘is in, is possible’), respelled to match.

title: Adjectives of the First and Second Declension
sub: ἀγαθός, δίκαιος, two-ending ἄδικος, and why the position of the article matters

blocks.p: Most Greek adjectives combine the two declensions you already know: the **second** for masculine and neuter, the **first** for feminine. Dictionaries list them as *ἀγαθός, -ή, -όν* ‘good’ — exactly like Latin *bonus, -a, -um*. There is nothing new to learn; only to recognise.

table.title: ἀγαθός, -ή, -όν ‘good’
table.note: Declined the same way: καλός ‘beautiful, fine’, κακός ‘bad’, σοφός ‘wise’, χαλεπός ‘difficult’, ἀνδρεῖος ‘brave’ (fem. ἀνδρεία), φίλος ‘dear’. As oxytones, ἀγαθός and καλός take a circumflex in the genitive and dative.

blocks.p: The feminine follows the rule of Chapter 4: after *ε, ι, ρ* it has **-α**, otherwise **-η**. So *δίκαιος, δικαία, δίκαιον* ‘just’, *μικρός, μικρά, μικρόν* ‘small’, *ἄξιος, ἀξία, ἄξιον* ‘worthy’, *ἐλεύθερος, ἐλευθέρα, ἐλεύθερον* ‘free’ — but *καλός, καλή, καλόν*.

table.title: δίκαιος, -α, -ον ‘just’
table.note: The feminine singular has a long α, so the accent cannot stay on the antepenult: δικαία. Final -οι and -αι count as short, so δίκαιοι and δίκαιαι can.

blocks.pitfall: A first-declension **noun** always has its genitive plural in *-ῶν* (*χωρῶν*), but the feminine of an **adjective** in *-ος* is accented in the genitive plural exactly like the masculine: *δικαίων*, not *δικαιῶν*; *ἀξίων*, not *ἀξιῶν*.

blocks.p: Many adjectives — above all **compounds** — have no separate feminine: the masculine forms do duty for both genders, and only the neuter is distinct. Dictionaries list them with two endings: *ἄδικος, -ον* ‘unjust’. Typical are compounds with the negative prefix *ἀ-* (*ἀν-* before a vowel): *ἀθάνατος* ‘immortal’, *ἀδύνατος* ‘impossible, powerless’, *ἄτιμος* ‘dishonoured’, *ἀνάξιος* ‘unworthy’; and a few simple words such as *βάρβαρος* ‘non-Greek’.

table.title: ἄδικος, -ον ‘unjust’
table.note: So ἡ ἄδικος πόλις ‘the unjust city’ and ψυχὴ ἀθάνατος ‘an immortal soul’: feminine nouns with -ος adjectives.

blocks.tip: The Greek negative prefix *ἀ-/ἀν-* is a cognate of Latin *in-* and English *un-*: *ἄδικος*, *iniūstus*, *unjust*. English is full of it: *atom* (*ἄτομος* ‘uncuttable’), *anonymous* (*ἀνώνυμος* ‘nameless’), *anarchy*, *agnostic*, *asymmetry*.

blocks.p: An adjective agrees with its noun in **gender, number and case** — which does not mean it has the same ending. *ἡ ὁδὸς μακρά* ‘the long road’ pairs a feminine noun in *-ος* with a feminine adjective in *-α*; *ὁ ἀγαθὸς πολίτης* ‘the good citizen’ pairs a masculine first-declension noun with a masculine adjective in *-ος*.

Because Greek has an article, word order tells you **what the adjective is doing**. An adjective inside the article–noun group, directly after an article, is **attributive**: it describes the noun (‘the good man’). An adjective outside that group is **predicative**: it makes a statement about the noun, with ‘is’ understood (‘the man is good’).

table.title: Where the adjective stands
table.note: The quick test: is the adjective directly preceded by an article? Then it is attributive. Type 2 repeats the article and stresses the adjective: ‘the man — the good one’.

blocks.tip: Latin has no article, so *vir bonus* can mean ‘a good man’ or ‘the good man’, and ‘the man is good’ needs *est*. Greek says all three without ambiguity — and can drop the verb in the third.

blocks.p: With the article, an adjective becomes a **noun**: *οἱ ἀγαθοί* ‘good men, the good’, *οἱ σοφοί* ‘the wise’, *τὰ καλά* ‘fine things’, *τὸ ἀγαθόν* ‘the good’ (a key term in Plato). The Athenian ideal of the perfect gentleman was *καλὸς κἀγαθός* ‘fine and good’, with *κἀγαθός* the crasis of *καὶ ἀγαθός*.

items.t: ὁ βίος βραχύς, ἡ δὲ τέχνη μακρή.
items.en: Life is short, the craft is long. (Hippocrates, Aphorisms 1.1 — Ionic μακρή for Attic μακρά)

items.t: ὁ δὲ ἀνεξέταστος βίος οὐ βιωτὸς ἀνθρώπῳ.
items.en: The unexamined life is not worth living for a human being. (Plato, Apology 38a)
Every soul is immortal. (Plato, Phaedrus 245c — two-ending ἀθάνατος with a feminine noun)
The road is long.

items.t: ὁ ἀγαθὸς πολίτης τοὺς νόμους φυλάττει.
items.en: The good citizen guards the laws.

items.t: οἱ δίκαιοι τοῖς ἀδίκοις οὐ πιστεύουσιν.
items.en: The just do not trust the unjust.
A big book is a big evil. (proverbial form of a saying of Callimachus; μέγα is the neuter of μέγας ‘big’)

blocks.p: Modern Greek adjectives in *-ος* decline just like their ancient models, minus the dative and with the plural feminine in *-ες* (Chapter 4): *καλός, καλή, καλό*. After a vowel the feminine usually has *-α*, as in Attic: *ωραίος, ωραία* ‘beautiful’, *νέος, νέα* ‘new, young’, *αρχαίος, αρχαία* ‘ancient’.

Meanings shifted. Ancient *καλός* ‘beautiful, fine, noble’ became the everyday word for **‘good’** (*καλημέρα* ‘good morning’, *καλό ταξίδι* ‘have a good trip’). *Αγαθός* lives on in a narrower sense — ‘kind, good-natured, simple-hearted’ — and as a noun, *τα αγαθά* ‘goods’ (*καταναλωτικά αγαθά* ‘consumer goods’). ‘Beautiful’ is now *ωραίος*, from ancient *ὡραῖος* ‘in season, ripe, in the bloom of youth’, a derivative of *ὥρα* ‘season, hour’ (English *hour*, *horoscope*).

Word order survives too: Modern Greek still says *ο καλός άνθρωπος* and, with emphasis, *ο άνθρωπος ο καλός* — the ancient type 2. But the predicate now needs the verb: *ο άνθρωπος είναι καλός*. The verbless sentence lives on mainly in proverbs and headlines.

compare.title: ‘The good person’ and ‘the person is good’
Adjectives in Modern Greek and English
compare.note: Kaleidoscope was coined in 1817 from καλός + εἶδος ‘shape’ + σκοπέω ‘look at’. Modern μακρύς ‘long’ has moved into another declension.

title: Third Declension I: Consonant Stems
sub: φύλαξ, σῶμα, δαίμων, ῥήτωρ, γέρων, ἐλπίς, νύξ and πατήρ

blocks.p: The **third declension** is the largest and most varied: nouns of all three genders, with a nominative that often looks nothing like the rest of the word. The key is the **genitive singular**, which always ends in *-ος*: remove the *-ος* and you have the **stem**, to which all the other endings are added. *φύλαξ, φύλακος* ‘guard’ → stem *φυλακ-*; *σῶμα, σώματος* ‘body’ → stem *σωματ-*. Dictionaries give the genitive ending and the article: *φύλαξ, -ακος, ὁ*.

table.title: Third-declension endings
table.note: Neuters: nominative, accusative and vocative singular are the bare stem (σῶμα); plural -α (σώματα).

compare.title: One declension, two languages
compare.note: Greek πούς, Latin pēs and English foot are the same Indo-European word, and the endings match too: Greek -ος ~ Latin -is, -ι ~ -ī, -α ~ -em, -ες ~ -ēs, -ων ~ -um. The Greek and Latin third declensions are one inherited system.

blocks.p: Most of the apparent irregularity comes from two endings that begin with *σ* — the nominative singular *-ς* and the dative plural *-σι* — and from what a stem consonant does when it meets that *σ*. Six rules cover almost everything:

table.title: Stem consonant + σ
rows: ντ drops, ο lengthens to ου

table.title: Masculine and feminine stems in a stop
table.note: Monosyllabic nouns such as νύξ accent the ending in the genitive and dative of both numbers: νυκτός, νυκτί, νυκτῶν, νυξί. Like φύλαξ: κῆρυξ, -υκος ‘herald’. Like ἐλπίς: πατρίς, -ίδος ‘fatherland’.

table.title: σῶμα, -ατος, τό ‘body’
table.note: Every noun in -μα is neuter with a stem in -ματ-: ὄνομα ‘name’, πρᾶγμα ‘thing, matter’, γράμμα ‘letter (of the alphabet)’, ποίημα ‘poem’, στόμα ‘mouth’, χρῶμα ‘colour’. The -τ- cannot stand at the end of a Greek word, so it disappears in the nominative.

blocks.h: Liquids and nasals: δαίμων, ῥήτωρ, γέρων

table.title: Stems in ν, ρ and ντ
table.note: The nominative has a long vowel (-ων, -ωρ), the other cases a short one (-ον-, -ορ-). The vocative singular is the bare stem: δαῖμον, ῥῆτορ, γέρον.

blocks.pitfall: The dative plural can disguise a noun completely. *γέρουσι(ν)* ‘to the old men’ looks exactly like a verb (*λύουσι* ‘they loosen’), and *φύλαξι*, *σώμασι*, *δαίμοσι* hide their stems. When you meet an unknown form in *-σι(ν)*, try undoing the rules above.

blocks.p: A few nouns in *-ηρ* shift their stem between three grades: long *πατήρ* in the nominative, *πατέρ-* in the accusative, vocative and plural, and the shortened *πατρ-* in the genitive and dative singular, with *πατρά-* before the dative plural ending.

table.title: πατήρ ‘father’, μήτηρ ‘mother’, ἀνήρ ‘man, husband’
table.note: θυγάτηρ, θυγατρός ‘daughter’ goes like μήτηρ. ἀνήρ slips a δ between ν and ρ (ἀνρ- → ἀνδρ-), just as English thunder grew a d that Old English þunor did not have. The vocatives throw the accent back: πάτερ, μῆτερ, ἄνερ.

compare.title: Family words across the languages
gloss: Greek: clansman; Latin and English: brother
compare.note: All cognates except Latin fīlia: Latin lost the old word for ‘daughter’ that Greek and English kept. Greek φράτηρ shifted from ‘brother’ to ‘member of a clan’; for a real brother Greek uses ἀδελφός ‘from the same womb’.

blocks.tip: Always learn **nominative, genitive and gender** together: *φύλαξ, -ακος, ὁ*. Some endings tell you the gender: *-μα* is always neuter; abstracts in *-της, -τητος* are feminine (*ἡ ἰσότης* ‘equality’, *ἡ νεότης* ‘youth’). And nouns in *-ις* with an **unaccented** *ι* make the accusative in *-ιν*, not *-ιδα*: *χάρις, χάριτος*, acc. *χάριν* ‘favour, grace’.

items.t: Πάτερ ἡμῶν ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς
items.en: Our Father in heaven (Matthew 6:9 — vocative πάτερ)
items.lit: Father of us, the one in the heavens

items.t: τὸ μὲν σῶμά ἐστιν ἡμῖν σῆμα.
items.en: The body is our tomb. (Plato, Gorgias 493a — a pun on σῶμα and σῆμα)
A man’s character is his destiny. (Heraclitus)
items.lit: character for a human being is a daimon

items.t: ἀνδρῶν γὰρ ἐπιφανῶν πᾶσα γῆ τάφος.
items.en: For famous men the whole earth is their tomb. (Thucydides 2.43, Pericles’ Funeral Speech)

items.t: ὁ γέρων τοῖς ῥήτορσιν οὐ πιστεύει.
items.en: The old man does not trust the speakers.

items.t: οἱ φύλακες διὰ τῆς νυκτὸς φυλάττουσιν.
items.en: The guards keep watch through the night.

items.t: ἐλπίδες ἐν ζωοῖσιν, ἀνέλπιστοι δὲ θανόντες.
items.en: Hopes are for the living; the dead have none. (Theocritus 4.42 — epic-Doric dative ζωοῖσιν)

blocks.p: A noun whose nominative (*νύξ*) looks different from all its other forms is awkward, and spoken Greek gradually fixed the problem. It took the **accusative singular** — the most frequent form — and built a new, regular noun on it. **Feminines** simply used the accusative as their new nominative: *γυναῖκα* → *η γυναίκα*, *ἐλπίδα* → *η ελπίδα*, *νύκτα* → *η νύχτα* (with the regular change of *κτ* to *χτ*). **Masculines** added *-ς*, like first-declension masculines in *-ας*: *πατέρα* → *ο πατέρας*, *φύλακα* → *ο φύλακας*. The nominative plural in *-ες* took over the accusative plural too — and spread from there to the first declension (*οι χώρες*, Chapter 4).

compare.title: ‘Woman’ then and now
compare.note: Ancient γυνή was irregular even by third-declension standards; Modern γυναίκα declines like any noun in -α.

compare.title: New nouns from old accusatives
compare.note: English derivatives are built on the stem, not the nominative: γυναικ- in gynaecology, ἀνδρ- in android, γεροντ- in gerontology, φυλακ- in prophylactic. Metropolis is μητρόπολις ‘mother city’.

blocks.p: The neuters in *-μα* needed no repair, and they survive **intact**, ancient stem, endings and accent shifts included: *το σώμα, του σώματος, τα σώματα, των σωμάτων*. Modern Greek keeps adding to the class: *πρόβλημα, πρόγραμμα, θέμα, σύστημα, μήνυμα* ‘message’.

compare.title: Neuters in -μα and their -ματ- stem
compare.note: English adjectives in -matic preserve the Greek stem -ματ-; learned plurals such as stigmata and schemata keep the Greek plural -ματα.

blocks.p: One more English footnote: *octopus* is *ὀκτώπους* ‘eight-foot’, a third-declension noun with stem *ὀκτωποδ-*. Its Greek plural would be *octopodes*; *octopi* is a false Latin plural.

parts.title: Liquids and nasals: δαίμων, ῥήτωρ, γέρων

title: Third Declension II: Vowel Stems and s-Stems
sub: πόλις, βασιλεύς, γένος, ἰχθύς — and two famous irregulars

blocks.h: When stems end in a vowel

blocks.p: The rest of the third declension consists of stems ending in a **vowel** (*ι, υ*), a **diphthong** (*ευ, αυ, ου*) or a **σ** that has since vanished. The endings are the familiar ones from Chapter 7, but two old sound changes blur them: vowels that came into contact after a *σ* or a *w*-sound dropped out between them **contracted**, and in a few forms a long and a short vowel **swapped their lengths** (*ηο* → *εω*), a change called quantitative metathesis.

table.title: πόλις, -εως, ἡ ‘city, city-state’
table.note: The stem is πολι- in the nominative, accusative and vocative singular, πολε- everywhere else. Declined the same way: the hundreds of feminine abstracts in -σις, such as φύσις ‘nature’, κρίσις ‘judgement’, ποίησις ‘making, poetry’, τάξις ‘order’, στάσις ‘civil strife’, and also δύναμις ‘power’.

blocks.pitfall: *πόλεως* and *πόλεων* break the accent rules: an acute on the antepenult despite a long ultima. The accent was fixed when the form was still *πόληος* (Homer has *πόληος* and *πόλιος*); then the vowels swapped lengths, *ηο* → *εω*, and the accent stayed where it was. Note too that the nominative and accusative plural are both *πόλεις*.

table.title: βασιλεύς, -έως, ὁ ‘king’
table.note: The stem once ended in -ηϝ- (with the lost w-sound digamma): Homer still says βασιλῆος, which became Attic βασιλέως by the same length-swap as πόλεως. Declined the same way: ἱερεύς ‘priest’, ἱππεύς ‘horseman’, γραμματεύς ‘clerk, secretary’, and the heroes Ὀδυσσεύς and Ἀχιλλεύς.

blocks.p: Neuters like *γένος* ‘race, kind, family’ had a stem *γενεσ-*. At the end of the word it appears as *γένος*; but between vowels Greek lost its *σ*, so *γένεσ-ος* became *γένεος* — the form still used by Homer and Herodotus — and Attic contracted that to *γένους*. The plural *γένεσ-α* went the same way: *γένεα* → *γένη*.

table.title: γένος, -ους, τό ‘race, kind, family’
table.note: Declined the same way: ἔθνος ‘nation, people’, ἔτος ‘year’, ὄρος ‘mountain’, μέρος ‘part’, τέλος ‘end’, τεῖχος ‘wall’, πάθος ‘experience, suffering’, ἦθος ‘character’.

blocks.pitfall: *γένος* and *ὄρος* look like second-declension masculines (*λόγος*), but they are third-declension **neuters**: genitive *γένους*, not *γένου*; plural *γένη*, not *γένοι*. Always check the article and the genitive in the dictionary — and do not confuse *τὸ ὄρος* ‘mountain’ with *ὁ ὅρος* ‘boundary’.

blocks.p: The same *σ*-stems are hidden in many personal names in *-ης* and *-κλῆς*. Their vocatives are among the best-known words in Greek literature — Plato’s dialogues are full of *ὦ Σώκρατες*.

table.title: Σωκράτης and Περικλῆς
table.note: Σωκράτης also has a first-declension accusative Σωκράτην. Like Περικλῆς: Σοφοκλῆς, Θεμιστοκλῆς, Ἡρακλῆς.

blocks.h: ἰχθύς: stems in υ, and two irregulars

table.title: ἰχθύς, -ύος, ὁ ‘fish’
table.note: No surprises except the contracted accusative plural ἰχθῦς. Like ἰχθύς: μῦς, μυός ‘mouse’, δρῦς, δρυός ‘oak’. Early Christians read ΙΧΘΥΣ as an acrostic: Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς Θεοῦ Υἱὸς Σωτήρ.

table.title: βοῦς ‘ox, cow’ and ναῦς ‘ship’
table.note: Two ancient words with Latin and English relatives: βοῦς, Latin bōs and English cow are cognates; ναῦς and Latin nāvis (navy, naval) are too. The Bosporus is the ‘ox-ford’.

items.t: ἄνδρες γὰρ πόλις, καὶ οὐ τείχη οὐδὲ νῆες ἀνδρῶν κεναί.
items.en: For men are the city, not walls nor ships empty of men. (Thucydides 7.77, Nicias to his army)
Let there be one lord, one king. (Iliad 2.204–205)
King of kings and Lord of lords. (Revelation 19:16)
What are you saying, Socrates?
Nature does nothing in vain. (an Aristotelian principle)
The priest sacrifices to the gods.

blocks.p: *πόλις* lost the final *-ν* of its accusative *πόλιν*, and since *ι* and *η* sound the same, it joined the feminines in *-η* such as *γνώμη*: **η πόλη**, everyday genitive *της πόλης*. But the plural is still the ancient one — *οι πόλεις, των πόλεων* — and formal Greek keeps the learned genitive *της πόλεως*, as in the title of the Ecumenical Patriarch, *Πατριάρχης Κωνσταντινουπόλεως*. All the abstracts in *-σις* did the same: *η φύση, η λύση, η ανάλυση, η κρίση, η τάξη*, plural *κρίσεις, τάξεις*. (*Εντάξει* ‘OK’ is the old dative *ἐν τάξει*, Chapter 3.)

*βασιλεύς* was rebuilt from its accusative, just like the consonant stems of Chapter 7: *βασιλέα* → *βασιλιά* → **ο βασιλιάς**, plural *οι βασιλιάδες*. Other nouns in *-εύς* turned into *-έας* in the same way: *ἱερέα* → *ο ιερέας* ‘priest’, *γραμματέα* → *ο γραμματέας* ‘secretary’, *συγγραφέα* → *ο συγγραφέας* ‘author’.

The neuter *s*-stems survive **unchanged**: *το γένος, του γένους, τα γένη, των γενών*; likewise *έθνος, έτος, μέρος, τέλος, πάθος, τείχος*, and *κράτος*, which has moved from ancient ‘might, power’ to Modern ‘state’.

compare.title: One stem, two fates
compare.note: Greek γένος and Latin genus are the same inherited s-stem (English kin is a native cognate). Between vowels Greek dropped the s and contracted the vowels; Latin turned it into r, as in flōs, flōris. Hence English generic and general beside Greek-derived genealogy.

compare.title: Third-declension words in Modern Greek and English
compare.note: Some everyday words were replaced: ψάρι comes from ὀψάριον, a diminutive of ὄψον ‘cooked food eaten with bread’, since fish was the relish par excellence; βόδι from the diminutive βοΐδιον; πλοίο from ancient πλοῖον ‘vessel’. ναῦς lives on in ναύτης ‘sailor’ and ναυτία ‘seasickness’, the source of nausea.
