ἰχθύς: stems in υ, and two irregulars

title: Middle and Passive
sub: λύομαι, λύεσθαι, the meaning of the middle voice, and deponent verbs

blocks.p: Latin and English have two voices, active and passive. Greek has three: **active** (*λύω* ‘I free’), **passive** (‘I am freed’) and **middle**, in which the subject acts on itself, for itself, or with some personal involvement (*λύομαι* ‘I free for myself’, i.e. ‘I ransom’). In the **present and imperfect** the middle and passive share one set of forms, and only context tells them apart; the future and aorist give the passive its own forms (later chapters).

table.title: λύομαι — present middle/passive indicative
table.note: Infinitive: λύεσθαι. Middle ‘I ransom, I free for myself’; passive ‘I am (being) freed’. The 2nd singular λύῃ is contracted from λύεσαι after the σ between vowels was lost; many Attic texts spell it λύει.

blocks.p: The endings are *-ομαι, -ῃ, -εται, -ομεθα, -εσθε, -ονται*, infinitive *-εσθαι*: thematic vowel plus the middle endings *-μαι, -σαι, -ται, -μεθα, -σθε, -νται*. The accent is recessive as always: *λυόμεθα* has a short ultima, so the accent sits on the antepenult.

compare.title: Greek middle, Latin passive
compare.note: ἄγω and agō are the same Indo-European verb. Latin built its passive with -r; Greek used its middle endings, so a Greek form like ἄγομαι can also be middle: ‘I lead for myself’, e.g. ἄγομαι γυναῖκα ‘I take a wife’.

blocks.p: A passive verb makes the object of the action its subject. The **agent** (the person doing it) is expressed with *ὑπό* + genitive, the **instrument** with the plain dative — just as Latin uses *ā/ab* + ablative for the agent and the bare ablative for the means: *ὁ παῖς ὑπὸ τοῦ διδασκάλου διδάσκεται* ‘the boy is taught by the teacher’; *ἡ πόλις τείχεσι φυλάττεται* ‘the city is guarded by walls’.

The middle shows that the action concerns the subject itself. Sometimes it is simply **reflexive** (*λούομαι* ‘I wash myself, bathe’); more often the subject acts **for its own benefit** (*λύομαι* ‘I free for myself’ = ‘ransom’); and in many verbs the middle has developed a **meaning of its own**. In the first book of the Iliad, the priest Chryses comes to the Greek camp to ransom his daughter: *λυσόμενός τε θύγατρα* ‘to free his daughter for himself’, with the middle.

blocks.tip: Think of the middle as ‘the subject is in it up to the elbows’. English has no such voice, but French and Spanish reflexives come close: *λούομαι* is *je me lave*, *me lavo*; *παύομαι* is *je m’arrête*, *me detengo*.

blocks.p: Many verbs exist only in middle form but have an active meaning. Latin grammar calls such verbs **deponents** (as if they had ‘laid aside’ their active forms). Several of them describe actions in which the subject is deeply involved — receiving, fighting, perceiving, becoming — exactly the territory of the middle.

blocks.pitfall: Two traps. (1) *βούλομαι* and *οἴομαι* always have the 2nd singular in *-ει*: *βούλει* ‘you want’, *οἴει* ‘you think’ — never *-ῃ*. (2) Attic *γίγνομαι* and *γιγνώσκω* ‘know’ are spelled *γίνομαι* and *γινώσκω* in Ionic and in the Koine — the New Testament has *γίνομαι* — so look up both spellings.

compare.title: Deponent in one language, not in another
compare.note: ἕπομαι and sequor are the same verb, deponent in both languages; the Greek h- comes from an earlier s-, as in ἑπτά and septem. γί-γν-ομαι and Latin gi-gn-ō share a reduplicated present from the root of genus. But deponency is no rule across languages: Latin pugnō and veniō are active.

items.t: πάντες ἄνθρωποι τοῦ εἰδέναι ὀρέγονται φύσει.
items.en: All human beings by nature desire to know. (Aristotle, Metaphysics 1.1 — ὀρέγομαι ‘reach out for’ is deponent)
I grow old, always learning many things. (Solon)
items.lit: I grow old ever being taught many things

items.en: What do you want?

items.t: ὁ παῖς ὑπὸ τοῦ διδασκάλου διδάσκεται.
items.en: The boy is taught by the teacher.
One must obey the laws.
The soldiers are fighting the enemy.
The general ransoms his son.
items.lit: the general frees the son for himself

blocks.p: Modern Greek kept the middle-passive conjugation alive — something Latin’s heirs did not do. Every transitive verb has a mediopassive in *-ομαι*: *λύνω* ‘I untie, solve’ → *λύνομαι* ‘I am untied, solved’; *γράφω* → *γράφεται* ‘it is written’. The endings have hardly moved.

compare.title: λύομαι and λύνομαι
compare.note: The Modern present λύνω is a new formation; the ancient λύω survives in the aorist έλυσα.

blocks.p: Three details changed. The 2nd singular *-εσαι* has its *σ* back, remodelled on forms like *δύνασαι* ‘you can’. The cluster *σθ* became *στ* in everyday speech, so *-εσθε* → *-εστε* (likewise *χθ* → *χτ*, *φθ* → *φτ*). And the infinitive *-εσθαι* disappeared, surviving only in learned fossils such as *το φαίνεσθαι* ‘appearances’.

The **deponents** are still there — *έρχομαι, γίνομαι, δέχομαι, αισθάνομαι* — joined by many more: *σκέφτομαι* ‘think’ (ancient *σκέπτομαι* ‘consider’), *κάθομαι* ‘sit’, *σέβομαι* ‘respect’, *χρειάζομαι* ‘need’. And so is the old reflexive sense of the middle: *λούζω* ‘wash (someone)’ / *λούζομαι* ‘wash oneself’, *ντύνω* ‘dress (someone)’ / *ντύνομαι* ‘get dressed’, *πείθω* ‘persuade’ / *πείθομαι* ‘become convinced’. Even ‘to be’ joined the class: *είμαι* (Chapter 5).

Latin went the other way. Its passive in *-r* vanished from all the Romance languages, replaced by ‘be’ + participle or by reflexive constructions, and its deponents turned active: *sequī* ‘to follow’ became Italian *seguire*, Spanish *seguir*, French *suivre*.

compare.title: Synthetic passive: kept in Greek, lost in Romance
compare.note: Modern Greek replaced ἕπομαι with ακολουθώ (ancient ἀκολουθέω), so ‘follow’ lost its deponent form on both sides.

title: The Imperfect and the Augment
sub: Past action in progress, and the little ἐ- that marks the past

blocks.p: The **imperfect** is the past tense of the present stem. It presents a past action as **going on**, **repeated** or **attempted**: *ἔλυον* ‘I was loosening, I used to loosen, I tried to loosen’. It corresponds closely to the Latin imperfect (*solvēbam*), and Greek grammarians named it *παρατατικός* ‘extending’, because the action is stretched out in time.

It is formed from **augment + present stem + secondary endings**. The secondary endings are the set used in past tenses: active *-ον, -ες, -ε(ν), -ομεν, -ετε, -ον*; middle-passive *-όμην, -ου, -ετο, -όμεθα, -εσθε, -οντο*.

table.title: Imperfect of λύω
table.note: Active: ‘I was loosening’ etc. Middle: ‘I was ransoming’; passive: ‘I was being loosed’. ἐλύου comes from ἐλύεσο: the σ between vowels was lost and εο contracted to ου. The imperfect has no infinitive of its own.

blocks.pitfall: In the active, the 1st singular and the 3rd plural are identical: *ἔλυον* is ‘I was loosening’ **or** ‘they were loosening’. A subject in the nominative plural, or the context, decides.

blocks.p: The **augment** is a prefix that marks **past time**. It appears only in the **indicative** of the past tenses — imperfect, aorist and pluperfect — never in infinitives or participles. It is old: Sanskrit has it too, and Sanskrit *ábharam* ‘I was carrying’ is letter for letter Greek *ἔφερον*. Latin has no augment and marks its imperfect with a suffix instead (*ferēbam*).

**Syllabic augment.** A verb beginning with a consonant adds a syllable *ἐ-*: *λύω* → *ἔλυον*, *γράφω* → *ἔγραφον*, *πέμπω* → *ἔπεμπον*. After the augment, initial *ρ* is doubled: *ῥίπτω* ‘throw’ → *ἔρριπτον*.

**Temporal augment.** A verb beginning with a vowel or diphthong **lengthens** it instead (*temporal* because it adds time, i.e. length). Short *α* and *ε* become *η*, *ο* becomes *ω*, and diphthongs lengthen their first element.

table.title: The temporal augment
table.note: ει and ευ are often left unchanged: εὑρίσκω → ηὕρισκον or εὕρισκον.

blocks.p: A few verbs augment unexpectedly because they once began with a consonant that has since disappeared. *ἔχω* ‘have’ originally began with *σ*: the augmented form was *ἐ-σεχον*, the *σ* dropped out, and *ἔεχον* contracted to **εἶχον** ‘I had’. In the same way *ἕπομαι* ‘follow’ makes *εἱπόμην*. And *ἐθέλω* and its shorter twin *θέλω* both make *ἤθελον*.

In a verb with a prepositional prefix, the augment goes **between the prefix and the verb**. A prefix ending in a vowel loses it (except *περι-* and *προ-*), and *ἐκ-* becomes *ἐξ-*: *ἀπο-φεύγω* → *ἀπέφευγον* ‘I was escaping’, *ἐκ-βάλλω* → *ἐξέβαλλον* ‘I was throwing out’, *προσ-φέρω* → *προσέφερον* ‘I was bringing to’, *προ-πέμπω* → *προὔπεμπον* ‘I was escorting’. The recessive accent cannot jump back over the augment: *παρ-έχω* ‘provide’ → *παρεῖχον*.

blocks.tip: To look up an augmented compound, undo the process: take out the augment from between prefix and stem and restore the prefix’s vowel. *ἀπέφευγον* → *ἀπο-* + *ἔφευγον* → *ἀποφεύγω*.

table.title: Imperfect of εἰμί ‘I was’
table.note: The ἦν of John 1:1, Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος. Unlike the present, these forms are not enclitic.

blocks.p: The imperfect has three main uses: **progressive** (‘was doing’), **habitual** (‘used to do’) and **conative** (‘tried to do’): *ἔπειθε* can mean ‘he tried to persuade’. In narrative it paints the background, the ongoing situation, while the aorist (next chapter) moves the story forward. Homer, by the way, often leaves out the augment altogether: *βῆ* for *ἔβη* ‘he went’.

items.en: Socrates used to teach the young.
The enemy were fleeing.

items.t: ἔπειθε τοὺς πολίτας, ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἐπείθοντο.
items.en: He tried to persuade the citizens, but they would not listen.
items.lit: he was persuading the citizens, but they were not obeying

items.en: I wanted to learn.
The Athenians had many ships.

items.t: ἦσαν ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ πολλοὶ ἄνθρωποι.
items.en: There were many people in the market-place.

items.t: βῆ δ’ ἀκέων παρὰ θῖνα πολυφλοίσβοιο θαλάσσης.
items.en: He went in silence along the shore of the loud-roaring sea. (Iliad 1.34 — βῆ is an aorist without augment)

blocks.p: Modern Greek still has the imperfect — its grammars use the very same name, *παρατατικός* — and still marks it with the augment. But the endings changed: the imperfect borrowed the *-α-* endings of the aorist (*έγραψα*, next chapter), so *ἔγραφον* became **έγραφα**.

Where has the augment gone in *γράφαμε*? The rule of the spoken language is that the past tenses are stressed on the **third syllable from the end**, and the syllabic augment survives **only when it carries that stress**. *έ-γρα-φα* needs an extra syllable to stress, so the augment stays; *γρά-φα-με* already has three syllables, so it drops. Verbs with longer stems never show it: *διάβαζα* ‘I was reading’, *αγόραζα* ‘I was buying’. Learned compounds keep an internal augment under the same condition: *υπογράφω* ‘sign’ → *υπέγραψα* ‘I signed’, but *υπογράψαμε* ‘we signed’.

The **temporal** augment is dead in the spoken language, apart from a few fossils inherited from ancient augmented forms: *ήθελα* ‘I wanted’ (from *ἤθελον*), which drops its *η-* in *θέλαμε*; and *είχα* ‘I had’ (from *εἶχον*), whose *ει-* has become part of the stem and stays everywhere: *είχαμε, είχατε*.

Latin and the Romance languages build the same tense in a completely different way, with a suffix, Latin *-bā-* (probably from the same root as *fuī* ‘I was’). The suffix survives in Spanish *-aba*, and in reduced form everywhere else.

compare.title: The Latin imperfect in Romance
gloss: I was singing, used to sing
compare.note: Romance kept the Latin distinction between an ongoing past (imperfect) and a completed past — the same contrast Greek draws between the imperfect and the aorist (Chapter 11).

title: The Future, the First Aorist and Aspect
sub: λύσω, ἔλυσα, and the difference between ‘was writing’ and ‘wrote’

blocks.p: A Greek verb is built on several **stems**, each carrying its own family of forms. So far you have met the **present stem** (*λυ-*), which gives the present and the imperfect. This chapter adds two more, both marked by a *σ*: the **future stem** *λυσ-* and the **aorist stem** *λυσα-*.

The future is formed by adding **σ** to the verb stem and then the endings of the present: *λύσω* ‘I shall loosen’. It has a middle (*λύσομαι* ‘I shall ransom’) — but here, unlike in the present, the middle is **only** middle: the passive future has forms of its own, met later.

When the stem ends in a consonant, the *σ* combines with it exactly as in the third declension (Chapter 7): a **labial** + *σ* gives *ψ* (*πέμπω* → *πέμψω*, *γράφω* → *γράψω*); a **velar** + *σ* gives *ξ* (*ἄγω* → *ἄξω*, *ἄρχω* → *ἄρξω*, *διδάσκω* → *διδάξω*, *φυλάττω* → *φυλάξω*); a **dental** disappears (*πείθω* → *πείσω*, *σῴζω* → *σώσω*). Verbs with stems in *λ μ ν ρ* form a contracted future instead (*μένω* ‘stay’ → *μενῶ*), which comes later.

Many common verbs — especially verbs of perceiving, moving and the body — have a **middle future with active meaning**: *ἀκούω* → *ἀκούσομαι* ‘I shall hear’, *φεύγω* → *φεύξομαι* ‘I shall flee’, *μανθάνω* → *μαθήσομαι* ‘I shall learn’, and *εἰμί* → *ἔσομαι* ‘I shall be’ (3rd sg. *ἔσται*).

The **aorist** is the Greek simple past: *ἔλυσα* ‘I loosened’. The **first** (or **sigmatic**) aorist is formed with **augment + stem + σα + endings**. Its infinitive, like every non-indicative form, has **no augment**: *λῦσαι* ‘to loosen’. The aorist middle is again only middle (*ἐλυσάμην* ‘I ransomed’); the aorist passive (*ἐλύθην*) is a separate formation.

table.title: First aorist of λύω
table.note: ἐλύσω comes from ἐλύσασο (σ lost, αο contracted to ω). λῦσαι has a circumflex because final -αι counts as short.

blocks.pitfall: Future and aorist share their *σ*; the **augment** and the **α** tell them apart. *λύσει* ‘he will loosen’, but *ἔλυσε* ‘he loosened’. And because the aorist infinitive *λῦσαι* has no augment, beginners often take it for a future — look for the *-σαι* ending.

blocks.p: What is the difference between the imperfect *ἔγραφον* ‘I was writing’ and the aorist *ἔγραψα* ‘I wrote’? Not time — both are past — but **aspect**, the way the speaker views the action. The **present stem** is **imperfective**: it shows the action from inside, as ongoing, repeated or unfinished. The **aorist stem** is **perfective**: it shows the action from outside, as a single complete event. Ancient grammarians called the aorist *ἀόριστος* ‘undefined, unbounded’ — it says nothing about duration. (A third aspect, the perfect, comes later.)

In the **indicative**, aspect combines with time: present, imperfect and aorist. **Outside the indicative** — infinitives, imperatives, subjunctives, participles — the difference is **purely one of aspect**, with no difference of time at all. *βούλομαι γράφειν* ‘I want to be writing, to write regularly’; *βούλομαι γράψαι* ‘I want to write (it, once)’. The aorist infinitive is by far the more common.

table.title: One verb, two aspects
table.note: γράφω ‘I write, am writing’; ἔγραφον ‘I was writing, used to write’; ἔγραψα ‘I wrote’; γράφειν ‘to be writing’; γράψαι ‘to write (once)’. There is no perfective present: an action seen as a complete whole cannot be in progress now. The future γράψω has one form, neutral as to aspect.

blocks.tip: With verbs describing a **state**, the aorist often marks the **entry** into that state — the ‘ingressive’ aorist: *ἐβασίλευε* ‘he was king, he reigned’, but *ἐβασίλευσε* ‘he became king’; *ἐπίστευε* ‘he believed, trusted’, but *ἐπίστευσε* ‘he came to believe’.

items.en: I wrote the letter and sent it.
The old man used to teach the children. (imperfect: habit)
The old man taught the children. (aorist: a completed fact)
And Abraham believed God. (Romans 4:3)
And I will give you rest. (Matthew 11:28)
The general saved the city.
The young man became king.
I want to write a letter.

blocks.p: If a single feature links Homer to a Greek speaking today, it is **aspect**. Every Modern Greek verb still has two stems, an imperfective one (*γράφ-*) and a perfective one (*γράψ-*), and almost every form must choose between them — not only in the past, but in the future, the subjunctive and the imperative: *θα γράφω* ‘I’ll be writing, I’ll write regularly’ versus *θα γράψω* ‘I’ll write (it)’.

table.title: The Modern Greek verb: two stems everywhere
table.note: The perfective non-past γράψω cannot stand alone; it needs θα or να (or another particle). Ancient imperatives: γράφε, γράψον.

blocks.p: The ancient future did not survive as such. The new future is built with **θα**, worn down in the Middle Ages from *θέλει να* ‘wants that’ (*θέλω* + *ἵνα*), followed by either stem. The perfective form after it, *γράψω*, continues the ancient **aorist subjunctive** *γράψω* — which by chance looked just like the ancient future.

compare.title: Present, future, aorist — then and now
compare.note: The σ of the ancient aorist is still the perfective marker; after ευ it now appears as ψ (πιστέψω). The temporal augment of ἤκουσα has gone, and the syllabic augment appears only under stress (Chapter 10).

blocks.p: Latin went another way. It merged the inherited aorist and perfect into one tense, the Latin **perfect**, so *scrīpsī* means both ‘I wrote’ and ‘I have written’ — and its *s* is the same old aorist *σ* as in *ἔγραψα*. Aspect survived in Latin only in the past, as imperfect versus perfect, and that is what Romance inherited: Italian *passato remoto* *scrissi* (from *scrīpsī*) against *imperfetto* *scrivevo*, Spanish *escribí* against *escribía*, French *j’écrivis* against *j’écrivais*. None of them distinguishes aspect in the future, as Modern Greek does.

compare.title: Where aspect is marked
compare.note: In the past, all six languages draw the line. In the future, only Modern Greek does: the ancient future, Latin and Romance have a single form.

title: The Second Aorist and Principal Parts
sub: ἔλιπον, ἦλθον, εἶδον, εἶπον — and how to learn a Greek verb

blocks.h: A second way to make an aorist

blocks.p: Many of the commonest Greek verbs do not form their aorist with *-σα*. Instead they have a **second** (or ‘strong’) **aorist**: a different, usually shorter stem with the **endings of the imperfect**. *λείπω* ‘I leave’ → *ἔλιπον* ‘I left’. The meaning is exactly that of a first aorist — a completed action seen as a whole — and a verb normally has one kind or the other.

table.title: Second aorist of λείπω ‘leave’
table.note: The infinitives break the recessive rule and accent the ending: λιπεῖν, λιπέσθαι. As always, the infinitive has no augment.

blocks.pitfall: Imperfect *ἔλειπον* ‘I was leaving’ and aorist *ἔλιπον* ‘I left’ have **identical endings**; only the stem differs. Always compare the stem with the present: if it is the present stem (*λειπ-*), the form is imperfect; if it is different (*λιπ-*), it is aorist.

blocks.p: Often the aorist stem is the **bare root**, and the present is the form that has been enlarged: by a nasal (*λαμβάνω* from *λαβ-*, *μανθάνω* from *μαθ-*, *τυγχάνω* from *τυχ-*), by *-ισκ-* (*εὑρίσκω* from *εὑρ-*), by doubling a consonant (*βάλλω* from *βαλ-*) or by a fuller vowel (*λείπω* from *λιπ-*, *φεύγω* from *φυγ-*). Aeschylus’ maxim *πάθει μάθος* ‘learning through suffering’ (Agamemnon 177) is made of two such roots: *παθ-* from *ἔπαθον* and *μαθ-* from *ἔμαθον*.

table.title: Common second aorists
table.note: ἤγαγον has a doubled (reduplicated) stem ἀγαγ-. Deponents such as γίγνομαι have a middle second aorist.

blocks.p: Some of the most frequent verbs take their aorist from an entirely **different root** — the phenomenon called **suppletion**, familiar from English *go – went* and Latin *ferō – tulī*. These forms are everywhere in Greek texts; learn them early.

table.title: Suppletive aorists
table.note: εἶδον goes back to ἐ-ϝιδ-ον, from the root ϝιδ- ‘see’ (with the lost w-sound digamma), the root of Latin vidēre and English wit and wise. εἶπον belongs with ἔπος ‘word’, originally ϝέπος, cousin of Latin vōx. ἤνεγκα mixes first-aorist endings into a second aorist.

blocks.tip: English is full of aorist stems: *ἰδεῖν* → *idea* (*ἰδέα* ‘look, form’); *ἔφαγον* → *sarcophagus* ‘flesh-eater’, *oesophagus*; *παθεῖν* → *pathos, sympathy*; *μαθεῖν* → *mathematics* (*μάθημα* ‘lesson’); *εὑρεῖν* → *heuristic*; *λαβεῖν* → *syllable* (*συλλαβή* ‘a taking together’).

blocks.p: Since a verb’s stems cannot be predicted from the present, Greek verbs are learned by their **principal parts**: up to six forms from which every other form can be built — **present, future, aorist, perfect active, perfect middle/passive, aorist passive**. Latin has the same habit on a smaller scale (*amō, amāre, amāvī, amātum*). You will meet the last three parts in later chapters; for now, learn present, future and aorist, but notice the full set.

table.title: Principal parts of ten verbs
table.note: Attic uses εἶμι ‘I shall go’ as the future of ἔρχομαι. λήψομαι, ὄψομαι and ἔδομαι are middle futures with active meaning. ὁράω uses three roots: ὁρα- ‘see’, ἰδ- in εἶδον, and ὀπ- in ὄψομαι and ὤφθην — the root of optics.

items.en: I came, I saw, I conquered. (Caesar’s veni, vidi, vici in Plutarch’s Greek, Life of Caesar 50)

items.t: καὶ εἶπεν ὁ θεός· γενηθήτω φῶς. καὶ ἐγένετο φῶς.
items.en: And God said, Let there be light; and there was light. (Genesis 1:3 in the Septuagint)
I escaped the bad, I found the better. (formula of a mystery rite, quoted by Demosthenes, On the Crown 259)
We ate and drank in your presence. (Luke 13:26)
Cyrus died in the battle.
The boy threw the stone.
The enemy fled.

blocks.p: The Modern Greek aorist is the ancient aorist — and many of the most common ones are ancient **second aorists**, now with the *-α* endings of the first aorist. The mixing had begun already in the Koine: the New Testament has *εἶπαν* ‘they said’ and *ἦλθαν* ‘they came’ (Luke 2:16) beside *εἶπον* and *ἦλθον*. Today: *έφαγα, έφαγες, έφαγε, φάγαμε, φάγατε, έφαγαν*, with the augment appearing only under stress (Chapter 10).

compare.title: Second aorists in Modern Greek
compare.note: The suppletive pairs survived even where the present was replaced: βλέπω · είδα, τρώω · έφαγα. ήρθα comes from Koine ἦλθα, with λ turning into ρ before θ (compare colloquial αδερφός for αδελφός). And βρήκα ‘I found’ continues Archimedes’ εὕρηκα — an ancient perfect.

blocks.p: The perfective forms after *να* and *θα* continue ancient **aorist subjunctives**, and they show the bare aorist roots very clearly: *να δω* ‘to see’ is *ἵνα ἴδω*, *να πω* ‘to say’ is *ἵνα εἴπω*. So the Modern Greek for ‘I want to see’ — *θέλω να δω* — contains the same root *ἰδ-* as *idea*.

compare.title: Ancient aorist subjunctives inside Modern Greek

blocks.p: The second aorist is an inheritance from Indo-European, and Latin and English show its relatives. The vowel shift of *λείπω – ἔλιπον – λέλοιπα* (*ει – ι – οι*), called **ablaut**, is the very same alternation as English *drive – driven – drove*; and suppletion is shared too.

compare.title: Roots and vowel shifts across the family
gloss: εἶδον, vīdī and English wit share one root
φέρω, ferō and bear are cognates; Greek and Latin took their past tense from other roots
λείπω and linquō are cognates; ει – ι – οι is the same ablaut series as English i – i – o

parts.title: A second way to make an aorist

title: Pronouns and Demonstratives
sub: ἐγώ and σύ, the three faces of αὐτός, and οὗτος, ὅδε, ἐκεῖνος

blocks.p: Greek verbs already show the person, so the nominatives *ἐγώ* ‘I’ and *σύ* ‘you’ appear only for **emphasis or contrast**: *ἐγὼ μὲν γράφω, σὺ δὲ παίζεις* ‘**I** am writing, but **you** are playing’. In the other cases of the singular there are two sets of forms: **emphatic**, accented ones (*ἐμοῦ, ἐμοί, ἐμέ*), used for stress and usually after prepositions (*πρὸς ἐμέ* ‘to me’), and **unemphatic** enclitic ones (*μου, μοι, με*). In the second person the two sets differ only in accent: *σοῦ* / *σου*.

table.title: ἐγώ ‘I’ and σύ ‘you’
table.note: ἡμ- ‘we, us’ and ὑμ- ‘you’ differ only in the first letter and the breathing — read carefully.

blocks.p: To say ‘my’ and ‘your’, the New Testament usually puts the enclitic genitive after the noun: *ὁ πατήρ μου* ‘my father’. Classical Attic prefers **possessive adjectives** in attributive position: *ὁ ἐμὸς πατήρ* ‘my father’, *ὁ σὸς φίλος* ‘your friend’, *ἡ ἡμετέρα πόλις* ‘our city’, *ὁ ὑμέτερος οἶκος* ‘your (pl.) house’.

Attic has no ordinary word for ‘he, she, it’ in the nominative: the verb ending does the work, and when emphasis is needed a demonstrative (*οὗτος, ἐκεῖνος*) steps in. For ‘him, her, it, them’ in the other cases Greek uses **αὐτός**.

table.title: αὐτός, αὐτή, αὐτό
table.note: Declined like ἀγαθός, except that the neuter singular has no -ν: αὐτό, like the article τό.

blocks.p: *αὐτός* has three distinct uses, and its **position** tells you which. **(1)** In predicate position next to a noun — outside the article — or alone in the nominative, it is **intensive**, ‘-self’: *αὐτὸς ὁ βασιλεύς* or *ὁ βασιλεὺς αὐτός* ‘the king himself’; *αὐτὸς ἦλθεν* ‘he came himself’. **(2)** In attributive position — after the article — it means **‘same’**: *ὁ αὐτὸς βασιλεύς* ‘the same king’, *τὸ αὐτό* (crasis *ταὐτό*) ‘the same thing’. **(3)** Alone in any case **except the nominative** it is the plain pronoun **‘him, her, it, them’**: *πέμπω αὐτόν* ‘I send him’.

blocks.tip: The followers of Pythagoras settled arguments with *αὐτὸς ἔφα* ‘he himself said so’ (Doric for Attic *ἔφη*) — the Master needed no other proof. Cicero translated it into Latin as *ipse dixit*, still used in English for an unsupported assertion.

blocks.pitfall: Breathings and accents matter here. *αὐτή* ‘she, the same, herself’ but *αὕτη* ‘this (woman)’; *αὐταί* ‘they (f.)’ but *αὗται* ‘these (women)’. And *αὑτός* with a rough breathing is the crasis of *ὁ αὐτός* ‘the same man’, while *αὑτοῦ* is the short form of the reflexive *ἑαυτοῦ* ‘of himself’.

blocks.p: Fused with personal pronouns, *αὐτός* forms the **reflexives**, which refer back to the subject and therefore have no nominative: *ἐμαυτόν* ‘myself’, *σεαυτόν* ‘yourself’, *ἑαυτόν* ‘himself’ (*ἑαυτήν* ‘herself’, *ἑαυτό* ‘itself’). Hence the Delphic *γνῶθι σεαυτόν* ‘know yourself’.

Greek has three demonstratives. **οὗτος** ‘this’ points to something near or **just mentioned**; **ὅδε** ‘this here’ points with emphasis, often to what **follows**; **ἐκεῖνος** ‘that’ points to something far away or to ‘the former’. With a noun, a demonstrative stands in **predicate position**, outside the article–noun group, and the noun keeps its article: *οὗτος ὁ ἀνήρ* or *ὁ ἀνὴρ οὗτος* ‘this man’ — never *ὁ οὗτος ἀνήρ*.

table.title: οὗτος, αὕτη, τοῦτο ‘this’
table.note: The feminine genitive plural is τούτων, like the masculine. Neuter singular τοῦτο, without -ν.

blocks.tip: *οὗτος* copies the article. Where the article has a rough breathing (*ὁ ἡ οἱ αἱ*), so does *οὗτος* (*οὗτος αὕτη οὗτοι αὗται*); everywhere else both begin with *τ-*. And where the article has an *ο*- or *ω*-sound, *οὗτος* has *ου*; where it has an *α*- or *η*-sound, *αυ*: *τοῦ* → *τούτου*, *τῶν* → *τούτων*, but *τῆς* → *ταύτης*, *τά* → *ταῦτα*.

table.title: ὅδε, ἥδε, τόδε ‘this here’
table.note: Simply the article + the enclitic -δε ‘here’; the accent follows the enclitic rules (ὅδε, τόνδε, τοῦδε).

table.title: ἐκεῖνος, ἐκείνη, ἐκεῖνο ‘that’
table.note: Declined like αὐτός, with neuter ἐκεῖνο. Related to ἐκεῖ ‘there’.

blocks.p: In practice *οὗτος* looks back and *ὅδε* looks forward: *ταῦτα εἶπεν* ‘he said this’ (what has just been reported), but *τάδε λέγει* ‘he says the following’. *ἐκεῖνος* can also mean ‘that famous’: *Σόλων ἐκεῖνος* ‘the famous Solon’.

items.t: οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ υἱός μου ὁ ἀγαπητός, ἐν ᾧ εὐδόκησα.
items.en: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. (Matthew 3:17)

items.t: ἐκεῖνον δεῖ αὐξάνειν, ἐμὲ δὲ ἐλαττοῦσθαι.
items.en: He must increase, but I must decrease. (John 3:30)
This is the presentation of the inquiry of Herodotus of Halicarnassus. (Herodotus 1.1, in Ionic — ἥδε points forward to the whole work)
Thus says the Lord. (a formula of the prophets in the Septuagint)

items.t: ποταμοῖς τοῖς αὐτοῖς ἐμβαίνομέν τε καὶ οὐκ ἐμβαίνομεν.
items.en: Into the same rivers we step and do not step. (Heraclitus)
The king himself came.
The same man said these things.

items.t: τὴν ἐπιστολὴν ἔγραψα καὶ ἔπεμψα αὐτὴν τῷ πατρί μου.
items.en: I wrote the letter and sent it to my father.

afterlife.title: From αὐτός to αυτός — and to τον, την, το

blocks.p: *αὐτός* had the most remarkable career of all Greek pronouns. In Modern Greek **αυτός, αυτή, αυτό** is the ordinary demonstrative **‘this’**, used exactly like ancient *οὗτος*, with the article and outside it: *αυτός ο άνθρωπος* ‘this man’. It is also the stressed pronoun **‘he, she, it’**: *αυτός δεν ξέρει* ‘**he** doesn’t know’. Its old meanings ‘-self’ and ‘same’ passed to **ο ίδιος**, from ancient *ἴδιος* ‘one’s own, private’: *ο ίδιος ο βασιλιάς* ‘the king himself’, *το ίδιο* ‘the same thing’. (English *idiot* comes from *ἰδιώτης* ‘a private person, a layman’.)

The **unstressed** forms of *αὐτός* lost their first syllable and became Modern Greek’s **weak object pronouns**: *αὐτόν* → **τον**, *αὐτήν* → **την**, *αὐτό* → **το**, *αὐτοῦ* → **του**, *αὐτῆς* → **της**, *αὐτούς* → **τους**. They look exactly like the article but stand before the verb: *τον βλέπω* ‘I see him’, *του το δίνω* ‘I give it to him’ — with the genitive *του* doing the old dative’s job. The 1st and 2nd persons did the same: *με, μου, σε, σου*, and *μας, σας* from *ἡμᾶς, ὑμᾶς*.

compare.title: Personal pronouns then and now
compare.note: Once η and υ both came to be pronounced [i], ἡμεῖς and ὑμεῖς sounded identical, and medieval scribes confused them constantly. Modern Greek rebuilt them as εμείς and εσείς. The possessive still follows the noun as in the New Testament: ο πατέρας μου, and the Lord’s Prayer begins Πατέρα μας.

blocks.p: Latin went through the same process. The demonstrative *ille* ‘that’ lost its first syllable when unstressed and became the Romance weak pronouns *lo, la, le* — and also the Romance definite article (*il, el, le*), something Greek did not need because it already had an article.

The other demonstratives fared differently. *ἐκεῖνος* lives on unchanged as *εκείνος, εκείνη, εκείνο* ‘that’, beside *εκεί* ‘there’. *οὗτος* survives only colloquially as *τούτος* ‘this one here’, and *ὅδε* has vanished from speech.

compare.title: Cognate pronouns
compare.note: Attic σύ comes from an earlier τύ, which Doric kept — matching Latin tū and English thou. And αὐτός gave English the prefix auto-: automatic, autonomy (‘own laws’), autopsy (‘seeing for oneself’); ταὐτό ‘the same’ gave tautology.

parts.title: From αὐτός to αυτός — and to τον, την, το

title: Contract Verbs
sub: -άω, -έω, -όω: what happens when vowels collide

blocks.p: A large group of verbs have stems ending in a vowel: *τιμά-ω* ‘I honour’, *ποιέ-ω* ‘I make, do’, *δηλό-ω* ‘I show’. In the **present** and **imperfect**, that stem vowel runs straight into the thematic vowel and the ending, and in Attic the two **contract** into one sound: *τιμάω* is actually pronounced and written *τιμῶ*, *ποιέω* is *ποιῶ*. Dictionaries list the uncontracted form so you can see which vowel the stem ends in; the endings themselves are the ones you already know from *λύω*.

Contraction is an Attic habit. Ionic often leaves *ε*-verbs open (Herodotus writes *ποιέει* where Attic has *ποιεῖ*), and Homer has both open and contracted forms, which is useful when reading epic: if a form looks odd, try ‘un-contracting’ or contracting it.

table.title: What the stem vowel does with each following sound
table.note: The infinitive ending -ειν contains a ‘spurious’ ει (it comes from -εεν), so it contracts as if it were a plain ε: τιμάειν → τιμᾶν (no iota subscript), δηλόειν → δηλοῦν.

blocks.tip: Three rules of thumb. **α-verbs**: an o-sound wins (→ ω), otherwise α wins (→ long ᾱ), and an ι survives as subscript. **ε-verbs**: ε + ε → ει, ε + ο → ου, and before any long vowel or diphthong the ε simply vanishes. **ο-verbs**: an o-sound everywhere (ου or ω), and an ι survives as οι.

blocks.p: **Accent.** Find the accent of the uncontracted form. If it stood on the **first** of the two vowels that merge, the contracted syllable takes a **circumflex**: *τιμάω → τιμῶ*, *ποιέει → ποιεῖ*. If it stood on the **second**, the result has an **acute**: *τιμαόμεθα → τιμώμεθα*. If neither vowel was accented, the accent is the normal recessive one: *ἐτίμαε → ἐτίμα*.

table.title: Present middle / passive
table.note: The 2 sg. comes from -άῃ / -έῃ / -όῃ (older -εσαι with the σ lost between vowels).

blocks.pitfall: Contraction creates look-alikes. *τιμᾷ* is both ‘he honours’ (from *τιμάει*) and ‘you are honoured’ (from *τιμάῃ*); *ἐτίμων* is both ‘I was honouring’ and ‘they were honouring’; and *τιμᾶτε* can be indicative or imperative. Context and the subject decide.

blocks.p: Contraction happens **only in the present and imperfect**. In every other tense the stem vowel is simply **lengthened** before the tense sign: *α → η* (but *ᾱ* after *ε, ι, ρ*), *ε → η*, *ο → ω*. So the principal parts of a contract verb are very regular.

table.title: Principal parts: the vowel lengthens
table.note: δράω keeps long ᾱ after ρ. A few verbs keep the short vowel, e.g. καλέω (aorist ἐκάλεσα), τελέω ‘finish’ (ἐτέλεσα), γελάω ‘laugh’ (ἐγέλασα). καλέω also has a contracted Attic future καλῶ, which looks exactly like a present.

table.title: Three irregular types
table.note: ζάω and χράομαι (also πεινάω ‘be hungry’, διψάω ‘be thirsty’) contract to η where other α-verbs have ᾱ. Two-syllable ε-verbs such as πλέω, πνέω ‘breathe’, θέω ‘run’ contract only ε + ε → ει and leave the other forms open. χράομαι takes its object in the dative.

items.en: The Father loves the Son. (John 3:35)
What are you doing, Socrates?
The Athenians used to honour the gods.
The Greeks were winning.
Deeds show the man.

items.t: Φιλοκαλοῦμέν τε γὰρ μετ’ εὐτελείας καὶ φιλοσοφοῦμεν ἄνευ μαλακίας.
items.en: We love beauty without extravagance, and we love wisdom without softness. (Thucydides 2.40, Pericles’ Funeral Oration)

items.t: Οὐ τὸ ζῆν περὶ πλείστου ποιητέον, ἀλλὰ τὸ εὖ ζῆν.
items.en: What we must value most is not living, but living well. (Plato, Crito 48b)
items.lit: Not the living is to be made of most account, but the living well.

afterlife.title: Conjugation B: the contract verbs never left

blocks.p: Modern Greek has two great verb classes. **Conjugation A** stresses the stem (*γράφω, γράφεις*). **Conjugation B** stresses the ending (*αγαπώ, μπορώ*) — and conjugation B is nothing other than the ancient contract verbs. The *α*-verbs became type **B1**, the *ε*-verbs type **B2**, and the endings are still recognisably Attic.

compare.title: B1: α-verbs
compare.note: The spoken variants αγαπάω, αγαπάει, αγαπάνε are new, remodelled on conjugation A; 1 pl. αγαπάμε has α where Attic contracted to ω.

compare.title: B2: ε-verbs, almost unchanged
compare.note: Apart from the monotonic accent and the lost final ν, a Pericles would recognise every form.

blocks.p: The **ο-verbs** did not survive as a type. They were rebuilt from their aorist: *ἐδήλωσα* suggested a new present *δηλώνω*, *ἐπλήρωσα* gave *πληρώνω*. And the odd verb *ζάω*, whose *ζῇς, ζῇ* came to be pronounced /zis, zi/, slid into the B2 pattern: Modern *ζω, ζεις, ζει, ζούμε*.

compare.title: Ancient contract verbs in everyday Modern Greek

items.en: I love you.
I can’t come tomorrow.

items.t: Ζει στην Αθήνα και οδηγεί ταξί.
items.en: He lives in Athens and drives a taxi.
They consider him the best pupil.

title: Perfect and Pluperfect
sub: Reduplication and the tense of results: λέλυκα, λέλυμαι

blocks.p: The Greek **perfect** describes a **present state** that results from a completed action. *τέθνηκε* does not just say ‘he died’ (that would be the aorist *ἀπέθανε*) but ‘he has died and is now dead’. *νενίκηκα* is ‘I have won — I am the victor’; *γέγραπται* ‘it has been written — it stands written’. The aorist tells a story; the perfect describes where the story has left us.
The **pluperfect** moves that state into the past: *ἐτεθνήκει* ‘he had died, he was (already) dead’. It is much rarer than the perfect, and you will meet it mostly in narrative.

The perfect stem is marked by **reduplication**: the first consonant of the verb is repeated with *ε*. Unlike the augment, reduplication belongs to the stem itself, so it stays in the infinitive, the participle and every mood: *λέλυκα, λελυκέναι, λελυκώς*.

table.title: How the perfect reduplicates
rows: φιλέω → πεφίληκα; θύω → τέθυκα; χορεύω → κεχόρευκα
two consonants, ζ, ξ, ψ, ῥ
στέλλω → ἔσταλκα; ζητέω → ἐζήτηκα; ῥίπτω → ἔρριφα
ἀγγέλλω → ἤγγελκα; ἐλπίζω → ἤλπικα; ὁρμάω → ὥρμηκα
ἀκούω → ἀκήκοα; ἐλαύνω → ἐλήλακα; ἔρχομαι → ἐλήλυθα
table.note: Note γιγνώσκω → ἔγνωκα: γν counts as a group that takes ε only.

blocks.p: The **first perfect** adds *-κα* to the reduplicated stem: *λέ-λυ-κα*. Contract verbs lengthen their vowel (*τετίμηκα*), and a dental drops before the *κ* (*πείθω → πέπεικα*). The **second perfect** adds plain *-α*, often aspirating a final stop or changing the root vowel: *γράφω → γέγραφα*, *πέμπω → πέπομφα*, *λείπω → λέλοιπα*, *γίγνομαι → γέγονα*, *φεύγω → πέφευγα*. The two types mean the same; which one a verb uses is a matter of vocabulary.

table.title: Perfect and pluperfect active
table.note: The perfect endings are those of the 1st aorist except the 3 pl. -ᾱσι(ν). The pluperfect adds the augment to the reduplicated stem; later Attic has 1 sg. ἐλελύκειν, 2 sg. ἐλελύκεις. A verb whose perfect already begins with a vowel or with ἐ- takes no further augment: ἤγγελκα → ἠγγέλκη. Participle genitive: λελυκότος, λελυκυίας, λελυκότος.

blocks.tip: Accent of the perfect active is easy: the infinitive is always stressed on *-έναι* (*λελυκέναι, γεγονέναι*) and the participle on *-ώς / -υῖα / -ός* (*λελυκώς*). Both are exceptions to recessive accent, so they are good recognition signs.

blocks.p: The middle/passive perfect adds the endings **directly** to the reduplicated stem, with no thematic vowel and no *κ*: *λέλυ-μαι* (compare present *λύ-ο-μαι*). As in the present, one set of forms serves for both middle and passive.

table.title: Perfect and pluperfect middle / passive
table.note: The infinitive is stressed on the penult (λελύσθαι) and the participle always on -μέ- (λελυμένος), whatever the case.

blocks.p: When the stem ends in a consonant, the endings collide with it and the usual sound changes apply: a labial becomes *μ* before *μ*, *ψ* before *σ*, *π* before *τ*; a velar becomes *γ, ξ, κ*; a dental becomes *σ*. The 3rd plural is impossible to pronounce (*-φνται*), so Greek uses the participle with *εἰσί(ν)* instead.

table.title: Consonant stems: γράφω, πράττω (πραγ-), πείθω
table.note: In the 2 pl. and the infinitive the σ of -σθε, -σθαι drops between two consonants: γέγραφ-σθε → γέγραφθε.

blocks.p: Because the perfect describes a present state, several common perfects are simply translated by an English present, and their pluperfects by a simple past: *μέμνημαι* ‘I remember’, *ἐμεμνήμην* ‘I remembered’.

table.title: Perfects with present meaning
table.note: Attic uses the simple τέθνηκα as the perfect of the compound ἀποθνῄσκω. The most famous of all, οἶδα ‘I know’, is treated with the μι-verbs.

blocks.pitfall: English ‘I have done’ and the Greek perfect are not the same thing. English uses its perfect for any recent or unspecified past event (‘I’ve just seen him’), where Greek normally uses the **aorist** (*ἄρτι εἶδον αὐτόν*). Use the Greek perfect only when a lasting result is the point.
Do not take the *ε-* of *ἔσταλκα* or *ἐζήτηκα* for an augment. It is reduplication, so it remains in the infinitive (*ἐσταλκέναι*) and participle (*ἐζητηκώς*), where an augment never appears.

items.en: The king is dead.
The enemy have broken down the bridge (and it is down).

items.t: Ὅτε ἀφίκοντο, οἱ πολέμιοι ἤδη τὴν γέφυραν ἐλελύκεσαν.
items.en: When they arrived, the enemy had already broken down the bridge.

items.t: Γέγραπται· Οὐκ ἐπ’ ἄρτῳ μόνῳ ζήσεται ὁ ἄνθρωπος.
items.en: It is written: Man shall not live by bread alone. (Matthew 4:4)
What I have written, I have written. (Pilate, John 19:22)
It is finished. (John 19:30)
items.lit: It has been brought to completion.

afterlife.title: The old perfect died; ‘have’ built a new one

blocks.p: Already in Koine the perfect and the aorist were drifting together: the New Testament has perfects with aorist endings such as *γέγοναν* for *γεγόνασι*. In spoken medieval Greek the synthetic perfect disappeared, and the aorist took over its meaning. Modern Greek then built a **new perfect** with *έχω* ‘I have’ plus an invariable verb form (the so-called *απαρέμφατο*), which descends from the old aorist infinitive: *έχω γράψει* ‘I have written’, *είχα γράψει* ‘I had written’, *θα έχω γράψει* ‘I will have written’.

This is exactly what happened in the West, where Latin *habeō scrīptum* ‘I have (it) written’ became the Romance perfect, and where English developed *I have written*. Greek and Romance arrived at the same structure independently: Greek with the old infinitive, Romance with the past participle.

items.en: I have read this book.
When I arrived, he had already left.

items.t: Το βιβλίο είναι γραμμένο στα αγγλικά.
items.en: The book is written in English.

blocks.p: The perfect **participle** in *-μένος* is the great survivor. Spoken Greek simply dropped the reduplication, so that *γεγραμμένος* became *γραμμένος*. Today it is the ordinary past participle of Modern Greek, and it forms a second, colloquial perfect: *τα έχω γραμμένα* ‘I have them written down’.

Learned Greek kept a handful of fully reduplicated perfect forms, now ordinary words. One of them travelled west: Euclid wrote a book called *Δεδομένα* ‘things given’, translated into Latin as *Data* — the source of English *data*.

parts.title: The old perfect died; ‘have’ built a new one

title: Aorist and Future Passive
sub: ἐλύθην, λυθήσομαι: the sixth principal part

blocks.p: In the present, imperfect and perfect, Greek uses one set of forms for both middle and passive: *λύομαι* can mean ‘I ransom (for myself)’ or ‘I am freed’. The **aorist** and **future** are different: they have separate **passive** forms, built on the sixth principal part, *ἐλύθην* ‘I was freed’. The sign of this tense is **-θη-** (first aorist passive) or plain **-η-** (second aorist passive).
Oddly, the endings are **active** ones: *-ν, -ς, -, -μεν, -τε, -σαν*, the same as in a root aorist like *ἔβην* ‘I went’. Don’t let them mislead you — *ἐλύθημεν* means ‘we were freed’.

table.title: Aorist passive
table.note: The imperative is λύθητι rather than λύθηθι: Greek avoids two aspirates in successive syllables. The participle declines like a 3rd-declension adjective: gen. λυθέντος, λυθείσης, λυθέντος.

blocks.p: The **future passive** takes the unaugmented aorist passive stem, adds the future sign *-σ-*, and uses **middle** endings: *λυθή-σ-ομαι* ‘I shall be freed’.

blocks.tip: Look for **θη / θε** right after the stem: *-θην, -θῆναι, -θείς / -θέντ-* = aorist passive; *-θήσ-* = future passive. The infinitive (*λυθῆναι*) and participle (*λυθείς*) always carry their accent in the same place.

blocks.p: The *θ* of the suffix affects a consonant before it, just as in the perfect middle: a labial becomes *φ*, a velar becomes *χ*, a dental becomes *σ*. Contract verbs lengthen their vowel, and a number of verbs insert a *σ*.

table.title: Common irregular passives
table.note: ἐτέθην (instead of ἐθέθην) shows the same dislike of two aspirates in a row as λύθητι.

blocks.p: A number of deponent verbs form their aorist with the passive suffix but keep an active or middle meaning. These are called **passive deponents**: *βούλομαι* ‘I want’ → *ἐβουλήθην* ‘I wanted’; *δύναμαι* ‘I can’ → *ἐδυνήθην* ‘I was able’; *πορεύομαι* ‘I travel, march’ → *ἐπορεύθην*; *φοβέομαι* ‘I fear’ → *ἐφοβήθην* ‘I took fright’; *ἥδομαι* ‘I am pleased’ → *ἥσθην*. Many ordinary verbs also use the passive aorist for an intransitive middle sense: *φαίνομαι* ‘I appear’ → *ἐφάνην*, *κοιμάομαι* ‘I sleep’ → *ἐκοιμήθην* ‘I fell asleep’.
As with other passives, the **agent** is expressed by *ὑπό* + genitive (*ὑπὸ τῶν πολεμίων*), the **instrument** by the plain dative (*λίθοις* ‘with stones’).

blocks.pitfall: Don’t confuse the **future passive** *λυθήσομαι* ‘I shall be freed’ with the **future middle** *λύσομαι* ‘I shall ransom’. Both have middle endings; only the *-θη-* tells you which is which. And remember the active-looking endings of the aorist: *ἐπέμφθησαν* is ‘they were sent’.

items.t: Ἡ πόλις ὑπὸ τῶν πολεμίων ἐλήφθη.
items.en: The city was taken by the enemy.
The messenger was sent to Sparta.
The soldiers took fright and fled.

items.t: Ὁ Κῦρος ἐπορεύθη διὰ τῆς Λυδίας.
items.en: Cyrus marched through Lydia.

items.t: Ἠκούσατε ὅτι ἐρρέθη τοῖς ἀρχαίοις· Οὐ φονεύσεις.
items.en: You have heard that it was said to the people of old: You shall not murder. (Matthew 5:21; Koine ἐρρέθη for Attic ἐρρήθη)
He is not here; for he has been raised. (Matthew 28:6)

items.t: Πᾶς ὁ ὑψῶν ἑαυτὸν ταπεινωθήσεται, καὶ ὁ ταπεινῶν ἑαυτὸν ὑψωθήσεται.
items.en: Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted. (Luke 14:11)

blocks.p: The aorist passive is one of the most faithful survivals of Ancient Greek grammar. In medieval Greek the endings *-θην, -θης, -θη* were extended with the *κ*-endings of aorists like *ἔδωκα* and *ἔθηκα*, giving *-θηκα*; and the augment, unstressed, fell away. The result is the Modern passive aorist: *ἐλύθην → λύθηκα*.

compare.title: The passive aorist then and now

blocks.p: In everyday speech the clusters *φθ* and *χθ* became *φτ* and *χτ*, so many Modern passives are spelt with *τ*: *γράφτηκα* ‘I was written, I enrolled’, *κρύφτηκα* ‘I hid’. Several ancient second aorists in plain *-η-* also survive, with no *θ* at all.

compare.title: Ancient passive aorists in Modern Greek
compare.note: Modern γράφτηκα is a new -θηκα formation; Attic used the second aorist ἐγράφην.

blocks.p: The **future passive** *λυθήσομαι* did not survive. Modern Greek makes its passive future with *θα* and the old aorist passive **subjunctive** (*λυθῶ*, see the subjunctive chapter): *θα λυθώ* ‘I will be freed’. The aorist passive **infinitive** *λυθῆναι* lives on in the perfect: *έχω λυθεί, έχει γραφτεί*.

The participle in *-θείς* is alive in formal Greek, especially in news reports and legal language: *οι συλληφθέντες* ‘those arrested’, *ο εκλεγείς* ‘the person elected’, *τα ληφθέντα μέτρα* ‘the measures taken’.

items.en: The book was written in 1920.
Very pleased to meet you!
items.lit: I was very glad.

items.en: I was very frightened.
We will be saved.

title: Participles
sub: Forms, and the three ways Greek uses them

blocks.p: No feature of Greek style is more characteristic than the **participle**. A participle is a **verb** — it has tense, voice and can take objects — and an **adjective**: it agrees with a noun in gender, number and case. Where English strings clauses together with ‘when’, ‘because’, ‘although’ and ‘who’, Greek prefers a participle. A single Greek sentence can carry three or four of them.

Greek has a participle for nearly every tense and voice. Latin, by comparison, had only three (*amāns, amātus, amātūrus*), which is why Latin writers had to fall back on *cum*-clauses and ablative absolutes where Greek simply says *λύσας* ‘having freed’.

table.title: The participles of λύω (nominative singular)
table.note: Second aorists take the endings of the present with the accent on the ending: λιπών, λιποῦσα, λιπόν (gen. λιπόντος). The participle of εἰμί is ὤν, οὖσα, ὄν.

blocks.p: All the active participles and the aorist passive belong to the **third declension** in the masculine and neuter (stems in *-ντ-*, or *-οτ-* in the perfect) and to the **first declension** in the feminine. All the *-μενος* participles decline like *ἀγαθός*.

table.title: Present active: λύων
table.note: ὤν, οὖσα, ὄν declines exactly like the endings: ὄντος, ὄντι, ὄντα; οὔσης, οὔσῃ; dat. pl. οὖσι(ν). The future λύσων, λύσουσα, λῦσον is identical apart from the σ.

table.title: Aorist passive: λυθείς
table.note: The perfect active λελυκώς has stem λελυκοτ-: gen. λελυκότος, dat. pl. λελυκόσι(ν); fem. λελυκυῖα, λελυκυίας.

blocks.h: Tense is aspect — and relative time

blocks.p: A participle’s tense shows aspect and its time **relative to the main verb**. The **present** participle describes something going on at the same time (*λέγων* ‘while saying’); the **aorist** usually something completed before (*εἰπών* ‘having said’); the **future** an intention (*ἐροῦντες* ‘in order to say’); the **perfect** a resulting state (*τεθνηκώς* ‘dead’).

blocks.h: 1. Attributive: the participle as adjective or noun

blocks.p: With the **article**, a participle works like an adjective or, standing alone, like a noun. English usually needs a relative clause or a noun: *ὁ παρὼν καιρός* ‘the present moment’; *οἱ παρόντες* ‘those present’; *οἱ τεθνηκότες* ‘the dead’; *τὰ ὄντα* ‘the things that are, reality’; *ὁ βουλόμενος* ‘anyone who wishes’ — the Athenian legal term for any citizen entitled to bring a prosecution.

**Without the article**, a participle that agrees with a noun adds a circumstance to the sentence: time, cause, condition, concession, purpose or manner. Greek leaves the exact relation to the context, but particles can make it explicit: *καίπερ* + participle ‘although’; *ἅτε* + participle ‘since, inasmuch as’ (the writer’s own reason); *ὡς* + participle ‘on the grounds that’ (an alleged reason); *ὡς* + **future** participle ‘in order to’. A conditional participle is negated with *μή*, the others with *οὐ*.

A participle with its own subject, both in the **genitive** and grammatically independent of the rest of the sentence, is the **genitive absolute** — the Greek counterpart of the Latin ablative absolute: *τοῦ ἡλίου δύνοντος* ‘as the sun was setting’. It is treated with the cases.
Some verbs are incomplete without a participle, much as *βούλομαι* needs an infinitive. The participle agrees with the subject.

table.title: Verbs that take a supplementary participle
table.note: With λανθάνω and φθάνω the main idea is in the participle: ‘he escaped notice running away’ = ‘he ran away secretly’. Compare φαίνεται σοφὸς εἶναι ‘he seems to be wise’ (infinitive). After verbs of knowing and perceiving the participle reports a fact; see indirect discourse.

blocks.pitfall: Position matters. *ὁ ἀνὴρ ὁ γράφων* (with a second article) is attributive: ‘the man **who is writing**’. *ὁ ἀνὴρ γράφων* (no article before the participle) is circumstantial: ‘the man, **while writing**’ or ‘**when** he writes’.

blocks.tip: When translating, resist ‘having …-ed’ for every aorist participle. Ask what the relation is — time, cause, concession — and use an English clause: *ἀκούσας ταῦτα ἀπῆλθεν* is best rendered ‘**when** he heard this, he left’.

items.en: When they heard this, the soldiers went away.
Although he was an old man, he was still learning.
He came to ransom his daughter. (after Iliad 1.13)
The sower went out to sow. (Matthew 13:3)
items.lit: The (one) sowing went out to sow.

items.en: I happened to be in the agora.

items.t: Ὁ μὴ δαρεὶς ἄνθρωπος οὐ παιδεύεται.
items.en: The man who has not been beaten is not educated. (Menander)
Live unnoticed. (Epicurus)
items.lit: Escape notice having lived.

afterlife.title: From a forest of participles to a gerund

blocks.p: Modern Greek kept only a fraction of this system. Spoken Greek retains the **active gerund** in *-οντας / -ώντας*, which no longer declines and always refers to the subject of the sentence; the **passive participle** in *-μένος* (see the perfect); and a few present middle participles in *-όμενος* used as adjectives. Fully declined active participles survive only in the learned register.

compare.title: What remains of the participle
compare.note: The gerund continues the participle stem in -οντ-; it has a single form for all genders, numbers and cases.

items.t: Περπατώντας στον δρόμο, είδα τον Νίκο.
items.en: Walking down the street, I saw Nikos.
He was talking and laughing.
items.lit: He was talking laughing.

items.en: Next, please!
The future is uncertain.

blocks.p: Many ancient participles were frozen into **nouns**, and these are everyday words in Modern Greek. The ‘ruling (man)’ became ‘a ruler’; ‘what is about to be’ became ‘the future’.

compare.title: Participles turned into nouns
compare.note: Modern άρχοντας was formed from the accusative ἄρχοντα, the usual path for 3rd-declension nouns.

compare.title: Greek participles in English
gloss: ‘(thing) appearing’, present middle participle of φαίνω
‘things left out’: the Greek and Latin Bible’s title for Chronicles

compare.title: Greek has more participles than Latin
compare.note: Where Greek says λύσας, Latin needs a clause (cum solvisset) or an ablative absolute.

From a forest of participles to a gerund

title: Third-Declension Adjectives and Comparison
sub: ἀληθής, εὐδαίμων, πᾶς, μέγας, πολύς; -τερος / -τατος and -ίων / -ιστος

blocks.p: Besides the familiar *-ος, -η, -ον* type, Greek has adjectives that follow the **third declension**. Two-termination adjectives have one set of forms for masculine and feminine and another for the neuter: **σ-stems** like *ἀληθής, ἀληθές* ‘true’ and **ν-stems** like *εὐδαίμων, εὔδαιμον* ‘fortunate, happy’. Others are **mixed**: third declension in the masculine and neuter, first declension in the feminine, like *πᾶς, πᾶσα, πᾶν* ‘all, every’ and *ἡδύς, ἡδεῖα, ἡδύ* ‘sweet’.

table.title: σ-stem: ἀληθής ‘true’
table.note: The stem is ἀληθεσ-. The σ vanished between vowels, which then contracted: ἀληθέσος → ἀληθέος → ἀληθοῦς — exactly as in the neuter noun γένος, γένους. Likewise σαφής ‘clear’, εὐγενής ‘noble’, ἀσθενής ‘weak’.

table.title: ν-stem: εὐδαίμων ‘fortunate’
table.note: The neuter and the vocative pull the accent back as far as it can go: εὔδαιμον. Likewise σώφρων ‘sensible’, ἄφρων ‘foolish’.

table.title: Mixed: πᾶς ‘all, every, whole’
table.note: Like other monosyllabic 3rd-declension stems, πᾶς accents the ending in the genitive and dative singular (παντός, παντί) — but not in the plural (πάντων, πᾶσι).

blocks.p: The meaning of *πᾶς* depends on its position. In **predicate position** (outside the article) it means ‘all, the whole’: *πᾶσα ἡ πόλις* or *ἡ πόλις πᾶσα* ‘the whole city’, *πάντες οἱ πολῖται* ‘all the citizens’. **Without the article** it means ‘every’: *πᾶσα πόλις* ‘every city’. In **attributive position** it stresses the totality: *ἡ πᾶσα πόλις* ‘the city as a whole’.

table.title: Mixed: ἡδύς ‘sweet’
table.note: Likewise ταχύς ‘swift’, βαρύς ‘heavy’, βραχύς ‘short’, γλυκύς ‘sweet’, ὀξύς ‘sharp’.

blocks.p: The two commonest adjectives of size and quantity have short forms only in the nominative and accusative singular of the masculine and neuter. Everything else is built on a longer stem (*μεγαλ-*, *πολλ-*) and declines like *ἀγαθός*.

table.title: πολύς ‘much, many’
table.note: With the article, οἱ πολλοί means ‘the majority, the masses’.

blocks.p: Most adjectives form the **comparative** with *-τερος, -τέρα, -τερον* and the **superlative** with *-τατος, -τάτη, -τατον*, both declined like ordinary first/second-declension adjectives. Adjectives in *-ος* lengthen the *ο* to *ω* when the syllable before it is short: *σοφός → σοφώτερος*, but *δεινός → δεινότερος*. Third-declension adjectives usually add *-εσ-*: *ἀληθέστερος, εὐδαιμονέστερος*.

blocks.tip: The *ο / ω* rule is about rhythm: Greek avoids a long run of short syllables. ‘Short before, long after’: *σο-φώ-τε-ρος*. ‘Long before, short after’: *δει-νό-τε-ρος*.

blocks.p: A group of very common adjectives uses an older set of suffixes: comparative **-ίων / -ων**, superlative **-ιστος**. Several also take their comparison from a different root, just as English *good* has *better, best*.

table.title: Irregular comparison
table.note: The ‘better’ words differ in shade: ἀμείνων ‘abler, better’, βελτίων ‘(morally) better’, κρείττων ‘stronger, superior’; ἥττων is ‘weaker, inferior’. Attic ττ corresponds to σσ in Ionic and Koine: ἐλάσσων, θάσσων, κρείσσων.

table.title: Declension of μείζων ‘bigger’
table.note: Like εὐδαίμων, but with short alternative forms in -ω and -ους, very common in Attic. Don’t mistake μείζους for a genitive.

blocks.p: ‘Than’ is either *ἤ*, with the same case on both sides, or simply the **genitive of comparison**: *σοφώτερος ἢ Σωκράτης* = *σοφώτερος Σωκράτους* ‘wiser than Socrates’. The amount of difference goes in the dative: *πολλῷ μείζων* ‘much bigger’ (literally ‘bigger by much’). *ὡς* or *ὅτι* with a superlative means ‘as … as possible’: *ὡς τάχιστα* ‘as quickly as possible’, *ὅτι πλεῖστοι* ‘as many as possible’. Without a comparison, the comparative can mean ‘rather, too’ and the superlative ‘very’.

blocks.pitfall: *οἱ πολλοί* already contains the article: it means ‘**the** many’. So the English phrase ‘the hoi polloi’ says ‘the’ twice. And *πᾶσα πόλις* ‘every city’ is not the same as *πᾶσα ἡ πόλις* ‘the whole city’.

items.en: Best of all is water. (Pindar, Olympian 1.1)
Man is the measure of all things. (Protagoras)
Everything flows. (attributed to Heraclitus)
A big book is a big evil. (attributed to Callimachus)
No one is wiser than Socrates.

items.t: Ἡ γῆ πολλῷ μείζων ἐστὶ τῆς σελήνης.
items.en: The earth is much bigger than the moon.
They went away as quickly as possible.

afterlife.title: πιο and -τερος: comparison in Modern Greek

blocks.p: Modern Greek compares in two ways. The analytic way puts **πιο** ‘more’ before the adjective — *πιο ψηλός* ‘taller’ — and *πιο* is a worn-down form of ancient *πλέον* ‘more’. The synthetic way keeps the suffix **-τερος**, now always spelt *-ότερος*: *ψηλότερος*. ‘Than’ is *από* + accusative. The superlative is the comparative with the article (*ο πιο ψηλός, ο ψηλότερος* ‘the tallest’), while *-ότατος* means ‘very’ (*ψηλότατος* ‘very tall’).

compare.title: Comparatives then and now
compare.note: καλύτερος and μεγαλύτερος are post-classical formations; χειρότερος is a ‘double comparative’, -τερος added to the old comparative χείρων.

blocks.p: The ancient superlatives in *-ιστος* survive in the learned vocabulary, often with a technical sense. In Greek schools the top mark is *άριστα* ‘excellent’; a car’s top speed is its *μέγιστη ταχύτητα*.

The third-declension adjectives in *-ής* live on in the formal language and in many everyday words: *ακριβής* ‘exact’, *συνεχής* ‘continuous’, *διεθνής* ‘international’, *ευγενής* ‘polite’; ‘true’ in ordinary speech is *αληθινός*. *πας* gave way to *όλος* ‘all, whole’ and *κάθε* ‘every’, but it survives in set phrases (*πάση θυσία* ‘at all costs’, *πάσης φύσεως* ‘of every kind’) and in the prefix *παν-* (*πανεπιστήμιο* ‘university’). *πολύς, πολλή, πολύ* still has its ancient irregularity; *μέγας* lives in titles such as *Αλέξανδρος ο Μέγας*, while ordinary ‘big’ is the regularised *μεγάλος*.

items.t: Ο Γιάννης είναι πιο ψηλός από τον αδελφό του.
items.en: Yannis is taller than his brother.

items.t: Αυτό είναι το καλύτερο βιβλίο που διάβασα.
items.en: This is the best book I have read.
She got top marks in the exams.

compare.title: In English
compare.note: μέγας is a cognate, not a source, of Latin magnus and English much: all three go back to one Indo-European root.

parts.title: πιο and -τερος: comparison in Modern Greek

title: Relatives and Interrogatives
sub: ὅς, ἥ, ὅ; ὅστις; τίς and τις

blocks.h: The relative pronoun ὅς, ἥ, ὅ

blocks.p: The relative pronoun ‘who, which, that’ looks like the article without its *τ*: it has the same endings, but every form has a **rough breathing** and an **accent**.

table.title: ὅς, ἥ, ὅ ‘who, which’
table.note: Compare the article ὁ, ἡ, τό; οἱ, αἱ, τά. The forms ἥ, οἵ, αἵ differ from the article only by their accent; ὅ (neuter relative) differs from ὁ (masculine article) by accent alone.

blocks.p: The rule is the same as in Latin and English: the relative takes its **gender and number** from its antecedent, but its **case** from its job in its own clause. In *ὁ ἀνὴρ ὃν εἶδες* ‘the man whom you saw’, *ὅν* is masculine singular because of *ἀνήρ*, accusative because it is the object of *εἶδες*. The antecedent is often left out: *ὃν οἱ θεοὶ φιλοῦσιν* ‘(he) whom the gods love’.

**Attraction.** Attic likes to pull a relative that should be accusative into the case of a genitive or dative antecedent. Xenophon’s Cyrus tells his Greeks to be *ἄξιοι τῆς ἐλευθερίας ἧς κέκτησθε* ‘worthy of the freedom which you possess’ — *ἧς* stands for the expected accusative *ἥν*, attracted by *ἐλευθερίας*.

*ὅστις, ἥτις, ὅ τι* means ‘whoever, whatever, anyone who’. It is simply *ὅς* + the indefinite *τις*, and **both halves decline**. It is also used to introduce indirect questions. The neuter *ὅ τι* is printed as two words to keep it apart from the conjunction *ὅτι* ‘that, because’.

table.title: ὅστις, ἥτις, ὅ τι ‘whoever, whatever’
table.note: The short forms ὅτου, ὅτῳ, ὅτων, ὅτοις are very common in Attic.

blocks.h: Who? and someone: τίς and τις

blocks.p: The **interrogative** *τίς, τί* ‘who? what?’ always carries an **acute** on its first syllable — it never turns grave, even in the middle of a sentence. The **indefinite** *τις, τι* ‘someone, something, a certain’ is **enclitic**: it leans on the word before it and has an accent, if at all, on its last syllable (*τινός, τινί*). Same letters, opposite meanings: the accent decides.

table.title: Interrogative and indefinite
table.note: Where two forms are given, the first is masculine/feminine, the second neuter. The short forms in brackets are frequent in Attic.

blocks.p: *τί* also means ‘why?’. The indefinite *τις* usually follows its noun: *ἀνήρ τις* ‘a certain man, some man’. With an adjective it softens: *δεινός τις* ‘somewhat terrible’. In indirect questions Greek can use either the direct interrogative or *ὅστις*: *ἐρωτᾷ τίς εἰμι* or *ἐρωτᾷ ὅστις εἰμί* ‘he asks who I am’.

Questions, indefinites and relatives form a neat grid. Interrogatives begin with *π-* and are accented; the indefinites are the same words enclitic; relatives begin with a rough breathing; and the indefinite relatives, also used in indirect questions, add *ὁ-*.

blocks.pitfall: Watch the small words: *τίς* ‘who?’ vs *τις* ‘someone’; *ὅ τι* ‘whatever’ vs *ὅτι* ‘that, because’; *ἥ* ‘who (fem.)’ vs *ἡ* ‘the’ vs *ἤ* ‘or, than’ vs *ᾗ* ‘where, how’; *οὗ* ‘of whom; where’ vs *οὐ* ‘not’. Breathings and accents are not decoration.

items.t: Ὃν οἱ θεοὶ φιλοῦσιν, ἀποθνῄσκει νέος.
items.en: He whom the gods love dies young. (Menander)
What is truth? (Pilate, John 18:38)
Who are you?

items.t: Ἦλθεν ἄνθρωπός τις εἰς τὴν πόλιν.
items.en: A certain man came into the city.
Whoever has friends is rich.
I don’t know what you are saying.

items.t: Ἄξιοι ἔσεσθε τῆς ἐλευθερίας ἧς κέκτησθε.
items.en: You will be worthy of the freedom which you possess. (after Xenophon, Anabasis 1.7.3)

afterlife.title: που, ο οποίος, ποιος: the modern system

blocks.p: Spoken Modern Greek replaced the declined relative with an **indeclinable** word, **που**, from ancient *ὅπου* ‘where’. It serves for every gender, number and case: *ο άνθρωπος που είδα* ‘the man (whom) I saw’, *η γυναίκα που μου μίλησε* ‘the woman who spoke to me’. It is the same solution as English *that* or Italian *che*. Formal Greek uses the declined **ο οποίος, η οποία, το οποίο**, built from the article and *ὁποῖος* ‘of what kind’.

compare.title: Relatives then and now
rows: ο οποίος, η οποία, το οποίο
compare.note: Modern spelling writes ό,τι ‘whatever’ with a comma to keep it apart from ότι ‘that’ — the same distinction ancient printing makes with ὅ τι and ὅτι. The ancient relative ὅς itself survives only in fossils like εξ ου (και το όνομα) ‘hence (the name)’.

blocks.p: Among the interrogatives, *τί* survives as indeclinable **τι** ‘what?’. But ‘who?’ is now **ποιος**, from *ποῖος* ‘of what kind?’, which pushed *τίς* out. Modern accents still mirror the ancient split between interrogative and indefinite: *πού;* ‘where?’ and *πώς;* ‘how?’ carry an accent, while relative *που* and *πως* ‘that’ do not.

compare.title: Question words
compare.note: Learned πόθεν ‘from where?’ lives on in το πόθεν έσχες ‘where did you get it from?’, the Greek name for the asset declaration required of politicians.

items.t: Ο φίλος που σου είπα έρχεται απόψε.
items.en: The friend I told you about is coming tonight.
Who is it?
How are you?
items.lit: What are you doing?

items.en: Do whatever you want.

blocks.p: *τίς* is a cognate of Latin *quis* and English *who*: all three continue one Indo-European question word beginning with kʷ-. In Greek that sound became *τ* before *ε* and *ι* (*τίς, τί*) but *π* before *ο* (*ποῦ, πότε, ποῖος*), which is why one family of Greek question words starts with τ and the other with π. English owes one philosophical word to this family: Plato coined *ποιότης* ‘what-sort-ness’ from *ποῖος*, and Cicero translated it into Latin as *quālitās*, our *quality*.

compare.title: One question word, three languages
gloss: a Latin calque on Plato’s coinage

title: μι-Verbs
sub: δίδωμι, τίθημι, ἵστημι, ἵημι — and εἶμι, οἶδα, φημί

blocks.p: So far almost every verb has been **thematic**: a vowel (*ο / ε*) stands between stem and ending, *λύ-ο-μεν, λύ-ε-τε*. A small but very common group is **athematic**: the endings are added straight to the stem, *δίδο-μεν, δίδο-τε*. Because the 1st singular ends in *-μι*, these are called **μι-verbs**. They are an older layer of the language — English *am* (from Indo-European -mi, like *εἰμί*) is a relic of the same type.

Three features recur. (1) The present stem is **reduplicated with ι**: *δί-δω-μι, τί-θη-μι, ἵ-στη-μι* (from older *σί-στη-μι*). (2) The stem vowel is **long** in the singular active (*δω, θη, στη*) and **short** elsewhere (*δο, θε, στα*). (3) Remove the reduplication and you have the **aorist** stem: *δο-, θε-, στα-, ἑ-*.

table.title: Present active
table.note: Infinitives in -ναι are always stressed on the penult. The participles decline like λυθείς: gen. διδόντος, τιθέντος, ἱστάντος, ἱέντος.

table.title: Imperfect active
table.note: In ἵστην and ἵην the augment only lengthens the ι, which the spelling does not show. The singulars ἐδίδουν, ἐτίθεις, ἐτίθει borrow contract-verb endings.

table.title: Present middle / passive
table.note: With no thematic vowel, the 2 sg. keeps its σ: δίδοσαι, not a contracted form like λύῃ. ἵσταμαι means ‘I stand’; τίθεμαι νόμους ‘I make laws (for myself, as a people)’; ἵεμαι ‘I hasten’.

blocks.p: *δίδωμι, τίθημι* and *ἵημι* have a curious mixed aorist: a **κ-aorist** in the indicative singular (*ἔδωκα* ‘I gave’), but **root** forms everywhere else (*ἔδομεν* ‘we gave’, *δοῦναι* ‘to give’, *δός* ‘give!’). *ἵημι* is nearly always found in compounds: *ἀφίημι* ‘let go, forgive’, *συνίημι* ‘understand’.

table.title: Aorist active
table.note: Aorist middle: ἐδόμην, ἐθέμην, εἵμην (2 sg. ἔδου, ἔθου). In compounds: ἀφῆκα, ἀφεῖμεν, ἀφεῖναι, ἄφες.

blocks.p: *ἵστημι* splits its tenses between a **transitive** meaning ‘make stand, set up’ and an **intransitive** meaning ‘stand’. The first (sigmatic) aorist *ἔστησα* is transitive, ‘I set up’; the second (root) aorist *ἔστην* is intransitive, ‘I stood, I halted’. The perfect *ἕστηκα* means ‘I have taken my stand’ = ‘I stand’.

table.title: Transitive and intransitive tenses
table.note: The perfect also has short forms: ἕσταμεν, ἑστᾶσι(ν), inf. ἑστάναι, ptcp. ἑστώς.

table.title: Root aorist ἔστην ‘I stood’
table.note: ἔβην ‘I went’ (βαίνω) and ἔγνων ‘I recognised’ (γιγνώσκω; imper. γνῶθι) go the same way.

blocks.p: A second group adds **-νυ-** to the root: *δείκνυμι* ‘show’ (*δείκνυμι, δείκνυς, δείκνυσι(ν), δείκνυμεν, δείκνυτε, δεικνύασι(ν)*; inf. *δεικνύναι*; ptcp. *δεικνύς*). Only the present system is athematic; the other tenses are regular (*δείξω, ἔδειξα*). Likewise *ὄμνυμι* ‘swear’, *ὄλλυμι* ‘destroy’, *ῥήγνυμι* ‘break’, *ζεύγνυμι* ‘yoke’.

blocks.h: Three irregular favourites: εἶμι, οἶδα, φημί

table.title: Present
table.note: The present indicative of φημί is enclitic except for φῄς.

table.title: Past tenses
table.note: ᾔδη is formally the pluperfect of οἶδα, so it means simply ‘I knew’. The future of οἶδα is εἴσομαι.

blocks.p: **εἶμι** is a present in form but in Attic its indicative means ‘**I shall go**’: it serves as the future of *ἔρχομαι*, while its infinitive *ἰέναι* and participle *ἰών* serve as the ordinary present ‘to go, going’. **οἶδα** is a perfect in form — ‘I have seen’, from the root of *εἶδον* ‘I saw’ — and therefore present in meaning: ‘I know’. **φημί** ‘say, affirm’ often stands parenthetically (*ὡς ἔφη* ‘as he said’), and *οὔ φημι* means ‘I deny, I say that … not’.

blocks.pitfall: Look-alikes abound. *εἶ* is ‘you are’ (*εἰμί*) and ‘you will go’ (*εἶμι*); *ἴσθι* is ‘be!’ and ‘know!’; *ᾖσαν* is ‘they were going’ and ‘they knew’. *εἶναι* ‘to be’ differs from *εἷναι* ‘to send’ only by its breathing; *ἧκα* ‘I sent’ is not *ἥκω* ‘I have come’. And *ἔστησαν* is the 3 pl. of both *ἔστησα* and *ἔστην*: ‘they set up’ or ‘they stood’.

items.t: Δός μοι ποῦ στῶ, καὶ τὴν γῆν κινήσω.
items.en: Give me a place to stand, and I will move the earth. (attributed to Archimedes; the wording varies)

items.t: Τὸν ἄρτον ἡμῶν τὸν ἐπιούσιον δὸς ἡμῖν σήμερον· καὶ ἄφες ἡμῖν τὰ ὀφειλήματα ἡμῶν.
items.en: Give us this day our daily bread, and forgive us our debts. (Matthew 6:11–12)

items.t: Ὁ θεὸς τοῖς ἀνθρώποις πολλὰ ἀγαθὰ δίδωσιν.
items.en: God gives people many good things.
The Athenians set up a trophy.

items.t: Ἔστη ὁ στρατὸς παρὰ τὸν ποταμόν.
items.en: The army halted beside the river.
Tomorrow I shall go to the agora.
One thing I know: that I know nothing. (traditional summary of Socrates’ position; cf. Plato, Apology 21d)

afterlife.title: No μι-verbs left — but their roots are everywhere

blocks.p: The athematic type was dying even in antiquity. Koine already turns many μι-verbs into ordinary *ω*-verbs: *δεικνύω* for *δείκνυμι*, and the Lord’s Prayer in Luke has *ἀφίομεν* ‘we forgive’ (Luke 11:4) where Attic would say *ἀφίεμεν*. Modern Greek has no μι-verbs at all. Each verb was rebuilt — often from its aorist or perfect — or replaced by another word.

compare.title: What became of them
compare.note: δίνω developed from δίδω, a thematic remake of δίδωμι. στέκω goes back to Koine στήκω, a new present built on the perfect ἕστηκα (Paul writes στήκετε ἐν τῇ πίστει ‘stand firm in the faith’, 1 Corinthians 16:13). αφήνω was built on the aorist ἀφῆκα. The everyday verb ‘put’ is βάζω, from a different root. ξέρω comes from ἐξευρίσκω ‘find out’ — ‘I have found out’ → ‘I know’, the same path that made οἶδα ‘I have seen’ mean ‘I know’. πηγαίνω goes back to ὑπάγω ‘go away’, and λέω is λέγω.

items.en: Give me a little water.
Leave me alone!
items.lit: Leave me quiet.

items.en: I don’t know.
He is standing at the door.

blocks.p: These verbs continue some of the oldest roots of Indo-European, so they have **cognates** in Latin and English as well as **loans**. Latin *sistō* ‘I set’ is even reduplicated just like *ἵστημι*, and English *do* is the same root as *τίθημι*.

compare.title: Cognates and borrowings
compare.note: The Latin words are cognates, not loans. In the English column, the words before the semicolon are borrowed from Greek (δόσις ‘a giving’, ἀνέκδοτα ‘unpublished things’, σύστημα, ἔκστασις, παράδειγμα, ἰδέα, ἱστορία, εὐφημισμός, προφήτης); those after it are native English cognates.
