title: The Subjunctive
sub: Let us…, shall I…?, so that…, whenever…

blocks.h: The mood of will and expectation

blocks.p: The indicative states facts. The **subjunctive** presents an action as **willed, expected or general**: ‘let us go’, ‘what am I to say?’, ‘so that he may see’, ‘whenever anyone steals’. It appears in main clauses (exhortations, deliberative questions, prohibitions) and, even more often, in subordinate clauses of purpose, fear, and — with the particle *ἄν* — in general and future conditions and relative clauses.

The subjunctive has a **present** and an **aorist** (a perfect exists but is rare). The difference between them is purely one of **aspect**, never of time: *ἵνα γράφῃ* ‘so that he may keep writing’, *ἵνα γράψῃ* ‘so that he may write (it)’. There is **no augment**, even in the aorist.

The subjunctive is easy to recognise: it **lengthens the thematic vowel**. Where the indicative has *ο*, the subjunctive has *ω*; where it has *ε* (or *ει*), the subjunctive has *η* (or *ῃ*). The endings are the primary ones. The aorist adds the same endings to the aorist stem; the aorist passive contracts, so it carries a circumflex.

table.title: Active and aorist passive
table.note: Second aorists use their own stem: λίπω, λίπῃς, λίπῃ… The 1 sg. λύω looks like the present indicative and λύσω like the future indicative: only context tells them apart.

table.title: εἰμί, contract verbs, μι-verbs
table.note: α-verbs have the same forms in the subjunctive as in the indicative. ο-verbs: δηλῶ, δηλοῖς, δηλοῖ, δηλῶμεν, δηλῶτε, δηλῶσι(ν). Aorists of τίθημι and ἵστημι: θῶ, θῇς, θῇ…; στῶ, στῇς, στῇ…

blocks.tip: Spot the long vowel: *λύομεν* is indicative, *λύωμεν* subjunctive; *λύετε* indicative, *λύητε* subjunctive. And an iota subscript under *η* in a verb ending (*λύῃς, λύσῃ*) almost always means subjunctive.

blocks.p: **Hortatory**: the 1st person, usually plural, means ‘let us…’; negative *μή*. **Deliberative**: a 1st-person question asks ‘am I to…? what are we to…?’; negative *μή*. **Prohibitive**: *μή* + **aorist** subjunctive in the 2nd person forbids a single act: *μὴ θαυμάσῃς* ‘don’t be surprised’. (For an ongoing action Greek uses *μή* + present imperative: *μὴ κρίνετε* ‘stop judging, don’t judge’.) **Emphatic denial**: *οὐ μή* + aorist subjunctive means ‘certainly not, never’.

**Purpose**: *ἵνα, ὅπως* or *ὡς* + subjunctive, ‘so that, in order that’; negative *ἵνα μή* or simply *μή*. After a past main verb, Attic may switch to the optative (see the next chapter), but the subjunctive is often kept for vividness. **Fear**: *φοβοῦμαι μή* + subjunctive ‘I am afraid that (something will happen)’; *μὴ οὐ* ‘that (something will) not’.

**Indefinite clauses with ἄν.** Combined with the particle *ἄν*, a conjunction or relative pronoun becomes general or open-ended, and takes the subjunctive. With a present main verb this makes a **general** statement (‘whenever, if ever’); with a future main verb, a **future** one (‘when, if (in the future)’). The aorist subjunctive here marks an action completed before the main verb, not a past one: *ὅταν ἔλθῃ* ‘when he comes, once he has come’.

blocks.pitfall: In a negative command, Greek never uses the aorist **imperative**: ‘don’t do it (now)’ is *μὴ ποιήσῃς*, with the aorist **subjunctive**, while *μὴ ποίει* (present imperative) means ‘don’t keep doing it, stop doing it’.

items.t: Φάγωμεν καὶ πίωμεν, αὔριον γὰρ ἀποθνῄσκομεν.
items.en: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die. (1 Corinthians 15:32, quoting Isaiah)
What then are we to do? (Luke 3:10)
Do not be surprised. (John 3:7)
Do not judge, so that you may not be judged. (Matthew 7:1)

items.t: Οἱ δὲ λόγοι μου οὐ μὴ παρέλθωσιν.
items.en: But my words will never pass away. (Matthew 24:35)
I am afraid that father will get angry.
If anyone steals, he is punished.
We are coming in order to see the city.

afterlife.title: ἵνα → να: the subjunctive takes over

blocks.p: No ancient mood had a brighter future than the subjunctive. In Koine, *ἵνα* + subjunctive spread far beyond purpose clauses and began to replace the infinitive: *θέλω ἵνα* … ‘I want that …’. Worn down to **να**, it is now one of the most frequent words of Modern Greek. The Modern ‘subjunctive’ is simply *να* + verb, with the old aspect contrast intact: *να γράφω* (from the present subjunctive, ongoing) and *να γράψω* (from the aorist subjunctive, single act).

The old long vowels did not survive the loss of vowel length: *λύῃς* and *λύεις* both came to be pronounced /ˈlis/. Modern spelling therefore writes subjunctive and indicative alike (*να γράψεις, γράφεις*), and the mood is marked instead by its particles: **να, ας, θα, μη(ν), αν, όταν**.

compare.title: Ancient subjunctive, Modern particles
compare.note: ας comes from ἄφες ‘let!’, already used with the subjunctive in Koine: ἄφες ἐκβάλω τὸ κάρφος ‘let me take out the speck’ (Matthew 7:4). θα is worn down from θέλει ἵνα (θε να) ‘it wants that’. The prohibition μη γράψεις is the ancient μὴ γράψῃς, unchanged but for spelling.

items.en: I want to learn Greek.
Let’s begin!
Don’t be afraid.
When you come, I will tell you.

blocks.p: Romance languages also lean on conjunction + subjunctive (*que, che*), but only when the subject changes: Italian *voglio che tu venga* ‘I want you to come’, yet *voglio venire* ‘I want to come’. Greek goes further and uses *να* even with the same subject: *θέλω να έρθω*, literally ‘I want that I come’. The one Romance language that does the same is **Romanian**, with *să* (from Latin *sī* ‘if’): *vreau să vin*. Bulgarian (*да*) and Albanian (*të*) work the same way — a shared Balkan trait taken up again in the chapter on the infinitive.

parts.title: The mood of will and expectation
ἵνα → να: the subjunctive takes over

title: The Optative
sub: Wishes, possibilities and the past seen from afar

blocks.h: The mood of wishes and possibilities

blocks.p: The **optative** (from Latin *optāre* ‘to wish’, translating the Greek grammarians’ *εὐκτική* ‘wishing (mood)’) is the most remote of the moods. Where the subjunctive says ‘let it happen’ or ‘if it happens’, the optative says ‘may it happen’ or ‘if it should happen’. It has four main uses: **wishes** for the future, the **potential** with *ἄν* (‘would, could, might’), the ‘should … would’ **condition**, and as a **replacement** for the subjunctive or indicative after a past main verb. Attic prose uses it freely; it was the first mood to die.

blocks.h: Forms: the mood sign ι / ιη

blocks.p: The optative is marked by an *ι* inserted after the stem: thematic tenses have **-οι-** (*λύ-οι-μεν*), the first aorist **-αι-** (*λύσ-αι-μεν*), and the aorist passive, contract verbs and μι-verbs **-ιη-** (*λυθε-ίη-ν*). The endings are the secondary ones, except that the active 1st singular of the *οι / αι* type ends in *-μι*. There is no augment. The present and aorist differ in aspect only; a future optative exists but is used only in indirect discourse (*λύσοιμι*).

table.title: Active and aorist passive
table.note: In the aorist, the so-called ‘Aeolic’ forms λύσειας, λύσειε(ν), λύσειαν are actually more common in Attic than λύσαις, λύσαι, λύσαιεν. Second aorists use the present endings on their own stem: λίποιμι, λίποις, λίποι…

table.title: εἰμί, contract verbs, μι-verbs
table.note: Likewise θείην (τίθημι) and σταίην (ἵστημι). δηλόω: δηλοίην, δηλοίης, δηλοίη, δηλοῖμεν…

blocks.pitfall: For accent, final *-οι* and *-αι* count as **long** in the optative but **short** everywhere else. Hence three forms that differ only in their accent: *λύσαι* ‘may he free’ (aorist optative), *λῦσαι* ‘to free’ (aorist infinitive), *λῦσαι* ‘ransom!’ (aorist middle imperative). Likewise *λύοι* ‘may he free’ vs. *λῦε* ‘free!’.

blocks.p: The optative alone, or introduced by *εἴθε* or *εἰ γάρ* ‘if only’, expresses a **wish for the future** that can still come true; the negative is *μή*. (A wish that can no longer be fulfilled uses a past indicative instead: *εἴθε παρῆσθα* ‘if only you were here’.)

With the particle **ἄν**, the optative states what **would, could or might** be the case: *τάχ’ ἄν τις εἴποι* ‘perhaps someone might say’. The negative is *οὐ*: *οὐκ ἂν δυναίμην* ‘I could not’. It is the Greek way of being tentative or polite: *βουλοίμην ἄν* ‘I would like’, *ἡδέως ἂν ἀκούσαιμι* ‘I would gladly hear’.

*εἰ* + optative in the ‘if’ clause and optative + *ἄν* in the main clause make the **future less vivid** condition: *εἰ ἔλθοι, ἴδοι ἂν τὴν πόλιν* ‘if he should come, he would see the city’. See the chapter on conditional sentences.

After a **past** main verb, Attic may replace a subjunctive in a subordinate clause, or an indicative in indirect speech, with the optative — as if to say ‘this was how it looked from the past’. The change is optional; the subjunctive or indicative may be kept for vividness. Clauses with *ἄν* + subjunctive drop the *ἄν*: *ἐάν* becomes *εἰ*, *ὅταν* becomes *ὅτε*.

table.title: Primary and secondary sequence
table.note: ‘He comes / came to see’; ‘they fear / feared that he may / might come’; ‘he says / said that he is / was ill’; ‘whenever he sees / saw (someone), he calls / used to call (him)’.

blocks.tip: Rule of thumb: **ἄν + optative** in a main clause = ‘would, could’. **ἄν + subjunctive** never stands in a main clause; it belongs to subordinate clauses (*ἐάν, ὅταν, ὃς ἄν*).

items.en: My son, may you be luckier than your father. (Sophocles, Ajax 550)
By no means! (Paul, Romans 6:2)
items.lit: May it not happen.

items.en: I would gladly listen.
I could not do this.
He came to see the city.
He said that his father was ill.
Whenever he saw anyone, he would call him.

items.t: Πῶς γὰρ ἂν δυναίμην, ἐὰν μή τις ὁδηγήσει με;
items.en: How could I, unless someone guides me? (Acts 8:31, Koine)

afterlife.title: The mood that died — and its fossils

blocks.p: The optative was already fading in Koine. The New Testament uses it only a few dozen times, mostly in fixed formulas like Paul’s *μὴ γένοιτο* and in the more literary Luke–Acts (*πῶς γὰρ ἂν δυναίμην* above). In medieval vernacular Greek it disappeared. Its jobs were shared out: **wishes** went to *να* + subjunctive (often with *είθε* or *μακάρι* ‘if only’), and the **potential** ‘would’ went to *θα* + imperfect.

compare.title: Who does the optative’s work now
rows: long may you live! (said on birthdays)
είθε να έρθει / μακάρι να έρθει

blocks.p: A few optatives survive as **fossils**. *Μη γένοιτο!* ‘God forbid!’ is still everyday Greek; *γένοιτο* ‘so be it’ is heard in church; *Θεός φυλάξοι!* ‘God forbid!’ (literally ‘may God protect’) preserves a later optative form; and *είθε* ‘would that’ lives on in elevated style, now followed by *να*.

items.en: Happy birthday! Long may you live!
I hope he comes too.
items.lit: If only he too may come.

items.en: I would like a coffee, please.

items.t: Να χάσω τη δουλειά μου; Μη γένοιτο!
items.en: Lose my job? God forbid!

blocks.p: Latin has no separate optative: its subjunctive took over the optative’s jobs (wishes with *utinam*, the potential ‘would’). But some Latin subjunctives **are** old optatives in form. Old Latin *siem, siēs, siet* ‘may I / you / he be’ (classical *sim, sīs, sit*) match Greek *εἴην, εἴης, εἴη*, from one Indo-European optative; so does *velim* ‘I would like’.

compare.title: Greek optatives and their Latin counterparts
compare.note: The Vulgate renders Paul’s μὴ γένοιτο as absit ‘far be it’.

parts.title: The mood of wishes and possibilities
Forms: the mood sign ι / ιη
The mood that died — and its fossils

title: Infinitives and Indirect Discourse
sub: Verbal nouns, ὅτι-clauses, the accusative + infinitive and the participle of knowing

blocks.p: The Greek **infinitive** is both a verb and a noun. As a verb it has tense (that is, aspect) and voice, and takes objects and adverbs; as a noun it is neuter and can take the article: *τὸ ζῆν* ‘living, life’. Its negative is normally *μή*; only in indirect discourse does it keep the *οὐ* of the original statement.

table.title: The infinitives of λύω
table.note: εἰμί: εἶναι, future ἔσεσθαι. Second aorists accent the ending: λιπεῖν, λιπέσθαι, ἐλθεῖν, ἰδεῖν. Contract verbs: τιμᾶν, ποιεῖν, δηλοῦν. μι-verbs: διδόναι, δοῦναι; τιθέναι, θεῖναι.

blocks.p: **Complementary**: after verbs of wishing, being able, trying, knowing how, and after impersonal expressions: *βούλομαι ἀπιέναι* ‘I want to leave’, *δύναμαι* ‘I can’, *ἐπίσταμαι* ‘I know how to’, *δεῖ* ‘it is necessary’, *ἔξεστι* ‘it is permitted’, *χρή* ‘one must’. With the impersonals the person goes in the accusative: *δεῖ ἡμᾶς ἀπιέναι* ‘we must leave’.

**Articular**: with the article the infinitive can stand in any case, and so after any preposition: *τὸ φιλοσοφεῖν* ‘doing philosophy’; *διὰ τὸ νοσεῖν* ‘because of being ill’; *πρὸ τοῦ ἐλθεῖν* ‘before coming’; *ἐν τῷ λέγειν* ‘while speaking’.

**Result and ‘before’**: *ὥστε* + infinitive gives a natural or expected result, ‘so as to, so that’ (with the indicative, an actual result). *πρίν* + infinitive means ‘before’: *πρὶν ἐλθεῖν τοὺς πολεμίους* ‘before the enemy came’. **Purpose** after verbs of giving and sending: *δίδωσί μοι πιεῖν* ‘he gives me (something) to drink’.

An infinitive with its own subject puts that subject in the **accusative**: *νομίζω αὐτὸν σοφὸν εἶναι* ‘I think that he is wise’. But if the subject is the **same** as that of the main verb, Greek leaves it out and anything agreeing with it stays in the **nominative**: *νομίζει σοφὸς εἶναι* ‘he thinks that he (himself) is wise’. Latin, by contrast, always uses the accusative, adding a reflexive: *putat sē sapientem esse*.
Reported statements and thoughts use one of three constructions, chosen by the introducing verb.

table.title: Which verb takes which construction
rows: οἶδα, γιγνώσκω, ὁράω, ἀκούω, αἰσθάνομαι, μανθάνω, ἀγγέλλω
table.note: λέγω and ἀγγέλλω also take an infinitive or participle; φημί always takes the infinitive. The participle construction belongs above all to verbs of knowing and perceiving: it presents what is said as a fact.

blocks.p: Three rules govern all three constructions. (1) The **tense of the original** statement is kept: a present stays present, an aorist stays aorist, even after a past verb — Greek has no ‘sequence of tenses’ like English. (2) The **negative** of the original (*οὐ*) is kept. (3) After a **past** introducing verb, a finite verb in a *ὅτι*-clause may change to the **optative** of the same tense.

table.title: One statement, reported three ways
rows: εἶπεν ὅτι ὁ Κῦρος νικῴη (or νικᾷ).
table.note: ‘Cyrus is winning.’ → ‘He says / said that Cyrus is / was winning’; ‘he knows / knew that Cyrus is / was winning’. Had the original been ἐνίκησε ‘he won’, the infinitive would be aorist (ἔφη τὸν Κῦρον νικῆσαι ‘he said that Cyrus had won’) and the participle too (νικήσαντα).

blocks.tip: Some verbs change meaning with the construction. *ἀκούω* + genitive + participle: ‘I hear (someone) doing’ (I hear it myself); + accusative + participle: ‘I hear that’ (a fact); + infinitive: ‘I hear it said that’ (a report). *μανθάνω* + infinitive: ‘learn how to’; + participle: ‘learn that’.

blocks.pitfall: English shifts tenses in reported speech (‘he said he **was** ill’), Greek does not: *ἔφη νοσεῖν* has a **present** infinitive because he said ‘I am ill’. Translate the Greek tense relative to the introducing verb, then adjust to English.

items.t: Πάντες ἄνθρωποι τοῦ εἰδέναι ὀρέγονται φύσει.
items.en: All human beings by nature desire to know. (Aristotle, Metaphysics 1.1)

items.t: Οὗτος μὲν οἴεταί τι εἰδέναι οὐκ εἰδώς.
items.en: This man thinks he knows something when he does not. (Plato, Apology 21d)

items.t: Ἔλεγον ὅτι Κῦρος μὲν τέθνηκεν, Ἀριαῖος δὲ πεφευγὼς ἐν τῷ σταθμῷ εἴη.
items.en: They said that Cyrus was dead, and that Ariaeus had fled and was at the camp. (Xenophon, Anabasis 2.1.3)
He said that the enemy were leaving.
I see that the soldiers are fleeing.

items.t: Δεῖ ἡμᾶς ἀπιέναι πρὶν τοὺς πολεμίους ἐλθεῖν.
items.en: We must leave before the enemy come.

items.t: Οὕτω σοφός ἐστιν ὥστε πάντας αὐτὸν θαυμάζειν.
items.en: He is so wise that everyone admires him.

blocks.p: Modern Greek has **no infinitive**. The decline began in Koine, where *ἵνα* + subjunctive steadily took over the infinitive’s jobs, and by the end of the Byzantine period the infinitive had vanished from speech. Today *να* + subjunctive does what the infinitive used to do after verbs of wanting and being able; *για να* (from *διά* + *ἵνα*) expresses purpose; and reported speech uses **ότι** or **πως** (from *πῶς* ‘how’) with an ordinary indicative.

compare.title: Ancient infinitives, Modern clauses
rows: λέει ότι ο βασιλιάς είναι σοφός
he says (that) the king is wise

blocks.p: Traces remain. The invariable form in *έχω γράψει* descends from an old aorist infinitive, and a few infinitives became nouns: *το είναι* ‘being’ in philosophical language, and everyday *το φαΐ* ‘food’ (medieval *φαγί*), from *φαγεῖν* ‘to eat’.

items.en: I want to tell you something.
Can you help me?
He said he would come.

items.t: Ήρθε στην Αθήνα για να σπουδάσει.
items.en: She came to Athens to study.

blocks.p: Greek is not alone. **Bulgarian** and Macedonian have lost the infinitive too (Bulgarian *искам да пиша* ‘I want to write’, with *да* + verb); **Albanian** (in its southern, Tosk form) says *dua të shkruaj*; and **Romanian**, though it keeps an infinitive (*a scrie*), normally prefers *vreau să scriu*. This shared loss is a textbook feature of the **Balkan linguistic area**, where centuries of contact made unrelated languages converge. Because the Greek development can be traced back furthest, Greek is often seen as its source, though that is debated.

In the West a related but smaller change happened. Latin reported speech used the **accusative + infinitive** (*dīcit rēgem sapientem esse*), just like Greek *φησὶ τὸν βασιλέα σοφὸν εἶναι*. The Romance languages replaced this with a ‘that’ clause (*che, que, că*) — but, unlike Greek, kept the infinitive after verbs like ‘want’ and ‘can’. English keeps a trace of the old construction in *I believe him to be wise*.

compare.title: Infinitive or clause?
rows: λέει ότι ο βασιλιάς είναι σοφός
dice che il re è saggio
dice que el rey es sabio
il dit que le roi est sage
he says that the king is wise
compare.note: Romanian also allows pot scrie, with a short infinitive, after ‘can’.

title: Conditional Sentences
sub: Real, vivid, remote and unreal: the system of εἰ and ἄν

blocks.p: A conditional sentence has two parts: the ‘if’ clause or **protasis**, introduced by *εἰ* and negated with *μή*, and the main clause or **apodosis**, negated with *οὐ*. Greek sorts its conditions by **time** (present, past, future, or ‘always’) and by how the speaker presents them: as simply open, as vivid and likely, as remote, or as contrary to fact. Two small words carry most of the load: the mood of the verbs, and the particle **ἄν**.

table.title: The Attic system at a glance
table.note: ἐάν (= εἰ + ἄν) also appears as ἤν or ἄν (with long α).

blocks.p: *εἰ* + any tense of the indicative states a condition **without implying** whether it is true: *εἰ ταῦτα λέγεις, ἁμαρτάνεις* ‘if you are saying this, you are wrong’; *εἰ ταῦτα ἔπραξεν, ἠδίκησεν* ‘if he did this, he did wrong’. The main clause can be any kind of sentence: a statement, a question, a command.

For the future, Greek offers two degrees of vividness. The **future more vivid** (*ἐάν* + subjunctive, future indicative) is the everyday English ‘if you come, you will see’: *ἐὰν ἔλθῃς, ὄψει τὸν πατέρα*. The main clause may also be an imperative. The **future less vivid** (*εἰ* + optative, optative + *ἄν*) is more hypothetical, English ‘if you should come, you would see’: *εἰ ἔλθοις, ἴδοις ἂν τὸν πατέρα*.

A **participle** often replaces the ‘if’ clause. The most famous future condition in Greek, the oracle given to Croesus, is phrased this way — and its ambiguity was the point: the great empire Croesus destroyed was his own.

When the speaker implies that the condition is **not** true, Greek uses past tenses of the indicative in both halves, with *ἄν* in the main clause. The **imperfect** refers to the present: *εἰ σοφὸς ἦσθα, οὐκ ἂν ταῦτα ἔλεγες* ‘if you were wise (but you aren’t), you would not be saying this’. The **aorist** refers to the past: *εἰ ἦλθες, εἶδες ἂν τὸν πατέρα* ‘if you had come (but you didn’t), you would have seen father’. The two can be mixed: a past ‘if’ with a present ‘then’.

A condition that holds **whenever** something happens uses *ἐάν* + subjunctive with a **present** main verb (‘if ever, whenever’); in the past, *εἰ* + optative with an **imperfect** (‘whenever … used to’). These are exactly the indefinite clauses met with the subjunctive and optative; *ὅταν, ἐπειδάν* and *ὃς ἄν* work the same way.

blocks.pitfall: There are two different *ἄν*. The **modal particle** *ἄν* (short α) never comes first in its clause and marks the main clause of potential and unreal conditions: *εἶδες ἄν* ‘you would have seen’. The **conjunction** *ἄν* (long α) is a contraction of *ἐάν* ‘if’, begins its clause, and takes the subjunctive. And *ἤν* ‘if’ is not *ἦν* ‘he was’.

blocks.tip: Look first at the main clause. *ἄν* + **past indicative** = contrary to fact (‘would be, would have been’). *ἄν* + **optative** = remote (‘would’). **No** *ἄν* in the main clause = simple, vivid or general.

items.en: If you are saying this, you are wrong.
If you seek, you will find.

items.t: Εἰ ἔλθοις, ἴδοις ἂν τὸν πατέρα.
items.en: If you should come, you would see father.

items.t: Εἰ σοφὸς ἦσθα, οὐκ ἂν ταῦτα ἔλεγες.
items.en: If you were wise, you would not be saying this.

items.t: Εἰ ἦλθες, εἶδες ἂν τὸν πατέρα.
items.en: If you had come, you would have seen father.

items.t: Ἢν δ’ ἐγγὺς ἔλθῃ θάνατος, οὐδεὶς βούλεται θνῄσκειν.
items.en: But when death comes near, no one wants to die. (Euripides, Alcestis 671–672)

items.t: Κροῖσος Ἅλυν διαβὰς μεγάλην ἀρχὴν καταλύσει.
items.en: If Croesus crosses the Halys, he will destroy a great empire. (the Delphic oracle, as quoted by Aristotle, Rhetoric 3.5)
items.lit: Croesus, having crossed the Halys, will destroy a great empire.

items.en: If anyone spoke against them, he was soon dead. (after Thucydides 8.66)

blocks.p: Modern Greek kept the conjunction and lost the particle. ‘If’ is **αν**, from *ἐάν* (already *ἄν* in Attic); the modal particle *ἄν* disappeared, and its work is done by **θα**. The many ancient types have been reduced to a simpler system: *αν* + indicative for real conditions, *αν* + subjunctive with *θα* for the future, and *αν* + imperfect or pluperfect with *θα* for unreal ones.

compare.title: Five conditions in four languages
rows: Αν το λες αυτό, κάνεις λάθος.
If you say this, you are wrong.
Αν έρθεις, θα δεις τον πατέρα.
If you come, you will see father.
Εἰ ἔλθοις, ἴδοις ἂν τὸν πατέρα.
Αν ερχόσουν, θα έβλεπες τον πατέρα.
If you should come, you would see father.
Εἰ παρῆσθα, ἑώρας ἂν τὸν πατέρα.
Αν ήσουν εδώ, θα έβλεπες τον πατέρα.
If you were here, you would see father.
Εἰ ἦλθες, εἶδες ἂν τὸν πατέρα.
Αν είχες έρθει, θα είχες δει τον πατέρα.
If you had come, you would have seen father.
compare.note: Modern Greek uses the same imperfect pattern for the remote future and the present unreal. In everyday speech αν + imperfect, θα + imperfect can even cover the past: Αν το ήξερα, θα σου το έλεγα ‘if I knew / had known, I would tell / have told you’.

blocks.p: **θα + imperfect** is the Modern Greek **conditional**: *θα έγραφα* ‘I would write’, and *θα είχα γράψει* ‘I would have written’. The recipe — a future marker put into the past — is the same one English and the Romance languages used: English *would* is the past of *will*, and Spanish *escribiría* is *escribir* + *(hab)ía*, ‘I had to write’.

items.t: Αν βρέξει, θα μείνουμε στο σπίτι.
items.en: If it rains, we will stay at home.

items.t: Αν ήμουν πλούσιος, θα ταξίδευα σε όλο τον κόσμο.
items.en: If I were rich, I would travel all over the world.

items.t: Αν είχες έρθει νωρίτερα, θα τον είχες δει.
items.en: If you had come earlier, you would have seen him.

title: Case Syntax and Prepositions
sub: What the genitive, dative and accusative do; the genitive absolute; prepositions with one, two and three cases

blocks.p: Indo-European had eight cases; Greek has five. The missing ones were absorbed: the **genitive** also does the work of the old ablative (‘from’), and the **dative** that of the instrumental (‘with, by means of’) and the locative (‘in, at’). That is why the uses of these two cases look so varied. Latin made a different merger, gathering ablative, instrumental and locative into its ablative. A useful rule of thumb: Greek genitive ≈ ‘of / from’, dative ≈ ‘to / for / with / in’, accusative ≈ ‘object / to / extent’.

table.title: Main uses of the genitive
rows: to keep away from the city

blocks.p: Many verbs take their object in the genitive. Most belong to a few families: **perceiving** (*ἀκούω τοῦ ἀνδρός* ‘I hear the man’ — the person heard), **remembering and forgetting** (*μέμνημαι, ἐπιλανθάνομαι*), **ruling** (*ἄρχω, κρατέω*), **touching and grasping** (*ἅπτομαι, λαμβάνομαι*), **sharing** (*μετέχω*), and **desiring** (*ἐπιθυμέω*).

table.title: Main uses of the dative
rows: he gives the book to the child
this has been done by us

blocks.p: Verbs of **trusting, obeying, helping, following, using, fighting** take the dative: *πιστεύω τῷ φίλῳ* ‘I trust my friend’, *πείθομαι τοῖς νόμοις* ‘I obey the laws’, *βοηθέω, ἕπομαι, χράομαι, μάχομαι*. So do adjectives of likeness and friendship: *ὅμοιος τῷ πατρί* ‘like his father’, *φίλος, ἐχθρός, ἴσος*.

table.title: Main uses of the accusative
rows: not at all; in this way
table.note: The accusative is also the subject case of the infinitive (see indirect discourse).

blocks.p: When a circumstantial participle has its **own subject** that plays no part in the main clause, both go into the **genitive** and stand apart from the rest of the sentence: *τοῦ ἡλίου δύνοντος ἀφικόμεθα* ‘as the sun was setting, we arrived’. This is the **genitive absolute**, the exact counterpart of the Latin ablative absolute (*sōle occidente*). The participle keeps its usual meanings — time, cause, condition, concession — and its tense shows time relative to the main verb: *ταῦτα εἰπόντος αὐτοῦ, ἀπῆλθον* ‘when he had said this, they went away’.
Impersonal verbs, which have no subject, use the neuter participle in the **accusative** instead: *ἐξόν* ‘it being possible’, *δέον* ‘it being necessary’ — the **accusative absolute**.

Prepositions began as adverbs that sharpened the meaning of a case, and the old case meanings still show through: with the **genitive** a preposition tends to mean motion **from**, with the **dative** rest **at**, with the **accusative** motion **to** or extent.

table.title: Prepositions with one case
table.note: ἐξ is used before vowels. Attic prose often writes ξύν for σύν in older texts (Thucydides).

blocks.tip: *παρά* shows the case logic perfectly: *παρὰ τοῦ βασιλέως* ‘from the king’ (genitive: from), *παρὰ τῷ βασιλεῖ* ‘at the king’s court’ (dative: at), *παρὰ τὸν βασιλέα* ‘to the king’ (accusative: to). English *para-dox* (*παρὰ δόξαν*) is ‘contrary to expectation’.

blocks.pitfall: *διὰ τοῦτο* means ‘**because of** this, therefore’, not ‘through this’: *διά* + accusative is causal. And the agent of a passive verb is *ὑπό* + genitive (*ὑπὸ τῶν πολεμίων*), not *ἀπό*.

items.en: When I am dead, let earth be mingled with fire. (a proverbial tragic verse; Suetonius reports that Nero capped it with ἐμοῦ ζῶντος, ‘no — while I live’)
We arrived as the sun was setting.

items.t: Ἐντεῦθεν ἐξελαύνει σταθμοὺς τρεῖς παρασάγγας εἴκοσι.
items.en: From there he marches three stages, twenty parasangs. (Xenophon’s recurring formula in the Anabasis)
Swift-footed Achilles. (Homer)
items.lit: Achilles, swift as to his feet.

items.en: I have a brother.
items.lit: There is to me a brother.

items.en: They left by night.

items.t: Καὶ νὴ τὸν κύνα, ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι…
items.en: And by the dog, men of Athens… (Socrates’ favourite oath, Plato, Apology 22a)
A messenger came from the king.

blocks.p: The dative was the first case to go. In Koine it was already weakening: *εἰς* + accusative began to replace *ἐν* + dative (‘in’ and ‘into’ merging), and the genitive took over indirect objects. In the course of the Middle Ages the dative vanished from everyday speech. Modern Greek expresses the indirect object in two ways: with **σε** (from *εἰς*) + accusative, fused with the article as *στον, στη(ν), στο*; or, with pronouns, with the **genitive** clitic: *μου δίνει* ‘he gives me’ (northern dialects use the accusative: *με δίνει*).

compare.title: Where the dative went
rows: I give the book to the child
compare.note: με ‘with’ comes from μετά, and για ‘for’ from διά.

blocks.p: The surviving prepositions now take the **accusative**, whatever case they once governed. Only learned prepositions, mostly in formal language, keep the ancient genitive.

Yet datives still turn up in Modern Greek, frozen in set phrases from the learned tradition. Some go back to antiquity or the Church; others were coined in the formal language (*καθαρεύουσα*) of the 19th and 20th centuries.

compare.title: Fossil datives in everyday Greek
compare.note: εντάξει is written as one word: most speakers no longer feel it as a phrase at all.

items.en: I give the book to Maria.
I give her the book.
items.lit: Of-her I give the book.

items.en: OK, I’ll come.

items.t: Δόξα τω Θεώ, είμαστε όλοι καλά.
items.en: Thank God, we are all well.

title: From Attic to Koine to Modern Greek
sub: Three thousand years of one language

blocks.p: Greek has the longest continuous written history of any European language: from the Mycenaean Linear B tablets of the late Bronze Age, through Homer, Plato and the New Testament, to the newspapers of today’s Athens. Its main stages are **Archaic and Classical** Greek (Homer to Aristotle), the **Koine** (from about 300 BC), **Medieval** or Byzantine Greek, and **Modern** Greek. These are not different languages but phases of one, and a modern Greek reader recognises a surprising amount of the Gospel of John.

Classical Greece had no standard language. Every region spoke and wrote its own dialect: **Attic** in Athens; **Ionic** on the coast of Asia Minor and the islands (Herodotus, Hippocrates); **Doric** in Sparta, Corinth and Syracuse; **Aeolic** on Lesbos (Sappho, Alcaeus); and others. Literary genres kept the dialect of their founders, so even Athenian tragedians gave their choral songs a Doric colouring. **Homer**’s language is an artificial poetic blend, mainly Ionic with Aeolic elements and many archaisms, never spoken by anyone.

table.title: Attic, Ionic and Koine
table.note: Koine took Attic as its base but adopted the more widespread σσ and ρσ. Doric kept the old long α where Attic-Ionic has η: μάτηρ ‘mother’, γᾶ ‘earth’, ἁμέρα ‘day’.

items.en: Sing, goddess, the wrath of Achilles, son of Peleus. (Homer, Iliad 1.1 — note the epic genitives in -εω and -ῆος)
This is the presentation of the inquiry of Herodotus of Halicarnassus. (Herodotus 1, in Ionic: ἱστορίης for Attic ἱστορίας)

items.t: Θουκυδίδης Ἀθηναῖος ξυνέγραψε τὸν πόλεμον τῶν Πελοποννησίων καὶ Ἀθηναίων.
items.en: Thucydides, an Athenian, wrote the history of the war between the Peloponnesians and the Athenians. (Thucydides 1.1, in Attic)
In the beginning was the Word. (John 1:1, in Koine)

blocks.p: The conquests of **Alexander the Great** (king 336–323 BC) carried Greek from Egypt to the borders of India. Out of the Attic used by the Macedonian court and administration grew **ἡ κοινὴ διάλεκτος**, ‘the common dialect’. For the next thousand years it was the language of government, trade and learning in the eastern Mediterranean — under the Hellenistic kings, and then in the eastern half of the Roman Empire. Its monuments include the historian Polybius and the biographer Plutarch; the **Septuagint**, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible begun in Alexandria in the 3rd century BC; the **New Testament**; and thousands of private letters and documents on papyrus from Egypt, which show everyday speech.

Much of what makes Modern Greek different from Attic was already under way in Koine. The **dual** disappeared; the **optative** became rare; **μι-verbs** turned into ω-verbs (*δεικνύω*); *ἵνα* + subjunctive began to replace the **infinitive**; the **dative** weakened, with *εἰς* taking over from *ἐν*; and first-aorist endings spread to other aorists (*εἶπαν* for *εἶπον*).

Above all, the **sound** of Greek changed. Vowel length was lost, the musical pitch accent became a stress accent, and many vowels and diphthongs merged into /i/ (**itacism**). The written accents themselves were invented in Hellenistic Alexandria, traditionally by the scholar Aristophanes of Byzantium around 200 BC, to help readers pronounce Homer correctly at a time when the old pitch accent was fading.

table.title: How the sounds changed
table.note: The changes took place over many centuries; υ and οι were the last to become /i/, in Byzantine times.

blocks.p: From the 1st century BC, and especially in the 2nd century AD, educated writers reacted against the Koine and set out to write like the Athenians of the 5th and 4th centuries BC. Lexicographers such as Phrynichus compiled lists of ‘correct’ Attic words to use instead of ‘vulgar’ Koine ones. This **Atticism** opened a gap between the written and the spoken language — a **diglossia** that lasted, in one form or another, until 1976.

In the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire, with its capital at Constantinople (founded 330), Greek became the language of state as well as of culture. Historians such as Procopius and Anna Komnene wrote in an Atticising style; the Church kept the Koine of the Bible and the Fathers; and the spoken language went its own way, surfacing in literature from the 12th century in satirical and epic poems. By the end of the period the vernacular had lost the dative and the infinitive, formed its future with *θα*, its passive aorist in *-θηκα*, and many nouns had been rebuilt from the accusative (*ὁ πατέρας* from *τὸν πατέρα*). Latin loans entered the language: *σπίτι* ‘house’ from *hospitium*, *φούρνος* from *furnus*, *κάστρο* from *castrum*.

After the fall of Constantinople to the Ottomans in **1453**, Greek lived on under foreign rule. Turkish gave words such as *καφές* and *χαλί* ‘carpet’; Venetian rule in Crete and the Ionian Islands brought Italian words such as *πόρτα* ‘door’ and *φουρτούνα* ‘storm at sea’, and a flowering of literature in Cretan Greek, crowned by Vitsentzos Kornaros’ verse romance *Erotokritos* (17th century).

When the modern Greek state was founded (1830), it had to decide what Greek to use. **Adamantios Korais** (1748–1833) had argued for a ‘middle way’: the living language, purified of foreign words and brought closer to ancient forms. This became **Katharevousa** (*καθαρεύουσα*, ‘the purifying (language)’), used by the state, the law courts, science, the press and most schools. The spoken **Demotic** (*δημοτική*) was the language of song and much poetry — of Dionysios Solomos, whose *Hymn to Liberty* (1823) became the national anthem, and later of Kostis Palamas. Ioannis Psycharis’ *Το ταξίδι μου* (‘My Journey’, 1888) became the manifesto of the demoticists.

The **Language Question** (*γλωσσικό ζήτημα*) was fought with real passion. In 1901 a translation of the Gospels into Demotic set off riots in Athens in which several people were killed (the *Ευαγγελικά*), and in 1903 a performance of Aeschylus in modernised Greek led to further violence. Demotic entered primary schools in 1917, was pushed back, and returned; Manolis Triantafyllidis’ grammar of Demotic (1941) became its standard description. The military dictatorship of 1967–74 imposed Katharevousa once more. After its fall, a law of **1976** made Demotic, as ‘Modern Greek’, the language of education and the state, and in **1982** the **monotonic** system replaced the ancient accents and breathings in official use.

The result, **Standard Modern Greek**, is Demotic in its grammar but rich in learned elements inherited from Katharevousa: vocabulary (*νοσοκομείο* ‘hospital’), formal genitives (*της πόλεως* beside *της πόλης*), participles (*οι συλληφθέντες*) and fixed datives (*εν τω μεταξύ*). In the end, the long quarrel ended in something like Korais’ middle way after all.

items.en: The turnings of the wheel (of fortune), which go up and down… (Kornaros, Erotokritos 1.1, Cretan Greek)

items.en: I recognise you by the fearsome edge of your sword. (Solomos, Hymn to Liberty, the Greek national anthem)

blocks.p: Follow a single simple sentence, ‘give me water to drink’, through the history of the language. Each stage shows one of the great changes: the infinitive giving way to *να*, the dative pronoun giving way to the genitive, and an old word for ‘water’ replaced by a new one.

items.en: Attic: aorist imperative, dative μοι, infinitive of purpose πιεῖν.
Koine: Jesus to the Samaritan woman (John 4:7). Still an infinitive, in the contracted Koine form πεῖν.
Medieval vernacular (illustrative): genitive μου for the dative, νὰ + subjunctive for the infinitive, νερόν for ὕδωρ.
Modern: a new imperative δώσε (from the aorist έδωσα), monotonic spelling, final ν gone. ‘Give me water to drink.’

blocks.p: The word for ‘water’ is a good example of how everyday vocabulary was renewed. Ancient *ὕδωρ* survives only in learned compounds (*υδραυλικός* ‘plumber’, English *hydraulic*); the spoken word *νερό* comes from *νεαρὸν (ὕδωρ)* ‘fresh (water)’. Many basic words changed in the same way, usually by a diminutive or a descriptive phrase taking over.

compare.title: The future, stage by stage
rows: Koine: ‘I want to write’ used as a future
Modern: θέλω να → θε να → θα

title: Greek inside English and Latin
sub: Transliteration, word-building, and the road through Latin into Romance

blocks.p: English contains tens of thousands of Greek words, but very few came straight from Greek. Most travelled **through Latin** — often with a stop in French — and English spelling still follows the way the Romans wrote Greek. Rome borrowed Greek words from its earliest days (trade, theatre, religion), then the vocabulary of philosophy, science and the Church; and from the Renaissance onwards scientists built new words from Greek parts (*thermometer, biology, telephone*). Learn the Roman spelling rules and you can see the Greek word through the English one.

table.title: How Latin spelled Greek
rows: ἄγγελος → angelus → angel; ἄγκυρα → ancora → anchor
οἰκονομία → oeconomia → economy; τραγῳδία → tragoedia → tragedy
εἰκών → īcōn → icon; μουσεῖον → mūsēum → museum
table.note: The Latin ch, ph, th were the Roman attempt to write the Greek aspirated stops kʰ, pʰ, tʰ; the Romans pronounced them roughly as k, p, t.

blocks.tip: Run the rules backwards to find the Greek: *ph* → φ, *th* → θ, *ch* → χ, *ps* → ψ, *y* → υ, *rh* → ῥ, initial *h* → rough breathing, *e* from *ae / oe* → αι / οι. *Hypothesis* is *ὑπόθεσις*, *rhapsody* *ῥαψῳδία*, *eucharist* *εὐχαριστία*, *economy* *οἰκονομία* ‘household management’.

blocks.pitfall: A Greek-looking spelling is not proof of Greek origin. English *rhyme* was originally *rime* (from French); the *h* and *y* were added in imitation of *rhythm*. Conversely, French-style spellings can hide Greek words: *blame* goes back to Greek *βλασφημεῖν*, through Late Latin *blasphēmāre* and Old French *blasmer*.

blocks.p: Most Greek prefixes are prepositions, and many have an exact Latin counterpart: *συν-* = Latin *con-*, *ὑπο-* = *sub-*, *ὑπερ-* = *super-*, *περι-* = *circum-*. Others that you will meet constantly in English are *ἀνα-* ‘up, back’ (*analysis*), *κατα-* ‘down’ (*catastrophe*), *δια-* ‘through’ (*diagnosis*), *μετα-* ‘change, after’ (*metamorphosis*), *παρα-* ‘beside, beyond’ (*paradox*), *περι-* ‘around’ (*perimeter*), *προ-* ‘before’ (*prologue*).

compare.title: Six productive prefixes
gloss: ‘not, without’ (ἄτομος ‘uncuttable’, ἀναρχία ‘having no ruler’); ἀν- before a vowel
‘under’ (ὑπόθεσις ‘placing under’); ὑποκριτής was the Greek word for an actor
‘with, together’; the ν assimilates: συμ- before labials, συλ- before λ, συ- before σ + consonant

blocks.p: Because the prefixes match, Latin writers often **translated** Greek compounds piece by piece. These calques gave English a second word for the same idea.

compare.title: Greek compounds and their Latin translations
gloss: ‘uncuttable’ (Cicero used individuum for the atoms of Democritus)

blocks.p: The Greek suffixes passed into Latin and from there into all the languages of Europe, where they are still productive: anyone can coin a new *-ism* or *-logy*. The British spelling *-ize* (*baptize, organize*) reflects the *ζ* of Greek *-ίζω*; *-ise* follows French *-iser*.

compare.title: Suffixes from Greek through Latin to English
gloss: adjective: ‘of the citizens, of the city’
compare.note: -μετρον ‘measure’ and -σκόπιον ‘instrument for viewing’ (σκοπέω ‘look at’) are mostly found in modern coinages: thermometer, barometer, telescope, microscope.

blocks.p: Many ‘Greek’ words of science were never Greek at all: they were assembled in modern Europe from Greek parts. *Dinosaur* (‘terrible lizard’) was coined by the English anatomist Richard Owen in 1842; *biology, photography* and *telephone* are 19th-century inventions; and *television* and *automobile* are hybrids, Greek *τῆλε* ‘far’ and *αὐτο-* ‘self’ joined to Latin *vīsiō* and *mōbilis*.

Some Greek words entered **spoken** Latin and then evolved with it like any native word, emerging in the Romance languages so changed that only the sound laws reveal their origin. Many came with Christianity. *ἐκκλησία*, the citizens’ assembly of Athens, became the Christian ‘assembly’, Latin *ecclēsia*, and then the word for ‘church’ from Italy to Portugal. *παραβολή* ‘comparison, parable’ became Church Latin *parabola*; since Christ ‘spoke in parables’, it came to mean simply ‘word’, displacing Latin *verbum*. Its verb *parabolāre* gave Italian *parlare* and French *parler*, while Spanish *hablar* and Portuguese *falar* come instead from Latin *fābulārī*.

compare.title: Greek words in Latin and Romance
compare.note: Romanian biserică ‘church’ comes from another Greek word: Latin basilica, Greek βασιλική ‘royal hall’; Romanian episcop and parabolă are learned words. English church is from yet another Greek word, κυριακόν ‘the Lord’s (house)’, borrowed early into Germanic (German Kirche). English palaver came via Portuguese palavra.

compare.title: More travellers
compare.note: English butter is another Greek word, βούτυρον, taken into Latin as būtȳrum and borrowed by Old English. The playing-card spade is the Italian and Spanish ‘sword’.

blocks.p: A Greek word can thus arrive **twice**: once by popular inheritance, worn down beyond recognition, and once as a learned borrowing that keeps its Greek shape. Italian has both *parola* ‘word’ and *parabola* ‘parabola’; English has both *govern* — from *κυβερνάω* ‘steer a ship’ through Latin *gubernāre* and French — and *cybernetics*, coined straight from the Greek in the 20th century.

items.en: Man is by nature a political animal. (Aristotle, Politics 1.2) — English political, zoology
Know yourself. (inscription at Delphi) — English diagnosis, agnostic
Nothing in excess. (inscription at Delphi)
In the beginning was the Word. (John 1:1) — English archaic, archaeology; logic, -logy

afterlife.title: Round trips: words that came home

blocks.p: The traffic did not run only one way. Modern Greek took back much of the international vocabulary that Western Europe had built from Greek parts: *τηλέφωνο, μικροσκόπιο, βιολογία, φωτογραφία, δεινόσαυρος*. Where the Western word was a Greek–Latin hybrid, Greek usually made a pure-Greek equivalent instead.

compare.title: International words in Modern Greek
gloss: Greek τῆλε + ὅρασις ‘sight’ instead of Latin visio
‘self-moving’, all Greek instead of Latin mobilis

blocks.p: Some words made a complete round trip, leaving Greece, travelling through Latin and Italian or French, and coming back centuries later in their new Western form — often alongside the learned descendant of the original.

compare.title: There and back again
rows: the market scene; taxi rank (via Italian piazza)
compare.note: Modern Greek πλατεία ‘square’, αποθήκη ‘storeroom’ and καμάρα ‘arch, vault’ continue the ancient words directly.

title: The Alphabet and Pronunciation
sub: Twenty-four letters, five vowels, and the letter pairs

blocks.h: The same alphabet, a new sound

blocks.p: Modern Greek uses the same 24 letters as Plato did, but reads them with a pronunciation that has been evolving for 2,500 years. The good news: reading is **almost perfectly regular**. Once you know the rules in this chapter you can pronounce any Greek word you see, and the written accent even tells you where the stress falls. Spelling is harder, because Greek keeps its historical spelling: the sound [i], for instance, can be written in six different ways.

table.title: The Greek alphabet
rows: [ɣ] a soft, voiced *ch*; before [e], [i] it is [ʝ], close to *y* in *yes*
[k], without the puff of air of English *k*
[s]; [z] before β, γ, δ, μ, ν, λ, ρ
[x] as in Scottish *loch*; before [e], [i] it is [ç], as in German *ich*
table.note: Sigma is written ς at the end of a word and σ everywhere else: *σεισμός* ‘earthquake’ has both.

blocks.p: Modern Greek has just **five vowel sounds** — [a], [e], [i], [o], [u] — all short and pure, like the vowels of Italian or Spanish. There is no difference of length: ο and ω sound exactly the same, and so do η, ι and υ. Some vowel sounds are written with two letters (**digraphs**), which are read as a single sound.

table.title: Vowel sounds and their spellings
rows: ι, η, υ, ει, οι, υι
table.note: *υι* is rare; you will meet it in *υιός* ‘son’, a formal word (everyday Greek says *γιος*).

blocks.p: So *και* ‘and’ is pronounced [ke], *είναι* ‘is’ [ˈine], *οι* ‘the’ (plural) [i], and *ούτε* ‘nor’ [ˈute]. A digraph is one vowel: in *είναι* the accent is written on the second letter, but it marks the stress of the whole sound.

In the pairs αυ and ευ the υ has become a **consonant**: [v] before a vowel or a voiced consonant (β, γ, δ, ζ, λ, μ, ν, ρ), and [f] before a voiceless consonant (θ, κ, ξ, π, σ, τ, φ, χ, ψ). When the pair is stressed, the accent goes on the υ: *αύριο*.
Some pairs of consonant letters stand for a single sound. The first three are how Greek writes [b], [d] and [g] — sounds that its letters β, δ, γ no longer have.

table.title: Consonant combinations
rows: [b] at the start of a word; [mb] or [b] inside it
table.note: Double consonants are pronounced as single ones: *θάλασσα* ‘sea’ is [ˈθalasa], *άλλος* ‘other’ [ˈalos].

blocks.h: γ, χ and the softening before e and i

blocks.p: γ is the voiced partner of χ: a soft, slightly gargled [ɣ] before [a], [o], [u] and consonants — *γάλα* ‘milk’, *γράμμα* ‘letter’. Before the sounds [e] and [i] — however they are spelled — it becomes [ʝ], close to the *y* of *yes*: *γέρος* ‘old man’, *γυναίκα* [ʝiˈneka] ‘woman’. In the same position χ softens to [ç], the sound of German *ich* (*χέρι* ‘hand’), and κ moves a little forward in the mouth (*κερί* ‘candle’).

An unstressed ι (or ει, οι…) before another vowel is often not a vowel at all, but only a sign of this softening: *γεια* [ʝa] ‘hi’, *γιατί* [ʝaˈti] ‘why’, *γιαγιά* [ʝaˈʝa] ‘grandma’, *ποιος* [pços] ‘who?’. After other consonants it becomes a quick glide: *παιδιά* [peˈðʝa] ‘children’, *καρδιά* [karˈðʝa] ‘heart’.

blocks.h: No h, no puff of air

blocks.p: Modern Greek has **no [h] sound**. Words that English borrowed with an *h* — *hero, history, hydrogen, harmony* — begin with a plain vowel in Greek: *ήρωας* [ˈiroas], *ιστορία* [istoˈria], *υδρογόνο* [iðroˈɣono], *αρμονία* [armoˈnia]. Nor do π, τ, κ have the puff of air (aspiration) that English gives *p, t, k* at the start of a word: Greek *πόλη* begins like the *p* of *spin*, not of *pin*.

blocks.pitfall: Beware the look-alikes. Greek **Η η** is [i], not *h*; **Ρ ρ** is [r], not *p*; **Ν ν** is [n], not *v*; **Υ υ** is [i], not *u*; **Χ χ** is the *ch* of *loch*, not *x*; **Β β** is [v]. And never read ου as in English *out* — it is always [u] — or ευ as in English *Europe*: *Ευρώπη* is [evˈropi].

blocks.tip: Since reading is regular, practise reading aloud from the very first day. Street signs, menus and shop fronts are perfect material: *ΦΑΡΜΑΚΕΙΟ* [farmaˈkio] ‘pharmacy’, *ΤΑΒΕΡΝΑ* ‘taverna’, *ΚΑΦΕΝΕΙΟ* ‘coffee house’. Words written entirely in capitals carry no accent marks.

afterlife.title: Where it comes from: itacism and the new consonants

blocks.p: The Attic Greek of around 400 BC had about a dozen vowel sounds, long and short, plus true diphthongs: η was a long open [ɛː], ω a long open [ɔː], υ a rounded [y] like French *u*, and αι, οι were two-part sounds like the vowels of English *eye* and *boy*. Over the following thousand years — through the Hellenistic Koine and into the Byzantine era — vowel length disappeared and the vowels collapsed into today’s five. The great winner was [i]: one after another, ει, η, οι, υ and υι merged with ι. This merger is called **itacism** (or iotacism), after the modern name of the letter η, *ήτα* [ˈita].

table.title: From Classical Attic to Modern Greek
table.note: Roughly: ει had become [i] by the 3rd century BC; αι became [e] and η became [i] in the first centuries AD; υ and οι first merged as [y] and finally became [i] around the 10th century.

blocks.p: That is why Modern Greek spelling, which keeps the ancient letters, has six ways of writing [i], and why Greek children learn spelling word by word. But the historical spelling has a great advantage: words still *look* like their ancestors, and like the English words borrowed from them. Latin took many of these words over before the vowels merged, so its spelling preserves the old distinctions: η became *ē*, υ became *y*, οι became *oe*, αι became *ae*, ου became *ū*.

compare.title: Old values frozen in Latin spelling
compare.note: In Modern Greek these vowels are simply [i], [e] and [u]: *ψυχή* [psiˈçi], *οικονομία* [ikonoˈmia], *σφαίρα* [ˈsfera].

blocks.p: The consonants moved too. β, γ, δ, once [b], [g], [d], softened into the fricatives [v], [ɣ], [ð]; and φ, θ, χ, once ‘aspirated’ [pʰ], [tʰ], [kʰ] — a *p, t, k* with a strong puff of air — became [f], [θ], [x]. The Romans heard that puff of air and wrote *ph, th, ch*, which is why English still spells *philosophy, theatre, chorus* that way. Greek, having lost its [b], [d], [g], rebuilt them from letter pairs: μπ, ντ, γκ.

The rough breathing — the [h] at the start of words like *ἥρως* ‘hero’ and *ἱστορία* ‘inquiry, history’ — fell silent during the Koine period. Latin had already written it as *h* (*hērōs, historia*), and English kept the letter; Modern Greek has neither the sound nor, since 1982, the sign (chapter 2).

If you learned Ancient Greek at school, you probably used the ‘Erasmian’ pronunciation, a Renaissance reconstruction in which β is [b] and η is [ɛː]. Greeks themselves read Homer and the New Testament aloud with the modern pronunciation described in this chapter.

title: Stress and Spelling
sub: The accent mark, the diaeresis and Greek punctuation

blocks.p: Modern Greek writes **one** accent mark, the *τόνος* (´), on the stressed vowel of every word of two or more syllables: *μητέρα* [miˈtera] ‘mother’, *άνθρωπος* [ˈanθropos] ‘person’, *καλά* [kaˈla] ‘well’. Words of one syllable normally have no accent: *και* ‘and’, *το* ‘the’, *θα* ‘will’, *φως* ‘light’.

Greek stress is **free** — it can fall on different syllables in different words — and it is **distinctive**: moving it can change the meaning. So the accent mark is not decoration. Learn every word together with its stress.

table.title: Same letters, different stress
table.note: *πόλη* and *πολύ* are spelled differently but sound the same apart from the stress: [ˈpoli], [poˈli].

blocks.p: The stress can only fall on one of the **last three syllables** of a word. Greek grammar has a name for each: the *λήγουσα* (last), the *παραλήγουσα* (second-to-last) and the *προπαραλήγουσα* (third-to-last).

Because of this rule, the stress has to move forward when a word stressed on the third-to-last syllable gains a syllable at the end: *το μάθημα* ‘the lesson’ but *τα μαθήματα* ‘the lessons’; *το όνομα* ‘the name’ but *τα ονόματα* ‘the names’. Some words shift for historical reasons even without growing — *ο άνθρωπος*, *του ανθρώπου* ‘of the person’ — as the ancestry panel below explains.

The accent sits on the vowel letter. In a digraph (αι, ει, οι, ου, αυ, ευ) it goes on the **second** letter: *είναι* ‘is’, *ούτε* ‘nor’, *αύριο* ‘tomorrow’. On a capital letter it is written in front of it, at the top: *Άννα*, *Όλγα*, *Ύδρα* ‘Hydra’. Words written entirely in capitals have no accents at all: *ΑΘΗΝΑ*.
A few one-syllable words are written with an accent to tell them apart from an identical unstressed word:

table.title: Monosyllables with an accent
table.note: *Πού μένεις;* ‘Where do you live?’ but *ο φίλος που μένει εδώ* ‘the friend who lives here’. *Πώς σε λένε;* ‘What’s your name?’ (literally ‘how do they call you?’) but *Λέει πως είναι άρρωστος* ‘He says that he’s ill’.

blocks.p: Little words such as *μου* ‘my’ and *σου* ‘your’ are **enclitics**: they have no stress of their own and lean on the word before, which counts them as an extra syllable. If that would push the stress outside the three-syllable window, the word takes a **second accent** on its last syllable: *το όνομα* + *μου* → *το όνομά μου* ‘my name’; *το τηλέφωνο* + *σου* → *το τηλέφωνό σου* ‘your phone’. Words stressed on the last or second-to-last syllable don’t change: *ο φίλος μου* ‘my friend’, *το σπίτι σου* ‘your house’.

Two dots (*διαλυτικά*) over ι or υ say: **this is not a digraph** — pronounce the two vowels separately. Compare *παιδάκι* [peˈðaki] ‘little child’, where αι is [e], with *κοροϊδεύω* [koroiˈðevo] ‘I tease’, where οϊ is [oi]. If the first of the two vowels carries the accent, the dots are unnecessary, because the accent already shows that the letters are not a pair: *τσάι* [ˈtsai] ‘tea’, *ρολόι* [roˈloi] ‘clock’. One letter can carry both marks: *καΐκι* [kaˈiki] ‘caique’.

Greek uses the comma, full stop and exclamation mark just as English does. But the **question mark is ;** — the sign that looks like an English semicolon: *Τι ώρα είναι;* ‘What time is it?’. The Greek semicolon is a raised dot, the *άνω τελεία* (·), and quotations are usually set in angle quotes: «Καλημέρα».

blocks.pitfall: Don’t read ; as a pause — it turns the whole sentence into a question. *Θέλεις καφέ.* ‘You want coffee.’ / *Θέλεις καφέ;* ‘Do you want coffee?’ The word order of statements and questions is often identical; only the rising intonation, and in writing the ;, makes the difference.

I never go there.
Do you want coffee or tea?
Where is Hydra?
What’s your phone number?

items.en: He said “thank you” to me and left.

blocks.tip: Learn each new word with its accent and say it aloud with the stress in the right place. Greeks will understand a slightly wrong vowel, but a misplaced stress can make a word unrecognisable — or turn it into a different word.

afterlife.title: Where it comes from: from three accents to one

blocks.p: Ancient Greek had a **pitch accent**: the accented syllable was spoken on a higher note, and on a long vowel the pitch could either rise or rise and fall. Around 200 BC scholars in Alexandria — tradition names Aristophanes of Byzantium — began to mark it with three signs: the acute (´), the grave (`) and the circumflex (῀). They also marked the presence or absence of [h] at the start of a word with the rough (῾) and smooth (᾿) **breathings**. Byzantine scribes later added the iota subscript (ᾳ, ῃ, ῳ) for an iota that had fallen silent.

By late antiquity the pitch accent had turned into a **stress accent**, vowel length had disappeared and the [h] was gone. The three accents and two breathings no longer stood for anything audible — yet Greeks went on writing them, in the **polytonic** (‘many-accent’) system, for well over a thousand years. In 1982 the Greek state officially adopted the **monotonic** (‘single-accent’) system you are learning: one stress mark and the diaeresis, with no breathings and no iota subscript.

compare.title: Polytonic and monotonic
compare.note: Breathings and the iota subscript vanish; acute, grave and circumflex all become the single *τόνος*; and words of one syllable lose their accent (*φῶς* → *φως*, *γῆ* → *γη*).

blocks.p: What survived the change is the **position** of the stress, which in most words is still where the ancient pitch accent was: *ἄνθρωπος* → *άνθρωπος*, *θάλασσα* → *θάλασσα*, *ποταμός* → *ποταμός* ‘river’. The ancient rule that the accent cannot stand further back than the third syllable from the end survived too — and so did a shift it caused. In Ancient Greek a long vowel in the last syllable pulled the accent forward: *ἄνθρωπος*, but genitive *ἀνθρώπου*. Modern Greek no longer has long vowels, yet it keeps the shift in many words, as a fossil of the old rule.

compare.title: The genitive shift, then and now
compare.note: Everyday Modern Greek keeps the shift in *άνθρωπος* and *θάνατος* but has given it up in *θάλασσα*.

blocks.p: The double accent before enclitics is ancient as well. Plato wrote *ἄνθρωπός τις* ‘some person’, with a second accent on the last syllable — exactly the rule behind Modern *το όνομά σου* ‘your name’. And where the stress *did* move, there is usually a reason. In *καρδία* → *καρδιά* ‘heart’ and *ἐλαία* → *ελιά* ‘olive’, the stressed ι turned into a [j] glide before the next vowel, and the stress slid on to that vowel.

parts.title: Where it comes from: from three accents to one

title: The Article and Masculine Nouns
sub: Gender, the two articles, and nouns in -ος, -ας, -ης, -ές

blocks.p: Like Ancient Greek and Latin, Modern Greek has **three genders**: masculine, feminine and neuter. Every noun has one. It is largely predictable from the ending, but the surest guide is the **article**, so learn every noun together with it: *ο δρόμος* ‘the road’ (m.), *η πόλη* ‘the city’ (f.), *το σπίτι* ‘the house’ (n.).

Nouns, articles and adjectives also change their endings for **case**. Modern Greek has four: the **nominative** (the subject), the **accusative** (the object, and after prepositions), the **genitive** (‘of’) and the **vocative** (for calling someone). Chapter 8 looks at how they are used; here we learn the forms.

table.title: The definite article ‘the’
table.note: The vocative has no article. *οι* serves for both masculine and feminine plural, and *των* for all three genders.

blocks.p: The masculine *τον* always keeps its final *-ν*: *τον φίλο*, *τον δρόμο*. The feminine *την* keeps it only before a vowel or before κ, π, τ, ξ, ψ and the pairs μπ, ντ, γκ, τσ, τζ: *την Άννα*, *την πόλη*, but *τη μητέρα*, *τη θάλασσα*. The negative *δεν* ‘not’ follows the same rule as *την*.

table.title: The indefinite article ‘a, an’
table.note: The indefinite article is simply the numeral ‘one’, so it has no plural: *ένας φίλος* ‘a friend’, *φίλοι* ‘friends’. The two-syllable *μία* is used when you mean ‘one’ rather than ‘a’.

blocks.p: Masculine nouns end in **-ος**, **-ας**, **-ης** or **-ές** (and a handful in *-ούς*). They share one simple principle: the nominative singular ends in *-ς*, and the other singular cases drop it.

table.title: Masculines in -ος
table.note: Most nouns stressed on the third syllable from the end move the stress one place forward in the genitive singular and in the genitive and accusative plural: *ανθρώπου, ανθρώπων, ανθρώπους*. The vocative plural is the same as the nominative.

blocks.p: The vocative of *-ος* nouns ends in *-ε*: *φίλε!* ‘mate!’, *κύριε!* ‘sir!’, *κύριε Παπαδόπουλε!*. But most two-syllable first names use *-ο* instead: *Γιώργο!*, *Νίκο!*, *Πέτρο!*.

table.title: Masculines in -ας and -ης
table.note: In the singular these nouns have only two forms: with *-ς* for the subject, without it for everything else. In the plural, nominative and accusative are the same. Nouns in *-ης* always stress the genitive plural on the last syllable (*των εργατών*), and so do many in *-ας* (*των αντρών*) — but not all (*των πατέρων*).

table.title: Masculines with a plural in -δες
table.note: Nouns stressed on a final *-άς*, *-ές* or *-ούς* — many of them loanwords or names of trades — add *-δες* in the plural. So do some nouns in *-ης*, such as *ο μανάβης* ‘greengrocer’, plural *οι μανάβηδες*.

blocks.tip: Think of the masculine pattern as ‘*-ς* for the subject’: *Ο Γιάννης έρχεται* ‘Giannis is coming’, but *Ξέρεις τον Γιάννη;* ‘Do you know Giannis?’ and *το σπίτι του Γιάννη* ‘Giannis’s house’. Greek speakers do this with every masculine name.

blocks.pitfall: Don’t forget to drop the *-ς*. Beginners often say *Βλέπω τον Νίκος*; it must be *Βλέπω τον Νίκο* ‘I see Nikos’. The same goes for surnames in the vocative: *Καλημέρα, κύριε Παπαδόπουλε!*

items.en: My father is a doctor.

items.t: Ο Νίκος έχει έναν αδερφό και μια αδερφή.
items.en: Nikos has a brother and a sister.
The coffee is very hot.
The pupils are asking the teacher.
Do you know Maria’s husband?
Where are you, mate?
Giorgos, come here!

afterlife.title: Where it comes from: the article and the accusative

blocks.p: The Modern Greek article is the ancient one, worn smooth. With the loss of [h], *ὁ, ἡ* became *ο, η*; the dative forms disappeared along with the dative case (chapter 8); and the feminine plural adopted the masculine *οἱ* and a new accusative, *τις*. Everything else is the ancient form without its breathings and extra accents.

compare.title: The definite article, then and now

blocks.p: Latin had no article at all: the Romance languages had to build theirs from the demonstrative *ille* ‘that’ (Italian *il*, Spanish *el*, French *le*, Romanian *-ul*). Greek never needed to. Its article has been in continuous use since Classical times, and its forms go back to a demonstrative pronoun already used by Homer.

The masculines in *-ας* and *-ης* tell a different story. Many of them were ancient **third-declension** nouns with awkward nominatives: *πατήρ* ‘father’, *ἀνήρ* ‘man’, *χειμών* ‘winter’. Spoken Greek took the **accusative** — the form heard most often — as its base, and simply added the masculine *-ς* to make a new nominative: *πατέρα* → *πατέρας*. The plural *-ες* (*πατέρες*) is the old third-declension plural, which later spread to the first-declension nouns in *-ης* as well: ancient *μαθηταί* ‘pupils’ is now *μαθητές*.

Exactly the same thing happened in the Romance languages, where most nouns continue the Latin **accusative**, not the nominative: Italian and Spanish *padre* come from *patrem*, not from *pater*. In both families, the form most used in everyday speech became the base of the whole word.

compare.title: Romance nouns from the Latin accusative

blocks.p: Finally, the plural in *-δες* also has an ancient seed: feminine nouns such as *λαμπάς* ‘torch’, plural *λαμπάδες*. In the Middle Ages this *-άδες* spread to masculines, and it became the standard way of fitting loanwords into Greek — *καφές* comes from Turkish *kahve*.

parts.title: Where it comes from: the article and the accusative

title: Feminine and Neuter Nouns
sub: -α, -η, -ος; -ο, -ι, -μα, -ος

blocks.p: Almost all feminine nouns end in **-α** or **-η**. Their pattern is the mirror image of the masculine one: the nominative has **no** *-ς*, and the genitive singular adds one. In the plural, nominative and accusative both end in *-ες*, and the genitive plural is usually stressed on its last syllable, *-ών*.

table.title: Feminines in -α
table.note: The vocative is the same as the nominative. A few nouns in *-α* keep the stress in place in the genitive plural: *η μητέρα*, *των μητέρων*.

table.title: Feminines in -η
table.note: *πόλη* represents a smaller group, mostly learned words, with the plural in *-εις* [-is]: *η λέξη* ‘word’, *οι λέξεις*; *η τάξη* ‘class’, *οι τάξεις*. In formal style its genitive singular may also be *της πόλεως*.

blocks.p: A small group of feminine nouns end in **-ος** and are declined exactly like the masculines, but with the feminine article. Most are learned words inherited from Ancient Greek — *η οδός* ‘street’ (in addresses), *η μέθοδος* ‘method’, *η είσοδος* ‘entrance’, *η έξοδος* ‘exit’ — and many are place names: *η Κύπρος* ‘Cyprus’, *η Ρόδος* ‘Rhodes’, *η Κόρινθος* ‘Corinth’.

Neuters are the easiest nouns in the language. Nominative, accusative and vocative are **always identical**, and the plural nominative/accusative nearly always ends in **-α**. There are four main types.

table.title: Neuters in -ο and -ι
table.note: In the *-ι* nouns the ι turns into a quick glide before the endings, and the genitive is stressed on the last syllable whatever the stress of the nominative: *το σπίτι*, *του σπιτιού*.

table.title: Neuters in -μα and -ος
table.note: The *-μα* nouns add a syllable (*-ματ-*) outside the nominative, so the three-syllable rule pushes the stress forward: *όνομα*, *ονόματος*, *ονομάτων*. The *-ος* neuters have their plural in *-η*, pronounced [i].

table.title: Gender at a glance
rows: ο δρόμος, ο πατέρας, ο μαθητής, ο καφές
η ώρα, η τέχνη, η πόλη, η είσοδος
το βιβλίο, το παιδί, το όνομα, το δάσος

blocks.tip: Diminutives in *-άκι* are always neuter, whatever the gender of the base word — and Greeks use them constantly: *ο σκύλος* ‘dog’ → *το σκυλάκι* ‘doggy’; *η πόρτα* ‘door’ → *το πορτάκι* ‘little door’; *ο καφές* → *το καφεδάκι* ‘a nice little coffee’.

blocks.pitfall: The ending *-ος* can be masculine (*ο δρόμος*), feminine (*η είσοδος*) or neuter (*το δάσος*), and the neuters are declined differently: *οι δρόμοι*, *οι είσοδοι*, but *τα δάση*. Whenever you meet a noun in *-ος*, check its article.

items.t: Η Αθήνα είναι μια μεγάλη πόλη.
items.en: Athens is a big city.
The child is reading a book.
The children are playing in the sea.

items.t: Η μητέρα της Άννας είναι καθηγήτρια.
items.en: Anna’s mother is a teacher.
The entrance is this way.
There’s no problem.

items.t: Κάθε μέρα έχει είκοσι τέσσερις ώρες.
items.en: Every day has twenty-four hours.

afterlife.title: Where it comes from: the triumph of the diminutive

blocks.p: The neuter nouns in *-ι* — among the commonest words in the language — are nearly all former **diminutives**. Ancient Greek made ‘little’ words with the suffix *-ιον*: *παῖς* ‘child’ → *παιδίον* ‘little child’. In everyday Koine these diminutives gradually lost their ‘little’ meaning and pushed out the plain words. Then the ending wore down: *-ιον* became *-ιν* in late antiquity, and the final *-ν* later dropped, leaving *-ι*: *παιδίον* → *παιδίν* → *παιδί*.

compare.title: From diminutive to everyday word
compare.note: Several of these replaced the old basic words: *ἄρτος* ‘bread’ gave way to *ψωμί*, *ἰχθύς* ‘fish’ to *ψάρι*, *ὀφθαλμός* ‘eye’ to *μάτι*. The old words live on in learned vocabulary — and in English *ichthyology* and *ophthalmology*.

blocks.p: *ψωμίον* meant a ‘morsel’ of food: in John’s Gospel it is the morsel that Jesus dips and hands to Judas. In Byzantine Greek it came to mean simply ‘bread’, and *ψωμί* is the bread on every Greek table today.

The most famous member of the family is a borrowing. Latin *hospitium* ‘hospitality, lodging’ entered Greek as *ὁσπίτιον* ‘lodging, house’, then lost its unstressed first syllable to become *σπίτι* ‘house, home’. English has the same Latin word, by way of French, in *hospice*.

Spoken Latin went through exactly the same fashion. *auris* ‘ear’ was replaced by *auricula* ‘little ear’, *genū* ‘knee’ by *genuculum* ‘little knee’ — and the Romance words descend from the diminutives:

compare.title: Latin diminutives in Romance
compare.note: Words in brackets come from a different source.

blocks.p: The other types are straight inheritance. The *-μα* neuters are ancient third-declension nouns, practically unchanged: *ὄνομα, ὀνόματος* → *όνομα, ονόματος*; *πρᾶγμα* → *πράγμα* ‘thing’. The *-ος* neuters keep the ancient contracted forms: *γένος, γένους*, plural *γένη*, are still the Modern forms of the word for ‘race, kind; gender’. The feminines in *-α* and *-η* continue the ancient first declension (*χώρα, χώρας*; *τέχνη, τέχνης*). And *πόλη* is ancient *πόλις* with a nominative rebuilt from the accusative *πόλιν* — the same trick as *πατέρα* → *πατέρας* in chapter 3 — while its plural *πόλεις* is pure Attic.

parts.title: Where it comes from: the triumph of the diminutive

title: The Present Tense (I)
sub: Conjugation A: γράφω; είμαι and έχω

blocks.p: Modern Greek has **no infinitive**. Verbs are listed in dictionaries under the first person singular of the present: *γράφω* is both ‘I write’ and the dictionary entry ‘to write’. Where English uses an infinitive, Greek uses *να* + a finite verb: *Θέλω να γράφω* ‘I want to write’, literally ‘I want that I write’.

Greek verbs fall into two great conjugations. **Conjugation A** verbs are stressed on the stem and end in unstressed *-ω*: *γράφω* ‘write’, *διαβάζω* ‘read, study’, *δουλεύω* ‘work’. **Conjugation B** verbs are stressed on the ending, *-ώ*: *μιλώ* ‘speak’, *μπορώ* ‘can’ (chapter 6).

table.title: Conjugation A — present
table.note: The 3rd plural has a longer, more colloquial form in *-ουνε*. In writing you will also meet an older 1st plural in *-ομε*: *γράφομε*.

blocks.p: The endings are the same for every A verb: **-ω, -εις, -ει, -ουμε, -ετε, -ουν**. Because they show the person, subject pronouns are normally left out, as in Latin, Italian or Spanish: *γράφω* ‘I write’, *γράφει* ‘he / she / it writes’.

One present covers all the English presents: *διαβάζω* is ‘I read’, ‘I am reading’ and ‘I do read’. With *εδώ και* ‘for (now)’ it also covers actions that began in the past and are still going on, where English needs the perfect: *Μένω στην Αθήνα εδώ και δύο χρόνια* ‘I have been living in Athens for two years’.

Put *δεν* ‘not’ before the verb: *Δεν ξέρω* ‘I don’t know’, *Δεν καταλαβαίνω* ‘I don’t understand’. Like *την*, it drops its *-ν* before most consonants other than κ, π, τ, ξ, ψ (*δε θέλω* ‘I don’t want’), though many writers simply keep *δεν* everywhere. A question has the same word order as a statement; only the intonation, and the ; in writing, are different: *Ξέρεις ελληνικά;* ‘Do you know Greek?’

blocks.pitfall: Greek has no helping verb ‘do’ in questions and negatives — the verb itself does the work. ‘Do you drink?’ is simply *Πίνεις;* and ‘I don’t drink’ is *Δεν πίνω*.

table.title: The two basic verbs
table.note: *είναι* is both ‘he / she / it is’ and ‘they are’. *είμαι* has the endings of the passive verbs in *-μαι* you will meet later; *έχω* is a perfectly regular A verb.

blocks.p: The 2nd plural doubles as the **polite** form of address, like French *vous*: *Τι κάνετε;* ‘How are you?’ to a stranger or an older person, but *Τι κάνεις;* to a friend. In everyday speech *έχει* on its own also means ‘there is, there are’: *Έχει πολύ κόσμο σήμερα* ‘There are a lot of people today’.
Many everyday expressions use *έχω* where English uses ‘be’: *έχω δίκιο* ‘I’m right’, *έχω άδικο* ‘I’m wrong’, *έχω γενέθλια* ‘it’s my birthday’.

blocks.h: Verbs with a vowel before the ending

blocks.p: A handful of very common A verbs have a stem ending in a vowel, and shorten some of their forms:

table.title: λέω, τρώω, ακούω, πάω
table.note: Others like them: *κλαίω* ‘cry’ (*κλαις, κλαίει…*), *φταίω* ‘be to blame’. *πάω* has a longer synonym, *πηγαίνω*, which is a regular A verb.

blocks.tip: In the present, an ending pronounced [i] or [is] is always spelled with **ει**: *γράφεις, γράφει*; and the 3rd plural is always **-ουν**. These spellings never vary, so they are free marks in any dictation.

items.en: How are you? — Fine, and you?

items.t: Είμαι από την Αγγλία. Εσύ από πού είσαι;
items.en: I’m from England. Where are you from?

items.t: Δουλεύουμε στην Αθήνα, αλλά μένουμε στον Πειραιά.
items.en: We work in Athens but live in Piraeus.
The children don’t drink coffee.
Do you have a room for tonight?
I don’t know what you want.
Shall we go for a coffee?

afterlife.title: Where it comes from: Plato’s endings, slightly worn

blocks.p: Conjugation A continues the ancient **thematic** verbs in *-ω*, and its singular has not changed in spelling for two and a half thousand years: Plato wrote *γράφω, γράφεις, γράφει* exactly as you do. The plural was remodelled. Ancient *γράφομεν* lost its final *-ν* to become *γράφομε*, then took the *ου* of the 3rd plural: *γράφουμε*. The 3rd plural *γράφουσι(ν)* was replaced by *γράφουν*, using the *-ν* that marked ‘they’ in the past tenses (*ἔγραφον* ‘they were writing’, *ἔγραψαν* ‘they wrote’).

compare.title: ‘write’ — present
compare.note: The two verbs are not related, but their endings are: Greek *-μεν*, *-τε* and *-ουσι* (from older *-οντι*, still found in Doric) and Latin *-mus*, *-tis*, *-nt* go back to the same Indo-European suffixes. Spelling hides a change of sound: Plato’s *γράφεις, γράφει* ended in [eːs], [eː]; today they end in [is], [i].

blocks.p: The verb ‘to be’ was rebuilt more radically. Ancient *εἰμί, εἶ, ἐστί(ν)* gave way in the Middle Ages to forms with **middle-passive** endings, *είμαι, είσαι*, like the passive verbs in *-μαι*. The 3rd person *είναι* is spelled like the ancient infinitive *εἶναι* ‘to be’, but it probably comes from Koine *ἔνι* ‘there is’ (short for *ἔνεστι*), reshaped to match *είμαι, είσαι*.

compare.title: ‘be’ — present
compare.note: Ancient *ἐστί* and Latin *est* are cognates — both from the Indo-European root *es-*, like English *is* and German *ist*.

blocks.p: *ἔχω* ‘I have’ needed no rebuilding: *ἔχω, ἔχεις, ἔχει* are Classical. In later Greek it took on a second job as a helping verb — *έχω γράψει* ‘I have written’ — just as Latin *habeō* did in the Romance languages: Italian *ho scritto*, Spanish *he escrito*, French *j’ai écrit*. You will meet that perfect later in the course.

parts.title: Verbs with a vowel before the ending
Where it comes from: Plato’s endings, slightly worn

title: The Present Tense (II)
sub: Conjugation B: αγαπάω / αγαπώ and μπορώ

blocks.p: Conjugation B verbs carry the stress on the ending. Their dictionary form ends in stressed *-ώ*, and they come in two types: **B1**, like *αγαπώ* ‘love’, with endings in *-α-*, and **B2**, like *μπορώ* ‘can’, with endings in *-ει-* and *-ου-*. The 2nd singular tells them apart at a glance: *αγαπάς* versus *μπορείς*.

B1 verbs have two sets of forms in several persons, and both are correct. The longer ones (*αγαπάω, αγαπάει, αγαπάνε*) are more colloquial; the shorter ones (*αγαπώ, αγαπά, αγαπούν*) a little more formal. Dictionaries list B1 verbs either as *αγαπώ* or as *αγαπάω*.

Common B1 verbs: *ρωτάω* ‘ask’, *απαντάω* ‘answer’, *ξυπνάω* ‘wake up’, *γελάω* ‘laugh’, *ξεχνάω* ‘forget’, *πεινάω* ‘be hungry’, *διψάω* ‘be thirsty’, *περνάω* ‘pass; spend (time)’, *βοηθάω* ‘help’, *ζητάω* ‘ask for’, *κοιτάω* ‘look at’, *τραγουδάω* ‘sing’, *πουλάω* ‘sell’, *σταματάω* ‘stop’.

table.title: B2 — present
table.note: B2 verbs have only one set of forms. *ζω* is the B2 pattern squeezed into one syllable; its one-syllable forms take no accent (*ζω, ζεις, ζει, ζουν*).

blocks.p: Common B2 verbs: *προσπαθώ* ‘try’, *ευχαριστώ* ‘thank’, *τηλεφωνώ* ‘phone’, *θεωρώ* ‘consider’, *χρησιμοποιώ* ‘use’, *αργώ* ‘be late’, *εξηγώ* ‘explain’, *καλώ* ‘call, invite’, *παρακαλώ* ‘request; please’. Many of them are learned or formal words.

blocks.tip: If a verb has a form in *-άω*, it is B1; B2 verbs never do — there is *μιλάω*, but nothing like ‘μποράω’. When a word list gives you only the *-ώ* form, look at the 2nd singular: *-άς* means B1, *-είς* means B2.

blocks.pitfall: Don’t mix the two patterns. The 2nd singular is *μιλάς* but *μπορείς*; the 3rd plural is *μιλάνε* or *μιλούν*, but only *μπορούν(ε)*. And note that the B1 1st plural *αγαπούμε* looks like B2 — it is the one place where the two types meet.

blocks.p: *μπορώ* ‘can’ and *θέλω* ‘want’ are followed by a *να*-clause, since Greek has no infinitive: *Δεν μπορώ να μιλάω τώρα* ‘I can’t talk now’; *Θέλω να πάω σπίτι* ‘I want to go home’. The verb after *να* has its own personal ending, which makes constructions like ‘I want you to go’ very simple: *Θέλω να πας*, literally ‘I want that you go’. Which form of the verb follows *να* is the subject of chapter 11.

items.en: I love you.
Do you speak English?
Are you hungry? — No, but I’m very thirsty.
Thank you very much! — You’re welcome.

items.t: Δεν μπορώ να μιλάω τώρα, οδηγώ.
items.en: I can’t talk now, I’m driving.
We live in Thessaloniki.

items.t: Με ρωτάει πάντα το ίδιο πράγμα.
items.en: She always asks me the same thing.
The children are laughing.

afterlife.title: Where it comes from: the ancient contract verbs

blocks.p: Conjugation B is the heir of the ancient **contract verbs** — verbs whose stem ended in a vowel that merged (‘contracted’) with the ending. Verbs in *-άω* such as *ἀγαπάω* became *ἀγαπῶ, ἀγαπᾷς…*; verbs in *-έω* such as *ποιέω* ‘make, do’ became *ποιῶ, ποιεῖς…*. Broadly, B1 continues the *-άω* verbs and B2 the *-έω* verbs.

compare.title: B2: almost unchanged
compare.note: Ancient *ὁδηγέω* meant ‘lead the way, guide’ (from *ὁδός* ‘road’ and *ἄγω* ‘lead’); the meaning ‘drive (a car)’ is modern.

compare.title: B1: the old forms and the new
compare.note: The short forms continue the ancient contracted ones, though *αγαπούμε, αγαπούν* have borrowed their *ου* from the *-έω* verbs. The long forms *αγαπάω, αγαπάει, αγαπάμε, αγαπάνε* were created in the Middle Ages on the pattern of vowel-stem verbs like *λέω* (*λέει, λέμε, λένε*).

blocks.p: The two classes did not stay neatly apart. Many everyday *-έω* verbs moved over to the livelier B1 type, while learned verbs stayed in B2:

The third ancient type, verbs in *-όω* such as *δηλόω* ‘show, make clear’, left conjugation B altogether and became regular A verbs in *-ώνω*: *δηλώνω* ‘declare’, *πληρώνω* ‘pay’ (ancient *πληρόω* ‘fill, fulfil’).

And *μπορώ* itself? It is not Classical. It comes from *εὐπορέω* ‘be well off, have the means’, which passed through medieval *ἠμπορῶ* to become *μπορώ* ‘I can’ — a verb of wealth turned into a verb of ability.

parts.title: Where it comes from: the ancient contract verbs

title: Adjectives
sub: Agreement and the four main patterns

blocks.p: A Greek adjective agrees with its noun in **gender, number and case**, using the same endings as the nouns you already know. It normally stands **before** the noun, between the article and the noun: *ο καλός φίλος* ‘the good friend’, *μια καλή ιδέα* ‘a good idea’, *τα καλά νέα* ‘the good news’. After *είμαι* it agrees in just the same way: *Ο καφές είναι καλός. Η μουσική είναι καλή. Το φαγητό είναι καλό.*

table.title: καλός ‘good’
table.note: This is the biggest group: *μεγάλος* ‘big’, *μικρός* ‘small’, *ζεστός* ‘warm, hot’, *όμορφος* ‘beautiful’, *ακριβός* ‘expensive’, *φτηνός* ‘cheap’, *άσπρος* ‘white’, *μαύρος* ‘black’.

blocks.p: Unlike nouns, adjectives stressed on the third syllable from the end usually keep the stress where it is throughout: *ο όμορφος*, *του όμορφου*, *των όμορφων*.

When the ending follows a **vowel** — usually in *-ιος, -αιος, -εος* — the feminine has *-α* instead of *-η*, and is declined like *η ώρα*: *ωραίος, ωραία, ωραίο* ‘lovely’; *νέος, νέα, νέο* ‘new, young’; *πλούσιος, πλούσια, πλούσιο* ‘rich’; *κρύος, κρύα, κρύο* ‘cold’; *παλιός, παλιά, παλιό* ‘old (of things)’; *αρχαίος, αρχαία, αρχαίο* ‘ancient’. One common adjective has a stressed feminine in *-ιά*: *γλυκός, γλυκιά, γλυκό* ‘sweet’.

table.title: βαθύς ‘deep’
