table.note: Like it: *βαρύς* ‘heavy’, *ελαφρύς* ‘light’, *μακρύς* ‘long’, *φαρδύς* ‘wide’, *παχύς* ‘thick, fat’. In all the forms with *ι* the ι is a glide, not a separate syllable: *βαθιά* has two syllables. The masculine and neuter genitive singular is rare in speech.

blocks.p: Learned adjectives in **-ής** have one set of forms for masculine and feminine and another for the neuter, with endings straight from Ancient Greek: *ακριβής* ‘exact’, *συνεχής* ‘continuous’, *διεθνής* ‘international’, *υγιής* ‘healthy’, *σαφής* ‘clear’.

blocks.pitfall: *ακριβής* ‘exact’ is not *ακριβός* ‘expensive’ — and some of their forms coincide: *ακριβή* can be ‘exact’ (accusative singular) or ‘expensive’ (feminine singular). *Η ακριβής ώρα* is ‘the exact time’; *η ακριβή τσάντα* is ‘the expensive bag’.

table.title: πολύς — irregular
table.note: Every form has a double λ except *πολύς* and *πολύ*. The neuter *πολύ* is also the adverb ‘very, a lot’: *πολύ καλός* ‘very good’, *Σ’ ευχαριστώ πολύ* ‘Thank you very much’.

blocks.tip: Comparison is easy: put *πιο* ‘more’ before the adjective and use *από* for ‘than’: *Η Αθήνα είναι πιο μεγάλη από τη Θεσσαλονίκη* ‘Athens is bigger than Thessaloniki’. Many common adjectives also have a one-word comparative in *-τερος*: *μεγαλύτερος* ‘bigger’, *καλύτερος* ‘better’.

items.t: Η Ελλάδα έχει πολλά ωραία νησιά.
items.en: Greece has many lovely islands.

items.t: Ο καφές σου είναι πολύ γλυκός.
items.en: Your coffee is very sweet.
A cold water, please.

items.t: Η θάλασσα εδώ είναι πολύ βαθιά.
items.en: The sea is very deep here.

items.t: Οι νέοι φοιτητές μένουν σε ένα παλιό σπίτι.
items.en: The new students live in an old house.
Enjoy your meal!
items.lit: good appetite

items.en: Have a good trip!

afterlife.title: Where it comes from — and where it went

blocks.p: Greek adjectives have changed remarkably little. The main type is the ancient *καλός, καλή, καλόν* minus the final *-ν* of the neuter. Ancient Greek had *-α* in the feminine after ε, ι and ρ (*νέα*, *δικαία*, *μικρά*); Modern Greek keeps *-α* after vowels but uses *-η* after ρ: Plato’s *μικρά, ἐλευθέρα* are today *μικρή, ελεύθερη*.

Two of these show sound change at work. In *βαθεῖα* the ει became [i] (chapter 1) and then a glide before the following vowel, giving *βαθιά*; the masculine plural *βαθιοί* was later built to match. And *μέγας* had an odd nominative but a regular stem *μεγαλ-* in most other forms (*μεγάλου, μεγάλῳ, μεγάλη*); spoken Greek rebuilt the masculine on that stem, making *μεγάλος* — the same instinct that turned *πατήρ* into *πατέρας*.
Greek adjectives are also one of the richest sources of English vocabulary, mostly by way of Latin and of modern scientific coinages:

compare.title: Greek adjectives in English
compare.note: Everyday *παλιός* ‘old’ is the worn-down form of *παλαιός*, which survives alongside it as a formal word.

parts.title: Where it comes from — and where it went

title: The Cases in Use
sub: Nominative, accusative, genitive, vocative — and σε

blocks.p: You have already met the forms of the four cases; this chapter is about what they do. In brief: the **nominative** names the subject; the **accusative** marks the object and follows almost every preposition; the **genitive** expresses ‘of’ (and, with pronouns, ‘to’); the **vocative** is for calling or addressing someone.

table.title: The cases at a glance
rows: direct object; after prepositions; time expressions

blocks.p: The nominative is the case of the subject, and also of a noun or adjective that describes the subject after *είμαι*: *Ο αδερφός μου είναι δάσκαλος* ‘My brother is a teacher’, *Η Μαρία είναι κουρασμένη* ‘Maria is tired’. The subject can follow the verb as easily as precede it: *Έρχεται ο Νίκος* ‘Nikos is coming’.

The accusative is the workhorse. It marks the **direct object** — *Ξέρω τη Μαρία* ‘I know Maria’ — and it follows **almost all prepositions**: *με* ‘with’, *για* ‘for, about’, *από* ‘from, by’, *σε* ‘in, at, to’, *χωρίς* ‘without’, *μέχρι* ‘until’. So: *με τον πατέρα μου* ‘with my father’, *για την Ελένη* ‘for Eleni’, *από την Αθήνα* ‘from Athens’.

The accusative on its own also expresses **time**, both when something happens and how long it lasts: *Την Κυριακή πάμε στη θάλασσα* ‘On Sunday we’re going to the sea’, *Δουλεύω όλη τη μέρα* ‘I work all day’, *κάθε πρωί* ‘every morning’.

The genitive follows the noun it belongs to and corresponds to English ‘of’ or ‘’s’: *το σπίτι του Γιάννη* ‘Giannis’s house’, *η πρωτεύουσα της Ελλάδας* ‘the capital of Greece’, *το τέλος της ταινίας* ‘the end of the film’. With weak pronouns it is also the case of the **indirect object**, the person *to* or *for* whom: *Μου δίνει το βιβλίο* ‘He gives me the book’ (chapter 9). With nouns, ‘to someone’ is normally *σε* + accusative: *Δίνω το βιβλίο στη Μαρία*.

blocks.pitfall: Quantities and containers take **no** genitive: the two nouns simply stand side by side. ‘A glass of water’ is *ένα ποτήρι νερό*, ‘a kilo of tomatoes’ *ένα κιλό ντομάτες*, ‘a bottle of wine’ *ένα μπουκάλι κρασί*.

blocks.p: The vocative is used to address people, without an article. Masculines in *-ος* take *-ε* (*φίλε!*, *κύριε Παπαδόπουλε!*), or *-ο* in most two-syllable first names (*Νίκο!*); masculines in *-ας* and *-ης* drop the *-ς* (*Κώστα!*, *Γιάννη!*). Feminines and neuters are the same as the nominative: *Μαρία!*, *παιδί μου!* ‘my child!’.

blocks.tip: Women’s surnames are genitives: the wife or daughter of *κύριος Παπαδόπουλος* is *κυρία Παπαδοπούλου*, literally ‘Mrs of-Papadopoulos’. Since it is a genitive, it never changes: *Καλημέρα, κυρία Παπαδοπούλου!*

blocks.p: The preposition *σε* covers ‘in’, ‘at’, ‘on’ and ‘to’ — both where something is and where it is going: *Είμαι στο σπίτι* ‘I’m at home’, *Πάω στο σπίτι* ‘I’m going home’. Before the definite article it loses its vowel and merges with it:

table.title: σε + the article
table.note: Before other words *σε* stays separate, and may drop its ε before a vowel: *σε μια ώρα* ‘in an hour’, *σ’ ένα λεπτό* ‘in a minute’. With clock times: *στις πέντε* ‘at five o’clock’.

items.en: Giannis is at home.
Shall we go to the beach?

items.t: Το αυτοκίνητο του πατέρα μου είναι παλιό.
items.en: My father’s car is old.
I’m giving the key to Maria.
The lesson starts at nine.

items.t: Μένουμε στην Ελλάδα από τον Μάιο.
items.en: We’ve been living in Greece since May.
I’d like a glass of wine.
items.lit: I want a glass wine

items.en: Good morning, Mrs Papadopoulou!

afterlife.title: Where it comes from: the vanishing dative

blocks.p: Ancient Greek had **five** cases: the four of Modern Greek plus the **dative**, which meant ‘to, for’ (the indirect object), ‘with, by means of’ and — with *ἐν* — ‘in’. During the Koine and Byzantine centuries the dative slowly died out of speech, and its work was shared out. The **genitive** took over the indirect object (*δίδωσί μοι* → *μου δίνει* ‘he gives me’), and prepositions with the **accusative** took over the rest.

The key preposition was *εἰς* ‘into’, which took the accusative. Already in the New Testament it is sometimes used for ‘in’ instead of *ἐν* + dative. In medieval Greek it lost its first vowel and merged with the article — *εἰς τόν* → *στον* — and became *σε*, the all-purpose preposition for both ‘in’ and ‘to’. Ancient *μετά* ‘with’, which took the genitive, shrank to *με* and switched to the accusative.

compare.title: Dative out, accusative in
gloss: I give the book to the child.
compare.note: Ancient Athens was a plural, *Ἀθῆναι*. Modern Greek does not distinguish ‘in’ from ‘to’: *στην Αθήνα* means both.

blocks.p: Latin went the same way, only further. Its six cases collapsed in the Romance languages, where prepositions — above all *dē* ‘from, of’ and *ad* ‘to’ — took over their work, and only the pronouns kept distinct case forms. The great exception is **Romanian**, which, like Greek, kept a single merged **genitive-dative**: *tatălui* means both ‘of the father’ and ‘to the father’. Albanian shares the same merger, and Bulgarian shows it in its pronouns — a hallmark of the Balkan languages, which shaped one another through centuries of contact.

compare.title: From Latin cases to Romance prepositions
rows: je donne le livre au père
gloss: I give the book to the father
compare.note: Romanian *tatălui* does both jobs, just as the Greek genitive *μου* is both ‘my’ and ‘to me’. And as Greek *σε* serves for ‘in’ and ‘to’, so do Italian *a*, French *à* and Romanian *la* with the names of cities.

parts.title: Where it comes from: the vanishing dative

title: Personal Pronouns
sub: Strong and weak forms, and where the weak ones go

blocks.p: Greek personal pronouns come in two sets. The **strong** forms (*εγώ, εμένα, εσύ, εσένα…*) are stressed words that can stand alone, carry emphasis and follow prepositions. The **weak** forms (*με, μου, σε, σου, τον…*) are short and unstressed, and must lean on a verb. In everyday speech the weak forms are by far the more frequent.

table.title: Personal pronouns
table.note: The weak genitive *τους* serves all three genders in the plural. The strong 3rd-person pronoun is the demonstrative *αυτός* ‘this’ (chapter 10).

blocks.p: Since the verb ending already shows the person, subject pronouns are used only for **emphasis or contrast**: *Εγώ δουλεύω κι εσύ κάθεσαι!* ‘I’m working and you’re sitting around!’. After prepositions, use the strong accusative, usually without its first ε: *για μένα* ‘for me’, *με σένα* ‘with you’, *από σας* ‘from you’, *χωρίς αυτόν* ‘without him’.

blocks.h: Weak forms: right before the verb

blocks.p: The weak forms go **immediately before** the verb, and nothing but another weak pronoun may come between them. *δεν*, *θα* and *να* stand in front of the whole group:

items.en: I see you.
I don’t know him.
She’s talking to me.
I’ll tell you.
I want to see her.

blocks.p: With an **imperative** the order flips: the weak pronoun comes **after** the verb and is pronounced as part of it. *Πες μου* ‘Tell me’, *Κοίτα με!* ‘Look at me!’, *Βοήθησέ με!* ‘Help me!’ (with the double accent of chapter 2).

The weak **accusative** is the direct object: *Με βλέπει* ‘he sees me’. The weak **genitive** is the indirect object, the person *to* or *for* whom: *Μου γράφει* ‘he writes to me’, *Σου φέρνω ένα δώρο* ‘I’m bringing you a present’. When both appear, the genitive comes first: *Μου το δίνει* ‘He gives it to me’, *Σου το λέω* ‘I’m telling you (so)’ — and after an imperative, *Δώσ’ μου το* ‘Give it to me’.

The same genitive goes with *αρέσει* ‘pleases’, Greek’s way of saying ‘like’: *Μου αρέσει η μουσική* ‘I like music’ (literally ‘music pleases me’), *Σου αρέσουν τα νησιά;* ‘Do you like the islands?’. The verb agrees with the thing liked, as in Spanish *me gustan* or Italian *mi piacciono*.

blocks.tip: To stress a weak pronoun, add the strong form as well — Greek happily says it twice: *Εμένα μου αρέσει, εσένα;* ‘I like it — do you?’, literally ‘to me it pleases me, to you?’. Likewise with nouns: *Τον Νίκο τον ξέρω* ‘Nikos — him I know’.

blocks.pitfall: Keep *με* and *μου* apart. *με* is the direct object, *μου* the indirect one: *Με ρωτάει* ‘she asks me’ but *Μου μιλάει* ‘she speaks to me’. Some verbs that take a direct object in English take the genitive in Greek: *Σου τηλεφωνώ* ‘I’ll phone you’, *Του μοιάζει* ‘he looks like him’.

items.en: I love you.

items.t: Πώς σε λένε; — Με λένε Ελένη.
items.en: What’s your name? — My name is Eleni.
items.lit: how do they call you? — they call me Eleni

items.t: Μου αρέσει πολύ αυτό το τραγούδι.
items.en: I really like this song.
Tell me the truth.

items.t: Το κλειδί; Σου το δίνω αμέσως.
items.en: The key? I’ll give it to you right away.
This is for you.
We see them every Saturday.

afterlife.title: Where it comes from: αὐτός, ille and the clitics

blocks.p: The strong pronouns are the ancient ones, lengthened. *ἐγώ* is unchanged; *σύ* gained an *ε-* to match it (*εσύ*); the accusatives *ἐμέ, σέ* were extended to *εμένα, εσένα*. The plurals show itacism at work: ancient *ἡμεῖς* ‘we’ and *ὑμεῖς* ‘you’ came to sound identical, [iˈmis], so ‘you’ was rebuilt on the singular *σύ, σέ* as *εσείς*, and ‘we’ became *εμείς* to match *εμένα*.

compare.title: Pronouns then and now
gloss: of me → of me, to me
of you → of you, to you

blocks.p: The weak 3rd-person forms have a story of their own. In Ancient Greek, *αὐτόν, αὐτήν, αὐτοῦ* in the oblique cases meant ‘him, her, of him’. Spoken without stress in front of a verb, they lost their first syllable — *(αὐ)τόν* → *τον* — and so came to coincide with the article *τον*.

Now the striking parallel. The Romance languages did **the same thing** with Latin *ille* ‘that’. Stressed, it gave the strong pronouns (Italian *lui*, Spanish *él*, French *lui*); unstressed before a verb, it lost its first syllable — *(il)lum* → *lo*, *(il)lam* → *la*, *(il)lī* → Italian *gli*, Spanish *le* — and these clitics look just like the definite article, which also comes from *ille*. Both families put clitics before an ordinary verb but after an imperative, and in both the indirect object comes first: Greek *μου το*, Italian and Spanish *me lo*.

compare.title: Clitic pronouns in Greek and Romance
compare.note: French is the odd one out after an imperative: *donne-le-moi* puts the direct object first. Spanish *le* covers both ‘to him’ and ‘to her’, just as Greek *τους* covers ‘to them’ for every gender.

blocks.p: Older stages of both families agree even more closely. Ancient Greek put unstressed pronouns second in the sentence, after its first word, whatever that word was. Medieval Greek, like Old Spanish and Old Italian, put them after the verb when the verb began the sentence — and Cypriot Greek still does: *Αγαπώ σε* ‘I love you’, where Athenians say *Σ’ αγαπώ*.

parts.title: Weak forms: right before the verb
Where it comes from: αὐτός, ille and the clitics

title: Possessives and Demonstratives
sub: μου, σου, του; δικός μου; αυτός, τούτος, εκείνος

blocks.p: Everyday Greek has no possessive adjectives like English *my* or French *mon*. Instead it puts the **weak genitive** pronoun after the noun, which keeps its article: *το σπίτι μου* ‘my house’, literally ‘the house of me’. The pronoun shows the owner; the article and noun show what is owned.

table.title: Possessives with ο φίλος ‘friend’
table.note: *σας* is also the polite ‘your’: *Το όνομά σας;* ‘Your name, please?’

blocks.p: Remember the double accent from chapter 2: a noun stressed on the third syllable from the end takes a second accent before the possessive — *το όνομά μου* ‘my name’, *το αυτοκίνητό σας* ‘your car’, *το τηλέφωνό του* ‘his phone’. With an adjective, the possessive can follow either word: *ο καλός μου φίλος* or *ο καλός φίλος μου* ‘my good friend’.
For emphasis, contrast or ‘mine, yours…’, Greek uses the adjective *δικός, δική, δικό* ‘own’, declined like *καλός*, followed by the weak genitive:

table.title: δικός μου ‘mine’
table.note: *δικός* agrees with the thing owned; the pronoun shows the owner: *Αυτή η τσάντα είναι δική του* ‘This bag is his’.

blocks.p: It has three main uses: as ‘mine, yours…’ after *είμαι* (*Αυτό είναι δικό μου* ‘That’s mine’); for emphasis (*το δικό μου σπίτι* ‘**my** house’, ‘my own house’); and for ‘a … of mine’ (*ένας δικός μου φίλος* ‘a friend of mine’). On its own, *οι δικοί μου* means ‘my family, my people’.

Greek has three demonstratives. *αυτός* ‘this, that’ is the everyday, neutral one; *εκείνος* ‘that (over there)’ points to things further away in space or time; *τούτος* ‘this (right here)’ is a more colloquial, emphatic ‘this’. All three are followed by the **article** and the noun: *αυτός ο άνθρωπος* ‘this person’ (literally ‘this the person’), *εκείνη η μέρα* ‘that day’, *τούτο το σπίτι* ‘this house’.

table.title: αυτός ‘this; he, she, it’
table.note: *εκείνος* (*εκείνου, εκείνον…*) and *τούτος* (*τούτου, τούτον…*) are declined the same way. Remember that αυ here is [af]: *αυτός* [afˈtos].

blocks.p: The demonstrative can also follow the noun, in a slightly more formal order: *ο άνθρωπος αυτός* ‘this person’. Without a noun, *αυτός* means ‘he, this one’ and *αυτό* ‘this, that, it’: *Ποιος είναι αυτός;* ‘Who’s he?’, *Τι είναι αυτό;* ‘What’s that?’.

blocks.pitfall: Don’t drop the article after a demonstrative: ‘this book’ is *αυτό το βιβλίο*, never *αυτό βιβλίο*. English makes do with one word before the noun; Greek needs two.

items.en: Where are my keys?

items.t: Η αδερφή μου μένει στη Θεσσαλονίκη.
items.en: My sister lives in Thessaloniki.

items.t: Ποιανού είναι αυτή η τσάντα; — Δική μου.
items.en: Whose bag is this? — Mine.
A friend of mine is a doctor.

items.t: Αυτή η πόλη είναι πολύ όμορφη.
items.en: This city is very beautiful.

items.t: Θέλω εκείνο το φόρεμα, όχι αυτό.
items.en: I want that dress, not this one.

items.t: Τούτο το σπίτι είναι του παππού μου.
items.en: This house is my grandfather’s.

afterlife.title: Where it comes from: from ‘self’ to ‘this’

blocks.p: Possession with the genitive of a pronoun is ancient. Classical Attic often used possessive adjectives (*ὁ ἐμὸς φίλος* ‘my friend’), but it also had the unemphatic genitive, and in the Koine — the Greek of the New Testament — the genitive became the normal way: *ὁ πατήρ μου* ‘my father’. The Lord’s Prayer even shows the double accent of Modern *το όνομά σου*: *ἁγιασθήτω τὸ ὄνομά σου* ‘hallowed be thy name’.
*δικός* is a worn-down *ἰδικός* ‘one’s own, particular’, from *ἴδιος* ‘own, private’ — the root of English *idiom* and *idiot*, originally a ‘private person’ who took no part in public life.

The demonstratives were reshuffled. Classical Greek said *οὗτος* ‘this’, *ἐκεῖνος* ‘that’ and *ὅδε* ‘this here’, while *αὐτός* meant ‘self’ (*αὐτὸς ὁ βασιλεύς* ‘the king himself’), ‘same’ (*ὁ αὐτός*) and, in the oblique cases, ‘him, her, it’. In post-classical Greek *αὐτός* drifted from ‘self’ to ‘this’ and took over from *οὗτος*. *ἐκεῖνος* survived intact as *εκείνος*, and *οὗτος* lives on in a rebuilt form, *τούτος*, made on its stem *τουτ-* (*τοῦτο, τούτου*). For ‘self’ Modern Greek turned to *ο ίδιος* (*ο ίδιος ο βασιλιάς* ‘the king himself’) and *ο εαυτός μου* ‘myself’.

compare.title: Demonstratives then and now
compare.note: Note the article after the demonstrative in both: *οὗτος ὁ ἀνήρ*, *αυτός ο άντρας*. That rule is Classical.

blocks.p: Latin and Romance went through a strikingly similar shuffle. Latin *ille* ‘that’ became the Romance article and 3rd-person pronoun; new demonstratives were built by reinforcing old ones with *eccum* or *ecce* ‘look!’; and ‘self’ was renewed too — Italian *stesso* from *istum ipsum*, Spanish *mismo* and French *même* from *metipsimus*, an emphatic form of *ipse* ‘self’.

compare.title: Romance demonstratives
compare.note: Italian *questo, quello* and Romanian *acest, acel* contain a reinforcing *eccum* or *ecce* before *iste* and *ille*; Spanish *este* is plain *iste*.

parts.title: Where it comes from: from ‘self’ to ‘this’

title: Aspect: The Two Stems
sub: Imperfective and perfective, and how to form the perfective stem

blocks.h: Two ways of looking at an action

blocks.p: Every Greek verb has **two stems**. The **imperfective** stem — the one you know from the present, *γράφ-* — presents an action as ongoing, repeated or habitual. The **perfective** stem, *γράψ-*, presents it as a single, complete event, seen as a whole. This difference is called **aspect**, and it runs through the whole verb system: Greek makes the choice in the past, in the future, after *να* and in the imperative.

English shows aspect only here and there — *I was writing* versus *I wrote*. Greek shows it almost everywhere. The one exception is the present tense: an action happening now is by definition still in progress, so the present has only the imperfective stem.

table.title: One verb, two stems
rows: έγραφα ‘I was writing, used to write’
θα γράφω ‘I’ll be writing, I’ll write (regularly)’
table.note: The past tenses and the imperative have their own chapters later. Here we concentrate on forming the perfective stem and using it after *να*; chapter 12 does the same for *θα*.

blocks.p: Verbs like *θέλω* ‘want’, *μπορώ* ‘can’, *πρέπει* ‘must’ and *μου αρέσει* ‘I like’ are followed by *να* + verb. Choose the perfective for a single, complete action, the imperfective for a habit or a process: *Θέλω να διαβάσω αυτό το βιβλίο* ‘I want to read this book’ (one complete reading), but *Θέλω να διαβάζω κάθε μέρα* ‘I want to read every day’ (a habit).

For most verbs the perfective stem is the present stem plus **σ**, which combines with the consonant before it. The perfective then takes the ordinary present endings: *(να) γράψω, γράψεις, γράψει, γράψουμε, γράψετε, γράψουν*. These are sometimes called the ‘dependent’ forms, because they never stand alone: they always follow *να*, *θα* or a similar word.

table.title: The regular patterns
rows: γράφω → γράψω, κόβω → κόψω, κρύβω → κρύψω, δουλεύω → δουλέψω, μαζεύω → μαζέψω
ανοίγω → ανοίξω, τρέχω → τρέξω, δείχνω → δείξω, ψάχνω → ψάξω, παίζω → παίξω, αλλάζω → αλλάξω
διαβάζω → διαβάσω, αρχίζω → αρχίσω, πείθω → πείσω, πιάνω → πιάσω, κλείνω → κλείσω, χάνω → χάσω
αγαπάω → αγαπήσω, μιλάω → μιλήσω; γελάω → γελάσω, ξεχνάω → ξεχάσω; φοράω → φορέσω
οδηγώ → οδηγήσω, ζω → ζήσω; μπορώ → μπορέσω, καλώ → καλέσω
μένω → μείνω, στέλνω → στείλω, πλένω → πλύνω
table.note: Verbs in *-ζω* are the one real uncertainty: most take *-σ-* (*αγοράζω → αγοράσω*), but a group, many of them describing sounds or quick movements, take *-ξ-* (*παίζω → παίξω*, *κοιτάζω → κοιτάξω*, *σφυρίζω → σφυρίξω* ‘whistle’). Learn them as you meet them.

table.title: Perfective forms after να
table.note: One-syllable irregular perfectives such as *δω* (from *βλέπω*), *πω* (from *λέω*) and *βρω* (from *βρίσκω*) take stressed endings like B2 verbs: *δεις, δει, δούμε, δείτε, δουν*.

blocks.p: Some of the commonest verbs have a perfective stem that looks nothing like the present. There is no way round them but to learn them — together with the simple past, which is built on the same stem:

table.title: Common irregular perfectives
table.note: *φάω* goes *φάω, φας, φάει, φάμε, φάτε, φάνε*; *πιω* goes *πιω, πιεις, πιει, πιούμε, πιείτε, πιουν*. A few verbs have no perfective at all — *είμαι*, *έχω*, *ξέρω* — and use the same form for both aspects: *να είμαι, να έχεις, να ξέρει*.

blocks.tip: When you see a form like *γράψω*, *πω* or *δω*, look to its left: there will be a *να*, a *θα* or a similar word. The perfective forms never stand alone as a present tense — *πω* by itself means nothing.

blocks.pitfall: The commonest mistake is using the perfective for a habit. *Πρέπει να πίνεις πολύ νερό* ‘You should drink a lot of water’ is a general rule, so imperfective; *Πρέπει να πιεις αυτό το φάρμακο* ‘You must take this medicine’ is one dose, so perfective. Ask yourself: one complete event, or a repeated or ongoing activity?

items.t: Μπορείς να μου δώσεις το αλάτι;
items.en: Can you pass me the salt?
I have to go now.
What do you want to eat?
I want to see you.
I like swimming.

items.t: Δεν μπορώ να βρω τα γυαλιά μου.
items.en: I can’t find my glasses.
I want to learn Greek.

afterlife.title: Where it comes from: the deepest continuity

blocks.p: Of everything in Greek grammar, the two-stem system is the oldest and most stable feature. Ancient Greek built its verbs on a **present stem** (*γράφ-*) and an **aorist stem** (*γραψ-*), and the difference between them was one of **aspect**, not time. Outside the indicative the aorist had no past meaning at all: *γράφε* meant ‘be writing, keep writing’, *γράψον* ‘write (it)’; *ἵνα γράφῃ* ‘so that he writes (habitually)’, *ἵνα γράψῃ* ‘so that he writes (it, once)’. Modern *να γράφει / να γράψει* is the same contrast after twenty-five centuries — the *να* forms are the old present and aorist subjunctives.

Even the irregular perfectives are ancient. Greek had always supplied some of its commonest verbs with aorists from a different root, and Modern Greek has kept them: the aorist of ‘see’ was *εἶδον*, of ‘say’ *εἶπον*, of ‘eat’ *ἔφαγον* — today’s *είδα, είπα, έφαγα*. Their subjunctives *ἴδω* and *εἴπω* were shortened to give *να δω, να πω*. And Modern *βρήκα* ‘I found’ is Archimedes’ *εὕρηκα* ‘I have found!’ — the old perfect, which took the place of the aorist *ηὗρον*.

compare.title: Ancient irregulars, still alive
compare.note: In ‘eat’ only the aorist survived: the ancient present *ἐσθίω* was replaced by *τρώγω* ‘gnaw, munch’, today *τρώω*.

blocks.p: Latin had the same contrast, but only in the past: the imperfect *scrībēbam* ‘I was writing’ against the perfect *scrīpsī* ‘I wrote’. The Romance languages kept it there — Italian *scrivevo / scrissi*, Spanish *escribía / escribí* — and nowhere else; Greek is unusual in marking aspect in the future and after *να* as well. The *-s-* of Latin *scrīpsī* and *dīxī*, by the way, is the same Indo-European suffix as the *-σ-* of Greek *έγραψα* and *έδειξα*.

compare.title: Imperfective and perfective past in Romance
gloss: I was writing, used to write
I was saying, used to say
compare.note: In everyday French, in much of Italy and in most of Romania, the simple perfect has given way to the *habēre* perfect: *j’ai écrit*, *ho scritto*, *am scris*.

parts.title: Two ways of looking at an action
Where it comes from: the deepest continuity

title: The Future
sub: θα + present and θα + perfective

blocks.p: The Greek future is made with the particle **θα** — unstressed and unchanging — placed before the verb. Because every verb has two stems (chapter 11), there are two futures: *θα* + the **present** gives the **continuous future**, and *θα* + the **perfective** gives the **simple future**.

table.title: More verbs
table.note: *είμαι*, *έχω* and *ξέρω* have only one future, which serves for both meanings.

blocks.p: The **simple future** is the default ‘will’: one event, seen as a whole, often with a result. *Θα σου τηλεφωνήσω αύριο* ‘I’ll call you tomorrow’. *Θα φάμε στις οχτώ* ‘We’ll eat at eight’.

The **continuous future** is for an action that will be in progress at a given moment, or that will be repeated or habitual — where English says ‘will be …-ing’ or ‘will (keep on) …’: *Αύριο στις οχτώ θα δουλεύω* ‘Tomorrow at eight I’ll be working’. *Θα σου τηλεφωνώ κάθε μέρα* ‘I’ll call you every day’.

Word order: *δεν* goes before *θα*, and weak pronouns go between *θα* and the verb: *Θα το κάνω αύριο* ‘I’ll do it tomorrow’; *Δε θα σε ξεχάσω ποτέ* ‘I will never forget you’ (often written *δεν θα*).

*θα* also expresses **probability**: *Θα είναι εννιά η ώρα* ‘It must be about nine o’clock’; *Θα είναι κουρασμένος* ‘He must be tired’. And with a past tense it forms the **conditional**, ‘would’: *Θα ήθελα έναν καφέ* ‘I would like a coffee’ — the most useful polite phrase in any Greek café.

blocks.tip: For plans in the near future Greek, like English, often uses the present: *Αύριο πάω στην Αθήνα* ‘Tomorrow I’m going to Athens’. *θα* is what you need for predictions, promises and decisions: *Θα πάω στην Αθήνα* ‘I will go to Athens’.

blocks.pitfall: Nothing but weak pronouns may stand between *θα* and its verb, and *δεν* always comes before *θα*, never after it: *Δε θα έρθω* ‘I won’t come’. And *θα* itself never changes: *θα έρθω, θα έρθεις, θα έρθουν*.

items.en: I’ll call you tomorrow.
I’ll write to you every week.
What are you doing this summer?
items.lit: what will you do the summer?

items.t: Δε θα έρθω απόψε, είμαι κουρασμένος.
items.en: I won’t come tonight, I’m tired.

items.t: Θα φάμε στο σπίτι ή έξω;
items.en: Shall we eat at home or out?
I’ll be waiting for you.
Will it rain tomorrow?

items.t: Θα ήθελα ένα ποτήρι νερό, παρακαλώ.
items.en: I’d like a glass of water, please.

afterlife.title: Where it comes from: ‘it wants that…’

blocks.p: Ancient Greek had a one-word future: *γράψω* ‘I shall write’, *λύσω* ‘I shall loosen’, formed with the same *-σ-* as the aorist. That was its weakness. The future *γράψω* was already identical to the aorist subjunctive *γράψω*, and once itacism and the loss of vowel length had merged future *γράψεις* with subjunctive *γράψῃς*, and *γράψει* with *γράψῃ*, the two could no longer be told apart. Speakers turned to phrases with a helping verb to say ‘will’.

Two rivals competed in the Koine and Byzantine centuries: *ἔχω* + infinitive, ‘I have to write’, and *θέλω* + infinitive or *θέλω ἵνα* + subjunctive, ‘I want to write’. The ‘want’ construction won. Its verb froze in the 3rd person — *θέλει να γράψω*, literally ‘it wants that I write’ — and then wore down, through *θε να*, to the tiny particle *θα*. The ‘have’ construction did not die: it lives on, with a new meaning, in the Modern perfect *έχω γράψει* ‘I have written’.

table.title: From ‘want’ to ‘will’
rows: I want to write; I want that I write
table.note: *να* itself is the ancient *ἵνα* ‘so that’, which lost its first vowel.

blocks.p: The Romance languages faced the same problem — Latin *amābit* ‘he will love’ came to sound like *amāvit* ‘he loved’ once *b* and *v* merged — and found a parallel solution with the other helping verb. Spoken Latin said *amāre habeō* ‘I have to love’, and the two words fused: Italian *amerò*, Spanish *amaré*, French *aimerai*, Portuguese *amarei*. The ending of the Romance future is literally the verb ‘have’.

compare.title: Romance futures from ‘have’
compare.note: Compare the present of ‘have’: Italian *ho, hai, ha*; Spanish *he, has, ha*; French *ai, as, a*.

blocks.p: Romanian, on the Balkan side of the Romance world, chose ‘want’, like Greek. Its literary future *voi cânta* ‘I will sing’ is built on the verb ‘want’ (Latin *volō*), and its everyday future is an almost exact copy of the Greek one: *o să cânt* — an invariable *o*, worn down from ‘it wants’, then *să* ‘that’ (the equivalent of *να*), then the subjunctive. English *will* is a ‘want’ verb too: Old English *willan* meant ‘to want’.

compare.title: Futures built on ‘want’
compare.note: Greek *θα* has swallowed its ‘that’ (*θε να* → *θα*); Romanian keeps it separate (*o să*). The literary Romanian future still conjugates the ‘want’ verb: *voi scrie, vei scrie, va scrie*.

blocks.p: Greek, Romanian, Albanian and Bulgarian all build their future on ‘want’ — one of the features of the Balkan linguistic area, where languages from four different branches of Indo-European grew alike over centuries of contact.

parts.title: Where it comes from: ‘it wants that…’

title: The Subjunctive with να
sub: Να-clauses, modal verbs, and purpose with για να

blocks.p: Modern Greek has **no infinitive**. Where English says ‘I want to write’ and Latin *scrībere volō*, Greek says *θέλω να γράψω* — literally ‘I want that I write’. The verb after *να* is fully conjugated, so its ending tells you who does the action. One construction therefore covers both ‘I want to write’ and ‘I want you to write’: only the ending changes.

items.en: I want to write a letter.
items.lit: I want that I write a letter.

items.en: I want you to write a letter.
items.lit: I want that you write a letter.

items.en: They want us to write.
items.lit: They want that we write.

blocks.p: The verb form after *να* is called the **subjunctive** (*υποτακτική*). It has no endings of its own: it is simply the present form or the perfective form you already use after *θα*. So, just as there are two futures (*θα γράφω*, *θα γράψω*), there are two subjunctives, one for each aspect.

table.title: Subjunctive of γράφω and αγαπώ
table.note: Verbs with only one stem — είμαι, έχω, ξέρω — have a single subjunctive: να είμαι, να είσαι, να είναι, να είμαστε, να είστε, να είναι; να έχω, να έχεις…

blocks.p: The **perfective** is the default: it presents the action as one whole event. The **imperfective** presents it as ongoing, repeated or habitual. English makes no such distinction, so let the meaning decide: one meal or a way of eating?

items.en: I want to eat something. (perfective: one act)
I want to eat more healthily. (imperfective: a habit)
Can you close the door?
Can you speak more slowly? (imperfective: keep it up)

blocks.tip: Verbs meaning ‘begin’, ‘stop’, ‘go on’, ‘learn to’ and ‘know how to’ take the **imperfective**, because what follows is an activity, not a single event: *Άρχισε να βρέχει* ‘It began to rain’, *Σταμάτησα να καπνίζω* ‘I stopped smoking’, *Ξέρεις να οδηγείς;* ‘Can you drive?’, *Μαθαίνω να κολυμπάω* ‘I’m learning to swim’.

blocks.p: The common verbs with irregular perfective stems (Chapters 11–12) use them after *να* too. Note the stressed endings of the short stems *πω*, *δω*, *βρω*, *πιω*, which follow the pattern of *μπορώ*.

table.title: Five irregular subjunctives
table.note: Also: πηγαίνω → να πάω (πας, πάει, πάμε, πάτε, πάνε); βρίσκω → να βρω (βρεις, βρει, βρούμε, βρείτε, βρουν); βγαίνω → να βγω; μπαίνω → να μπω. Formal style has έλθω for έρθω.

blocks.p: Inside a *να*-clause the negative is **μη(ν)**, never *δεν*. The pieces come in a fixed order — *να* + *μη(ν)* + object pronouns + verb — and nothing else can come between them: *να μην το πεις* ‘(that you) not say it’. *Μην* keeps its *-ν* on the same terms as the article *τη(ν)*: before a vowel and before κ, π, τ, ξ, ψ, μπ, ντ, γκ, τσ, τζ (*να μην έρθει*, *να μην το πεις*); before other consonants it is traditionally dropped (*να μη φύγεις*).

items.en: I want to tell you something.

items.t: Σου είπα να μην το αγγίξεις.
items.en: I told you not to touch it.
I don’t want to go.
I’d rather not go.

blocks.pitfall: *Δεν* negates the main verb, *μην* the *να*-clause: *Δεν θέλω να έρθεις* ‘I don’t want you to come’ vs *Θέλω να μην έρθεις* ‘I want you not to come’. Never write *να δεν*, and never put the pronoun after the verb: *να το δω*, not *να δω το*. And no *θα* after a modal verb: *θέλω να πάω*, never *θέλω θα πάω*.

table.title: Common verbs + να
table.note: I want to leave. May I come in? You must leave. She knows how to cook. I’m trying to understand. It’s starting to rain. It stopped raining. I hope you come. I like reading.

blocks.p: *Πρέπει* is **impersonal**: it never changes for person. The person is carried by the verb after *να*: *πρέπει να πάω*, *πρέπει να πας*, *πρέπει να πάμε*. In the past it becomes *έπρεπε*: *Έπρεπε να φύγω* ‘I had to leave’. In the same way *μπορεί να*, frozen in the 3rd singular, means ‘may, might’: *Μπορεί να έχεις δίκιο* ‘You may be right’, *Μπορεί να βρέξει* ‘It might rain’.

blocks.h: Purpose: για να; and χωρίς να, πριν (να)

blocks.p: Purpose — English ‘(in order) to’ — is **για να** + subjunctive. After verbs of motion *για* is often left out: *Πάω (για) να φέρω ψωμί* ‘I’m going to get bread’. Two other words introduce *να*-clauses: *χωρίς να* ‘without (doing)’ and *πριν (να)* ‘before (doing)’, where *να* is optional.

items.en: I came to see you.

items.t: Μαθαίνω ελληνικά για να διαβάζω Καζαντζάκη.
items.en: I’m learning Greek so that I can read Kazantzakis. (imperfective: reading as an activity)
She left without saying anything.
Before you leave, turn off the light.

blocks.p: A *να*-clause can stand alone. As a question it makes offers and suggestions: *Να σε βοηθήσω;* ‘Shall I help you?’, *Να πάμε;* ‘Shall we go?’. As a statement it gives a softened command or a wish: *Να προσέχεις!* ‘Take care!’, *Να μου γράψεις!* ‘Do write to me!’, *Να είσαι καλά!* ‘Be well!’ — the everyday way of saying ‘thank you, bless you’.

*να* is the Ancient conjunction **ἵνα** ‘in order that’. In Classical Attic it took the subjunctive and expressed purpose only: *ἦλθον ἵνα σε ἴδω* ‘I came so that I might see you’. After verbs such as ‘want’, ‘be able’ and ‘must’, Classical Greek used the **infinitive**, exactly like Latin and English.

compare.title: From infinitive to να-clause
compare.note: The Ancient aorist infinitive (γράψαι, ἐλθεῖν) and present infinitive (γράφειν) distinguished aspect exactly as the two Modern subjunctives do (να γράψω, να γράφω). The aspect survived; only its vehicle changed. Μπορώ goes back, through medieval ημπορώ, to Ancient εὐπορῶ ‘to be well supplied, to manage’.

blocks.p: In Koine, *ἵνα* + subjunctive spread from purpose clauses to verbs of wanting, asking and ordering, competing with the infinitive. The New Testament is full of it: *θέλω ἵνα ἐξαυτῆς δῷς μοι… τὴν κεφαλὴν Ἰωάννου τοῦ βαπτιστοῦ* ‘I want you to give me at once… the head of John the Baptist’ (Mark 6:25). Over the following centuries the infinitive retreated, and by the end of the Middle Ages it had all but vanished from speech. Used as an unstressed particle before the verb, *ἵνα* lost its first vowel: *ἵνα* → *να*. The same particle hides in the future *θα* (*θέλει να* → *θε να* → *θα*), and *για* (from *διά*) was added to purpose clauses once *να* alone no longer meant ‘in order to’.

Relics of the infinitive survive in disguise. The form *γράψει* in *έχω γράψει* is an old infinitive (Chapter 18), and a few nouns were infinitives used with the article: *το είναι* ‘being, existence’, *το φαγί* ‘food’ (from *τὸ φαγεῖν* ‘eating’).

Greek did not lose its infinitive alone. Romanian, Bulgarian, Macedonian and Albanian (in its southern, Tosk variety) also replaced it, wholly or largely, with a particle + finite verb, matching the Greek construction word for word. This is one of the classic features of the **Balkan Sprachbund**: languages of different families that converged through centuries of bilingualism. Greek, with its long prestige in the region, is usually seen as the source.

table.title: ‘I want to write’ around the Balkans
table.note: Romanian, alone in Romance, does what Greek does: it has an infinitive (a scrie) but uses it far less than its sisters.

compare.title: Same subject, different subject
compare.note: When the subjects differ, Italian and Spanish too switch to a finite clause with che / que + subjunctive — the pattern Greek and Romanian use everywhere. Romanian also allows pot veni, with a bare infinitive.

blocks.p: Latin had its own *ἵνα*: **ut** + subjunctive, used for purpose (*vēnī ut tē vidērem* ‘I came to see you’) and after verbs of asking and ordering (*rogō ut veniās* ‘I ask you to come’). Latin, however, kept the infinitive after *volō* and *possum*, and so did its western daughters.

compare.title: Purpose and request clauses
compare.note: The second Greek example is Koine; Classical Attic would use an infinitive there. Latin ut, like ἵνα, triggers the subjunctive, and Spanish para que, Italian perché and French pour que + subjunctive continue the same idea.

title: The Simple Past
sub: The aorist, the augment, and the irregular pasts

blocks.p: The **simple past** (*αόριστος*, the aorist) presents a past action as a single, completed whole: *Έγραψα ένα γράμμα* ‘I wrote a letter’. It is built on the same **perfective stem** you use in *θα γράψω* and *να γράψω*, with a set of past endings and, where the stress needs it, an **augment**.

Greek uses the simple past much more widely than English uses ‘I wrote’. For recent events and anything just completed, where English says ‘have you…?’, Greek normally uses the aorist: *Έφαγες;* ‘Have you eaten?’, *Τι έγινε;* ‘What’s happened?’

table.title: Simple past, conjugation A
table.note: The 3rd plural has a colloquial variant in -ανε, stressed one syllable later: γράψανε, διαβάσανε, ακούσανε.

blocks.p: All past tenses obey one rule: **the stress falls on the third syllable from the end**. In *διά-βα-σα* or *ά-κου-σα* the stem provides that syllable. In *γράψα* it does not — so a syllable is added in front, the **augment** *ε-*, to carry the stress: *έ-γρα-ψα*. In *γρά-ψα-με* the word is already long enough, and the augment disappears.

table.title: Augment or not?
table.note: Conjugation B verbs make their perfective stem in -ησ- (αγάπησα, τηλεφώνησα), a few in -ασ- or -εσ- (γέλασα ‘laughed’, ξέχασα ‘forgot’, μπόρεσα, κάλεσα ‘invited’). Their pasts are usually long enough to need no augment.

blocks.tip: Count back three syllables from the end and put the stress there; if you run out of syllables, add *ε-*. That one rule gives you *έγραψα / γράψαμε*, *έμαθα / μάθαμε*, *αγόρασα / αγοράσαμε* — and, in the next chapter, the imperfect as well.

blocks.pitfall: Don’t keep the augment when it is no longer stressed: *φάγαμε*, not *έφαγαμε*; *μάθαμε*, not *έμαθαμε*. (Some regional speech, for example in Crete and Cyprus, does keep it — *εγράψαμε* — but the standard drops it.) The exception is the irregular pasts whose first syllable is part of the stem: *ήρθαμε*, *είδαμε*, *είπαμε*, *ήπιαμε*, *βρήκαμε* keep it throughout.

blocks.p: The commonest verbs have pasts that must simply be learned, usually together with their perfective forms. Most of them are very old (see below).

table.title: Irregular pasts
table.note: είμαι and έχω have no aorist: their only pasts, ήμουν and είχα, are in Chapter 15. Formal Greek also uses ήλθα for ήρθα.

blocks.p: Verbs of learned origin made up of a preposition + verb put the augment **after** the prefix, where it replaces or merges with the prefix’s last vowel: *υπογράφω* → *υπέγραψα* ‘I signed’, *περιγράφω* → *περιέγραψα* ‘I described’, *επιστρέφω* → *επέστρεψα* ‘I returned’, *παραδίδω* → *παρέδωσα* ‘I handed over’, *εκλέγω* → *εξέλεξα* ‘I elected’. Like the ordinary augment, it appears only when stressed: *υπογράψαμε*, *επιστρέψαμε*. Everyday compounds simply follow the stress rule: *καταλαβαίνω* → *κατάλαβα*, *ξαναγράφω* → *ξανάγραψα*.

items.en: Yesterday I wrote three letters.

items.t: Είδες τον Νίκο; — Ναι, τον είδα το πρωί.
items.en: Did you see Nikos? — Yes, I saw him this morning.
We came to Athens in 2019.
What did you say?
Have you eaten? — Not yet.
I’ve found my keys!
We had a glass of wine and left.
Sorry, I didn’t understand.

blocks.p: The Greek aorist is one of the oldest tenses in the Indo-European family, and Modern *έγραψα* is Ancient *ἔγραψα* letter for letter. Ancient Greek had two main types. The **first (sigmatic) aorist** added *-σ-* to the root, with endings in *-α*: *γράφ-σ-α* → *ἔγραψα*, *λύ-σ-α* → *ἔλυσα*. The **second aorist** used a bare, often shorter root with the endings of the imperfect: *ἔφαγον*, *εἶδον*, *ἦλθον*. Modern Greek keeps both — its ‘irregular’ pasts are mostly old second aorists.

compare.title: First aorists: almost unchanged
compare.note: In Ancient Greek the augment was a fixed part of every past indicative, whether stressed or not (ἐγράψαμεν, ἐδίδαξα). Verbs beginning with a vowel lengthened it instead — the ‘temporal augment’: ἀγοράζω → ἠγόρασα. Modern Greek has turned the augment into a mere stress-carrier, so δίδαξα and αγόρασα no longer need it.

blocks.p: The augment itself is inherited: Sanskrit has it too, so that Greek *ἔφερε* ‘he carried’ matches Sanskrit *ábharat* exactly. Latin lost it entirely before written records begin.

The second aorist had its own endings: *-ον, -ες, -ε, -ομεν, -ετε, -ον*. In medieval Greek these were replaced by the first aorist’s *-α* endings, so that all Modern pasts now share one set. The old stems, however, survived intact — which is why they look irregular today.

compare.title: Second aorists and their heirs
compare.note: ἦλθον became ήλθα (still formal) and then ήρθα, with λ → ρ before a consonant. In είδα and είπα the old augment ει- has fused with the stem, which is why it stays in είδαμε, είπαμε.

blocks.p: *βρήκα* has a different history: it continues *ηὕρηκα*, a form of the Ancient **perfect** ‘I have found’ — the *εὕρηκα* of Archimedes — which took over the role of the simple past. The *-ηκα* of *ανέβηκα*, *μπήκα* and *βγήκα* has another source: Ancient root aorists in *-ην* such as *ἀνέβην* ‘I went up’, lengthened with *-κα* — exactly as the passive *-θην* became *-θηκα* (Chapter 16).

The *-σ-* of the first aorist is an Indo-European formation that Latin inherited too. There it merged into the perfect: *dīxī* (*dīc-s-ī*) and *scrīpsī* (*scrīb-s-ī*) are old s-aorists, and Italian *dissi*, *scrissi* and Spanish *dije* still carry the *s* (or *x*). Greek *ἔδειξα* ‘I showed’ and Latin *dīxī* ‘I said’ even share their root, Indo-European *deik-* ‘point out’.

compare.title: The s-past in Greek and Latin
gloss: I showed (Greek) · I said (Latin, Romance): one root
compare.note: Spanish escribí has been regularised, but dije still keeps the x of dīxī — one of the ‘irregular preterites’ every learner of Spanish meets.

title: The Imperfect
sub: The continuous past: έγραφα, αγαπούσα, μπορούσα

blocks.p: The **imperfect** (*παρατατικός*, ‘the extended tense’) is the past of the **imperfective** stem — the same stem as the present. It presents a past action as ongoing, repeated or habitual, or as the background to something else: *έγραφα* ‘I was writing, I used to write, I wrote (regularly)’. The simple past *έγραψα* (Chapter 14) is its perfective partner.

For conjugation A, the imperfect needs nothing new: present stem + the same endings as the simple past (*-α, -ες, -ε, -αμε, -ατε, -αν*), with the same stress rule — third syllable from the end, augment *ε-* where the stem is too short.

table.title: Imperfect, conjugation A
table.note: Verbs whose present ends in a vowel + -ω insert -γ-: λέω → έλεγα, τρώω → έτρωγα, ακούω → άκουγα, κλαίω → έκλαιγα. The 3rd plural also has the colloquial -ανε: γράφανε, λέγανε.

blocks.p: Conjugation B verbs form the imperfect with the stressed suffix **-ούσα**, added to the stem. Because the stress is fixed on *-ού-*, these verbs never take an augment.

table.title: Imperfect, conjugation B
table.note: Verbs of type αγαπάω also have a colloquial imperfect in -αγα, very common in speech: ρώταγα, πέρναγα, ξέχναγα (= ρωτούσα, περνούσα, ξεχνούσα).

blocks.h: είμαι, έχω and other one-past verbs

table.title: The past of είμαι and έχω
table.note: These verbs have no separate aorist: ήμουν and είχα serve for every kind of past. The same goes in practice for ξέρω → ήξερα and πρέπει → έπρεπε; θέλω has an aorist θέλησα, but its everyday past is ήθελα (we: θέλαμε).

blocks.p: The difference is **aspect**, not time: both are past. Ask whether the action is seen as one completed whole (simple past) or as a process, a habit, or a state of affairs (imperfect). English often hides the choice — ‘I read a lot as a child’ and ‘I read the book yesterday’ use the same verb form — but Greek always makes it.

items.t: Έγραφα ένα γράμμα, όταν χτύπησε το τηλέφωνο.
items.en: I was writing a letter when the phone rang.
Every summer we used to go to Naxos.
Last year we went to Naxos.
When I was a child, I read a lot.
Yesterday I read the whole book.

items.t: Ήταν Κυριακή, έβρεχε και δεν ήθελα να βγω.
items.en: It was Sunday, it was raining, and I didn’t want to go out.
I lived in London for ten years. (simple past: a closed period)

blocks.tip: In a story, the **imperfect paints the scene** — what was going on, what things were like, what used to happen — and the **simple past moves the plot**: what happened next. Signals of the imperfect: *κάθε μέρα*, *συνήθως* ‘usually’, *συχνά* ‘often’, *πάντα* ‘always’, *ενώ* ‘while’. Signals of the simple past: *χθες*, *ξαφνικά* ‘suddenly’, *μια φορά* ‘once’, *τελικά* ‘in the end’.

blocks.pitfall: Length alone does not make an action imperfective. A long but **closed** period counts as one whole and takes the simple past: *Έμεινα δέκα χρόνια στο Λονδίνο*, *Δούλεψα όλη τη νύχτα* ‘I worked all night’. Use the imperfect only when the period is the background to something else, or a habit: *Όταν έμενα στο Λονδίνο, δούλευα σε μια τράπεζα* ‘When I lived in London, I worked in a bank’.

blocks.p: With *θέλω*, *μπορώ*, *πρέπει* and the like, the imperfect is the normal past: *ήθελα να*, *μπορούσα να*, *έπρεπε να*. The imperfect *ήθελα* is also a polite softener — ‘I wanted to’ for ‘I would like to’ — and *θα* + imperfect is the Greek ‘would’ (Chapter 23).

items.en: I’d like to ask you something.
items.lit: I wanted to ask you something.

items.en: I couldn’t sleep.
We had to leave early.

blocks.p: Modern *έγραφα* continues the Ancient imperfect *ἔγραφον*: the same present stem, the same augment, and above all the same **aspect contrast** with the aorist *ἔγραψα*. The distinction between ‘I was writing’ and ‘I wrote’ has been made in exactly this way for some three thousand years. What changed is the endings: the Ancient imperfect had a set of its own, which medieval Greek replaced with the aorist’s *-α* endings.

compare.title: The imperfect of γράφω, then and now
compare.note: Ancient ἔγραφον meant both ‘I was writing’ and ‘they were writing’; the new -α endings removed the ambiguity. The 2nd and 3rd singular came through unchanged.

blocks.p: The Ancient **contract verbs** — the ancestors of conjugation B — had imperfects that contracted the stem vowel with the ending and took an augment: *ἠγάπων* ‘I was loving’, *ἐζήτουν* ‘I was asking for’. These did not survive. The *-ούσα* type is a **medieval innovation**. It grew out of the Koine 3rd plural ending *-σαν*, which spread from the aorist to the imperfect: forms like *ἐδολιοῦσαν* ‘they were deceiving’ (Attic *ἐδολίουν*) already appear in the Greek Bible (Romans 3:13). From the 3rd plural, speakers extracted a whole new paradigm: *-ούσα, -ούσες, -ούσε…*

compare.title: Contract verbs: old and new imperfects
compare.note: The new forms are perfectly regular — one stressed suffix, no augment, no contraction to work out — which is why they won.

blocks.p: Latin too had a dedicated imperfect, *scrībēbam* ‘I was writing, used to write’, and the Romance languages kept it everywhere. The Greek choice between *έγραφα* and *έγραψα* is the choice between Spanish *escribía* and *escribí*, or Italian *scrivevo* and *scrissi*: a learner who has mastered one has, in effect, mastered the other.

compare.title: Imperfect and perfective past
gloss: I was writing, used to write
compare.note: Latin scrīpsī covered both ‘I wrote’ and ‘I have written’. Spoken French and Romanian now use the compound past (j’ai écrit, am scris) for the second row.

title: Verbs in -ομαι
sub: Passive and middle: present, imperfect, past in -θηκα, future

blocks.h: One set of forms, several meanings

blocks.p: Greek verbs have a second complete set of endings, the one in **-ομαι**. Grammars call it the ‘passive voice’ (*παθητική φωνή*), but passive is only one of its meanings. An *-ομαι* form can be **passive** (*γράφεται* ‘it is written’), **reflexive** (*πλένομαι* ‘I wash (myself)’), **reciprocal** (*φιλιούνται* ‘they kiss (each other)’), or just a verb that happens to exist only in this form (*έρχομαι* ‘I come’). It is really the old **middle** voice — the voice of things that happen to or within the subject.

table.title: Present of -ομαι verbs
table.note: Type A is by far the commonest. Like θυμάμαι go κοιμάμαι ‘sleep’, φοβάμαι ‘be afraid’, λυπάμαι ‘be sorry’. The B2 type in -ούμαι belongs mostly to learned verbs: θεωρούμαι ‘be considered’, στερούμαι ‘lack’, αρνούμαι ‘refuse’ (also αρνιέμαι).

blocks.tip: Learn the type A endings as a chant — *-ομαι, -εσαι, -εται, -όμαστε, -εστε, -ονται* — and notice that the 1st plural moves the stress forward: *γράφομαι* but *γραφόμαστε*.

table.title: Imperfect of -ομαι verbs
table.note: The endings echo the past of είμαι (ήμουν, ήσουν, ήταν…). Colloquially the 1st and 2nd plural are also γραφόμαστε, γραφόσαστε, identical with the present. So: ερχόμουν ‘I was coming’, καθόμουν ‘I was sitting’, κοιμόμουν ‘I was sleeping’.

blocks.p: The simple past of *-ομαι* verbs is built on a special perfective stem ending in **-θ-** (or **-τ-** after φ, χ, σ) + **-ηκα**, with the regular past endings. The stress rule is the usual one — third syllable from the end — and there is never an augment.

table.title: Common -ομαι verbs and their pasts
table.note: The last three are deponents with active-looking pasts. χάρηκα has -ηκα without θ.

blocks.p: The perfective forms used after *θα* and *να* come from the past stem: drop *-ηκα* and add stressed endings, the same as those of *μπορώ*: *-ώ, -είς, -εί, -ούμε, -είτε, -ούν*. So *γράφτηκα* → *θα γραφτώ*, *θυμήθηκα* → *να θυμηθώ*. The imperfective forms are simply the present: *θα κοιμάμαι* ‘I will be sleeping’, *να θυμάσαι* ‘(that you) remember (always)’.

table.title: Perfective future
table.note: The same forms follow να: να γραφτώ, να μη θυμηθεί.

blocks.pitfall: Keep the voices apart in the perfective: *θα γράψει* ‘he will write’, *θα γραφτεί* ‘it will be written’; *να χάσω* ‘to lose’, *να χαθώ* ‘to get lost’. The stressed *-ώ* of *να χαθώ* is the passive perfective, not a conjugation B verb.

blocks.p: The agent — English ‘by’ — is **από** + accusative: *Το βιβλίο γράφτηκε από τον Καζαντζάκη*. Greek uses passives with an agent much less than English; it prefers an active sentence with the object moved to the front and repeated as a pronoun: *Το βιβλίο το έγραψε ο Καζαντζάκης* ‘The book was written by Kazantzakis’.

items.en: What’s your name? — My name is Maria.
items.lit: How are you called? — I am called Maria.

items.t: Δεν θυμάμαι πού έβαλα τα κλειδιά.
items.en: I don’t remember where I put the keys.
Pleased to meet you!
items.lit: I was very glad!

items.en: I’m tired, I’m off to sleep.
items.lit: I got tired, I go to sleep.

items.en: When did you get married?
The house was built in 1920.
Don’t be afraid!
I’ll be thinking of you.

blocks.tip: Greek often reports a **changed state** with the simple past where English uses a present: *Κουράστηκα* ‘I’m tired’, *Χάρηκα* ‘(I’m) pleased to meet you’, *Θύμωσα* ‘I’m angry’, *Πείνασα* ‘I’m hungry’.

blocks.p: Ancient Greek had three voices: active (*λύω* ‘I untie’), **middle** (*λύομαι* ‘I untie for myself, I ransom’) and passive. Outside the future and aorist, middle and passive shared one set of forms, so *λύομαι* meant both ‘I am untied’ and ‘I untie for myself’. Modern *-ομαι* continues that **middle-passive**, and its range of meanings — passive, reflexive, reciprocal, ‘inner’ verbs like ‘fear’ and ‘sit’ — is the old middle range.

compare.title: Present middle-passive, then and now
compare.note: Four forms of six are unchanged after 2,500 years. The 2nd singular -εσαι restores an s that Attic had lost between vowels; Koine already shows it — φάγεσαι καὶ πίεσαι ‘you shall eat and drink’ (Luke 17:8).

blocks.p: The Ancient **aorist passive** was built with *-θη-* and endings of its own: *ἐλύθην* ‘I was untied’, *ἐλύθης*, *ἐλύθη*, *ἐλύθημεν*… In medieval Greek it was extended with *-κα*, on the model of active aorists like *ἔθηκα* ‘I placed’ and *ἔδωκα* ‘I gave’ — and the augment was dropped by the usual stress rule: *ἐλύθην* → *λύθηκα*. Inside every Modern *-θηκα* sits the Ancient *-θη-*.

compare.title: Aorist passive: -θην → -θηκα
compare.note: θυμάμαι comes from Ancient ἐνθυμοῦμαι ‘take to heart, ponder’. γράφτηκα shows the regular change φθ → φτ (as in φθάνω → φτάνω ‘arrive’); Attic itself had a θ-less aorist ἐγράφην.

blocks.p: Ancient Greek also had many **deponents** — verbs found only in middle or passive form but with active meaning. Several survive with the same quirk. Even the odd mixture in *έρχομαι* / *ήρθα*, a middle present beside an active past, is Ancient: *ἔρχομαι* / *ἦλθον*.

Latin also had a synthetic middle-passive, in *-r* (*amor* ‘I am loved’, *lavor* ‘I wash myself, bathe’), and deponents such as *sequor* ‘I follow’ and *nāscor* ‘I am born’. The Romance languages lost it all: the passive is now *be* + participle, the reflexive uses a pronoun, and *sequor* became active *seguire / seguir / suivre*. Greek, by contrast, kept its synthetic middle-passive alive — so where Romance needs two words, Greek needs one.

compare.title: Synthetic in Greek, analytic in Romance

parts.title: One set of forms, several meanings

title: The Imperative
sub: Commands: γράφε and γράψε, and the negative μη(ν)

blocks.p: Like every other part of the Greek verb, the imperative comes in two aspects. The **perfective** imperative (*γράψε* ‘write!’) is the normal one for a single, specific request. The **imperfective** (*γράφε* ‘write! keep writing!’) is for an ongoing or repeated action, a general instruction, or an encouraging ‘go on’. Imperatives exist only in the 2nd person, singular and plural; other persons use *ας* or *να* (see below).

table.title: Active imperative, conjugation A
table.note: The singular ends in -ε and is stressed, like the past, on the third syllable from the end if there is one (διάβασε, άνοιξε). The perfective plural is the perfective stem + -τε (γράψ-τε; σ-stems give -στε: διαβάστε, κλείστε); fuller forms like γράψετε, ανοίξετε also occur. The imperfective plural is identical to the present: γράφετε.

table.title: Active imperative, conjugation B
table.note: B2 verbs (μπορώ, τηλεφωνώ, οδηγώ) have no imperfective singular; use the perfective, or να + present (να τηλεφωνείς).

blocks.p: The verbs with irregular perfective stems have short, irregular imperatives. They are among the most frequent words in the language — you will hear *έλα*, *πες μου* and *κοίτα* dozens of times a day.

*-ομαι* verbs have a perfective imperative in **-σου** (singular) and **-θείτε / -τείτε** (plural), built on the stem of the passive past. There is no imperfective singular; use *να* + present instead: *Να θυμάσαι!* ‘Remember (always)!’

With a positive imperative, object pronouns **follow** the verb: *Γράψε το!* ‘Write it!’, *Πες μου* ‘Tell me’, *Δώσε μου το βιβλίο* ‘Give me the book’. When the imperative is stressed on the third syllable from the end, the added pronoun brings a **second accent** onto the last syllable of the verb: *Διάβασέ το* ‘Read it’, *Κοίταξέ με* ‘Look at me’.

There is **no negative imperative** in Greek. To forbid something, use **μη(ν)** + the subjunctive — the form you would use after *να*, with the *να* itself usually left out. The perfective forbids a single act; the imperfective forbids a habit or tells someone to stop. The pronoun moves to its normal place in front of the verb: *Γράψε το!* → *Μην το γράψεις!*

table.title: Positive and negative
rows: Think about it! / Don’t think about it!
table.note: A full να μην… is also possible, and sounds more insistent: Να μην το ξαναπείς! ‘Don’t you ever say that again!’

blocks.pitfall: Never combine *μη* with an imperative form: *μη γράψεις* or *μη γράφεις*, never *μη γράψε*. And remember to move the pronoun: *Πες το!* but *Μην το πεις!*

blocks.p: For ‘let’s…’ and ‘let him/her…’ Greek uses **ας** + subjunctive forms (without *να*): *Ας πάμε* ‘Let’s go’, *Ας περιμένει* ‘Let him wait’. In speech *πάμε* alone is the usual ‘let’s go!’. And, as you saw in Chapter 13, *να* + subjunctive works as a softer or more emphatic command for any person: *Να μου γράψεις!* ‘Be sure to write to me!’

items.en: Come here!
Tell me the truth.
Please switch off your mobile phones.

items.t: Μην ανησυχείς, όλα θα πάνε καλά.
items.en: Don’t worry, everything will be fine.
Wait a moment!
Read it carefully.
Please sit down.
Let’s speak Greek.

blocks.tip: *Παρακαλώ* softens any imperative. The imperfective often sounds like encouragement or a standing rule: *Τρώγε!* ‘Go on, eat!’, *Διάβαζε κάθε μέρα* ‘Read every day’; the perfective is the everyday one-off request: *Φάε το φαγητό σου* ‘Eat your food’.

blocks.p: Ancient Greek had imperatives in each aspect, as Modern Greek does: present *γράφε* ‘keep writing’, aorist *γράψον* ‘write (once)’. The present imperative has come down unchanged. The aorist imperative was remodelled: its odd *-ον* was replaced by the *-ε* of the present, giving *γράψε*, and the plural *γράψατε* was replaced by *γράψετε*, shortened to *γράψτε*.

compare.title: Imperatives then and now
compare.note: In Luke 12:19 the rich fool says to himself: ἀναπαύου, φάγε, πίε, εὐφραίνου ‘take your ease, eat, drink, be merry’. A Greek today would say: ξεκουράσου, φάε, πιες, διασκέδασε.

blocks.p: The *-σου* of *ξεκουράσου*, *σκέψου* combines the *-σ-* of the aorist with the Ancient **present middle** imperative ending *-ου* — the very ending of *ἀναπαύου* ‘rest!’ in that same verse.

For prohibitions, Ancient Greek avoided the aorist imperative altogether. It said either **μή + aorist subjunctive** (*μὴ γράψῃς* ‘don’t write’) or μή + present imperative (*μὴ φοβοῦ* ‘stop being afraid’). Modern Greek generalised the subjunctive pattern, so *μη γράψεις* is Ancient *μὴ γράψῃς* almost unchanged.

compare.title: Prohibitions
compare.note: μὴ κλέψῃς is the commandment as quoted in the Gospels (Mark 10:19); μὴ φοβοῦ is the angel’s ‘Fear not’ (Luke 1:30).

blocks.p: The Romance languages share the same reluctance to negate an imperative. Latin itself, in ordinary prose, said *nōlī* ‘be unwilling’ + infinitive (*nōlī loquī* ‘don’t speak’) or *nē* + perfect subjunctive (*nē dīxeris* ‘don’t say it’). Its daughters each found a substitute: Italian and Romanian use the **infinitive**, Spanish and Portuguese the **subjunctive** — the Greek solution.

compare.title: ‘Speak!’ and ‘Don’t speak!’
compare.note: Only the singular is affected: Italian non parlate and French ne parlez pas use ordinary plural forms. Spanish no hables and Greek μη μιλάς both borrow the form from the subjunctive.

title: The Perfect Tenses
sub: έχω γράψει, είχα γράψει, θα έχω γράψει — and έχω γραμμένο

blocks.p: Greek builds its perfect tenses as English does, with **‘have’**: a form of *έχω* + an unchanging verb form in *-ει*. Greek grammars call that form the *απαρέμφατο* ‘infinitive’ — and historically it is one, the only place where the old infinitive survives (see below). In practice it is easy: it is identical to the **3rd singular perfective**, the form you use in *θα γράψει*, *να γράψει*.

table.title: The three perfects of γράφω
table.note: I have written, I had written, I will have written. Only έχω changes; γράψει never does.

table.title: The -ει form of common verbs
rows: I have been written; I have enrolled
table.note: Passive-form verbs work the same way: their -ει form is the 3rd singular perfective (να γραφτεί → έχω γραφτεί). είμαι and έχω have no perfect: ‘I have been to Crete’ is έχω πάει στην Κρήτη.

blocks.p: The Greek present perfect is narrower than the English one. Use it for **experience** (‘ever’, ‘never’), for a past action whose **result** matters now, and with *ακόμα* ‘(not) yet’ and *ήδη* ‘already’. For a recent, specific event Greek is happy with the simple past, and whenever a **past time is named** the simple past is required: *Χθες έφαγα στο σπίτι*, never *χθες έχω φάει*.

items.en: Have you ever been to Crete?

items.t: Δεν έχω δει ακόμα την ταινία.
items.en: I haven’t seen the film yet.
I’ve lost my keys (and still haven’t found them).

items.t: Όταν έφτασα στον σταθμό, το τρένο είχε φύγει.
items.en: When I got to the station, the train had left.

items.t: Μου είπε ότι είχε διαβάσει το βιβλίο.
items.en: She told me she had read the book.

items.t: Μέχρι τις οκτώ θα έχω τελειώσει.
items.en: By eight I will have finished.

blocks.pitfall: Duration up to now — English ‘I have lived here for five years’ — takes the **present** in Greek, with *εδώ και* ‘for, since’: *Μένω στην Αθήνα εδώ και πέντε χρόνια*; *Τον ξέρω εδώ και χρόνια* ‘I’ve known him for years’. *Έχω μείνει πέντε χρόνια στην Αθήνα* means ‘I have spent five years in Athens (in total)’ — an experience, not a situation that is still going on.

blocks.tip: The pluperfect is the safest of the three: it means ‘had done’ exactly as in English. The present perfect is where English speakers overuse it — when in doubt, especially with ‘just’ (*μόλις*), Greek prefers the simple past: *Μόλις ήρθα* ‘I’ve just arrived’.

blocks.p: In the perfect tenses, *έχω* behaves like any other finite verb: the negative *δεν* and the object pronouns go **in front of it**, never between *έχω* and the *-ει* form. Questions simply change the intonation.

items.en: I’ve seen it three times.
I haven’t met her yet.
I had told you so!

items.t: Θα το έχουν μάθει ως αύριο.
items.en: They will have found out by tomorrow.

blocks.p: Greek has a second, older-looking construction: **έχω + the participle in -μένος**, which agrees with the object like an adjective: *Έχω το γράμμα γραμμένο* ‘I have the letter written’. It focuses on the **resulting state** — the letter is ready — where *έχω γράψει* focuses on the action. With *είμαι* the same participle describes a state of the subject: *Το γράμμα είναι γραμμένο* ‘The letter is written’ (Chapter 19).

items.t: Το έχω διαβασμένο αυτό το βιβλίο.
items.en: I’ve read that book (I know it).
items.lit: I have it read, this book.

items.en: I’ve got my things packed.
items.lit: I have my things gathered.

items.en: The table is laid.

blocks.p: Ancient Greek had a **synthetic perfect**, built with reduplication and endings of its own: *γέγραφα* ‘I have written’, *λέλυκα* ‘I have untied’, pluperfect *ἐγεγράφειν* ‘I had written’. It described a present state resulting from a past action. In Koine its meaning drifted towards that of the aorist, and by the early Middle Ages it had disappeared from speech. Only its passive participle lived on — minus the reduplication.

compare.title: Synthetic and analytic perfects
compare.note: Learned Greek still keeps some reduplicated participles: δεδομένος ‘given’ (τα δεδομένα ‘data’), πεπεισμένος ‘convinced’, τετριμμένος ‘trite’, and the noun γεγονός ‘fact, event’, an old perfect participle of γίγνομαι ‘become, happen’.

blocks.p: The modern perfect grew out of **έχω + infinitive**. Already in Classical Greek this meant ‘I am able to’: *οὐκ ἔχω εἰπεῖν* ‘I cannot say’. In late Antiquity and the early Middle Ages *ἔχω* + infinitive became one way of expressing the **future**, and its past, *εἶχα* + infinitive, came to mean ‘I would have…’ and then ‘I had…’ — a pluperfect. The present perfect *έχω γράψει* followed by analogy, and became fully established only in the early modern period. Meanwhile the infinitive itself was remade: aorist *γράψαι* became *γράψειν* on the model of present *γράφειν*, and then lost its final *-ν*: **γράψει**.

The Romance languages reached the same goal by a different road. Spoken Latin said *epistulam scrīptam habeō* ‘I have the letter (in a) written (state)’, with the participle agreeing with the object — precisely Greek *έχω το γράμμα γραμμένο*. This hardened into the Romance compound past: Italian *ho scritto*, Spanish *he escrito*, French *j’ai écrit*. ‘Have’-perfects are a hallmark of western and central Europe (Romance, English, German) and of the Balkans (Greek, Albanian, Macedonian): a classic **areal** feature, spread across language families by contact.

compare.title: Have + participle, agreeing
compare.note: Spanish tengo escrita la carta keeps the agreeing type alive beside the grammaticalised he escrito, just as Greek keeps έχω γραμμένο beside έχω γράψει.

compare.title: The perfect tenses across Europe
compare.note: Portuguese uses the simple past escrevi for ‘I have written’; tenho escrito means ‘I have been writing (lately)’. Romanian keeps a one-word pluperfect, scrisesem, from the Latin pluperfect subjunctive — a reminder that the ‘have’ perfect spread unevenly. Romanian am scris itself uses ‘have’ (am < habeō).

title: Participles and the Gerund
sub: -οντας and -ώντας, -μένος, and the learned -ων, -ουσα, -ον

blocks.h: What is left of the participle

blocks.p: Ancient Greek was famous for its participles; Modern Greek has kept only a few, and they behave quite differently. There are three kinds to know: the active **gerund** in *-οντας / -ώντας*, which never changes; the passive participle in **-μένος**, which is a full adjective; and a set of **learned participles** with Ancient endings, used mostly as adjectives and nouns.

table.title: Forming the gerund
table.note: Conjugation A adds -οντας to the present stem, keeping the stem stress; conjugation B has stressed -ώντας. Verbs in vowel + -ω insert -γ- (τρώγοντας, λέγοντας, ακούγοντας). Only active verbs have a gerund, and only from the present stem. It never changes for gender, number or case.

blocks.p: The gerund describes something the **subject of the main verb** is doing at the same time, and covers English ‘by …ing’, ‘while …ing’, ‘(since) …ing’. With *έχοντας* + the *-ει* form it makes a perfect gerund: *έχοντας τελειώσει* ‘having finished’.

items.en: We learn by speaking.

items.t: Περπατώντας στην παραλία, συνάντησα έναν παλιό φίλο.
items.en: Walking on the beach, I met an old friend.
He came running into the room.
Laughing, she told me the truth.

items.t: Έχοντας τελειώσει τη δουλειά, πήγε σπίτι.
items.en: Having finished work, he went home.
One learns by making mistakes.

blocks.pitfall: The gerund must share its subject with the main verb. *Μπαίνοντας στο δωμάτιο, χτύπησε το τηλέφωνο* is as wrong as English ‘Entering the room, the phone rang’; say *Όταν μπήκα στο δωμάτιο, χτύπησε το τηλέφωνο*. And English ‘-ing’ after verbs is **not** a gerund in Greek: ‘I like reading’ is *Μου αρέσει να διαβάζω*, ‘I stopped smoking’ is *Σταμάτησα να καπνίζω*.

blocks.p: The participle in **-μένος, -μένη, -μένο** is an ordinary adjective, declined like *καλός*. It is formed mostly from the stem of the passive past and describes a **state resulting from an action**: ‘written’, ‘tired’, ‘married’. You have already met it with *έχω* and *είμαι* (Chapter 18).

table.title: Common participles in -μένος
table.note: The stem changes are those of the passive past, with assimilation before -μ-: γραφ- + -μένος → γραμμένος, ανοιχ- + -μένος → ανοιγμένος, κουρασ- stays: κουρασμένος.

items.en: I’m very tired. (said by a woman)
He’s married to an Italian woman.

items.t: Το αγαπημένο μου φαγητό είναι ο μουσακάς.
items.en: My favourite dish is moussaka.
The window is broken.

items.t: Θέλω ένα ψημένο ψάρι και μια χωριάτικη.
items.en: I’d like a grilled fish and a Greek salad.

blocks.p: From the learned tradition (Chapter 24) come participles with Ancient endings. The active present has **-ων, -ουσα, -ον** (genitive *-οντος*); the passive present has **-όμενος** (*-ούμενος* in conjugation B). They are not formed freely in speech, but many are everyday words — above all *ενδιαφέρων* ‘interesting’.

table.title: ενδιαφέρων ‘interesting’
table.note: Ενδιαφέρον! ‘Interesting!’; ένα ενδιαφέρον βιβλίο, μια ενδιαφέρουσα ιδέα. The neuter is also a noun: το ενδιαφέρον ‘interest’. Like it: ο υπάρχων ‘existing’, ο παρών, η παρούσα, το παρόν ‘present’, ο απών ‘absent’.

table.title: Learned participles in everyday words
rows: that which is about to be

blocks.tip: Treat learned participles as vocabulary, not as a pattern. You cannot say ‘writing’ as *γράφων* in everyday Greek — use *γράφοντας* or a clause — except in set phrases like *ο γράφων* ‘the present writer’, *οι ενδιαφερόμενοι* ‘those interested’.

blocks.p: Ancient Greek had one of the richest participle systems of any language. Every tense and voice had its own fully declined participle: present *λύων* ‘untying’, aorist *λύσας* ‘having untied’, perfect *λελυκώς*, future *λύσων*, with middle and passive counterparts (*λυόμενος*, *λυσάμενος*, *λελυμένος*, *λυθείς*). Classical prose built whole sentences around them. In Koine and medieval Greek the system collapsed: the active participle lost its declension and froze into a single form, the gerund, while the passive perfect participle survived as an adjective.

compare.title: From declined participle to frozen gerund
compare.note: The gerund goes back to the accusative form γράφοντα, which in medieval Greek was used without agreement and gained an adverb-like -ς: γράφοντα → γράφοντας. The aorist participles vanished from speech; Modern Greek uses έχοντας + -ει instead.

blocks.p: The participle phrases that Ancient Greek used everywhere — above all the **genitive absolute**, a participle phrase with its own subject in the genitive (*ἡλίου ἀνατείλαντος* ‘the sun having risen’) — gave way to clauses: *όταν βγήκε ο ήλιος*. A handful survive as frozen formulas, perfectly normal in Modern Greek:

Latin went through a strikingly similar change. Its present participle *cantāns, cantantis* largely gave way in Romance to the ablative of the gerund, *cantandō* ‘by singing’, which became the invariable Italian, Spanish and Portuguese *cantando* and Romanian *cântând* — doing exactly the job of Greek *τραγουδώντας*. The old present participle survived mainly as an adjective or noun: Italian *cantante* ‘singer’, Spanish *estudiante* ‘student’, French *amant* ‘lover’ — just as Greek kept *ενδιαφέρον* and *περιβάλλον*. The passive participle *scrīptus* lives on as *scritto*, *escrito*, *écrit*, *scris*, as *γεγραμμένος* lives on in *γραμμένος*.

compare.title: Gerunds and passive participles
compare.note: Like the Greek gerund, the Romance gerund is invariable and normally shares the subject of the main verb: Imparo leggendo / Aprendo leyendo / Μαθαίνω διαβάζοντας ‘I learn by reading’.

parts.title: What is left of the participle

title: Comparison
sub: πιο, -τερος, -τατος: comparing adjectives and adverbs

blocks.p: Greek compares adjectives in two equally correct ways: **analytically**, with *πιο* ‘more’ (*πιο μεγάλος* ‘bigger’), or **synthetically**, with the suffix *-τερος* (*μεγαλύτερος*). *Πιο* works with every adjective and is the safe choice; *-τερος* is common with frequent, short adjectives and in writing. The comparative is an ordinary adjective in *-ος, -η, -ο*: *μεγαλύτερος, μεγαλύτερη, μεγαλύτερο*.

table.title: The comparative
table.note: -τερος is added with a linking -ό- (ωραι-ό-τερος, φτην-ό-τερος), or -ύ- for adjectives in -ύς (βαρ-ύ-τερος). The stress always falls on that linking vowel.

blocks.pitfall: Use one or the other, never both: *πιο μεγάλος* or *μεγαλύτερος*, but not *πιο μεγαλύτερος* — a mistake Greeks themselves make, and are corrected for.

blocks.p: ‘Than’ is **από** + accusative before a noun or pronoun (strong pronoun forms: *από μένα*, *από σένα*). Before a clause, use **από ό,τι** (‘than what’). **Παρά** is used before anything that is not a simple noun phrase — an adverb, a prepositional phrase, a second adjective — and in set phrases.

items.t: Η Αθήνα είναι μεγαλύτερη από τη Θεσσαλονίκη.
items.en: Athens is bigger than Thessaloniki.

items.t: Ο αδερφός μου είναι δύο χρόνια μικρότερος από μένα.
items.en: My brother is two years younger than me.

items.t: Ήταν πιο εύκολο από ό,τι περίμενα.
items.en: It was easier than I expected.
Better late than never.

items.t: Αυτό το κρασί είναι πιο ακριβό, αλλά όχι καλύτερο.
items.en: This wine is more expensive, but not better.

table.title: Irregular forms
table.note: πιο καλός and πιο κακός are also heard and correct, but καλύτερος and χειρότερος are more usual. The absolute superlatives in this table are learned and appear mostly in fixed uses: άριστα ‘excellent’ (the top school grade), η μέγιστη ταχύτητα ‘maximum speed’, ως επί το πλείστον ‘for the most part’.

blocks.p: The **relative superlative** — ‘the biggest’ — is simply the **article + comparative**: *ο μεγαλύτερος*, *ο πιο μεγάλος*. The group is given with a genitive or with *από* / *σε*: *ο πιο ψηλός της τάξης*, *ο πιο ψηλός απ’ όλους*, *ο πιο ψηλός στην τάξη*.

The **absolute superlative** — ‘very…, extremely…’ — has the suffix **-τατος** (*ωραιότατος*, *νοστιμότατος*), or more often *πολύ* / *πάρα πολύ* + adjective. Colloquial Greek also loves intensifying prefixes: *πανέμορφος* ‘gorgeous’, *πανάκριβος* ‘outrageously expensive’, *κατακόκκινος* ‘bright red’, *ολοκάθαρος* ‘spotless’.

blocks.pitfall: *-τατος* does **not** mean ‘the most’ but ‘very’: *ωραιότατος* is ‘extremely beautiful’. ‘The most beautiful’ is *ο ωραιότερος* or *ο πιο ωραίος* — the article plus the comparative.

items.t: Είναι η πιο όμορφη παραλία του νησιού.
items.en: It’s the most beautiful beach on the island.

items.t: Ποιο είναι το ψηλότερο βουνό της Ελλάδας; — Ο Όλυμπος.
items.en: What is the highest mountain in Greece? — Olympus.
The food was absolutely delicious!
Thank you very much!

blocks.p: Adverbs formed from adjectives end in *-α* (*ωραία*, *γρήγορα*, *καλά*). They compare the same way: *πιο γρήγορα* or *γρηγορότερα*; the absolute superlative is in *-τατα* (*ωραιότατα*, *άριστα*).

items.en: Speak more slowly, please.
I’ll come later.
I like summer more.
The sooner, the better.

blocks.tip: *Όσο πιο…, τόσο πιο…* (or with *-τερος*) is ‘the more…, the more…’: *Όσο περισσότερο διαβάζεις, τόσο καλύτερα καταλαβαίνεις* ‘The more you read, the better you understand’.

blocks.p: *-τερος* and *-τατος* are Ancient Greek, and *-τερος* is older still: an Indo-European suffix that marked a contrast between two, seen also in Latin *alter* ‘the other (of two)’ and English *other* and *whether*. Ancient Greek compared adjectives exactly as Modern Greek does with them: *σοφός*, *σοφώτερος*, *σοφώτατος*. The only change is the linking vowel. Ancient Greek used *-ο-* after a long syllable (*δεινότερος*) and *-ω-* after a short one (*σοφώτερος*); Modern Greek has generalised *-ό-*: *σοφότερος*.

compare.title: Comparison, then and now
compare.note: The irregular Ancient comparatives in -ων (ἀμείνων, μείζων, πλείων) died out; the superlatives survived in learned use. χειρότερος is a ‘double comparative’: Ancient χείρων ‘worse’ with -τερος added on top. καλύτερος and μεγαλύτερος are new formations whose -ύ- spread from adjectives in -ύς (βαθύς ‘deep’ → βαθύτερος). περισσότερος is built on περισσός ‘extra, excessive’.

blocks.p: The analytic *πιο* comes from Ancient **πλέον** ‘more’, the neuter of *πλείων*: *πλέον* → medieval *πλιο* → *πιο*. The full form survives too, in a learned sense: *πλέον* ‘any more, now’ (*Δεν μένει πλέον εδώ* ‘He doesn’t live here any more’) and ‘plus’ on price lists (*πλέον ΦΠΑ* ‘plus VAT’). *Πάρα πολύ* ‘very much’ uses *παρά* ‘beyond’.

Latin made the same journey. Classical Latin had a synthetic comparative, *altior* ‘higher’, like Greek *ψηλότερος*. Spoken Latin replaced it with ‘more’ + adjective, using either *plūs* (hence Italian *più*, French *plus*) or *magis* (hence Spanish *más*, Portuguese *mais*, Romanian *mai*). Greek, unusually, keeps both systems side by side.
And just as Greek prefers *καλύτερος* and *χειρότερος* to *πιο καλός* and *πιο κακός*, the commonest Latin comparatives survived in Romance as irregular one-word forms.

compare.title: Irregular survivors
compare.note: French dropped the synthetic form for ‘bigger’ (majeur survives only as a learned word meaning ‘major’), but kept moindre from minor.

title: Prepositions and Numbers
sub: σε, από, με, για and friends; counting, dates and the time

blocks.p: In everyday Modern Greek nearly every preposition takes the **accusative**. You met *σε* and its contractions with the article (*στο*, *στη(ν)*, *στον*…) in Chapter 8; the others work the same way. A few learned prepositions take the genitive (see the end of the chapter).

table.title: The core prepositions
rows: Μένω στην Αθήνα. — I live in Athens.
Είμαι από την Κύπρο. — I’m from Cyprus.
Πάω με το λεωφορείο. — I go by bus.
Ένα δώρο για σένα. — A present for you.
Καφέ χωρίς ζάχαρη. — Coffee without sugar.
until, up to, as far as
Δουλεύω μέχρι τις πέντε. — I work until five.
Θα έρθω κατά τις οκτώ. — I’ll come at around eight.
Μετά το φαγητό. Μετά από δύο ώρες. — After the meal. After two hours.
Πριν από τρία χρόνια. — Three years ago.
Πάμε προς τη θάλασσα. — We’re heading for the sea.
table.note: μετά and πριν take από before a number or a noun without the article (μετά από δύο ώρες, πριν από πολύ καιρό); with the article από is optional (μετά το φαγητό). With pronouns, use the strong forms: για σένα, με μένα, χωρίς αυτόν.

blocks.p: Many expressions of place are an **adverb + σε or από**. With personal pronouns, these adverbs drop the preposition and take a short genitive pronoun instead: *πίσω μου* ‘behind me’, *κοντά σου* ‘near you’, *δίπλα του* ‘next to him’, *μαζί μας* ‘with us’.

table.title: Compound prepositions
rows: μέσα στο σπίτι, μέσα σε μια ώρα
πάνω από τη θάλασσα, πάνω από εκατό
