blocks.pitfall: Time expressions don’t map one-to-one onto English. ‘In two hours (from now)’ is *σε δύο ώρες*; ‘within two hours’ is *μέσα σε δύο ώρες*. ‘For two weeks’ is *για δύο εβδομάδες* when planned, but past durations usually take no preposition at all: *Έμεινα δύο εβδομάδες* ‘I stayed (for) two weeks’. Days and dates take a bare accusative: *τη Δευτέρα* ‘on Monday’.

table.note: The forms in brackets are the everyday spoken variants; both are standard.

table.title: Tens, hundreds, thousands
table.note: Compound numbers follow each other without ‘and’: 23 είκοσι τρία, 145 εκατόν σαράντα πέντε, 1821 χίλια οκτακόσια είκοσι ένα. εκατό becomes εκατόν before another number. From 2000 on, thousands are counted with the feminine noun χιλιάδες: τρεις χιλιάδες.

blocks.p: Most numbers are invariable, but **1, 3, 4** (and every compound ending in them: 13, 24, 101…), the **hundreds from 200** and **1000** agree in gender with the noun: *τρεις γυναίκες* but *τρία παιδιά*; *διακόσιες σελίδες* ‘200 pages’, *χίλια ευρώ*.

table.title: Ordinals
table.note: Ordinals are ordinary adjectives in -ος, -η, -ο: η πρώτη μέρα, ο δεύτερος όροφος. Written with a figure: 1ος, 1η, 1ο. Note ένατος with a single ν.

blocks.p: Dates use **cardinal** numbers with the month in the **genitive**, except the first of the month, which is ordinal: *(στις) είκοσι πέντε Μαρτίου* ‘(on) 25 March’, but *(την) πρώτη Μαΐου* ‘(on) 1 May’. Formal names of national days use ordinals throughout: *η 25η Μαρτίου* (*εικοστή πέμπτη*). Years take the neuter article and no preposition: *Γεννήθηκα το 1990*.
For the time, the numbers are **feminine**, agreeing with the understood *ώρα* ‘hour’: *μία η ώρα*, *τρεις*, *τέσσερις*. ‘At’ is *στις*: *στις τρεις*, but *στη μία*.

table.title: Telling the time
rows: στις οκτώ το πρωί / το βράδυ
στις δώδεκα το μεσημέρι / τα μεσάνυχτα
table.note: και ‘and’ = past, παρά ‘less’ = to. Timetables use the 24-hour clock: 20:30 είκοσι και τριάντα.

items.t: Τι ώρα φεύγει το πλοίο; — Στις επτά και μισή.
items.en: What time does the ferry leave? — At half past seven.
I was born on 3 April 1988.

items.t: Το μουσείο ανοίγει στις εννιά και κλείνει στις τρεις.
items.en: The museum opens at nine and closes at three.

items.t: Έχω δύο αδερφές και τρία ξαδέρφια.
items.en: I have two sisters and three cousins.
It costs a hundred and fifty euros.

items.t: Μένω στον τρίτο όροφο, δίπλα στο ασανσέρ.
items.en: I live on the third floor, next to the lift.

blocks.p: Ancient prepositions could govern three cases, each with its own meaning: *παρά* + genitive ‘from beside’, + dative ‘beside’, + accusative ‘to the side of’. When the dative died out and the genitive retreated, the **accusative** became the default case after prepositions. Some prepositions vanished from speech (*ἐν* ‘in’, *ὑπό* ‘under’, *σύν* ‘with’); others were worn down or changed meaning: **σε** < *εἰς* ‘into’, **με** < *μετά* ‘with’ (+ genitive), **για** < *διά*, **ως** < *ἕως*. *Από*, *κατά*, *προς*, *χωρίς* and *μέχρι* kept their Ancient forms.

compare.title: Same preposition, new case
compare.note: Modern σε covers both Ancient εἰς (motion) and ἐν (position). The learned genitive survives in formal style: κατά + genitive ‘against’ (κατά της βίας ‘against violence’), υπέρ ‘in favour of’, μεταξύ μας ‘between us’, and in fixed phrases such as από καιρού εις καιρόν ‘from time to time’.

blocks.p: Numerals are among the most stable words in any language. Most Greek numbers are Ancient forms with Modern sound changes: *ἕξ* gained a final vowel (*έξι*), *τέσσαρες* changed its vowel (*τέσσερις*), and *εἷς, ἑνός* ‘one’ was rebuilt on its oblique stem *ἑν-*: accusative *ἕνα* + *-ς* → *ένας*. The ordinals *πρῶτος, δεύτερος, τρίτος, τέταρτος, πέμπτος, ἕκτος, ἕβδομος, ὄγδοος, ἔνατος, δέκατος* survive unchanged except for the accents.

Because Greek and Latin both inherited their numerals from Indo-European, the two sets are visibly cognate — and through Latin, so are the Romance ones. Note how a Greek rough breathing often corresponds to a Latin *s-*: *ἕξ : sex*, *ἑπτά : septem*.

compare.title: Numbers across the family
compare.note: τέτταρες is Attic, τέσσαρες Ionic and Koine; Modern Greek continues the second. ἑκατόν and centum share a root, as do εἴκοσι and vīgintī. Romanian douăzeci is ‘two tens’, and o sută ‘a hundred’ is a Slavic loan; o mie comes from Latin mīlia.

title: Relative Clauses and Conjunctions
sub: που, ο οποίος, ό,τι — and the words that join clauses

blocks.p: The everyday relative word is **που** — unstressed and invariable. It serves for people and things, for subjects and objects, and even for places and times: English *who*, *whom*, *which*, *that*, *where* and *when* can all be *που*. Unlike English *that*, it can never be left out.

items.t: Ο άνθρωπος που μου μίλησε είναι ο θείος μου.
items.en: The man who spoke to me is my uncle.

items.t: Το βιβλίο που διαβάζω είναι πολύ καλό.
items.en: The book I’m reading is very good.

items.t: Το χωριό που γεννήθηκα είναι στην Κρήτη.
items.en: The village where I was born is in Crete.
The day you came, it was raining.

blocks.p: Because *που* itself carries no case, Greek often adds a **resumptive pronoun** inside the clause to show the relative’s role — obligatorily for indirect objects and possessors: *ο φίλος που του έδωσα το βιβλίο* ‘the friend I gave the book to’ (literally ‘that I gave him the book’); *η γυναίκα που ο άντρας της είναι γιατρός* ‘the woman whose husband is a doctor’.

items.t: Ο φίλος που του έστειλα το μήνυμα δεν απάντησε.
items.en: The friend I sent the message to didn’t reply.
items.lit: The friend that I sent him the message didn’t reply.

items.t: Είναι ένα σπίτι που η πόρτα του είναι πάντα ανοιχτή.
items.en: It’s a house whose door is always open.
items.lit: …a house that its door is always open.

blocks.pitfall: Don’t confuse **που** (relative ‘who, which, that’, no accent) with **πού;** (‘where?’, accented): *Πού είναι το βιβλίο που αγόρασες;* ‘Where is the book you bought?’ In the same way **πως** ‘that’ is distinct from **πώς;** ‘how?’.

blocks.p: **ο οποίος, η οποία, το οποίο** is the more formal relative. It declines with the article, takes its gender and number from the noun it refers to, and its case from its role in the clause. It is the natural choice after **prepositions** and for **possessors** (‘whose’), and it can follow a comma where *που* would be ambiguous.

table.title: ο οποίος
table.note: With σε the article contracts as usual: στον οποίο, στην οποία, στο οποίο.

items.t: Η εταιρεία για την οποία δουλεύω είναι γερμανική.
items.en: The company I work for is German.

items.t: Ο φίλος με τον οποίο ταξίδεψα μένει στον Βόλο.
items.en: The friend I travelled with lives in Volos.

items.t: Το σπίτι στο οποίο μένω είναι πολύ παλιό.
items.en: The house I live in is very old.

items.t: Ο καθηγητής, του οποίου το βιβλίο διαβάσαμε, έρχεται αύριο.
items.en: The professor whose book we read is coming tomorrow.

blocks.p: The ‘free’ relatives — English *whatever*, *whoever*, *wherever* — carry their antecedent inside them: **ό,τι** ‘what(ever)’, **όποιος, -α, -ο** ‘whoever, whichever’, **όπου** ‘where(ver)’, **όσος, -η, -ο** ‘as much / as many as’.

items.en: Do whatever you like.
Whoever wants to can come.
Sit wherever you like.
Take as many as you like.

blocks.pitfall: **ό,τι** (with a comma) means ‘whatever, what’; **ότι** means ‘that’. They sound identical: *Θα κάνω ό,τι μπορώ* ‘I’ll do what I can’ vs *Είπε ότι θα έρθει* ‘He said that he would come’.

table.title: Subordinating conjunctions
rows: Ξέρω ότι έχεις δίκιο. — I know (that) you’re right.
Όταν έρθεις, θα φάμε. — When you come, we’ll eat.
Ενώ μαγείρευα, άκουγα ραδιόφωνο. — While I was cooking, I listened to the radio.
Καθώς έβγαινα, χτύπησε το τηλέφωνο. — As I was going out, the phone rang.
Δεν ήρθα επειδή ήμουν άρρωστος. — I didn’t come because I was ill.
Γιατί; — Γιατί έβρεχε. — Why? — Because it was raining.
Αφού δεν θέλεις, δεν πειράζει. — Since you don’t want to, never mind.
Δεν ξέρω αν θα έρθει. — I don’t know whether he’ll come.
Μόλις φτάσεις, τηλεφώνησέ μου. — As soon as you arrive, call me.
Μίλα δυνατά, ώστε να σε ακούνε όλοι. — Speak up so that everyone can hear you.
table.note: Plus the coordinating basics: και ‘and’, ή ‘or’, αλλά, όμως ‘but, however’, ούτε… ούτε ‘neither… nor’, είτε… είτε ‘either… or’. μόλις + past also means ‘just’: Μόλις ήρθε ‘He has just arrived’.

blocks.p: **Future after όταν, μόλις, αν, αφού, πριν.** In a clause about the future, these take the **perfective form without θα** — just as English says ‘when I finish’, not ‘when I will finish’: *Όταν τελειώσω, θα σου τηλεφωνήσω* ‘When I finish, I’ll call you’. The present after *όταν* means ‘whenever’: *Όταν βρέχει, μένω σπίτι* ‘Whenever it rains, I stay home’.

**ότι / πως / που.** After verbs of saying, thinking and knowing, ‘that’ is *ότι* or *πως* (interchangeable; *πως* is a little more colloquial). After verbs of **emotion** — *χαίρομαι* ‘I’m glad’, *λυπάμαι* ‘I’m sorry’, *ντρέπομαι* ‘I’m ashamed’ — ‘that’ is **που**: *Χαίρομαι που ήρθες* ‘I’m glad (that) you came’.

items.en: He told me he’d be late.
I’m glad to see you.

items.t: Όταν ήμουν μικρός, ζούσαμε στην Πάτρα.
items.en: When I was little, we lived in Patras.
As soon as I finish, I’ll call you.
Since you’re tired, sit down for a bit.

blocks.tip: **Γιατί** answers its own question: *Γιατί; — Γιατί…* ‘Why? — Because…’. In the answer *γιατί* and *επειδή* are interchangeable, but only *επειδή* can open a sentence before the main clause: *Επειδή έβρεχε, μείναμε σπίτι* ‘Because it was raining, we stayed in’.

blocks.p: Modern **που** is Ancient **ὅπου** ‘where’, which lost its unstressed first vowel. Already in later Greek *ὅπου* was used loosely as a relative (‘in which case, where’), and in the Middle Ages *που* became the universal relative ‘who, which, that’, displacing the Ancient relative pronoun *ὅς, ἥ, ὅ*. That pronoun survives only in learned fragments: *εξ ου και* ‘hence (also)’, *αφ’ ης στιγμής* ‘from the moment that’. The question word **πού;** ‘where?’ is a different word, Ancient *ποῦ;* — the two merged in sound but are kept apart in spelling by the accent.

compare.title: Relatives and conjunctions, then and now
rows: the city where I was born
he says that he is coming
compare.note: ὅταν + subjunctive in Ancient Greek corresponds exactly to όταν + perfective in Modern Greek. The comma in ό,τι is an old printers’ convention, used to keep ὅ,τι ‘whatever’ apart from ὅτι ‘that’.

blocks.p: Most of the conjunctions are Ancient words or phrases that have fused: **ενώ** < *ἐν ᾧ* ‘in which (time)’, **αφού** < *ἀφ’ οὗ* ‘from which (time)’, **γιατί** < *διὰ τί;* ‘on account of what?’, **μόλις** < *μόλις* ‘with difficulty, barely’, **πως** < *πῶς* ‘how’. *Ὅτι*, *ὅταν* and *ἐπειδή* came through unchanged.

compare.title: Conjunctions with a past
rows: on account of what? → why; because
compare.note: Ancient ὁποῖος meant ‘of what kind’; its use with the article as a relative is post-classical.

blocks.p: The formal *ο οποίος* — article + ‘which’ — has exact counterparts in Romance: Italian *il quale*, Spanish *el cual*, French *lequel*, Portuguese *o qual*, all from Latin *quālis* ‘of what sort’ — the same meaning as Ancient *ὁποῖος*. And the everyday *που* has a twin in Romance *che / que*: Latin’s relative *quī, quae, quod* and its conjunction *quod* collapsed into an all-purpose connector that serves as relative (‘the book that…’), as ‘that’ after verbs of saying, and after verbs of emotion — the full range of Greek *που* and *ότι* combined. Colloquial Italian even adds resumptive pronouns like Greek (*la ragazza che le ho parlato*, frowned on in the standard), and standard Romanian does so routinely.

compare.title: Greek and Romance connectors
rows: sono contento che tu sia venuto
me alegro de que hayas venido
je suis content que tu sois venu
compare.note: Romanian care comes from quālis, and in cartea pe care o citesc the clitic o ‘it’ resumes the relative — exactly like Greek ο φίλος που του έδωσα.

title: Conditionals and Wishes
sub: αν, θα + past, and μακάρι να

blocks.p: Greek conditionals need no new forms. The if-clause has **αν** ‘if’ + an ordinary verb form; the main clause has a present, an imperative, or **θα** + a verb. What tells you how real the condition is, is the choice of **tense** in each half.

When the condition is a real possibility, the if-clause takes the **present** (for general truths and the here and now) or the **perfective form without θα** (for a single event in the future) — exactly as after *όταν* (Chapter 22). The negative is *αν δεν*.

items.en: If it rains (whenever it rains), we stay home.
If you like, come with us.

items.t: Αν βρέξει αύριο, θα μείνουμε σπίτι.
items.en: If it rains tomorrow, we’ll stay home.

items.t: Αν δεις τη Μαρία, πες της να μου τηλεφωνήσει.
items.en: If you see Maria, tell her to call me.

items.t: Αν δεν φύγεις τώρα, θα χάσεις το τρένο.
items.en: If you don’t leave now, you’ll miss the train.

blocks.pitfall: Don’t put *θα* in an ordinary if-clause: *Αν βρέξει, θα μείνουμε σπίτι*, not *Αν θα βρέξει…* — English likewise says ‘if it rains’, not ‘if it will rain’. (*Αν θα* does exist, but only in the sense ‘if it’s true that it will…’ or ‘whether it will…’: *Δεν ξέρω αν θα βρέξει* ‘I don’t know whether it will rain’.)

blocks.p: Greek has no separate conditional mood. English ‘would’ is **θα + imperfect**: *θα έγραφα* ‘I would write’, *θα πήγαινα* ‘I would go’, *θα ήθελα* ‘I would like’. For an imagined or unlikely condition, use *αν* + imperfect in the if-clause and *θα* + imperfect in the main clause.

table.title: θα + imperfect
table.note: θα + imperfect has two readings: ‘would (now, in other circumstances)’ and, in narrative, ‘was going to, would (later)’: Ήξερα ότι θα ερχόταν ‘I knew he would come’.

items.t: Αν είχα χρόνο, θα διάβαζα περισσότερο.
items.en: If I had time, I would read more.

items.t: Αν ήμουν στη θέση σου, δεν θα το έκανα.
items.en: If I were you, I wouldn’t do it.
items.lit: If I were in your place…

items.t: Τι θα έκανες αν κέρδιζες το λαχείο;
items.en: What would you do if you won the lottery?
I’d like a coffee, please.

items.t: Θα μπορούσατε να μου πείτε πού είναι ο σταθμός;
items.en: Could you tell me where the station is?

blocks.tip: Three formulas cover most polite speech: *θα ήθελα* ‘I would like’, *θα μπορούσα / θα μπορούσατε* ‘I could / could you’, and *θα έπρεπε* ‘ought to, should’: *Θα έπρεπε να φύγουμε* ‘We ought to leave’.

blocks.p: For a past condition that was not fulfilled — ‘if I had known, I would have come’ — the full form uses the **pluperfect** in both halves: *αν είχα* + *-ει*, *θα είχα* + *-ει*. In everyday speech the plain **imperfect** is just as common in both halves; context shows that the past is meant. Verbs with no perfect, such as *ξέρω* and *είμαι*, always use the imperfect: *αν το ήξερα* ‘if I had known’, *αν ήμουν εκεί* ‘if I had been there’.

items.t: Αν το είχα μάθει νωρίτερα, θα είχα έρθει.
items.en: If I had found out earlier, I would have come.

items.t: Αν το ήξερα, θα σου το έλεγα.
items.en: If I’d known, I’d have told you. / If I knew, I’d tell you.

items.t: Αν δεν είχε βρέξει, θα είχαμε πάει στην παραλία.
items.en: If it hadn’t rained, we would have gone to the beach.

items.t: Θα σου είχα τηλεφωνήσει, αλλά δεν είχα το τηλέφωνό σου.
items.en: I would have called you, but I didn’t have your number.

blocks.p: Wishes use **μακάρι (να)** ‘if only, I hope’ + verb, and the tense again shows how realistic the wish is: the subjunctive for a wish that may come true, the **imperfect** for an unreal present, the **pluperfect** for an unreal past. Formal Greek also has *είθε (να)* ‘may it be that’.

items.en: I hope he comes! / If only he’d come!
I hope you’re well.
If only I were rich.

items.t: Μακάρι να μην το είχα πει.
items.en: If only I hadn’t said it.

blocks.tip: Many everyday wishes use *να* alone: *Να ζήσεις!* ‘Happy birthday!’ (literally ‘may you live!’), *Να τα εκατοστήσεις!* ‘May you live to a hundred!’, *Να ’σαι καλά!* ‘Bless you!’ / ‘Thanks!’ (literally ‘may you be well!’).

blocks.p: **αν** is Ancient **ἐάν** ‘if’ — itself *εἰ* ‘if’ + the modal particle *ἄν* — which already in Koine was often written *ἄν*. Ancient Greek had an elaborate system of conditions, and the Modern one preserves its logic remarkably well. A possible future condition was *ἐάν* + subjunctive, as Modern *αν* + perfective is. An unreal condition put past tenses in both halves, with the particle *ἄν* in the main clause marking it as hypothetical — the job that *θα* does today.

compare.title: Ancient and Modern conditionals
rows: If he comes, he will see.
If I had money, I would buy (it).
Αν είχες έρθει, θα είχες δει.
If you had come, you would have seen.
compare.note: In Ancient Greek an imperfect in both halves meant ‘if it were so (now)’ and an aorist ‘if it had been so (then)’. Modern Greek keeps the imperfect for the first and uses the pluperfect for the second.

blocks.p: *θα* began as a future marker (*θέλει να* → *θα*, Chapter 12). Combined with a past tense, ‘will’ became ‘was going to’ and then ‘would’: *θα έγραφα*. This is exactly how the Romance **conditional** arose. Latin *scrībere habeō* ‘I have to write’ gave the future (Italian *scriverò*, Spanish *escribiré*, French *j’écrirai*); the same infinitive with a **past** of *habēre* gave the conditional: *scrībere habēbam* → Spanish *escribiría*, French *j’écrirais*, Portuguese *escreveria*, while Italian used the perfect *habuī* → *scriverei*. Future + past = ‘would’, in Greek and Romance alike — only Greek keeps the pieces apart.

compare.title: ‘Would’ in Greek and Romance
compare.note: Romanian builds its conditional with a separate auxiliary (aș). Spanish quisiera and Portuguese queria soften a request with a past form, just as Greek ήθελα να σας ρωτήσω ‘I wanted to ask you’ does.

blocks.p: Ancient Greek expressed wishes with *εἴθε* or *εἰ γάρ* + the **optative**, a mood that Modern Greek has lost: *εἴθε γένοιτο* ‘may it happen!’. Fossils remain — formal *είθε*, and the exclamation *μη γένοιτο!* ‘God forbid!’, which is St Paul’s *μὴ γένοιτο* ‘by no means!’. Everyday **μακάρι** comes from Ancient *μακάριος* ‘blessed, happy’ — the word of the Beatitudes, *μακάριοι οἱ πτωχοὶ τῷ πνεύματι* ‘Blessed are the poor in spirit’ (Matthew 5:3) — through its vocative *μακάριε* ‘O blessed one!’, used as an exclamation.

compare.title: ‘If only…’
compare.note: Italian magari is the same word as μακάρι, borrowed from Byzantine Greek μακάριε. Spanish ojalá and Portuguese oxalá come instead from Arabic law šāʾ Allāh ‘if God wills’. All three take a past subjunctive for an unreal wish, as Greek takes the imperfect.

title: Diglossia and the Learned Layer
sub: Katharevousa, Demotic, and the Ancient fossils in everyday Greek

blocks.p: For most of its modern history Greece had two written standards. **Katharevousa** (*καθαρεύουσα* ‘the purifying (language)’) was an archaising form shaped in the early 19th century, above all under the influence of Adamantios Korais, who wanted to ‘correct’ the spoken language towards Ancient Greek rather than revive Attic outright. It restored Ancient endings, the dative and much Ancient vocabulary on a Modern core, and grew more archaic as the century went on. **Demotic** (*δημοτική* ‘(the language) of the people’) was the language actually spoken, the language of folk song and, increasingly, of literature. The struggle between them — the **γλωσσικό ζήτημα** ‘language question’ — was as much political as linguistic.

Katharevousa was the language of the state, the law, the universities and the press. Demotic was the language of poetry (Solomos, Palamas) and, after Psycharis’s manifesto *Το ταξίδι μου* ‘My Journey’ (1888), of more and more prose. Feelings ran so high that a Demotic translation of the Gospels provoked deadly riots in Athens in 1901 (the *Ευαγγελικά*), and a Demotic-flavoured *Oresteia* more riots in 1903 (the *Ορεστειακά*). Demotic entered primary schools in 1917, was pushed back and brought back several times, and was expelled again by the military junta of 1967–74. In **1976** new laws finally made Demotic — now called **Standard Modern Greek** (*Νεοελληνική*) — the language of education and the state; in 1982 the monotonic accent replaced the polytonic.

The settlement did not simply erase Katharevousa. Standard Modern Greek is Demotic in its grammar, but it absorbed a vast **learned layer** of vocabulary, set phrases and some morphology from Katharevousa — and through it from Ancient Greek. Educated speakers move along a scale from plain to learned, and recognising the learned end is essential for reading newspapers, signs, official letters, even menus.

table.title: Everyday and learned
table.note: The everyday word is what you say; the learned word lives on in compounds, derivatives, signs and official language. Some learned words are themselves in everyday use with a special sense: ο άρτος is also the bread blessed in church.

blocks.p: Many phrases that everyone uses, in the most casual conversation, are frozen pieces of Ancient or Katharevousa grammar — often containing a **dative**, a case that otherwise vanished from the language centuries ago.

table.title: Learned set phrases
table.note: εν + dative and εκ + genitive are the commonest patterns. Dative forms such as τω, τη, τοις are recognisable by the article; in the old polytonic spelling they had an iota subscript (τῷ Θεῷ).

blocks.p: Learned **adverbs** end in **-ως** instead of Demotic *-α*: *ακριβώς* ‘exactly’, *ευτυχώς* ‘fortunately’, *δυστυχώς* ‘unfortunately’, *αμέσως* ‘immediately’, *προφανώς* ‘obviously’, *κυρίως* ‘mainly’, *βεβαίως* ‘certainly’. Some adverbs exist only in *-ως*, many only in *-α*, and some in both — often with a difference in meaning.

blocks.pitfall: Doublets in *-α* and *-ως* are not always interchangeable: *ακριβά* ‘expensively’ but *ακριβώς* ‘exactly’; *απλά* ‘simply, plainly’ but *απλώς* ‘merely, just’; *τελικά* and *τελικώς* both mean ‘finally’, the second more formal.

blocks.p: Nouns in *-ση, -ξη, -ψη* (the Ancient *-σις* type) have a learned genitive singular in **-εως** beside the Demotic *-ης*. It is very much alive on forms, packets and tickets.

table.title: Two genitives
rows: η Άλωση της Πόλεως ‘the Fall of Constantinople’
table.note: The plural forms are the same in both registers: οι λήξεις, των λήξεων. Among Greeks, η Πόλη ‘the City’ still means Constantinople.

table.title: Signs and notices
table.note: Greek written in capitals normally drops the accents. Lower-case: ωθήσατε, έλξατε, απαγορεύεται, ενοικιάζεται, πωλείται.

blocks.p: Newspaper Greek is Standard Modern Greek with a high density of learned vocabulary and fossils. Watch for Ancient-style pasts with the **internal augment** (Chapter 14) and the old aorist passive in *-η* / *-ησαν*: *εξελέγη* ‘was elected’, *συνελήφθη* ‘was arrested’, *ελήφθησαν* ‘were taken’, *διεξήχθη* ‘took place’, *απεβίωσε* ‘passed away’. And for prepositions that are really frozen datives: *λόγω* + genitive ‘because of’ (dative of *λόγος*), *βάσει* ‘on the basis of’ (dative of *βάσις*), *δυνάμει* ‘by virtue of’. Even the everyday abbreviation *π.χ.* ‘e.g.’ is learned: *παραδείγματος χάριν* ‘for the sake of example’.

items.t: Λόγω της κακοκαιρίας, ακυρώθηκαν όλα τα δρομολόγια.
items.en: Due to the bad weather, all sailings were cancelled.

items.t: Εξελέγη νέος δήμαρχος ο κ. Παπαδόπουλος.
items.en: Mr Papadopoulos was elected the new mayor.

items.t: Ελήφθησαν έκτακτα μέτρα για την προστασία των δασών.
items.en: Emergency measures were taken to protect the forests.

items.t: Η συνάντηση διεξήχθη σε καλό κλίμα.
items.en: The meeting took place in a good atmosphere.

items.t: Η είσοδος επιτρέπεται μόνο στους κατόχους εισιτηρίου.
items.en: Entry is permitted to ticket holders only.

blocks.tip: You do not need to produce learned forms, but you do need to recognise them. When an unfamiliar form has an Ancient look — *εν* + dative, a genitive in *-εως*, an internal augment, a past in *-η* or *-ησαν* — ask what the Ancient Greek would be. That question usually unlocks it.

afterlife.title: Where it comes from: one sentence, three Greeks

blocks.p: Here is one sentence — ‘When the king heard this, he immediately ordered the soldiers to return to the city’ — in Classical Attic, in Katharevousa (in the polytonic spelling it always used), and in Standard Modern Greek.

table.title: Attic, Katharevousa, Demotic
cols: ‘When the king heard this, he immediately ordered the soldiers to return to the city.’
rows: Ταῦτα ἀκούσας ὁ βασιλεὺς εὐθὺς ἐκέλευσε τοὺς στρατιώτας ἐπανελθεῖν εἰς τὴν πόλιν.
Ἀκούσας ταῦτα ὁ βασιλεὺς διέταξεν ἀμέσως τοὺς στρατιώτας νὰ ἐπανέλθωσιν εἰς τὴν πόλιν.
Μόλις το άκουσε αυτό ο βασιλιάς, διέταξε αμέσως τους στρατιώτες να γυρίσουν στην πόλη.

blocks.p: Katharevousa kept Ancient endings (*βασιλεύς*, *στρατιώτας*, *πόλιν*), the participle and the preposition *εἰς*, but its syntax was Modern: it normally used *νὰ* + subjunctive (with the Ancient ending *-ωσιν*) rather than the infinitive, which had been dead in speech for centuries. Demotic is the spoken language made standard — yet even it keeps learned *διέταξε*, with its internal augment, and *αμέσως* in *-ως*.

Much of everyday Demotic vocabulary is itself Ancient, only humbler. Hellenistic and Byzantine Greek loved **diminutives** in *-ιον*; worn down to *-ι*, they became the ordinary words, while the grand Ancient words withdrew into the learned layer.

compare.title: Where the everyday words come from
compare.note: The ending -ιον lost its -ο- and then its -ν: -ιον → -ιν → -ι. σπίτι has a more surprising source: Latin hospitium ‘lodging’, through Byzantine σπίτιον.

blocks.p: Greek diglossia became a textbook case: in 1959 the linguist Charles Ferguson named the phenomenon **diglossia** using four classic examples — Greek, Arabic, Swiss German and Haitian Creole. Latin offers a historical parallel. For centuries Europe wrote Latin while speaking Romance, and when the Romance languages began to be written, they borrowed heavily back from Latin. The result is pairs of **doublets**: one word inherited through speech and worn down by sound change, one re-borrowed from books.

compare.title: Popular and learned doublets in Romance
compare.note: Greek pairs like νερό / ύδωρ or μάτι / οφθαλμός are the same phenomenon — except that for Greek the ‘Latin’ is its own older self.
